News.title: Dark world of ‘predatory’ penis filler clinics after Brit’s death as patients left with ‘disfigured & infected genitals’
News.content:
LYING on the operating table under white lights, Igho Ubiribo was about to go under the needle to fix his biggest insecurity.

But hours after his penis enlargement procedure, the Brit influencer, 43, was rushed to hospital and pronounced dead.



Igho suffered a pulmonary embolism shortly after his surgery in Thailand on March 6, a UK inquest heard last week.

Coroners found hyaluronic acid – a clear gel-like substance commonly used in penis enlargement ops – in his lungs.



Businessman Igho had undergone five penis enlargement surgeries before his death.

The tragedy marked the latest in a series of botched penis filler ops – a trend that has left behind a trail of horrors across the globe, including in the UK, US, Mexico, Russia, France, Thailand and Turkey.



Self-professed “King of Penis Filler” Chris Bustamante said there were “predatory” unlicensed clinics taking advantage of girth-seeking patients.

The practitioner, who helps clients temporarily achieve larger appearing penises and testicles at his New York clinic, warned that some surgeries are prioritising cash over safety.



The Lushful Aethetics CEO told The Sun: “As more men engage in cosmetic procedures, you’re gonna have way more predatory clinics abroad, but also within the US and the UK as well.

“I’ve heard of clinics where the locations change all the time… you’re not really sure who’s injecting you.”

Igho’s story may just be the tip of the iceberg, Ashton Collins, the director of UK practitioner vetting platform Save Face, warned.



He said the “true scale is likely to be underestimated” because of limited data on Brits travelling abroad for girth-enhancement surgeries.

Patients on the quest for thicker penises without going under the knife have two options – temporary or permanent enlargement ops.

Both paths have contributed to the skyrocketing penis filler demand – which has boomed alongside “unscrupulous operators” at a dangerous pace, Collins said.

He told The Sun: “Penile enlargement is an area where demand has grown far faster than the evidence, regulation and safeguards needed to protect patients.”

His organisation recorded a whopping 1,100 per cent increase in penile enlargement procedure complaints since 2022.



There is also a seemingly endless host of overseas clinics using social media accounts to lure Brits abroad with the promise of cheap hassle-free ops, he warned.

A string of grisly penis enlargement stories have laid bare the dark side of the rising manhood augmentation trend.

In August last year, a Russian man died after doctors injected hyaluronic acid into his member.

The failed operation caused the moisture-binding molecule to reach his lungs, medical experts in Moscow ruled in a chilling echo of Igho’s case.

In 2019, a 65-year-old Israeli-Belgian diamond-trading billionaire died from a heart attack during a penis enlargement operation in Paris.



Two surgeons were cleared of any wrongdoing in his death, but were handed suspended prison terms and banned from practising for having improper qualifications.

And in October 2025, a dodgy Thai doctor known as “Chang Yai Modify” was arrested for performing illegal penis enlargement surgeries in the back of his Toyota Corolla.

Boasting his services on platforms like TikTok, bogus medic Pittaya Moolin, 51, charged just over £200 per penis filler injection.

Penis fillers also made headlines at the Winter Olympics as rumours swirled of male skiers using them to increase the surface area of their suits so they could jump further.

Temporary fillers, as opposed to permanent ones, use dissolvable materials like hyaluronic acid, a type of naturally occurring sugar molecule.



They increase the thickness of the penis but do not make it longer, cost around £6,000 per jab, and can last about nine months.

These types of ops have seen a meteoric rise in popularity over recent years, and Bustamante says he gives out three to five of them per day.

The procedure can take just 30 minutes, and sees men receiving multiple injections.

But those looking for a long-term solution usually go down the route of permanent fillers.

These ops use non-biodegradable synthetic substances like liquid silicone or PMMA – tiny plastic microspheres.



The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in the US has not approved their use for body augmentation surgeries, nor have UK medical authorities.

While offering lifetime volume, they carry the risk of severe complications including painful hard lumps, filler migration, infection, tissue necrosis, and permanent damage to erectile tissue.

Bustamante doesn’t offer any permanent fillers and he strongly advises against them.

Even though temporary jabs are considered safer than their lifelong counterparts, risks such as swelling, bruising, infection, and lumps still exist.

Bustamante outlined a horror story where one of his patients had gone to Mexico for permanent filler – only to come back with a “very deformed” penis.



The practitioner said: “He saved a lot of money going to Mexico, but he ended up having this permanent product migrate on him immediately.”

Bustamante said in another shock case, someone seeking larger testicles was left with the illusion of having a third testicle.

He said: “They had gone to Mexico to get filler injected inside their scrotum, which ended up creating this sort of pseudo-effect of having almost like an extra larger ball inside.

“This filler became infected, and they ended up having to cut this person’s scrotum open in order to clear out the infection, drain everything out, and it was horrific.”

He suspects the practitioner may have injected the filler directly inside the scrotum – rather than its skin.



Surgical andrology expert Vaibhav Modgil said permanent fillers are “particularly concerning” as opposed to temporary ones which are “generally preferable”.

But he warned neither procedure is completely risk-free.

Describing permanent fillers, he told The Sun: “Once injected, they cannot simply be dissolved.

“They can provoke chronic inflammation, granuloma formation, infection, fibrosis and significant penile deformity, sometimes presenting months or even years later.”

Those with disfigured private parts may have to go under the knife for reconstructive surgery or have parts of their genitals removed, he warned.



Fertility expert Dr Steven Palter warned some of these jabs could have life-changing implications due to the glaring lack of regulation – including sperm checks.

He told The Sun: “The scrotum’s purpose is to regulate the temperature of sperm, anything that interferes with this ability could pose a risk.

“Unapproved, non-sterile techniques can cause temporary or permanent damage to the testicle.

“If you have blot clots or an infection, you could lose your penis or testicles.”

Igho, who had four previous temporary penis enlargement surgeries at the same clinic according to Thai authorities, took a substantial dose of hyaluronic acid, Bustamante said.



The cosmetic clinic claimed they advised Igho to split the procedure into two parts rather than one session.

But he allegedly requested the surgery to be completed all in one go, the doctors said.

Bustamante said: “I’ve injected guys all throughout that range, and there isn’t a single person that I have encountered who could handle 40 milliliters in one sitting.

“I think the most I’ve ever injected in one sitting has probably been around, like 26 or so, 28 for someone who’s especially long.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It gets more risky as people are injecting so much.”



The practitioner said it was crucial to use the correct instrument, as some needles which are too thin risk perforating the penis and entering blood vessels.

News.title: My ‘first love’ committed one of UK’s most shocking sex crimes on a pensioner, 92… then tried to pin the blame on me
News.content:
TEENAGER Katie Uphill arrived home from a family holiday to find police officers waiting for her on the driveway.

Aged just 15 at the time, her 19-year-old boyfriend had been arrested for raping a 92-year-old woman multiple times and stealing £70 – and he claimed she had put him up to it.





Katie, now 43, was hauled in for questioning and quickly released with no further action, but couldn’t believe her ears as she learned of the crimes Philip Green was accused.

The evil sex attacker was described as a “psychopath” by a judge while experienced detectives labelled it one of the worst crimes they had ever been involved with.

Katie, who had been in a relationship with Green for six months by the summer of 1998, has spoken out for the first time and described him as “lovely and charming” when they first met – and there was no indication of what the monster was capable of.

In court he was told by Justice Turner that life in prison should mean life for him – however, in 2019 the Parole Board opted to greenlight his release.

Katie, who was not informed at the time, told The Sun this week: “He is a dangerous psychopath and what he did was beyond evil.

“I am scared now he is back on the streets if he might come and find me. He should never have been released and left to rot in jail.”

Katie recalled she had returned from the two-week trip with her parents to Ibiza to find police at her house and at the centre of one of the most shocking sexual crimes the UK had ever seen.

Late in the evening on July 3 1998, Green, having drank large amounts of cider and sniffed 13 cans of butane gas, crawled through a window the frail pensioner, 92, had left open for her cat in a bid to steal money, Cardiff Crown Court heard during his trial the following year.





The unsuspecting OAP was watching the Nine O’Clock News on TV when she turned to see Green.

Prosecutor Huw Evans said: “She was asked for money but before she could answer she was hit to the head and knocked to the floor face down.

“He then violently and repeatedly raped her while punching her to the face with his fists.

“She could feel herself drifting in and out of consciousness.”

The court also heard how, once the victim was allowed to get up, she went to her bedroom and gave Green £70 from one of the drawers.

Mr Evans said the attacker then told her: “If you are going to tell the police something terrible will happen to you.”

She was left clutching photographs of her dead husband and brother – and later told officers she wished she’d died, the prosecutor added.

Evil Green was identified by fingerprints on a packet of cigarettes and a disposable lighter he dropped during the attack.



Stephen Hopkins, defending, described the attack as “inhuman” but added his client was “grateful” his victim “is a courageous lady” and “in his own inarticulate way he is remorseful”.

Green pleaded guilty to two counts of rape, burglary and wounding with intent after subjecting her to what the judge described as a “prolonged and brutal physical assault such that any younger person might have found more than they could bear”.

Judge Turner labelled Green a “psychopath” who presented a “grave and immediate danger to the general public for the foreseeable future” and sentenced him to two life terms.

The parole board confirmed this week a decision was made to release Green in 2019 after serving 20 years – although his whereabouts since are unknown.

But Katie, of Cardiff, said she was not told he was now free and has been living in fear of ever seeing him again.

She said: “He should never have been released. He should have been detained in a psychiatric unit for the rest of his life.

“If he was here could he walk past me. I am of course scared of what he might do.

“My message to the government is they should not have let him and he needed to stay in jail.

“I will never forget his face. His evil actions. I loved this man as a teenager. He was my first love.



“But I now realise how possessive he was. He never wanted to leave my side or let me talk to anyone.

“All I did was go on holiday and then I came back and my life was changed forever.”

Katie said Green had tried to tell cops that she had “put him up to it” and was coerced into storing his gas under her bed.

She was interviewed by detectives but quickly ruled out of any enquiries and Green was arrested after going on the run in Bristol.

She added: “When I got back from holiday police were at my house. He told police he had done it for me.

“I was interviewed at the time and was only 15. He was 19 so he should not have been with me.

“My voice was supposed to have told him to do the crime, so he told the police my name and address.

“Detectives were at my house as they thought I was a accomplice, but I wasn’t even in the country.

“I was just young and stupidly in love.”

Katie said after his arrest he would send her letters from prison about how he “still loved and missed me” that forced her parents to take out an injunction against her.



She added: “We had been together for six months and I still to this day have no idea why he did that. It is just so disgusting.

“”He made me hide the gas cylinder under my bed. After I found out the details of what he did I never wanted to see him again. It was so bad. It was like torture. I was only young but I thought he loved me and did everything for me.

“I was just 15 and was disgusted and scared. It could have been me, or even my mum.

“School was hard and I was bullied a lot because of it. It was horrible and I am still suffering to this day. I am still on medication and worried one day he might came and try and find me.”

Katie recalls a whirlwind romance that saw them get engaged despite her age but now sees how controlling and coercive he was.

She added: “He proposed to me in the middle of town centre and I said yes. To celebrate we went to the cinema and for a meal.

“He used to ply me with alcohol as I was too young to drink.

“We would just spend time in the park. Just talking. I loved him. He was an older boy but he was charming and nice.

“We would go to the cinema, and everything. I don’t recall him ever being nasty or malicious to me but he was controlling.

“That was until I went on the holiday and we went a bit nuts that I was going away without him. But my parents had paid for it already.



“He broke my heart as I thought we were in love. I went back to school after in the sixth form and was really badly bullied. I was called a granny rapist and all sorts.”

Katie said the last time she saw him was when they “said goodbye” as she left for the trip and had no idea what had happened until she got back.

“He had given them my address and told police I made him to do that,” she recalled.

“The police took loads of fingerprints and told him what he had done.

“It was horrific. My mum was a carer and when she found out she cried her eyes out. She had let him into the house, made him tea.

“I was not allowed to be a witness. My mum said no so I was not involved in court.

“People told me he was supposed to have died – but I see he has now been released. I haven’t been told anything and have no idea what happened to him.

“I do not want anything to do with him. I thought he was a decent guy, he had dark hair, dark eyes and was tall. But he was so evil for what he did.

“My parents told me the detectives had said in 25 years it was the most horrific crime they had ever seen. It was so bad. It has never got out of my head.

“I still have nightmares and in torture about it. I cry all the time and have self-harmed. I just want it to go away. What an evil man for doing what he did to that poor and defenceless elderly woman



During the sentencing, the Judge described the crime and said after gaining entry to the victim’s flat he had “set about degrading, violating her person.”

He told the court: “Words fail adequately to convey the horror that a person so young as yourself could behave in such an inhuman fashion against such an elderly person.”

Green was given life for the two counts of rape and gave no additional sentence for the other two charges.

At the time the judge said it was “unthinkable” Green should be released from prison in the near future and no minimum sentence was given.

The court had heard how Green had broken into the woman’s home one evening through a window left open for her cats.

He went on to hit the woman on the head, pushed her to the floor and raped her before stealing her money.

He was identified by fingerprints left on a packet of cigarettes and a lighter left at the victims flat.

The parole board confirmed this week that a decision to release Green was made in December 2019. His exact release date after the decision is not known.

The uncertainty has brought all the trauma back for Katie as she lives in fear of coming face to face with Green.

She said: “I still have nightmares and wake up crying, where he’s trying to catch me.”

News.content:

'MURDER' PROBE Horror as elderly woman, 88, found ‘murdered’ at home as man, 36, arrested

AN 88-YEAR-OLD woman found dead at home has been pictured – with a man, 36, arrested on suspicion for murder.

Victim Jill Grant was discovered in Abingdon, Oxfordshire, on Thursday afternoon.

Her family has released an image in tribute – while the suspect remains in custody.

The force said: “Thames Valley Police can confirm the identity of the victim in its Major Crime Unit’s ongoing murder investigation in Abingdon.





“The investigation was launched after officers were called to an address in Appleford Drive at around 2.20pm on Thursday (10/9).

“The victim has been identified as Jill Gant, aged 88, of Appleford Drive, Abingdon.

“Her family have released the image below.”

Senior Investigating Officer Detective Chief Inspector Stuart Brangwin, of the Major Crime Unit, said: “Our thoughts remain with Jill’s family.



“We would ask, on their behalf, that their privacy is respected at this difficult time.”

“Specially trained officers continue to support Jill’s family.

“The 36-year-old man, from Abingdon, we arrested on suspicion of murder remains in our custody at this time.”

News.title: Saudi Arabia shuts key ‘East-West’ oil pipeline after Iraq drone strikes as ‘triple blockade’ chokes Middle East
News.content:
SAUDI Arabia has been forced to shut down a key oil pipeline after it was hammered by drones launched from Iraq.

The East-West pipeline – which carries around 5 percent of global oil – has been closed as a triple blockade chokes the Middle East‘s fuel supplies.



The Saudi Ministry of Energy described the closure as a “precautionary measure”.

Running 745 miles across the Arabian peninsula, the pipeline bypassed both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb Strait.



The two vital waterways are currently patrolled by Iran‘s vicious Islamic Guards and the pariah’s proxy Houthi rebels.

As such, global oil prices have skyrocketed with crude prices surpassing $100 a barrel again this week, giving Tehran more leverage in talks.



The Saudi kingdom has chosen not to retaliate to the drone strike to give the Iraqi government “an opportunity to take the necessary measures.”

The attack originated from one of the provinces on the Iranian border where Iranian-backed militias operate.



Satellite images showed smoke billowing where the pipeline was hit just south of Medina in the Hejaz Region.

Riyadh said it would support the efforts of the Iraqi government” to prevent attacks” launched from the country against neighbouring states.

The statement added: “Saudi Arabia reserves its right to take all necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty and security, protect its facilities, and ensure the safety of its citizens and residents.”



Iraq responded by saying the operations commander in Maysan – a southern province bordering Iran – had been sacked following the drone launch.

The Gulf Co-operation Council – made up of the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Oman, Qatar and Kuwait – condemned the attack.

Secretary General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said it represents a “dangerous escalation and an unacceptable threat” to Saudi security.

He added that it was also a “flagrant violation of the principles of international law“.

It comes amid fears that Houthi rebels threaten to paralyse global trade completely after seizing a critical island in the Bab al-Mandab Strait.



The key waterway, also known as the Gate of Tears, is critical choke point at the mouth of the Red Sea.

Ships have to pass through the 20-mile channel between Djibouti and Yemen to get goods to or from the Suez canal – the vital artery linking Europe and Asia.

A huge 12 per cent of all global trade flows through Suez.



The seizure of the Perim island is the Houthis’ biggest territorial gain in years and puts them in a strong position to threaten vessels in the Gate of Tears.

Markets fear that it could lead to a terrifying triple blockade that would spark an economic meltdown.

Oil exported from the Gulf now has to travel through three huge barriers to reach Europe – the US blockade of Iranian ports, the IRGC blockade of Hormuz and the threat from the Houthis in the Gate of Tears.

Retired Major General Chip Chapman, former senior British military commander to US Central Command, told The Sun that the chance of this triple blockade will send the price of petrol shooting up.

He said: “Not only have you got the Strait of Hormuz, which is a choke point where you’ve got a double blockade, but this also leads to a triple blockade with the Bab al-Mandab.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“That’s the significance of both the capture of Perim Island and Mocha.

“A barrel of Brent Oil, the real benchmark that people use, is $104 today. It was $100 earlier in the week. That means that you’ll see your prices of your petrol going up.”

News.title: Portsmouth braces for fresh protest chaos as rival anti-migrant groups to descend on city & cops slap down mask ban
News.content:
HIGH ALERT Portsmouth braces for fresh protest chaos as rival anti-migrant groups to descend on city & cops slap down mask ban

PORTSMOUTH is bracing for fresh protest chaos today as rival anti-migrant groups are set to descend on the city.

The two groups, as well as a counter protest by the Stand up to Racism campaign, are set to converge from around midday.



It comes as Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary confirmed ahead of today’s chaos that it would use its new powers to ban masks.

The measures will apply to parts of Portsmouth from 10am Saturday until Sunday morning – with anyone breaching the restrictions potentially facing arrest.



The demonstration comes days after hundreds of anti-migrant protesters clashed with police last Sunday when around 140 Channel migrants were brought ashore by the RNLI at Portsmouth’s Eastney Marina.

Demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying the migrants from leaving the city on Sunday night.

Vehicles were damaged and a small number of officers injured following the disorder which the government branded “thuggish”.

Demonstrators left the area at around 3am on Monday morning after Hampshire Constabulary issued a Section 14 dispersal order.



The action followed a separate protest at the UK’s busiest ferry port the previous day where hundreds of men in balaclavas and wearing black blocked a road at the terminal.

Swathes of masked “stop the boats” protesters brought the Port of Dover to a standstill as holidaymakers and lorries were stuck in huge queues for hours.

Kent Police monitored the march but said no one was arrested – and the group had been dispersed by midday.

Both protests last weekend were organised by Patriotic Platform, a group which wants to build a group of voters to influence political parties on the right.

The group’s leader, Daniel Thomas, aka Danny Tommo – an associate of Tommy Robinson – is not expected to be present at the march in Portsmouth today.



In a statement on Friday he penned: “No member, organiser, representative, or affiliate of Patriot Platform will attend, speak at, steward, or take part in any event in Portsmouth.”

He added: “Anyone who claims to be from Patriot Platform, to represent Patriot Platform, or to be a member acting on our behalf in Portsmouth is not authorised and is not telling the truth.”

On Friday, cops arrested 42-year-old Del Leon Somerville on suspicion of violent disorder and assaulting a constable in the execution of their duty during last Sunday’s demonstrations in Portsmouth.

He was subsequently charged with both offences and remanded to appear at Portsmouth Magistrates Court later today.

Both marches are expected to begin at All Saints Church on Commercial Road as local colleges have been warned to stay away from the area.



It comes as Hampshire police will use new powers to arrest anyone wearing a mask at today’s demonstration.

The force said the mask ban was to “reduce opportunities for violence, intimidation and criminality”.

They added the move followed “recent incidents of violence and intimidation by a minority of those who have been intent on disrupting peaceful protest”.

Last month, Sadiq Farhad Azad, an Iraqi national, was charged with raping a 14 year old boy in Portsmouth on August 11.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said Azad, 33, had also been charged with allegedly stalking a woman in her 20s over the course of a year, and criminal damage of a car belonging to a family member of the alleged victim, police said.



Latest figures from the Home Office show 768 migrants crossed the channel by small boat in the last seven days to September 11.

Around 17,250 migrants have crossed the channel in small boats since the start of the year.

Quarterly Home Office data shows that at the end of June 2026 there were 16,021 asylum seekers housed in hotels, approximately 17% of all those in receipt of support.

That’s figure is down from 20,885 at the end of March 2026, and 29,561 in June 2024.

The number of hotels used for this purpose has also decreased. As of August 2026 the government said “fewer than 160” hotels were being used to house asylum seekers, compared to 213 in July 2024.



A Home Office statement previously said: “This Government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border.

“Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We are making progress, with the number of small boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020.

“But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40 per cent more boots on the ground on French beaches.”

News.title: Labour’s ‘wrecking ball’ holiday tax will turn popular UK resorts into ghost towns & drive millions abroad, Reform warns
News.content:
By Alex Nelson

BRITS planning a domestic getaway could soon face an extra charge on their hotel bills under government plans to hand regional mayors power over a “tourist tax”.

Formally known as the Overnight Visitor Levy, the charge will allow local leaders across England to add a fee to hotel rooms, bed-and-breakfasts, and holiday lets like Airbnb.

The charge is a new levy added directly to overnight accommodation bills in participating regions.

The tax will apply to everyone staying overnight, whether you’re an overseas tourist visiting London or a British family taking a weekend staycation in Yorkshire.

How much will it cost?

The law itself will not set a hard national cap, giving regional mayors powers to set rates.

Unlike flat-rate schemes used in some cities, ministers have designed the tax as a percentage of the total room rate.

Labour’s regional mayors have committed to keeping any tax rate under 5% to avoid driving away visitors.

With the national average hotel room sitting around £198 a night, a 5% levy would add nearly £10 per night to a stay.

Over a week-long family staycation, that could add up to £70 extra on accommodation costs.

Because the tax is calculated as a percentage, cheaper accommodation will incur lower fees than luxury five-star hotels.

Day-trippers who do not stay overnight will not have to pay.

Where will it apply?

The powers will be available to elected mayors across English regions.

Destinations set to receive these tax-raising powers include:

Greater Manchester

Liverpool City Region

London

North East England

West Yorkshire

York and North Yorkshire

Existing voluntary schemes, such as Manchester’s flat £1-a-night city charge, are expected to be replaced by the new percentage levy.

Similar capped levies are already live in Edinburgh and due in Wales by April 2027.

Why is it controversial?

Supporters say the move brings England in line with popular international destinations like Paris, Venice, and Rome.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner and London Mayor Sadiq Khan have said the raised funds will stay local, funding public transport, high streets and cultural attractions without having to rely on Treasury coffers.

But hospitality leaders and small business owners have criticised the plan.

Trade body UKHospitality warns the levy could cost the sector up to £1.6billion and put jobs at risk by making UK holidays less competitive during an ongoing cost-of-living squeeze.

Major domestic operators and local traders fear the policy will hit hard-working families worst.

Resorts like Butlin’s have warned that an unlimited tax risks making UK family breaks unaffordable, damaging demand, and hurting youth employment.

Independent business owners are equally worried.

Caron Cooper, who has run the Fosse Farmhouse B&B in the Cotswolds for 42 years, said the tax comes as small operators struggle with rising costs.

“Just as we felt like we are coming through it and tourism’s back, this is like a hammer blow really,” she said.

Urging ministers to swap a percentage penalty for a flat £1 charge, she added: “If it was a pound on each booking then I could understand that, they would just be able to afford [it].

“Just to add a percentage, I think, no, it’s unfair and it will hit the poorest the most.”

Could Brits be exempt?

Under current government plans, the Overnight Visitor Levy is designed to apply to everyone staying in paid accommodation.

It will apply regardless of whether you’re an overseas tourist, a Brit on a family staycation, visiting relatives, attending a university open day, or someone travelling for business.

Everyone paying for an overnight stay in a participating area will see the charge added to their final bill.

Ministers and local authorities have ruled out creating “Brit discounts” or local exemptions for several reasons.

For instance, forcing hotel staff and B&B owners to verify passports, driving licences, or council tax bills to prove local residency would create administrative chaos for small hospitality businesses.

The charge only targets commercial, paid accommodation – crashing on a spare bed or sofa will remain tax-free.

News.title: Burnt body of missing dancer, 21, found washed up on beach after vanishing on night out with friend
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

DEATH RIDDLE Burnt body of missing dancer, 21, found washed up on beach after vanishing on night out with friend

AN URGENT probe is underway after the burnt body of a missing dancer washed up on a beach.

Sindy Loany Matute Morales, 21, stopped answering her phone after leaving home to attend a party in Honduras, Central America.



Tragically, the mum-of-one never returned home – and was found dead in the Santa Rosa de Aguán region the following evening on September 6.

In a harrowing revelation, cops said that her body was scorched with burn marks.



It is unclear whether the mum-of-one was already dead when her body was burned.

The glam dancer had previously said she was being stalked by “suspicious people”, according to her heartbroken mum Marlen Yesenia Matute Morales.



She said that her daughter had even quit her job over fears of strange people lurking outside her workplace.

Chillingly, Sindy had often told her: “Mum, I won’t last.



“I know I’m not going to live forever.”

The young mum leaves behind a four-year-old daughter.

Sindy’s mum said: “I went out to look for her and, when I tried to act, they had already brought her dead to Tocoa [morgue].

“They didn’t just kill her; they burned her as well.”

Sindy had been a keen dancer who regularly performed in local fiestas with heartbreaking videos showing Sindy laughing and twirling through a street parade.



Sindy had celebrated her 21st birthday just days earlier.

Police have launched a major probe into the horrifying killing – but so far no arrests have been made and no motives identified.

It comes after an influencer was found stabbed to death with her boyfriend chillingly claiming he had been “forced to kill her”.

Katerin Mejía Argueta, 20, was discovered dead by the Aguán River in the city of Tocoa, Honduras.

In a harrowing reveal, cops said the body showed signs of torture.



Three people have been arrested in connection with the horror killing.

News.title: Shocking moment cops uncover almost one-tonne of meth disguised as hundreds of cabbages
News.content:
THIS is the shocking moment cops uncover around one-tonne of meth disguised as hundreds of cabbages at the US-Mexico border.

Footage shared by the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) shows officers seizing a shipment of cabbages packed into several boxes.



Cops wearing blue nitrile gloves can be seen peeling back outer layers of cabbages to reveal a large latex pellets of methamphetamine.

The camera pans to show hundreds of cabbages being unwrapped, with six wheelbarrows and dozens of boxes full to the brim with drugs.



The DEA said that it had netted an around one-tonne stash.

The agency added that the seizure was made by its team in McAllen, a border city across from Reynosa, Mexico.



The DEA said: “On Tuesday, the McAllen office seized over 2,000 pounds of methamphetamine concealed in a commercial tractor-trailer shipment of cabbage,

“No arrests have been made, and the investigation remains ongoing.”

It added that the seizure was part of a Homeland Security Taskforce probe, conducted jointly with federal border agencies and Texas enforcement.

Strong partnerships and relentless enforcement produce real results,” the DEA said.



Police have been battling a meth epidemic across the US, caused in part by Mexican drug runners smuggling it into California.

Border cops discovered a similar shipment of suspected meth hidden in cabbage near McAllen in July.

A sniffer dog and imaging scan found half a tonne of the drug at the Pharr International Bridge.



Informally known as crystal meth, or ice, methamphetamines are highly addictive stimulants.

It is also known as “speed” or “crank” for its ability to give people a false sense of energy.

It can cause a person to lose weight quickly and lead to dental problems, skin sores and other health issues.

The dangerous drug also severely damages the brain, causing memory loss, paranoia and even psychosis.

In March, a man bled to death after cutting off his own penis with a penknife while high on the drug.



Ryan Dexter Sutherland, 31, was found with more than 20 stab wounds while also trying to chop off his arm after he had taken an “extreme” dose.

Although it wasn’t noted as a cause of death, he had a deadly blood concentrations of 1.9 ug/mL for meth and .24 ug/mL for amphetamines.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The wound to his private parts was nearly a foot in circumference, exposing his testes and causing a “degloving” of his penis, per a police report.

He is presumed to have died from cuts to an artery and vein in his right arm and injuries in his neck that damaged his jugular vein and trachea.

News.title: Putin's chilling response when asked about striking Britain after WW3 warning
News.content:
Putin's chilling response when asked about striking Britain after WW3 warning

Russia this week insisted that threats of nuclear strikes were 'not a scare tactic' and accused the West of 'acts of aggression capable of triggering a Third World War'

View 2 Images Putin was asked whether Russia might strike British military facilities (file) (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Vladimir Putin gave a chilling one-sentence response when asked whether Russia may launch direct strikes against the UK.

‌



Earlier this week Dmitry Medvedev, former Russian president and current Deputy Chairman of its Security Council, warned that Moscow’s threats to use nuclear weapons are "reality" and "not a scare tactic".

‌



He accused western leaders of a "Neanderthal mindset and abysmal ignorance", and warned they were "trying to push the world to the brink of nuclear apocalypse". It was in reference to Western countries - including the UK - supporting Ukraine in its fight against Putin’s illegal invasion.

‌



There have already been "acts of aggression capable of triggering a Third World War", Medvedev warned.

View 2 Images Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev (file) (Image: Ekaterina Shtukina/Pool Sputnik)

NATO fighter jets scrambled over Europe as emergency alert issued in Poland READ MORE :

He added: "Such a conflict would obliterate the entire history of human civilization and plunge it back into a primitive state - assuming any of the planet's billions of people survived at all."

‌



Russia has also made threats against sites in the UK which produce weapons used by Ukraine to strike Russian territory.

When asked earlier this month whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine, Putin said: "That's a secret. A military secret."

Medvedev also claimed this week that Putin could turn to nuclear weapons in a bid to "secure an end to the [Ukraine] conflict on our terms". He said: "It must end on our terms to prevent any possibility of it recurring in the future or escalating into a global conflict."

‌



He also urged the West to take Russia's threats about nuclear war seriously: "These are not hints. Everyone needs to understand: nuclear weapons could be used in certain circumstances.

"This is not a scare tactic - it is reality. Russia’s nuclear doctrine - under which our country reserves the right to use such weapons in the event of a threat to our state’s security - can hardly be described as a mere hint.”

"The list of military threats requiring nuclear deterrence measures has also been expanded."

Article continues below

Medvedev added: "We have every right to respond to a critical threat to our sovereignty. The final decision will rest with the Head of State [Putin]."

News.title: Portsmouth protestors issued mask warning by police ahead of another feared shutdown
News.content:
Portsmouth protestors issued mask warning by police ahead of another feared shutdown

As police brace for a second day of demonstrations in Portsmouth, anyone wearing face coverings could face arrest with Stand Up to Racism also planning a counter protest in the city

View 3 Images Police are desperately trying to prevent further violence in Portsmouth today (Image: Jamie Lashmar/PA Wire)

Police have warned of a crackdown ahead of another planned protest in Portsmouth today.

‌



The Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary has announced it will employ new powers under the Crime and Policing Act to prevent people involved in protest activity from concealing their identity by wearing face coverings. The move comes after a man was arrested on Friday as part of an investigation into the violent disorder at an anti-migrant protest in the city last Sunday, the first of several people expected to face justice in the aftermath of the clashes.

‌



Hundreds of protesters gathered at Eastney Marina on Sunday night after 120 people arrived in a boat that had crossed the English Channel. The man, assaulting a police constable. He remains in custody.

‌



View 3 Images Discarded life jackets are collected following the protest last weekend (Image: Joe Sene/PA Wire)

In a bid to avoid similar scenes, the force has announced that officers will use new powers banning coverings, warning mask-wearers could be arrested on the spot in the area designated by the order.

Extra police will be on duty with a unity demonstration, Stand Up to Racism's counter protest, also planned in what the group call "a response to the scenes of far right thugs intimidating refugees".

‌



Groups from South Coast Patriots have called for a peaceful march in Portsmouth city centre this afternoon but police say they will not tolerate a repeat of Sunday's violent scenes.

Hampshire Police will use this new tactic under the Crime and Policing Act, saying it will help officers and "allow peaceful protest". The measures will apply in parts of the city from 10:00am on Saturday until Sunday morning.

View 3 Images New measures are being employed to avoid a repeat of the scenes on Sunday

‌



Assistant Chief Constable Paul Bartolomeo said: “Where a minority of people try to take advantage of the situation to cause violence and disruption, it is right that we use all our policing powers robustly to protect the local community as well as the right of others to peaceful protest.

“We have listened to the concerns of our communities and know how intimidated they feel when they see masked groups descend on their neighbourhoods. This is why we are making use of these new policing powers, to ensure we have every tactic at our disposal, should we need it.

“It is important to stress that this power will apply to any groups that attend the protest and will be enforced equally and impartially. Let me be clear, these powers are not being implemented to prevent protest, but they are being used to help prevent crime and disorder, while making communities feel safer.

‌



“We will support those who want to express their views peacefully and lawfully, but we will not tolerate those whose only aim is to create fear and incite violence.”

Assistant Chief Constable Tony Rowlinson said Del Leon Somerville's arrest on Friday is the "first of what we fully anticipate to be a number of arrests" and hoped it would send a "clear warning" to those planning future disruption and disorder.

Several police, Coastguard and Border Force vehicles were damaged on Sunday, and a small number of officers were injured at the scene, Hampshire Police said. Around 200 people were dispersed at around 4am on Monday.

Article continues below

Daniel Thomas the leader of Patriot Platform behind the Portsmouth and Dover protests last weekend, said in a statement that "no organiser, representative, or affiliate of Patriot Platform will attend, speak at, steward, or take part" in the event.

News.title: UK clocks to go back in October – exact 2026 date confirmed
News.content:
UK clocks to go back in October – exact 2026 date confirmed

The clocks will go back an hour next month, marking the end of daylight saving time in the UK and the start of darker evenings

View 2 Images Summer is nearly over as the clocks are set to go back in October (Image: Studio4 via Getty Images)

The UK moves to British Summer Time (BST) during the warmer months, with clocks pushed forward by one hour to give people lighter evenings. Come autumn, the clocks are turned back and the country returns to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).

‌



The twice-yearly clock change takes place on the last Sunday of March and the last Sunday of October. There have been calls for the UK to scrap the clock changes altogether, with various proposals suggesting keeping BST all year round or adopting another permanent time zone.

‌



However, there are currently no confirmed plans to change the existing system.

‌



As those long, dark winter evenings are fast closing in. Nightfall is now arriving noticeably earlier and temperatures are set to plummet.

The autumn season will also mark the end of daylight saving time, which is rarely welcomed across the UK. Those early sunsets mean workers can miss almost all of the day's natural light.

On the bright side, there will be an extra hour in bed when the clocks are turned back.

‌



And that date will come around sooner this year than in 2025, reports the Express.

View 2 Images Autumn will mean less daylight and earlier darker evenings (Image: Justin Paget via Getty Images)

UK clocks will go back by one hour on Sunday, October 25, 2026. At 2am BST, the clocks will move back to 1am GMT, marking the end of British Summer Time and the return to Greenwich Mean Time.

‌



This means that on the night of Saturday, October 24, clocks will remain on BST before changing in the early hours of Sunday.

Most smartphones, computers and smart devices should update automatically, but it’s worth checking manual clocks, car clocks and household timers to make sure they are showing the correct time.

However, in 2026 they will shift back an hour at 2am on Sunday, October 25, bringing daylight saving time to a close.

Article continues below

A handy way of remembering which direction the clocks will change is "spring forward, fall back".

According to timeanddate.com, sunset today (September 12) occurs at 7.22pm in London. However, the days will gradually shorten, with sunset arriving at 6.48pm by Wednesday, September 30, and dipping further to 4.50pm on Sunday, October 25 - the day the clocks go back.

Looking further ahead, the clocks will spring forward next year on Sunday, March 28, 2027, and fall back on Sunday, October 31, 2027 - which happens to be the latest possible date the clocks could go back in any given year.

News.title: Ant and Dec's 'biggest challenge' after NTA snub as they make surprising statement
News.content:
Ant and Dec's 'biggest challenge' after NTA snub as they make surprising statement

EXCLUSIVE: Ant McPartlin and Declan Donnelly have dominated British TV for decades, but after walking away from the NTAs empty handed for the first time in 25 years, The Mirror explores their changing fortunes...

View 6 Images Ant McPartlin and Declan Donnelly failed to secure any wins at the National Television Awards (Image: WireImage)

For more than two decades, Ant McPartlin and Declan Donnelly have seemed to be untouchable, beloved by fans and the industry.

‌



But the pair suffered a bruising night at the National Television Awards earlier this week, walking away empty-handed for the first time in 25 years.

‌



The Geordie duo were trumped in four categories including TV Presenter, Reality Competition, Quiz Show and Talent Show. Sir David Attenborough took the presenter prize, while their long-running ITV reality show, I'm A Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here lost out to BBC's The Traitors.

‌



Their quiz show Limitless Win was beaten by Lee Mack's The 1% Club and Britain's Got Talent lost out to Strictly Come Dancing. Speaking on their podcast, Hanging Out With Ant & Dec, they predicted who the winners might be ahead of the show. Dec said: "So National Television Awards this week. We are recording this before the event, so we have no idea what is going to happen.

"We are nominated in a few categories, most notably Entertainment Presenter… Think you’re going to win it this year Ant?"

"I don't think we’re going to win it this year," Ant admitted. Dec replied: "Do you not? Who do you think is going to win it this year?" Ant said: "David Attenborough." Dec even admitted he had voted for the wildlife presenter, to which Ant replied: "So did I."

‌



So what is going on? Since finding fame in kids' TV series, Byker Grove and fronting SMTV Live - one of the most popular Saturday morning shows in history - the pair have been indestructible.

Ant and Dec lose out at NTAs again as David Attenborough scoops Best Presenter READ MORE :

View 6 Images Ant and Dec are renowned for their winning streak and are pictured here in 2024

When Ant went public with his addiction to pain medication in 2017, leading to two rehab spells, the public was firmly behind him. When he pleaded guilty to drink driving after a three-car smash in April 2018, TV execs were more than supportive of his recovery, letting him take the rest of the year off. He even bounced back seamlessly from his messy split from Strictly make-up artist Lisa Armstrong and subsequent marriage to their former PA, Anne-Marie Corbett.

‌



But it seems to be now - when they're at the top of their game having just signed another three-year contract with ITV - that the tide has turned. A question that would once have seemed unthinkable is becoming harder to ignore: has Britain's love affair with Ant and Dec started to change?

"There's no shame in losing out to Sir David Attenborough, but I do think it's significant that this was the first NTAs where they went home with nothing at all. They almost always win something," says Sean O'Meara, managing director of public relations and reputation management consultancy Essential Content.

View 6 Images Ant and Dec met on kids' TV show, Byker Grove (Image: BBC)

‌



PR expert Chad Teixeira believes the duo could be the latest victims of changing trends and audiences, especially given the relatively luke-warm reception of their podcast, Hanging Out With Ant and Dec. Launched in January 2026, it received mixed reviews with one Times critic giving the show two stars and arguing that their relaxed banter did not translate to long-form audio.

Writing for the Observer, podcast critic Miranda Sawyer said: "The show is just as you might imagine: funny but not uproarious, upbeat but not manic, teasing but not mean. The 35 minutes of the first show tumble by, a froth of good vibes and not much else."

It also got two stars in the Telegraph, where they noted: "The Georgie duo’s naughty schoolboy schtick doesn’t work nearly as well without their usual primetime TV backdrop."

‌



But fans were more positive, with the podcast currently rated 4.9 stars with 1,700 reviews. One recent commenter wrote: "Totally loving the pod! Respect guys!". Another added: "The pod is amaing! You are both phenomenal. Like a fine wine that gets better with age."

It got off to a bad start after their promo video - which showed their feet dangling off the ground as they were hung up on a washing line - was deemed insensitive. The pair quickly apologised.

"Ant and Dec built their careers when Saturday night television could attract huge numbers of viewers and presenters became household names almost by default," Chad tells The Mirror. "What has changed massively during this time is the audience, and how the pair are perceived.

‌



"Younger audiences today are just as likely to be watching TikTok, YouTube or listening to podcasts as they are sitting down for a traditional entertainment show. So I don't necessarily think younger people dislike Ant and Dec, but they may simply not have the same relationship with them that older audiences have built over 20 or 30 years."

View 6 Images The pair have turned their attentions to podcasting, with mixed reviews (Image: Hanging Out With Ant & Dec)

"Their biggest challenge will be in remaining relevant, not popular," Sean adds. "They can't appeal to younger audiences forever. Nobody can, it's why DJs move from Radio 1 to Radio 2."

‌



But over the past 12 months, I'm A Celebrity (Series 19) ranked as the number one commercial broadcast series for 16–34s, second overall only to BBC One's Celebrity Traitors. Nearly a quarter (23 percent) of its audience falls into the 16–34 demographic. The series reach for 16-34's was 5.6million.

All three of their flagship series have also landed in the top 20 commercial broadcast series for 16–34s over the last year. However, Chad believes their decision to quit their prime time TV show, Saturday Night Takeaway, in 2024, has somewhat impacted their visibility.

"Saturday Night Takeaway coming to an end in 2024 was significant too. That was arguably Ant and Dec at their most 'Ant and Dec', and their personalities, friendship and chemistry were the whole premise of the programme.

‌



"They still front enormous shows like I'm a Celebrity and Britain's Got Talent, but those are formats where the show itself is the star to a greater extent. Takeaway gave audiences a weekly dose of them as a duo and losing that regular vehicle inevitably changes their visibility."

View 6 Images Ant with wife Anne Marie and their son Wilder (Image: Tim Merry/Staff Photographer)

Ant and Dec's brand has also undergone something of a transformation in recent years. While once they were the inseparable poster boys of the heady nineties and noughties generation, sailing close to the wind with their cheeky chat and lad banter, these days they lead increasingly separate lives.

‌



They famously lived next door to each other in London. But Ant has since left the capital, moving to a £10million mansion in leafy Surrey with Anne-Marie, their toddler son Wilder and her two daughters. Dec is father to Isla, eight, and Jack, four, with wife Ali Astall.

"We both became fathers and we became fathers later in life," Dec told The Times about their decision to 'reappraise' their careers and priorities. Ant added: "What changes as you get older, especially being sober as well, for me, is the purpose. When you're live on I'm a Celebrity in Australia and you're in the moment with your best friend, there's nowhere else I want to be, but as soon as we finish, we go back to our apartments by the beach and we're with our families. That's where we want to be right then."

View 6 Images Dec pictured with wife Ali Astall. The couple have two children together (Image: PA)

Article continues below

But has the shift from relatable boys-next-door to settled and separate family men impacted their brand? "As a pair, they influence one another's reputation and they've faced challenges together," Sean says. "They've evolved into adults dealing publicly with serious and well publicised hurdles. They're fathers, husbands and co-owners of a production company. That's going to influence how they connect with youth audiences."

However, with a fresh ITV deal in the bag and three decades of success under their belts, Chad says it will be their decisions about the next chapter that determine their fate.

"Staying relevant in entertainment for more than 30 years is an achievement in itself, and they've successfully reinvented themselves several times already," he says. "The challenge now is whether they can do that again and find something that connects with a younger generation while keeping the familiarity, humour and chemistry that made them such a huge part of British television in the first place."

News.title: I tax my daughter's £3 a week pocket money - she is 7 but it's her house too
News.content:
I tax my daughter's £3 a week pocket money - she is 7 but it's her house too

Phoebe says her two younger children will also soon starting paying up

View 4 Images Phoebe Lee

A mum has explained why she "taxes" her seven year old daughter's pocket money - and says her two younger kids will soon start forking out too. Phoebe Lee, 35, has established what she describes as a "mini democracy" within her home in Twickenham, where her young children cast votes on certain household choices and contribute small portions of their pocket money into a shared family fund.

‌



Phoebe lives with her husband Alex and their three children, aged seven, four and two. While the couple foot the bill for all major household expenses, she says the aim is to give their children a sense of ownership, responsibility and an understanding of how public systems operate.

‌



The AI architect and founder of Inherit Health, said: "I am aware there are so many decisions that are made for our kids, and they have a lot of agencies in a lot of areas, and we try to give them control when we can. While Alex and I pay for everything, this is their house too - we want them to feel like they can make decisions in their home."

‌



View 4 Images Phoebe wants her kids to understand the meaning of money

The system kicked off with straightforward voting exercises at home, sparked by Phoebe's passion for ethical technology and her husband's background as a public servant. She explained that they were keen to introduce concepts such as contribution, community responsibility and decision-making in a manner suited to their ages.

She said: "Being in ethical tech - I want them to learn a lesson. My husband is a public servant and we wanted them to feel that community contribution. We encourage the children to understand where money goes, including donations and public services.

‌



"We handle donations and make sure we donate time or second-hand bits, or my daughter sells bracelets." At the heart of the approach is what the family playfully dubs a "fun tax", where both parents and youngsters chip in modest weekly sums into a communal kitty used for optional extras like treats or larger household purchases.

Her seven year old currently puts in roughly 20p a week from her pocket money, with her four and two year old set to join once they're old enough for some cash as well. She explained: "She gets £3 a week in pocket money and £1 goes into savings. Then she can make other money from chores, but we are very strict on what they are.

View 4 Images Phoebe runs things differently in her home

‌



"We haven't got much in the pot yet, but we are hoping to increase our side and have around £300 by December. The contribution is symbolic rather than financially significant - my husband and I are paying far larger amounts into the same system.

"It's supposed to be fun tax - we are not making them pay the Wi-Fi or the rent." She revealed her and her husband each put in approximately £4 a week, with intentions to boost adult contributions as the scheme develops, while maintaining the children's amounts steady as an educational device.

She added: "The tax is about everyone. She will feel like she has contributed, even though it's much less than us. There's something in that where she feels like she's paid for it too."

‌



Phoebe explains the goal is to instil lessons about budgeting and delayed gratification, while demonstrating how collective decision-making operates in the real world. Under the system, the family also votes on shared purchases such as activities or items, with the youngsters allowed to put forward their own ideas.

For Phoebe, the method is intimately linked to broader lessons she hopes her children will grasp about society, public services and fairness.

View 4 Images Family time with Phoebe and one of her children

‌



She has also discussed introducing concepts around taxation and public services in an age-appropriate manner, pointing to the NHS and state education as examples of systems financed through collective contribution. She said: "We are trying to keep her informed in an age-appropriate way.

"She benefits from things like the NHS and state school because we pay taxes for them - I want her to start to understand them. I want her to understand the system is designed in the UK to avoid entitlement while still giving children a sense of inclusion in family life.

"It is about bringing them into decisions in a way that doesn't feel burdensome," she said. The household anticipates the shared "fun tax" pot will build up steadily over time as contributions mount, with Phoebe joking it might eventually stretch to larger household purchases like a trampoline.

Article continues below

She said: "We anticipate to grow the funds... which could buy a great second-hand trampoline. It's not about control, it's about understanding how things work in a family, and eventually in the world."

News.title: Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Sunday with 24 counties at risk
News.content:
Met Office names areas facing heavy rain on Sunday with 24 counties at risk

Sunday morning is expected to bring heavy rain to some parts of the UK, despite Met Office forecasters predicting that temperatures will improve this weekend

UK weather: Met Office forecasts heavy rain in the south

Heavy rain is expected to sweep across some parts of the UK on Sunday morning.

‌



It has been a miserable week of weather for the most part, with temperatures remaining in the low-20s across much of the country, and rain falling earlier in the week. Although temperatures are set to improve slightly this weekend, rising to 25C today, more rain is on the cards too.

‌



In this morning’s Met Office video forecast, meteorologist Alex Deakin explained some heavy spells of rain could move across southern and central parts of the UK in the early hours of Sunday morning.

‌



“We could see some further heavier pulses coming in, particularly across parts of Wales, then into the Midlands and across southern England, as we go through the night [into Sunday morning],” he said.

View 3 Images Met Office outlook for 5am on Sunday (Image: Met Office)

UK weather maps show 31 counties facing heavy rain this weekend – full list READ MORE :

“With more cloud and the rain, and still the warm air tucked in, it will be a much milder night across the south compared to the one just gone - so a warmer start, but it will be a wetter start if you’re up early on Sunday morning.”

‌



Thankfully, the heavy rain is expected to clear throughout the day. Most areas should be bright and dry by the afternoon.

Mr Deakin continued: “We’re not exactly sure on the timing of when that rain will clear on Sunday but it certainly could be a wet start, so some useful rain in parts of the south through the first part of Sunday.

View 3 Images Met Office outlook for 5am on Sunday (Image: Met Office)

‌



“The heavier pulses of rain should clear through and it’s likely to stay pretty drab across the southernmost counties of England [as we head into the afternoon] with a little bit of rain and drizzle.

“Elsewhere, a much brighter day generally. Some good spells of sunshine, especially for parts of north-east England. And the winds will be a lot lighter as well.”

The Met Office predicts afternoon highs of 22C in the south-east and western England on Sunday afternoon, with 21C coming in the Midlands and the south coast, 18C in Edinburgh, and 17C in Northern Ireland.

‌
