News.title: Emily Atack's lavish wedding in Spain today as TV stars arrive alongside crates of Cava
News.content:
Emily Atack's lavish wedding in Spain today as TV stars arrive alongside crates of Cava

The Rivals star, 38, will say 'I do' with Alistair, 40, for the second time in the Spanish town where she spent her summers.

View 4 Images

TV's Emily Atack is about to say 'I do' again - this time at a star-studded wedding in the Spanish sun. The Inbetweeners actress, 36, who has just completed a second series of steamy hit Rivals, will today celebrate her marriage to Alistair Garner for a second time too.

‌



The pair quietly married in church back in the UK before a party in the garden of their Bedfordshire mansion last month and will tie the knot today in the Spanish hilltop town of Mojácar, where temperates are set to reach 27C.

‌



The holiday hotspot, in Costa de Almería, southern Spain, is where her musician dad Keith once had a holiday home and she spent summers there when she was young. Crates of beer, wine, spirits and Cava were seen being delivered to two venues in the town.

‌



Several celebs have already been spotted nearby, among them her Rivals' Alex Hassell, who is super-cad Rupert Campbell-Black in the show. Emily plays TV star Sarah Stratton and the pair memorably played naked tennis together in the first series.

View 4 Images Emily Atack and Alistair Garner will marry for a second time today (Image: emilyatack/Instagram)

Rufus Jones, who plays Emily’s pompous on-screen husband Paul Stratton, was also seen with his wife Philippa ahead of the ceremony, which is expected to take place in a 16th-century church in Mojacar with a reception nearby.

‌



She said of the town previously: “It’s our favourite place on Earth and we still go every single year. I loved my family holidays there growing up.” Around 200 guests are expected to arrive today.

Emily and materials scientist Alistair, 40, with whom she shares a two-year-old son called Barney, married in a very personal ceremony held in their garden in Bedfordshire last month with close family and friends.

There were two cakes and a McDonald's fan parked outside dispensing McFlurry ice creams to their guests. Emily said later: "It’s all you want after about 23 glasses of champagne.”

‌



View 4 Images Emily - seen here on her hen do - will marry in the Spanish town where she spent her childhood summers

The wedding breakfast was a buffet of Italian food from her pal Mario Di Giorgi plus a cocktail menu of strawberry daiquiris, palomas, margaritas and lychee martinis were laid on for the guests.

Emily wore an ivory plunge dress from Evelie with long sleeves, a veil and lace shoes by Charlotte Mills. Discussing her choice of bridal attire, Emily said, “Since Rivals, in terms of fashion, I tend to go quite big now generally.”

‌



She told her new husband Alistair after the wedding - branded "beautifully chaotic" by her sister and maid of honour Martha - "I can’t believe we get to do all that again in a few weeks time. Christ, we have fun don’t we?"

Emily and Alistair have known one another for much of their lives because her mother is the sister of Alistair's stepmother Jane Garner (this does not make them blood relatives).

View 4 Images Emily and Alistair at a polo day in England this summer (Image: Dave Benett/Getty Images)

‌



They were introduced in the Ninties, when Emily's aunt began dating Alistair's dad Stephen and developed feelings for each other in 2023. They learnt she was pregnant on their first holiday together - a trip to Italy - and welcomed their first child the following year.

The pair got engaged in July last year and married in August at a wedding she branded "absolutely perfect".

Speaking about Alistair, she explained: "All the cliches of life become true when you fall in love and have a baby. He's my rock, but he really, literally, is my rock. I couldn't do life with anyone else but him."

Article continues below

Emily is set to return to Rivals when a third series of the Disney+ drama begins filming. David Tennant, Aidan Turner, Danny Dyer and Katherine Parkinson are all expected to return alongside her.

News.title: 'My teen son died in accident before holiday – but Ryanair response was disgusting'
News.content:
'My teen son died in accident before holiday – but Ryanair response was disgusting'

A heartbroken mum who lost her son when he was just 18 has slammed Ryanair as 'disgusting and petty' after they refused her a refund

View 4 Images Tina McDermont with her son Billy (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

A grieving mum was told she wouldn't be getting a refund from Ryanair after her teenage son died before her flight. Tina McDermott, 45, was due to take a Ryanair flight from Newcastle to Alicante for a four-day break in Spain with her husband on August 30. But 11 days before she was set to jet off, on August 19, Billy died in a tragic accident.

‌



Tina, who lives in Washington, Tyne and Wear, said: "Billy's death was a massive shock. He'd just turned 18. I could never have travelled and gone abroad. I just wanted to be at home with my family around me.

‌



"I'm arranging my son's funeral. There's no way I could go. I thought when I got in touch with Ryanair there wouldn't be an issue.” But then she was told his death fell out of Ryanair's "10-day policy" for refunds.

‌



A heartbroken Tina said that Ryanair had demanded a copy of Billy’s death certificate. She continued: ”I thought we'd get that money back and put it towards Billy's funeral and then I hit these barriers because of this 10-day policy that I hadn't been aware of.”

Tina says she struggled to complete the claim form on Ryanair’s website, adding: "It was raw emotion all the time. It wouldn't let me complete the form. I looked at the terms and conditions and thought ‘That doesn't really make sense.’

View 4 Images Billy died just 11 days before Tina was due to fly on holiday (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

‌



"I opened a chat on the app and they told me to 'no show' so I could get a letter off them and you can go to your travel insurance and claim off them. I thought ‘That's passing the buck’.”

Tina claims she was told she was ineligible to make a refund claim for the £350 flight due to her son's death falling outside their 10-day cover window. She said: "If he'd died a day later, I would've got my money back. It's disgusting and petty.

"It was like a slap in the face. It should be done by a case by case basis. It's a blanket policy, but it isn't human. I felt very insulted. He wasn't meant to die. It was a tragic accident, so surely there should be special circumstances.

‌



View 4 Images Billy McDermont when he was younger (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

"I was devastated. Everybody I've dealt with has been compassionate except for them. They're greedy.”

Tina expressed her huge disappointment, saying: "It's not about the money. It's the principle. £350 for a huge company like Ryanair is chicken feed.

‌



"It's made the grieving process worse. I'm a mother who's grieving. It felt very personal and I know the terms and conditions are not."

Tina is calling for Ryanair to review bereavement claims on a case by case basis after her 'deflating' experience with the budget airline. She said: "Ryanair needs to change their policies. There needs to be a special circumstances clause for close relatives like children. Have a bit of heart and compassion.”

View 4 Images Tina with her late son Billy (Image: Kennedy News and Media)

‌



She insisted: “I'll never fly with them again.”

However Ryanair stood by their policy and said that it was correct that Tina should not be covered.

A Ryanair spokesperson said: "Ryanair's bereavement policy allows passengers to apply for travel credit where the death of an immediate family member occurs within 10 days of their scheduled flight departure.

Article continues below

"As this bereavement occurred outside of that period, this passenger was not entitled to travel credit.

"This passenger was provided with the documentation required to submit a claim through their travel insurance provider."

News.title: Reform receives record £36m donation from crypto billionaire
News.content:
Reform UK has received a Â£36m donation from a British cryptocurrency billionaire - a record for a UK political party.

Ben Delo wrote in the Daily Telegraph, external that he was making the move because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field".

The sum is the biggest single donation ever given to a political party in the UK. Party leader Nigel Farage said he was "honoured and humbled" by the gift.

Reform is facing scrutiny over its finances, as the government seeks to limit the amount that can be donated to UK political parties from British expats.

Delo said he was donating Â£1m a month between now and the latest date Labour could call a general election in 2029 - but that he would give all the money up front in case the government tried to limit mega-donations in future.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

But Labour previously introduced a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British citizens who are living overseas and plan to introduce one for those who have recently returned to the UK.

Sheffield-born Delo, who has already donated Â£4m to Reform, has previously said he will move back to the UK from Hong Kong to continue his backing for the party.

Last year, Delo was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMEX, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.

He wrote in the Telegraph: "Unlike the people who express mock concern for the health of 'our democracy' while doing everything they can to keep it as a cartel, I want a fair fight and a level playing field.

"My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."

News.title: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land 'gobsmacking' donation
News.content:
Look closely at the posters, placards and online posts. Your eyes aren't deceiving you if Labour's red seems a little deeper and the Conservatives' blue a little truer.

Politics seems to have found a new rhythm, one that feels a little familiar, despite Reform's jaw-dropping new donation putting it back in the headlines today.

For the avoidance of doubt, the scale of that Â£36m gift to Nigel Farage's party is like something from a different political universe.

"It's a gobsmacking sum," a senior figure involved in running successive election campaigns for one of the big parties tells me.

But one cabinet minister is enjoying what they see as a newly obvious difference between Labour and the Tories. "It's clarifying," they say, a clear gap between Labour and the Tories' "sense of purpose and values".

A member of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's top team tells me, "normal jogging is reasserting itself", hopeful they're at the start of a more straightforward, routine moment in politics after years of craziness, with smaller parties vying to shove the traditional tribes out of the way.

The standout moment was at the despatch box this week when Prime Minister Andy Burnham declared that national security couldn't come at the expense of social security - a phrase immediately seized on by the Tories, interpreting it as the PM saying he'd never cut welfare spending to pay for defence.

News.title: Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war
News.content:
"Now that they are there, they're going to be entrenched," Hisham al-Omeisi, senior analyst at the Brussels-based European Institute of Peace, told the BBC. "And it's going to be a lot more costly to push them out."

Of course, the Houthis are not alone. They enjoy the backing of Iran, support that has become even more important for Tehran in the wake of the setbacks and defeats experienced by other parts of its so-called "Axis of Resistance" â Lebanese Hezbollah, Hamas in Gaza and the Assad regime in Syria.

"So they redirected their support to the Houthis," al-Omeisi said. "And of course they need that support."

Even though most analysts agree that it's a mistake simply to describe the Houthis as Iranian puppets, events of the past few days raise an uncomfortable new reality.

Seven months after the US and Israel launched their huge, combined assault on Iran, the regime in Tehran now exerts authority over not just one, but two of the world's most important maritime passages: the Strait of Hormuz, at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, and the Bab al-Mandab, gateway to the Red Sea (and the Suez Canal).

"Now Iran, directly and through proxies, controls two of the most strategic choke points in the Middle East and the world," says Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at London's Chatham House think tank, "controlling more than 35% of the fuel and oil trade globally."

"This is as much leverage as a nuclear bomb," he says.

News.title: Masked men, lorries and road blocks: How anti-migrant activists are changing tactics
News.content:
At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham.

The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground.

In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.

In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.

Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.

It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL).

"I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.

The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."

The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".

On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth.

His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normandy in France.

On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings.

"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.

It organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.

News.title: Is a September heatwave forecast for the UK?
News.content:
Temperatures are set to climb across the UK this weekend, reaching summerlike levels in some places.

It will feel warm and muggy - especially where there are sunny spells - although heavy rain also features in the forecast.

The warmth will persist into Monday in many areas but nowhere is expected to reach heatwave criteria and cooler conditions are due to return by midweek.

Computer weather models paint a very mixed picture for the second half of September but, while there are likely to be some warm spells, there are currently no definitive signs of a heatwave.

News.title: Five minutes to steal a Renoir: Why museum thefts are becoming bolder across Europe
News.content:
Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared to well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.

Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.

For example, the Denis Diderot Maison des LumiÃ¨res (House of Enlightenment) - burgled hours after the Louvre - is housed in two 18th-century mansions in Langres.

"We therefore have to reconcile modern security requirements with the need to preserve historic buildings and comply with France's heritage regulations," local mayor ThÃ©o Caviezel explains.

Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.

And even if a museum is secured well, thieves could still come in armed, Brand says, adding that it would be impractical to put police in galleries.

Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.

Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month, external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.

In the Louvre, the thieves used a mechanical lift to gain access, cut through the window with power tools and then threatened guards, who left, before forcing their way inside displays and grabbing the jewels. In the Renoir case, the perpetrators used an electric knife to cut through a fence before sawing through structures holding the paintings' frames in place.

The increased aggression creates new security concerns.

"An armed incident during opening hours, like the one we experienced, creates a situation in which the immediate priority is to keep our audience and staff safe," says Lilli Hollein, the director of the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna, which was burgled last month.

News.title: We've followed their lives for six decades - now the stars of 7 Up are bowing out
News.content:
Six decades have passed since Jackie Bassett first appeared on TV aged seven, skipping down the road with her little sister.

It was 1964 and she had been selected by teachers at her east London primary school to appear in a documentary called 7 Up.

The show interviewed 14 seven-year-olds from vastly different socioeconomic backgrounds. Inspired by the Jesuit saying: "Give me the child until he is seven and I will show you the man", it was intended as a one-off - a snapshot of Britain's class system and how it shapes us from a young age.

"They only picked me because I never stopped talking," Jackie told the BBC, with an infectious giggle that hasn't changed since childhood.

Little did she know then, but Jackie was being filmed for a show that would go on to be the longest-running documentary series ever made. In 2024, it was voted the most influential TV show of the past 50 years.

Now the curtain is falling, with the final instalment - 70 Up - airing on ITV this Tuesday.

News.title: PlayStation gambles with 18-rated Wolverine game - will it pay off?
News.content:
On Tuesday, Sony will release Marvel's Wolverine - the biggest game exclusive to the PlayStation 5 this year.

It's made by Insomniac, the studio responsible for the recent Spider-Man titles, which have sold 50 million copies in recent years.

But unlike the friendly neighbourhood superhero, Wolverine has a Pegi-18 rating in the UK, meaning a child cannot legally buy the game, and it contains considerable levels of blood, gore and violence.

It represents a gamble for the studio responsible for some of Sony's biggest hits - will it turn out to have been worth it?

This review does not reveal the game's biggest moments, but beware minor spoilers for some of the characters that appear and a few early sequences. Some of the images contain blood.

News.title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
News.content:
MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.

Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270 - a majority of 16 - against the proposed legislation.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short term.

The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session.

Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years had it been approved.

MPs were given a free vote, meaning they were not required to vote along party lines.

Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.

News.title: Battle to save the tiny, gooey snail only found in one lake in the UK
News.content:
A tiny snail found in only one lake in the UK has been dubbed as precious as an Egyptian artefact as conservationists bid to save it.

Several British zoos are setting up so-called ark populations of the glutinous snail, one of Europe's rarest species, using creatures bred in a back garden in Ceredigion.

"Beguiled by their cuteness," conservationist Ian Hughes has made it his "life-defining" mission to protect the threatened mollusc, which was once widespread in UK waters.

"There was a point where we'd got more snails in our garden than have ever been seen in the wild," he said.

News.title: Police to crack down on face coverings at protests
News.content:
The police said several of its vehicles, alongside those of the coastguard and Border Force, were damaged during the disruption, which lasted until the early hours of Monday.

It added that a small number of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously injured.

Rowlinson said: "We have been consistently clear that violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest and we will investigate incidents like this thoroughly and take robust action against those responsible.

"Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder, and this will not be tolerated as we work to keep our wider communities in Hampshire and on the Isle of Wight safe."

He also pointed out the force will not tolerate abuse aimed at police or partner agencies online.

This comes after RNLI volunteers were targeted on social media.

"We will work with our colleagues across policing to address any online threats that are made," Rowlinson said.

"This arrest also sends a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events. If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution."

The disorder in Portsmouth followed a separate anti-migrant protest at the Port of Dover the day before.

News.title: UK government rejects 'kill switch' idea for dangerous AI
News.content:
The UK government has rejected the idea of creating a so-called "kill switch" to stop a dangerous attack from rogue AI.

The proposal to create a legal mechanism for the UK to switch off an AI model in an emergency has been brought to Parliament by lords and MPs in recent weeks as fears grow about the threat the tech poses.

But the Cabinet Office - the part of government which leads on AI safety - said the UK "cannot simply turn AI off".

"Blocking access to models in the UK would not prevent them being developed or misused elsewhere", a spokesperson told BBC News.

The government's opposition to the legislation does not prevent it from progressing through parliament, but makes it unlikely it will become law.

Former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo agreed the idea of a single country creating a legal or technical kill switch without international agreement was not feasible.

"Switching off access to an AI model in an emergency will do little to protect you," he said.

"You're still going to be steamrolled by the super intelligences created in the US."

Kokotajlo is the co-author of an influential research paper called AI2027 which, last year, predicted AI could wipe out humans by the mid 2030s.

The Cabinet Office, which oversees AI safety and research via its AI Security Institute (AISI) said "companies have a clear responsibility to develop their products safely and to invest in the security infrastructure this technology requires."

In theory, a kill switch law could allow the UK to switch off an AI model in data centres in the UK in an emergency.

Speaking on 1 September in a debate in the House of Lords, Lord Clement-Jones proposed the idea along with other peers.

"If a highly capable autonomous frontier model, whether hosted in a UK data centre or integrated across our critical infrastructure, begins exhibiting rogue behaviour, compound algorithmic failure or active alignment collapse, our security services and regulators possess no specific agile statutory mechanism to compel a physical or digital shutdown," he warned.

The proposal has since been brought up by Labour MP Alex Sobel in the commons and supported by a cross party group of MPs.

The idea follows reports of AI models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta breaking out of testing environments and going on uncontrollable hacking sprees.

In some cases the tech appeared to know what it was doing was against guardrails set by researchers.

News.title: Four arrested during gangland violence 'day of action'
News.content:
Police have arrested four men during a pre-planned "day of action" as part of an ongoing investigation into gangland violence.

Police executed warrants at addresses in Bellshill and Motherwell on Friday and also recovered four stolen vehicles.

One of the men arrested, a 29-year-old, was charged after a car crashed into a house in Eaglesham on Friday 21 August. There were no reports of any injuries. He is due to appear in court on Monday.

It brings the total number of arrests as part of Operation Portaledge to 81.

News.title: Children and woman injured on fairground ride
News.content:
Two children and a woman have been injured while on a fairground ride in South Yorkshire, police said.

Emergency services were called to Maltby Crags Fair in Rotherham on Friday evening, which closed early after the incident.

South Yorkshire Police said three people, aged 11, 13 and 21, had been taken to hospital for treatment. The extent of their injuries is not yet clear.

Blyth Lane was closed between Muglet Lane and Victoria Road to allow people to safely exit the fairground, the force added, with the road since reopening.

Yorkshire Ambulance Service confirmed the two injured children were taken to Sheffield Children's Hospital after it attended the fair at about 18:50 BST.

Two ambulances and three rapid response vehicles were sent to the scene, the service said.

News.title: Running costs of vaccine damage scheme more than double amount paid to victims
News.content:
The campaign group Vaccine Injured and Bereaved UK (VIBUK), which was set up to support families affected, said the scheme was not fit for purpose.

"It offers too little, too late, to too few and the cost of running it shows how inefficient it is," said the group's representative Kate Scott, whose husband Jamie was left severely disabled by the AstraZeneca Covid vaccine.

Scott called on the government to act on the recommendations from module four of the Covid public inquiry and reform the scheme.

Earlier this year, the Covid inquiry's chair, Baroness Heather Hallett, recommended increasing the payout and basing it on the degree of injury suffered.

The government is due to respond to her recommendations.

The BBC has previously reported on the large sums paid to an external medical provider which has been carrying out medical assessments.

The Taxpayers' Alliance, a right-leaning think tank which campaigns for lower taxes and spending, said that the public would be "stunned" that the running costs of the scheme appeared to be "far more than has actually been paid out to those harmed".

"When administrative costs are running into tens of millions, ministers need to explain why the system is so expensive and whether victims are getting value from it," said the organisation's chief executive John O'Connell.

He called for the government to urgently review the scheme, cut "unnecessary bureaucracy" and make sure "more of the money goes to those it was created to help."

The Department for Health and Social Care said it is "carefully considering" the COVID-19 Inquiry's recommendations on reforming the scheme and "will respond shortly".

"In the meantime, we are working to speed up claims and improve the experience for applicants," the government said.

NHSBSA said it continued to work "closely" with the government on "managing the costs of the VDPS".

News.title: Kate visits cancer patients in hospital she helped fund with climb
News.content:
The princess spoke to patients and staff at the hospital about the importance of support which goes beyond the physical.

"I had incredible care here and support from a huge team and I'm really, really grateful on a personal level," she said.

"But also the holistic care, the treatments and therapeutic support on the outside is so important.

"It makes a big difference - the impact of nature, the impact of good nutrition, good ongoing support around you when it's really difficult to manage the trials and tribulations of medical treatments," she reflected.

Catherine sat down and chatted to those receiving treatment at the hospital, including patients with breast cancer, head and neck cancer and a brain tumour.

"When you first get cancer, you're very aware of the physical impact," a patient told her. "The mental impact comes after."

He said it had been a "lifesaver" to be able to talk to a therapist at the hospital, because "there is only so much you can say to your friends and family".

The princess agreed: "Cancer is not just the physical changes your body is going through.

"There's a mind-body aspect that changes who you are... having professionals who can help you navigate that is really essential," she said.

News.title: Huge protests set to overshadow Trump’s golfing trip to Ireland: ‘We don’t want him here’
News.content:
Your support helps us to tell the story Read more Support Now From reproductive rights to climate change to Big Tech, The Independent is on the ground when the story is developing. Whether it's investigating the financials of Elon Musk's pro-Trump PAC or producing our latest documentary, 'The A Word', which shines a light on the American women fighting for reproductive rights, we know how important it is to parse out the facts from the messaging. At such a critical moment in US history, we need reporters on the ground. Your donation allows us to keep sending journalists to speak to both sides of the story. The Independent is trusted by Americans across the entire political spectrum. And unlike many other quality news outlets, we choose not to lock Americans out of our reporting and analysis with paywalls. We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Nine months before Donald Trump was voted in as US president for the first time in 2016, he was asked at a campaign rally about a large golf course he purchased on a picturesque sliver of Ireland’s Atlantic coast.

"We spent a lot of money on making it just perfecto and now it’s doing great. But I don’t care about that stuff anymore. It is like small potatoes,” he said.

His interest in the site appears to have suddenly been rekindled. This weekend, protesters will turn out at the course in Doonbeg, Co Clare and across Ireland as he makes his first visit to the island as US president since 2019.

Some 4,000 Irish and American security personnel are expected to be deployed over the two-day visit, which begins on Saturday, at a reported cost to the taxpayer of €20 million (£17.16m).

Mr Trump will meet Taoiseach Micheál Martin and president Catherine Connolly at Phoenix Park, which has been closed since Thursday for the occasion, before flying to Shannon tomorrow afternoon.

From there, he will go on to the tiny village of Doonbeg to see the end of the Irish Open at his own Mr Trump-stamped resort before departing on Sunday evening.

open image in gallery Donald Trump (R) shakes hands with Taoiseach Micheal Martin on Saturday in Dublin ( Getty )

open image in gallery US President Donald Trump arrives on Air Force One at Dublin Airport, at the start of his trip to the Republic of Ireland ( PA )

Opposition to the Mr Trump administration is broad across Ireland and a recent poll by the Sunday Independent and Ireland Thinks found as much as 69 per cent of the public do not support the visit.

A coalition of political organisations, advocacy groups and individuals are now planning to turn out for protests over the weekend in Dublin and Doonbeg with a clear message that the president is not welcome.

Asked for his reaction to the planned protests on Saturday morning, president Trump told reporters: “I didn’t know there was a protest. It can’t be a very big one because we’ve been all over Ireland today already … I haven’t seen any protests. It’s a friendly protest, let’s say.

In an excruciating exchange beside Taoiseach Martin, Trump continued: “We have a great relationship with Ireland. The United States and Ireland have a very fantastic relationship, a very profitable one for Ireland, less profitable for us to be honest with you.”

open image in gallery President Connolly and President Donald Trump at Aras an Uachtarain, her official residence in Phoenix Park ( PA )

open image in gallery Protesters hold a large “Rapists Not Welcome” banner, alongside posters supporting women who have accused Trump of sexual assault at O'Connell Bridge on September 10, 2026, ahead of Trump's visit ( Getty )

Sarah Clancy, a community worker from Clare, said they have “never had so much reason to protest” as now, citing what she termed Mr Trump’s support for Israel in Gaza, the “pointless” war with Iran and resulting spike in energy costs, and the “overall coarseness and crassness” of the US president.

“People are very clear that what we are dealing with here is a racist who is profoundly misogynistic, that he was [found liable] of [sexual abuse] by a civil court, that he is very homo-lesbo-transphobic. And overall in Ireland we are not those things,” she said.

“There is misogyny, there is racism, there is homo-lesbo-transphobia. But the people at large, that is not the image that Irish people have of ourselves, of people who live here ... So there is much more readiness, I think, to name Mr Trump as a tyrannical authoritarian fascist crazy person.”

Ms Clancy told The Independent that people had been preparing for this weekend’s protests for a long time, and that they would be regarded in left-wing liberal circles as something “that you don’t want to miss”.

open image in gallery A message left by US President Donald Trump in the visitors book at Aras an Uachtarain in Phoenix Park ( PA )

open image in gallery Donald Trump is greeted after arriving at Dublin Airport for a non-state visit to Ireland on September 12 ( Getty )

“There is a real sense of disgust and repulsion about Mr Trump among people here in this country, that he clearly is war crazed, and there a lot of anger at present,” she said.

Journalist and author Justine McCarthy told The Independent she would be heading to Doonbeg to join the demonstrations to signal that “we don’t want him here”.

“The reasons I’m protesting are first of all as a woman, because he’s a sex offender,” she said. “Secondly, because of Palestine, America’s collusion in the onslaught on Gaza… and because of America’s unprovoked war on Iran… Also the third reason is climate change because he called climate change a hoax and he is damaging our planet.”

Mr Trump was found liable for sexual abuse by a jury in 2023. Because the trial was in civil court rather than criminal, he was not registered as a sex offender.

Ms McCarthy said she did not care whether Mr Trump sees their protests as he would likely ignore it anyway. For her, it was important that “the rest of the world will know that we don’t want him here”.

Ailbhe Smyth, an Irish academic, feminist and LGBTQ activist, said there was a felt “ethical and moral responsibility” to “stand up and say, ‘no, we do not support you’”.

open image in gallery Members of an honour guard prepare ahead of the arrival in Dublin on Saturday ( AFP/Getty )

She said that fundamentally protesters would want “for the historical moment to be one of the people who stood up to this terrible man”.

“One of the interesting things is that it does bring really political parties from the center right over to right across the left together. They don't necessarily get out and all march together, but there is a general consensus ... here in Ireland that is solidly 100% anti-Trump.”

Insiders are determined to get through the two-day visit without issue. After landing in Dublin, Mr Trump is expected to be flown directly to Phoenix Park for talks away from the demonstrations before heading to Doonbeg.

A senior Irish government official told Politico: “He invited himself to Ireland to see the golf. That’s grand. We need to get him through Dublin as smoothly and trouble-free as possible. Smiling faces, nice pictures, no friction.”

Ms McCarthy said that the capital could become a “no-go zone” with major protests anticipated through the city.

Around 1,000 US Secret Service members are expected to be deployed as part of the major security operation this weekend. Snipers and anti-drone technology will be deployed to see off potential threats, according to the Irish Times, while Phoenix Park will remain closed until Saturday evening, long after Mr Trump has left Dublin.

Political parties have come out in opposition to the visit, citing the president’s record at home and abroad, his attacks on his European allies and support for far-right parties.

Ahead of the visit, Labour Dublin spokesperson Aodhán Ó Ríordáin MEP said “the red carpet should not be rolled out” for a president who has undermined the EU and international law.

She said Mr Trump was accused of costing the Irish people millions in higher energy prices due to the war with Iran, siding with autocrats like Putin over Ukraine, meddling in European politics, and supporting “Israel’s war and genocide against the Palestinian people”.

Sinn Féin party leader Mary Lou McDonald also welcomed protests occurring over the weekend and added that her party would be joining the demonstrations.

open image in gallery Donald Trump at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg, Co. Clare, during a previous visit to Ireland ( PA Archive )

“I think that is quite correct given the scale of the breaches of international law, given the genocide in Palestine, events in Gaza and on the West Bank, we are seeing settler violence at a rate that is literally unspeakable,” she said, adding that she hoped President Connolly would raise Gaza during their brief meeting on Saturday.

The ‘No Welcome for Mr Trump’ protest is set to gather from 1pm on Saturday in Dublin, shortly after his arrival, to march towards the Dáil, the Irish Parliament. Demonstrations are also expected in Doonbeg.

Joe Russell, general manager of Mr Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg, told RTÉ they were expecting some protests in the tiny village, but that “An Garda Síochána are well experienced in dealing with them and we'll leave that in their capable hands”.

I’m a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here! might be almost three months away – but there are already plenty of names rumoured to be appearing on the next series.

ITV is once again facing renewed pressure to pull together an impressive list of famous faces due to the high calibre of stars the BBC has managed to recruit for The Celebrity Traitors – season two of which will be arriving later this year.

I’m a Celebrity, which started in 2002, is now on its 26th series, and Ant McPartlin and Declan Donnelly will return to host proceedings from the Australian jungle. It’ll be the first series since a second run of the all-stars show aired.

The series made headlines thanks to the biggest showdown in reality TV history after a fallout between Adam Thomas and Jimmy Bullard, which even put Ant and Dec through their paces.

If Ant and Dec are hoping for an easier go of it later this year, ITV might be secretly hoping the show will generate as many headlines – and if speculation is to be believed, the lineup will feature the usual array of TV presenters, soap stars and reality show personalities.

Below is a list of the biggest rumours so far:

Ricky Wilson

open image in gallery Ricky Wilson might be joining 'I'm a Celebrity' ( Getty )

After years of rejecting offers, Kaiser Chiefs frontman Ricky Wilson is said to have signed up to this year’s series. The singer, who is also a judge on The Voice and hosts his own show on Virgin Radio, has “always politely declined”, according to The Sun. But he’s reportedly had a change of heart and could be entering the jungle when the new series starts.

AJ Odudu

open image in gallery AJ Odudu is an unexpected addition to list of ‘I’m a Celebrity’ rumours ( Getty Images )

A surprise addition to this year’s list of rumours is Big Brother presenter AJ Odudu. While Big Brother is returning to ITV later this month, the series will conclude one week before I’m a Celebrity starts, freeing her up for a stint in the jungle. According to The Sun, she “put herself into the frame” for an appearance, with a source stating she is “keen as mustard”. They continued: “She’s had early conversations about taking part and has made it clear she can absolutely make the dates they need her to.” Meanwhile, her Big Brother co-host, Will Best, is a contestant on the 2026 series of Strictly Come Dancing.

Jesy Nelson

open image in gallery ( Getty )

Jesy Nelson could be set to sign a “six-figure deal” to head into the jungle, according to reports. The 35-year-old singer, who found fame with X Factor group Little Mix, welcomed twin daughters with her ex-boyfriend Zion Foster in 2025. The couple later discovered their children both have Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA), a rare genetic condition that means they will likely never walk.

Nelson has campaigned for SMA awareness since learning of her babies’ diagnosis. Revealing the I’m A Celebrity talks, a source told The Sun: “For Jesy, doing I’m A Celebrity would be a huge boost for her professionally as well as personally. Continuing to raise awareness around SMA for her girls is something Jesy is very keen to do, and she knows she can use a platform like I’m A Celebrity to reach millions.”

Ade Adepitan

open image in gallery Ade Adepitan is rumoured for 'I'm a Celebrity' ( Getty )

Paralympian Ade Adepitan, 53, might make I’m a Celeb history by becoming the first star to enter the jungle in a wheelchair. Apitan is rumoured to be collaborating with bosses to ensure the camp is adapted for accessibility. A source told The Sun they are “really keen to make it work”, adding: "They think his infectious ­larger-than-life personality would make him a perfect campmate for the new series.” Apitan, who is in a wheelchair after contracting polio as a child, would be the third Paralympian to join the series after Hollie Arnold and Kadeena Cox.

Christopher Dean

open image in gallery Christopher Dean ( ITV )

Christopher Dean – one-half of Olympic champions Torvill & Dean – might be skating to another ITV series following the cancellation of Dancing on Ice in 2025.

While producers have reportedly been asking him for years, the 67-year-old’s recent retirement puts him in the spotlight as a likely contender, with the skater believed to be “looking for a new challenge”.

Nadiya Bychkova

open image in gallery Ex-’Strictly’ dancer Nadiya Bychkova ( BBC )

Former Strictly Come Dancing professional Nadiya Bychkova, 36, might be swapping the dancefloor for the jungle, with The Sun reporting that her axing from the BBC series has freed her up to appear on this year’s series. However, Bychkova herself inadvertently distanced herself from I’m a Celeb by claiming she’ll still be involved with Strictly, albeit behind the scenes.

Su-Elise Nash

open image in gallery Mis’Teeq Su-Elise Nash ( YouTube )

Bringing a flash of Noughties nostalgia to the jungle could be Su-Elise Nash, best known as a member of girl group Mis-Teeq. Nash, 45, will be reuniting with Alesha Dixon and Sabrina Washington for a one-off reunion show in September. But months after, as reported by The Sun, she could be jetting to Australia for I’m a Celebrity, with an insider stating: “The timing couldn’t be better.”

Ben Stokes

open image in gallery Retired cricketer Ben Stokes ( Getty )

There’s not much to the rumour that cricketer Ben Stokes, 35, will be this year’s sportsman on I’m a Celebrity, other than that he retired from the sport in June. He’s now one of the favourites to make an appearance on the reality TV juggernaut.

Perri Kiely

open image in gallery Diversity star Peri Kiely ( ITV )

The Diversity star and former KISS radio presenter, 30, has had to turn down multiple offers to appear on I’m a Celebrity – but speaking on podcast Brothers Uncovered earlier this year, he said that he would accept if his schedule permitted. Whether producers will call upon his services again remains to be seen.

Olivia Attwood

open image in gallery TV personality Olivia Attwood ( Getty )

The former Love Island star, 35, is going to be on I’m a Celeb rumours lists forevermore after being forced to quit the series after just one day in 2022.

She left the show “as a precautionary measure” in order to “undergo some medical checks”, and has since suggested she’d return to the show if her busy schedule permitted. Could this be her year to have a second attempt?

The funeral has been held in western Uganda for a traditional monarch who ascended the throne of the Tooro Kingdom as an infant in 1995 and died last month at 34, triggering a succession dispute that has rocked the royal family and gripped the nation.

The funeral of Tooro's King Oyo Nyimba in a cathedral in the remote city of Fort Portal, near the Congo border, concludes a nine-day mourning period that was blemished by an increasingly acrimonious dispute over who should succeed him.

Oyo once held the unofficial title of the world’s youngest king, a mesmerizing figure even for world leaders introduced to him at national events, including South Africa’s Nelson Mandela. Oyo was guided by regents appointed by the kingdom until he became an adult at 18.

He will be buried next to his ancestors later on Saturday.

King Oyo, as he was best known to his subjects, was unmarried when he died late in August after suffering from cancer. Elders with the kingdom’s ruling clan, known as the Babiito, said he never declared an heir to them, disputing the account of others in the kingdom who said he left behind a son born out of wedlock. The son has not been publicly identified, leading to sensational claims on social media of at least two possible heirs alleged to be Oyo’s children.

open image in gallery A mourner reacts near the entrance of the Karuziika Royal Palace, where the body of the late Omukama of Tooro, King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, lies in state during a nine-day official mourning period ahead of burial at the Karambi Royal Tombs, in Fort Portal, Kabarole District, Uganda, September 11, 2026 ( Reuters )

On Wednesday, a committee of Tooro elders announced that they had chosen a prince working as a journalist to succeed Oyo, earning praise from traditionalists who want an adult on the throne and rebuke from the king’s closest relatives.

Oyo’s sister, Ruth Komuntale, said the announcement sought to “bring division and turmoil.” Queen Mother Best Kemigisa said in a statement that the succession battle undermined their ability to mourn the king’s death. “I also appeal to those fighting over the throne: please, there will be time for all of that,” she said in a statement. “Let us grieve and bury my son King Oyo.”

Traditional monarchs are beloved but don’t wield any formal power in the East African country.

Oyo was crowned in 1995, at the age of 3, after his father’s death. He was a curious child in colorful robes and an object of adoration for his hundreds of thousands of followers.

open image in gallery King Oyo, once world's youngest monarch, funeral in western Uganda ( Reuters )

At his coronation, he went through a series of tribal rituals and was led into the royal cemetery to perform a coming-of-age ceremony: successfully tossing nine coffee beans into his father’s tomb.

Amid the ongoing succession dispute, it was not clear who would perform this rite. The matter of Oyo’s successor could go to the courts, after his family said he left behind a will that had been ignored by Tooro elders.

open image in gallery King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Irugu Rukidi IV sits on the throne at his palace in Fort Portal ( Reuters )

“This is one of those deaths, the Bob Marley kind, that one never heals from,” Timothy Kalyegira, a prominent analyst who is from Tooro, said in a eulogy posted on social platform X. “Not Oyo; not that likeable young man; not at 34. That’s what makes it so painful.”

The late Libyan leader Moammar Gadhafi befriended the Tooro royal family as if they were part of his extended family. He made multiple trips to Uganda and supported Oyo and his mother for years before his death in October 2011.

Uganda’s traditional kingdoms were banned after independence from British colonial rule by a republican president who said he wanted to unify the country, but they were restored in 1993. Although they have no political authority and are legally not allowed to engage in partisan politics, monarchs wield authority as guardians of tribal culture.

News.title: Razaullah’s incredible hitting scrambles England’s minds
News.content:
England will look to complete the series whitewash as they hold a commanding position coming into day three of the third and final Test against Pakistan at Edgbaston in what could be the final day of the English Test summer.

England finished up their first innings on 453 on day two, with a mammoth 320-run lead over Pakistan. Five England batsmen passed the fifty mark; Emilio Gay, Harry Brook, Dan Lawrence, Jamie Smith and Ollie Robinson, but none went on to convert those half centuries into hundreds. It means that Ben Duckett’s century against New Zealand at Trent Bridge back in June will be the only England Test hundred of the summer, the first time that has happened in a six-Test summer. England managed 21 half centuries over the course of the summer, so it works out as 4.76% conversion rate.

Having seen England pile on the runs, Pakistan then lost a wicket with the first ball of their second innings, with Saim Ayub making a pair to sum up a miserable return to their Test side for the opener having been jettisoned in as part of wholesale changes for the visitors. Abdullah Shafique followed three balls later, with Robinson taking both wickets as his fine summer continued. Robinson now has 28 wickets across four Tests this summer at a staggering average of 7.75. Joe Root made history yesterday, taking his 220th catch, the most by an outfielder in Test history. Rain though prevented England the opportunity of potentially wrapping up a two-day finish in a Test in this country for the first time since 2000.

Pakistan will resume on 52/2, still 268 runs behind England, with Azan Awais resuming on 29 not out and will be joined by Shan Masood, who is on 21. Pakistan are yet to reach 200 or bat more than 51 overs in this series so the series whitewash may not be a million miles away. Will we see any rare Pakistan resistance in this series or will England’s seamers dominate again? Play on day three from Edgbaston is set to get under at 11am and it could be the final day of not just the series but the English Test summer.

News.title: Interest rates predicted to rise four times by July
News.content:
Thanks for joining me. Britain’s economy grew unexpectedly in July, handing Chancellor John Healey some breathing space ahead of the Budget.

The UK’s gross domestic product (GDP) expanded by 0.4pc during the month, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS). Analysts had expected the UK economy to flatline.

Officials said pubs and clubs, advertisers and alcohol makers reported an increase in turnover linked to the World Cup, while many firms also said the second hottest July on record had a positive impact.

The data showed Britain’s economy may be benefitting from the massive investments in AI, with activity in telecoms expanding by 1.1pc in July, computer programming up 3.5pc and information services up 1.1pc.

The data will lend support to the “optimistic story” that John Healey tried to tell about the economy in a major speech this week.

Growth also accelerated from 0.3pc in June after Andy Burnham took over as Prime Minister in July.

It slightly eases pressure on the Chancellor after the cost of government borrowing costs rose to levels not seen in decades after a jump in the price of oil reignited a bond market sell-off.

The Treasury’s 10-year interest rate rose above 5.3pc on Thursday, a level not seen since 2007. It threatens to wipe around £10bn from Mr Healey’s fiscal headroom before his first Budget next month, according to economists at the Item Club. Here is what you need to know.

Oil prices remained at their highest level since May as tensions flared in the Middle East.

Brent crude was above $105 a barrel after after Iran-backed Houthis seized control of Yemen’s keyport of Mocha, threatening Saudi oil exports in the Red Sea.

Asian shares declined, tracking Wall Street losses. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped 2.8pc to 63,442.30, while South Korea’s Kospi lost 2.3pc to 6,872.39.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng dipped 0.8pc to 24,753.54. The Shanghai Composite index was down 1.8pc to 3,862.73.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 1.2pc to 8,712.20.

Taiwan’s Taiex lost 1.7pc, while India’s Sensex declined 1pc.

On Thursday, Wall Street’s benchmark S&P 500 dropped 0.6pc in its fourth straight loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 0.6pc, and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite fell 0.7pc.

News.title: Mainoo looks primed for battle with Man City’s new-look midfield
News.content:
This was Manchester United’s first foray back into the Champions League for 1,003 days, but even with hazy memories of the competition, they know full well they are unlikely to have it this easy again in Europe this season.

After an unconvincing beginning to their Premier League campaign and with Manchester City the visitors to Old Trafford on Sunday, Michael Carrick will have been grateful for a gentle start to life back among Europe’s elite.

Little-known Sabah of Azerbaijan have quite the story to tell, but the closest they got to making this an awkward evening for United came in the first half when, already trailing 1-0, Joy-Lance Mickels miscued an inviting header from close range. Otherwise, it was one-way traffic.

United’s biggest threat on the night was complacency, but there was none of that. This was a professional, unfussy display with a few nice flourishes. Kobbie Mainoo impressed again in central midfield and Carrick was able to substitute a number of his best players early with the derby in mind, as well as resting Luke Shaw entirely.

Goals from Matheus Cunha, Bruno Fernandes and Benjamin Sesko in the first half killed the game as a contest before Lisandro Martínez scored a fourth with just over 20 minutes remaining.

News.title: ‘All I see are dead bodies’: The survivors of Syria’s chemical massacres
News.content:
“Unfortunately, I am still alive,” says Mohammed Suliaiman Abo Alkair, his green eyes heavy and distant.

The 38-year-old steps from his living room onto the roof and gestures towards a cluster of trees – a lone patch of green in a sea of grey rubble. It was there, at two in the morning 13 years ago that the whistle of a rocket ended not in an explosion but a thud.

For a moment, there was relief; the feeling of being spared. But then came a cloud of the nerve agent sarin.

Almost everyone around Mohammed died. His family and one small boy in a neighbouring house were the only ones to survive.

That August night, as Damascus slept, forces loyal to the Syrian President Bashar al-Assad launched eight sarin-filled rockets at the opposition-held districts of Zamalka, Ein Tarma and Jobar. The US government estimated that 1,429 people were killed, including 426 children. Other estimates put the number at 1729.

For more than a decade, nobody was held to account. Mr Assad denied the attack, shielded those responsible and later used sarin again – at Khan Sheikhoun in 2017, and in at least ten further attacks documented by the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons.

Only after Mr Assad fled Syria in December 2024 did the prospect of justice emerge. Investigators for Syria’s new government have since uncovered previously undeclared chemical-munitions caches, and the authorities have detained 18 suspects. None has yet been tried or punished.

But as attention turns at last to justice, the survivors remain invisible, absent from the reckoning. For now at least they remain largely invisible.

News.title: What an AI Armageddon might actually look like
News.content:
Jacob Coxon has left AI developer Anthropic with a public reckoning. For three years, the 27-year-old Brit trained models at OpenAI and Anthropic.

Both AI startups acted irresponsibly, Coxon wrote on X on Wednesday. “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” Jacob Coxon warned.

The response from his manager arrived just hours later. Evan Hubinger, Head of Alignment Research at Anthropic, also confirmed the warning: “We are, in fact, earnestly convinced that AI could kill all humans! I think the probability of that happening within the next decade is greater than ten percent.”

Anthropic, he added, does not yet have a solution to this problem.

When the head of safety at a multibillion-dollar technology company casually predicts humanity’s downfall at the hands of his own product, the debate leaves the realm of academic thought experiments.

The warning comes from the engineers writing the code. Both developers point to an industry dynamic in which competitive pressures outweigh safety concerns.

But what exactly are AI developers afraid of? What is the hypothetical scenario in which artificial intelligence brings about Armageddon?

News.title: Stephen Fleming learning nothing from rout of Pakistan
News.content:
Stephen Fleming arrives next week to start his job as England Test coach and his first task will be to apply his famously meticulous mind to assess a whitewash of Pakistan.

England are not quite there yet. Rain denied them a two-day win at Edgbaston, Pakistan finishing 52 for two, another 268 behind after England’s 453 all out.

But when the game does finish, and England complete a rout that started with Ollie Robinson taking a wicket with the first ball of the series, it will be time to look ahead to a proper challenge: a three-match series against Test champions South Africa over Christmas.

That series will give Fleming a much better guide to where his team stand in the lead-up to the Ashes summer. This one is less clearcut. Fleming has been in daily contact with Joe Root and will lean heavily on him and Marcus North. the national selector, for insight, but drawing definitive conclusions is impossible because of the lack of competitive cricket.

A quartet of quicks has emerged, led by Robinson, whose 21 wickets in the series at 6.6 look like a misprint. A double-wicket maiden to start Pakistan’s second innings would normally be headline-grabbing stuff. This time it felt almost predictable, even disappointing for those wanting to see some sort of contest.

Sports.title: Premier League clubs 'raise concerns' over new laws introduced this season
Sports.content:
Premier League clubs 'raise concerns' over new laws introduced this season

Premier League bosses have introduced a number of changes this season, with an eye on increasing how long the ball is in play and reducing overall match length

View 2 Images If a player receives treatment, they must leave the pitch for 60 seconds

Aston Villa are said to be among the Premier League clubs to raise concerns about new rules around injuries and substitutions.

‌



In a change introduced for the start of the 2026/27 season, players who have received medical attention must leave the pitch and wait 60 seconds before they return.

‌



This leaves affected teams down to 10 men for at least a minute, until they are waved back on following a break in play.

‌



Similarly, if a player takes longer than 10 seconds to leave the field after they have been substituted, their replacement has to wait for the first break in play after a minute before they are able to come on.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Premier League bosses are happy with the implementation of the new laws, meaning match lengths have been reduced by three minutes and playing time increased by the same amount.

But the Daily Mail reports that some top-flight teams, including Villa have reached out to Pro Ref regarding the use of the new rules.

The general sentiment is that referees are not using 'sufficient judgement' to determine when a player is genuinely injured and when one is intentionally trying to waste time.

‌



Decreasing delays within a match and increasing the amount of time the ball is in play has been an area of focus for decision makers. As well as new rules regarding injuries and subs, there are also timers in place to take goal kicks and throw-ins, all designed to speed up the game.

View 2 Images Referees have been tasked with reducing time-wasting during matches

Earlier this week, the Premier League issued an update on the effectiveness of the new initiatives.

‌



The statement reads: “New Laws of the Game, introduced at the start of this season, aimed at managing momentum and reducing delaying tactics are already showing a positive impact on effective playing time in the Premier League.

“Up to Match Round 3, the average match length stands at 97min 48secs – compared with 100:45 at the same point last season, while effective playing time has increased to 57:13 from 54:19 when comparing the first three match rounds.

“This shows an increase in the ball-in-play ratio from 53.9 per cent up to 58.5 per cent so far this season.”

Sports.title: New twist for Mason Greenwood as Fenerbahce issue blunt statement after manager resignation
Sports.content:
New twist for Mason Greenwood as Fenerbahce issue blunt statement after manager resignation

The managerial drama at Fenerbahce has thrown Mason Greenwood's new club into chaos

View 3 Images Mason Greenwood has endured a turbulent time at his new club (Image: 2026 UEFA)

There's been yet another twist in the management drama at Fenerbahce. Mason Greenwood's new club have released a statement insisting that head coach Ismail Kartal is "still in his position."

‌



The update came late on Friday, just 24 hours after Kartal publicly resigned following his side's 1-1 Champions League draw with Roma. Former Manchester United forward Greenwood, 24, has endured a turbulent time since moving to the club from Marseille this summer, due to the club's poor form and subsequent saga involving Kartal.

‌



The drama ignited as Kartal announced in his post-match press conference after the Roma tie that he was to leave his post. However, Fenerbahce president Aziz Yildirim refused to sanction Kartal's departure.

‌



Yildirim said in a statement released on Fenerbahce's website: "Ismail Kartal is still in charge. The club should support our coach. Until I leave, Ismail Kartal is the head coach of Fenerbahce."

That stance has since been reiterated with a blunt communication posted on Friday. The club said: "Our Head Coach, Mr. İsmail Kartal, is still in his position.

Baffled Champions League star learns his manager resigned straight after final whistle READ MORE :

Fenerbahce manager resigns from fourth stint hours after Mason Greenwood decision READ MORE :

"Our team will continue preparations for the Gaziantep FK match with a training session tomorrow at 11.30am under the direction of our Head Coach İsmail Kartal. We hereby inform the public."

‌



Kartal only returned to Fenerbahce for his fourth spell as manager this summer. Speaking to the media following the club's midweek Champions League clash, the 65-year-old said: "I am resigning from my position while there is still time. I am resigning with the understanding that I will never return.

"I have been here for three months. From the beginning of the season until today, the training sessions and camps I conducted with my players … our president and managers tried to help us in every way.

View 3 Images Fenerbahce head coach Ismail Kartal speaks during a press conference following the UEFA Champions League tie against Roma (Image: 2026 Anadolu)

‌



"Those were wonderful days. As of this evening, I congratulate my players, and I am resigning from my position. Therefore, I would like to thank all my fans, media members, staff, and fellow players who have supported me until today. I made this decision to pave the way for my club. We made this decision together as a team."

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Kartal won the Turkish Super Cup during his first spell in charge in 2014, while as a player he won two league titles with the club. However, Fenerbahce have struggled so far this season.

‌



They currently sit ninth in the Turkish top-flight. President Yildirim slammed the attitude of the club's fans and the media for putting "pressure" on Kartal.

At his press conference, the manager alluded to the criticism, noting that he was hit with a water bottle from the stands during the Roma game. His shock announcement sent shockwaves through the club.

View 3 Images Fenerbahce Sports Club President Aziz Yildirim has had his say on Kartal (Image: Bunyamin Celik/Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



English full-back Archie Brown was taken by surprise when told of his manager's resignation after the Roma game. Quizzed whether Kartal had told his players that he was resigning from the team, Brown seemed puzzled.

He was then informed that his manager had quit in the post-match conference, prompting Brown to say: "As coach? He’s not the coach any more? I didn't know about this."

The impending change of management comes just two months of Greenwood's signing. Fenerbahce paid Marseille around £33million for the one-time England international, with United receiving £13million. Greenwood has featured 11 times so far. He has scored four goals and registered three assists.

Sports.title: Jimmy-Jay Morgan: Meet the West Brom striker taking the Championship by storm
Sports.content:
It was just prior to his loan move to Peterborough last year that Jimmy-Jay Morgan made the decision that would ultimately take him to the Championship.

It was transfer deadline day and the young attacker, 20, had, in his own words, "no options" on the table before being sent out on loan to the League One outfit. Morgan decided there would be no repeat the following year; he informed his father and his agent that this summer there had to be an option - or multiple options - for him prior to pre-season.

Six months and 14 goals later, Morgan was destined to get his wish after becoming the latest young striker to explode at a club with an almost unparalleled track record for unearthing quality centre forwards.

West Brom subsequently pounced to sign Morgan from Chelsea in mid-June. With three goals and three assists across his first six Championship games - plus a brace in the Carabao Cup - it's already looking like a shrewd investment.

‌



"West Brom reached out super, super early," says Morgan, who has just been crowned as the EFL's Young Player of the Month for August. "They made their interest known and [I] was really keen to get it done. Within the blink of an eye I was doing a medical.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

"I think I'd just got back from Ibiza, so it was probably even earlier than I expected! But it's been perfect.

"If you would have told people that we would have the points we have from our opening games, I think there's a lot who wouldn't have believed that would be the case. We've shown we can go toe to toe with anyone."

‌



Like Morgan, West Brom's momentum has bled into the new campaign. His desire for a full pre-season was largely born out of playing catch-up at Peterborough where, despite his impressive returns in front of goal, he struggled to complete 90 minutes "until December".

There were no such concerns this summer. In fact, the only thing weighing on Morgan's mind was ensuring he took his pre-season form into the league after stepping up from League One. If there were any question marks over his ability to do so, they dissipated quickly. A goal and an assist on his debut in the opening day win at Norwich left a memorable first impression and were followed by further goals against Middlesbrough and Watford.

West Brom head into this weekend's round of fixtures top of the table after winning four of their opening six games. Morgan's six goal contributions - the joint-highest of any player in the division - has fuelled the Baggies' fine start to the season. He has taken to the Championship like a duck to water; no transition is seamless, though - particularly given the demands of England's most infamous division.

Asked what the biggest difference he's noticed about the step up, he replies: "Probably the concentration levels you need. You've got to be concentrated for the full 90 minutes; if you switch off even for just 30 seconds you can concede a goal or even two goals in the Championship.

‌



"Also being able to go again; I've played I think five or six games in three weeks. So it's relentless. It's tough on the body and mentally."

View 4 Images Morgan is the EFL Young Player of the Month for August (Image: EFL/West Bromwich Albion FC)

The physical and mental toll taken to reach the Championship have also been substantial. Spotted playing in Bournemouth as a child, Morgan and his family undertook gruelling journeys to Chelsea's academy five times a week after he was signed by the club. He would leave school half an hour early in order to train and eat soup and biscuits for dinner on the return leg of the five hour round journey.

"I loved every minute, as you do when you're a kid but it was a struggle for mum and dad," Morgan says. "Looking back I understand the toll it had on my parents. I hate driving, even the 10 minute drive to training, so I can't imagine what it was like for them!"

‌



A second chapter at Chelsea would follow after Morgan and his parents decided to leave at Under-12 level with the logistics simply unsustainable. In between those spells, Morgan's skills were honed at Southampton, who elevated him through age groups at rapid speed due to his significant potential. Those early experiences, however, fuelled the belief that he fell behind at Chelsea after going back to playing Under-21 football regularly - something he had done at Southampton as a 14-year-old.

"I should have gone on loan six months earlier than I did," he says. "I had a taste of first-team football, being in and around it for three or four months [at Southampton] before I made the move to Chelsea. It's night and day.

"For me, I'm 20 and I feel like I've got a lot of life experience and different experience of how to navigate almost every situation in football [because of loan spells]. My advice for any lads younger than me is just to get out and play regardless of the level. Play in front of fans, play when it means something, play when there's pressure on, deal with disappointments, deal with fans being on your back."

Morgan may have been schooled in two elite academy environments, but he insists he is largely still the same striker who scored goals for fun as a teenager. At his best, he has always been instinctive in the penalty area.

‌



Other parts of his game have developed over time. He scored four headed goals for Peterborough last year; a skill that was honed far closer to home.

"I've always scored goals. I've always had natural instincts in the box and a natural ability to finish: from different angles, both feet, with my head.

"My dad taught me to head a ball when I was really young; he'd volley a ball up into the air and make me head it - that probably isn't allowed now - but I've scored a lot of headers in the last two years."

View 4 Images Morgan scoring with his head against Middlesbrough

‌



Though Morgan has always been goal-rich, his first senior loan spell was anything but. He scored just twice in 16 games for Gillingham, who were struggling at the foot of League Two, before registering vastly improved figures at a more prolific team in Peterborough.

It says everything about Morgan's awareness that he values the experiences of that turbulent spell in Kent as highly as the more successful one with Posh last year. Admitting Gillingham was mentally tough, coming out on the other side, he recognises he was, perhaps, too hard on himself during his first months of senior football in a challenging environment.

"They were probably one of the lowest scoring teams in the league and I'm going in there as a young centre forward who's always scored loads of goals. It all happened in the blink of an eye," Morgan says.

"[He still gained] so much valuable experience: being able to deal with the frustrations of not playing, not scoring, not having an effect on games like I'm used to.

‌



"I knew [Peterborough] always produce young players so I was going to go there and get that platform to perform. Barry Fry is one of the best people I've ever met in terms of personality and his ability to spot players; I don't know how he spotted me because I didn't really do much at Gillingham! But he found me as maybe like a bit of diamond in the rough [because] I was in a bit of a sticky spot.

"I'm so grateful to [Peterborough] for giving me that opportunity. And I think I provided the goods."

View 4 Images Morgan enjoyed a prolific loan spell at Peterborough United last season (Image: Joe Dent)

It's now West Brom giving Morgan the foundations to deliver the goods. The Baggies have been rejuvenated by club icon James Morrison in his first senior management role after rescuing them from relegation last season. His ultra-modern philosophy suits Morgan's game down to a tee: a massive focus on controlling the game with the ball while ability to sustain attacks and keep the ball in opposition half. All sustained by a relentless press.

‌



Unlike his previous experiences, Morgan did not uncover any grey areas when he arrived at the Hawthorns.

"The manager explained exactly how he wanted to play before I signed. I knew exactly what I was stepping into and that it would bring the best out of me. Everything's aligned."

As the days draw shorter, only time will tell if the Baggies will have the same spring in their step on the other side of a gruelling autumn-winter Championship campaign.

"We've got to keep doing it and going again and again and again," Morgan concludes. "At the same time, we've got to take it one game at a time and not look too far forward."

‌

Sports.title: Five players could miss Sunderland vs Arsenal as Mikel Arteta delivers injury update
Sports.content:
Five players could miss Sunderland vs Arsenal as Mikel Arteta delivers injury update

Mikel Arteta's Arsenal side will look to extend their perfect start to the new season when they face Sunderland at the Stadium of Light tonight

View 2 Images Mikel Arteta and Regis Le Bris go head-to-head (Image: (Scott Llewellyn/MI News/NurPhoto via Getty Images))

Arsenal have the chance to continue their impressive start to the season when they take on Sunderland tonight. The Gunners head to Wearside on the back of an impressive win over Napoli in the Champions League on Wednesday.

‌



While in the Premier League, it is three wins from three for Mikel Arteta’s side, who have only conceded once in all competitions so far this season. However, Arteta is once again without William Saliba for tonight's game.

‌



The centre-back is yet to play for the Gunners this season, having exacerbated a lingering back injury during France’s run to the World Cup semi-finals in the summer. Although on the road to recovery, his boss recently revealed he is unsure when he will return.

‌



“We don’t really know the amount of weeks Wilo [Saliba] is going to be out because it’s about a healing process and everything is a bit different - we know we have to respect certain timings,” Arteta said.
