JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Jurrien Timber is working his way back to full fitness, with Arteta revealing on Friday: "[With Jurrien], let's see. We have another training session. He's been doing really well, he's been training with us now for a few days, and he looks in good shape."

While Arsenal could be set to welcome back Cristhian Mosquera, who has missed his side’s last two matches after picking up a muscular injury against Aston Villa. "[Cristhian's] doing really well, let's see if he can get [back] for this game or the next one,” Arteta said.

Ben White was also spotted limping towards the end of the 1-0 victory over Napoli, but Arteta confirmed the defender is "fine" and could feature tonight. While also speaking on Friday, Sunderland boss Regis Le Bris confirmed Romaine Mundle and Habib Diarra are his side’s only injury absentees for tonight’s game.

‌



View 2 Images Ben White started for Arsenal against Napoli midweek (Image: (Franco Romano/NurPhoto via Getty Images))

On Mundle, Le Bris said: “Romaine has a knee injury, which is a shame because he had a good pre-season. We will support him and hope he is ready by the end of the year.”

Diarra is continuing his recovery from a hamstring injury, and Le Bris added: “Habib is in the middle of his recovery.” And Le Bris also believes his side stand every chance of ending Arsenal’s perfect start to the new campaign.

‌



He said: “They are the best team in Europe at the minute and they have good momentum as well. We can’t get complacent otherwise it is finished very quickly.

“If you think that you are already a European team, it’s going to be a big problem. They are flying right now and they have many threats on the pitch but we have a good team as well. It is a good challenge and we need these challenges to get better.”

Sports.title: Chris Kamara health latest after diagnosis left him 'not the same person' as he enters Great North Run
Sports.content:
Chris Kamara health latest after diagnosis left him 'not the same person' as he enters Great North Run

Chris Kamara is taking on the Great North Run

View 3 Images Chris Kamara has been open about his health struggles in recent years (Image: Prostate Cancer UK/PA Wire)

Chris Kamara is set to participate in the Great North Run over four years since he was diagnosed with speech apraxia. The former footballer and Sky Sports pundit revealed his diagnosis in 2022 and stepped away from his broadcasting career that same year.

‌



The neurological disorder affects the brain's ability to plan and coordinate movements needed to speak clearly. Kamara, 68, has been open about his journey with the condition and recently discussed his health during an appearance on ITV's This Morning last month.

‌



Speaking to Cat Deeley and Ben Shephard, Kamara said: "I'm feeling great, my voice has quickened up and I'm so much better." The former midfielder will be joined by his son Jack and Shephard for Sunday's race, which is the largest half-marathon in the world and will be broadcast live on BBC One.

‌



He discussed the impact the TV presenter has had during his speech apraxia journey, telling Shephard: "You kept onto me, my carer there, he's been amazing. He's been there for me the whole time, he looks after me so much, but having someone behind you keep saying, 'You're still the same person as you were before', is amazing."

He further detailed his experience with the diagnosis in May on Good Morning Britain when asked by host Ranvir Singh how he was coping. Kamara replied: "Ah, I'm great. Yeah, I'm fine. I'm not the same person as I was, but I accept the new me now, and everybody else seems to accept it, so you get on with life.

"I had apraxia of speech, a brain injury. So, the message from the brain to the mouth is interrupted. So, sometimes you can't speak, or you speak slower." He admitted it's important to "accept the person you are now and not crave the person you were before. And then you can get on."

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Chris Kamara shares huge update after revealing prostate cancer scare READ MORE :

Kamara will be entering the Great North Run in support of Prostate Cancer UK and last month revealed his own cancer scare after going through testing in 2024. He had undergone a routine blood test that showed an above-average PSA level - a potential sign of the disease.

He then went through several more checks and monitoring before being informed that he didn't have prostate cancer. Taking to X to describe the experience, Kamara wrote: "Had some good news from @ProstateUK that blokes using the risk checker after my appeal in the paper last week, went up by a THIRD.

‌



View 3 Images The former footballer will be running the Great North Run with Ben Shephard today (Image: Prostate Cancer UK/PA Wire)

"They know from experience that this will prompt a number men to see their doctor. Unfortunately, some will get a diagnosis- BUT thankfully early enough to save their lives." Kamara has enjoyed a decade-long association with Prostate Cancer UK and told the Mirror how vital early diagnosis.

He said: "Any man would feel scared about the prospect of getting prostate cancer. I've been working with the charity for more than a decade, so I know that early diagnosis is absolutely key.

‌

Sports.title: Arsenal told they ‘dodged a bullet’ by NOT signing Vinicius Jr after transfer saga
Sports.content:
Arsenal told they ‘dodged a bullet’ by NOT signing Vinicius Jr after transfer saga

Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta was desperate to land a superstar attacking talent, but failed in his pursuits of Julian Alvarez and Real Madrid forward Vinicius Jr

View 3 Images Real Madrid star Vinicius Jr was a target for Arsenal during the summer window

Arsenal title winner Emmanuel Petit believes his former side had a lucky escape after missing out on Vinicius Jr this summer.

‌



The Gunners were crowned Premier League champions for the first time in 20 years back in May, but Mikel Arteta wasted no time on upgrading his squad.

‌



Bruno Guimaraes, Ezri Konsa and Christos Tzolis have all made an immediate impact, but Arsenal did fail to land a new top-tier attacker. Arteta had earmarked the need for a new striker after a difficult first season for Viktor Gyokeres.

‌



Atletico Madrid frontman Julian Alvarez was linked for the entire window, although his reluctance over a move to the Emirates ultimately scuppered any chance of a deal.

But a move for Real Madrid superstar Vinicius Jr was on the cards for a certain period of the window. The Gunners felt they were in pole position to land the Brazilian, who had reached an impasse in talks over a new contract.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Arsenal were optimistic about completing a deal, before he eventually signed a new contract to stay at the Bernabeu. However, rather than seeing that as a negative, Petit, who won the double with Arsenal in 97/98, thinks Arteta may have struggled to incorporate the ego of a player like Vinicius.

Speaking to Boyle Sports, Petit said: "I think Vinicius Jnr is a really talented player but in terms of his mentality I am not sure he is a good fit for Arsenal. That’s just my opinion.

‌



"I see so many humble players at Arsenal so if you all of a sudden bring in someone who is completely different, it can be a problem, especially with Arteta’s style of management.

View 3 Images Emmanuel Petit had fears over Vinicius Jr fitting in at Arsenal (Image: Robbie Jay Barratt - AMA/Getty Images)

"Look at what happened between Vinicius Jnr and Jose Mourinho in the last game between Real Betis and Real Madrid. It reminded me of what happened with Xabi Alonso last season when he didn’t want to shake his hand.

‌



He added: "Vinicius Jnr receives so much stick from the fans, the press and social media but in those moments he is sending the wrong message. I think he is probably a bullet dodged for Arsenal looking at that moment.

"I would have loved to see a player with the talent of Vinicius Jnr play for Arsenal but with his mentality and his ego I think it would have made for a really difficult situation to cope with."

Failing to sign Alvarez was a blow though, according to Petit, who thinks the Argentinian would have slotted in seamlessly.

‌



View 3 Images Arsenal missed out on signing Julian Alvarez (Image: Cesar Ortiz Gonzalez/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Petit continued: "Julian Alvarez is the striker Arsenal need. Why? Because he knows the Premier League. He’s such a talented player. He has great movement, great technical skills, and he would perfectly fit the DNA of this Arsenal team in how he plays one touch football. I really like everything about him as a player.

"But obviously he wants Barcelona, and if he didn’t leave Atletico Madrid in the summer transfer window, do you really think he’s going to leave that club during the winter transfer window? I wouldn’t be so sure about that."

Sports.title: 'Joining Liverpool from Fulham was the biggest failure of my career - my mum got me in trouble'
Sports.content:
'Joining Liverpool from Fulham was the biggest failure of my career - my mum got me in trouble'

The former Liverpool defender had a tough time at Anfield during the 12 months he spent on Merseyside

View 2 Images Paul Konchesky moved to Liverpool in 2010 (Image: Matthew Ashton/AMA/Corbis via Getty Images)

Paul Konchesky says joining Liverpool from Fulham was a dream come true - until it quickly turned into a nightmare. The left-back had a tough time at Anfield, with his mother also getting him in trouble with fans.

‌



Konchesky's two former clubs face off on Saturday afternoon as the Cottagers travel to Anfield to face Andoni Iraola's Reds. The 45-year-old joined Liverpool on deadline day in 2010, signing a £3.5million deal with Lauri Dalla Valle and Alex Kacaniklic heading the other way to west London.

‌



However, the defender did not arrive to much fanfare at Anfield as he followed unpopular new manager Roy Hodgson in moving from Fulham to Liverpool.

‌



Konchesky made just 18 appearances at Liverpool and was loaned out to Nottingham Forest mid-way through his only season. The defender struggled and admitted that the "dream" move was the biggest failure of his career.

Liverpool given worrying Bradley Barcola verdict after Andoni Iraola injury update READ MORE :

Alexis Mac Allister backs up contract demand as Liverpool beat Atletico - 5 talking points READ MORE :

When asked if he believed he was good enough to play for Liverpool, Konchesky told the ECHO in 2025: "Yeah, I do, yeah. I obviously wouldn’t have gone if I didn't back myself to play for a football club like that because you don't want to embarrass yourself.

"But it didn't work out. I think you just have to bite the bullet on that one. And I have to say that it is probably one of the biggest failures in my 20-year career."

‌



Things got particularly bad for Konchesky when his mum went viral for branding the Reds' supporters "Scouse scum" on social media in response to the backlash her son had received after a defeat by Stoke City.

She wrote at the time: "To all you Liverpool Scouse scum out the (sic) never mind the cockney c**t. Take a real look at you team stop living off the past. the team are s**t. Anyone made a mistake, it's the cockney c**t. Never should have left Fulham."

View 2 Images Konchesky struggled at Liverpool (Image: PAUL ELLIS / AFP via Getty Images)

‌



The post was taken down not long after it was published, and a club spokesperson told the ECHO at the time: "Mrs Konchensky's comments are inappropriate and have already been removed from Facebook. This does remain, however, a private family matter."

Despite all the chaos caused at Anfield, Konchesky still believes he would've made the same decision and signed for them. "Listen, I don't regret many things in my career. You look at it now, do I regret it? Only because of what happened. But I was 29 and going to one of the biggest clubs with a massive history. You can't turn that down," he said.

"I knew the club was trying to change hands with the owners, but obviously not as much as it probably was behind the scenes. So I knew it was going to be difficult, it was a difficult time for the club. But if someone comes to you at 29 years old and it’s a club like Liverpool with that massive history, I think everyone will bite their hands off. And it was a dream come true.

Article continues below

"I learned loads from it, I played with some fantastic players and I met some fantastic people along the way."

Following his time at Liverpool, Konchesky had stints at Leicester City, Gillingham and Queens Park Rangers before retiring in 2018. He was most recently the manager of Women's Super League side West Ham United.

Sports.title: Enceladus takes on Christmas Day and Pienne Bonnard in 250th St Leger
Sports.content:
Enceladus takes on Ballydoyle duo Christmas Day and Pierre Bonnard in the latest renewal of the St Leger.

3.35 Doncaster - Enceladus faces Christmas Day and Pierre Bonnard in St Leger

The 250th renewal of the Group 1 Betfred St Leger looks a cracker, with Aidan and Joseph O'Brien set to dominate a field of 11.

Joseph O'Brien took this race with Galileo Chrome in 2020 and looks to have a super chance with Enceladus.

The son of Sea The Stars has progressed with each start, including when winning the King George V at the Royal meeting. He warmed up for a crack at this with a ready success in the Gordon Stakes and may go off the market leader under Billy Loughnane.

Nine-time winner Aidan O'Brien saddles four runners with Derby hero Christmas Day a big player under Ronan Whelan. Any rain would be a positive given his Epsom triumph in wet conditions, and he will be 5lbs better off with stablemate Pierre Bonnard - who finished ahead of him at York.

Great Voltigeur runner-up Pierre Bonnard should be suited by this extra distance after defeat at the hands of Arc hopeful Maltese Cross, while Amelia Earhart is a quirky but talented filly. She looked like showing signs of revival when a runner-up in Group 3 company at Cork, but this is a huge step up from that assignment.

Of the others, Andrew Balding pair Galiyan and Hatteen rate each-way alternatives, with Saffie Osborne picking up the ride on Joseph O'Brien's second string, Highwayman.

1.45 Doncaster - 2000 Guineas favourite Desert Castle bids to go 2-2

The 2000 Guineas favourite Desert Castle is the headline act in a quality edition of the Group 2 Betfred Champagne Stakes.

The Charlie Appleby-trained Frankel colt burst onto the scene with a runaway success at Newmarket last month and he will be all the rage to follow up under Billy Loughnane - who will be eyeing more winners to fend off Oisín Murphy at the summit of the jockeys' championship.

Gentle Hurricane scored on debut before improving to claim second in the Acomb Stakes and granted further progress he can put it up to the favourite. Jason Watson replaces Oisin Murphy in the plate here, with the champion otherwise engaged at Leopardstown.

William Muir has spoken glowingly about Breacher and having landed a Salisbury maiden on his first start, he ran a solid third in Group 3 company. That form entitles him to hit the frame here.

Ballydoyle raider Sergei Diaghilev looks the pick of the remainder, with Rosberg and Silver Dominion also in situ.

2.55 Doncaster - Red-hot favourite More Thunder drops in trip

More Thunder drops back to seven furlongs in a strong-looking Group 2 Betfred Park Stakes at 2.55pm.

The William Haggas-trained five-year-old has been running with credit at the top table all season and this dip back in class and distance should see him hard to beat under Tom Marquand.

Never So Brave landed a first Group 1 victory last season but has failed to fire this season, while the same applies to last year's Middle Park victor Wise Approach.

Image: Never So Brave (centre) takes on More Thunder

Ralph Beckett's 2025 Sussex Stakes winner Qirat ran another fine race in defeat when chasing home Zavateri at Goodwood and cannot be ruled out, while Flora Of Bermuda and Volterra complete the shortlist.

Also on Town Moor...

Berkshire Regal locks horns with Hmas Perth in the opening 1.10pm British Stallion Studs EBF Maiden Stakes, worth £25,770 to the winner. Ed Dunlop won this race last year and will be eyeing further success in it, with Beloved Country his representative.

A typically competitive Betfred Portland (2.20pm) sees Getreadytorumble and Twilight Calls towards the top of the market. The team surrounding the latter have already tasted success at this year's Festival, with Speed Of Sound soaring to success in Thursday's opener.

Bullet Point tops a field of 17 assembled for a strong renewal of the Pertemps Network Handicap, although Moonfall is also likely to attract support for the popular George Boughey and Billy Loughnane combination.

Elsewhere...

The day begins with top-quality action from Australia. Sir Delius (formerly Delius) takes on Sheza Alibi in a classy looking Grade 1 Crown Makybe Diva Stakes.

Back on home soil, Solar Edge and Kylian do battle in Lingfield's feature - the Free Race Replays On attheraces.com Handicap at 4pm.

Woodbine plays host to top-class action in the evening, headlined by Notable Speech taking on Archivist and company in the feature Woodbine Mile at 10.20pm. Just 35 minutes later, Diamond Rain, Sea The Fire and Jancis all hold good chances in the E. P. Taylor Stakes.

Sports.title: 'Let's do this for the USA' - Shelton sets up Zverev showdown in US Open final
Sports.content:
Ben Shelton ‌defeated compatriot Frances Tiafoe in ‌an electric US Open semi-final on Friday to ​secure a title showdown with Alexander Zverev.

On a poignant evening that began with commemorations marking the 25th anniversary of ​the September 11 attacks, Shelton ‌came from a set down to beat Tiafoe 4-6 6-3 6-3 7-5 and move closer ​to ending a 23-year ‌American wait for a men's singles Grand Slam ​champion.

No home male player has won a Grand Slam singles title since Andy Roddick triumphed in Flushing Meadows in 2003. Shelton will now have a chance to claim his maiden Grand Slam crown.

The German had played all his previous matches during the night sessions, existing in a perpetual loop of darkness and midnight finishes.

The 29-year-old has capitalised on the absence of Jannik Sinner and defeats for Carlos Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic, as well as a kind draw, to reach a third consecutive Grand Slam final.

"I really started off the tournament, and I ​was like, 'Well, this is pointless because I'm not going to do anything here,' and here I am sitting and preparing for a Sunday final," Zverev ​told reporters.

A solitary break was all Zverev needed to pinch a tight first set from his opponent and when he broke again at start of the second, a routine afternoon looked on the cards.

However, a double fault allowed Khachanov back on serve and instead Zverev became embroiled in a tie-break, at one point trailing 5-3 and only winning it after a lung-busting 35-shot rally.

The third set went the same way and Khachanov had set points at 6-4, but two wayward forehands and a Zverev ace gave him match point, which he took at the first attempt.

Sports.title: Nelson: Benn's graduation day is here but Garcia could be a class above
Sports.content:
Conor Benn must prove he belongs at world level in this weekend's fight against Ryan Garcia, but the WBC champion might be too fast and too sharp, says Sky Sports expert Johnny Nelson.

Benn will challenge for his first world title when he takes on Garcia for the WBC welterweight belt at the T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The Californian floored and outpointed Mario Barrios to become the new WBC champion in February, while he has previously fought elite champions such as Devin Haney and Gervonta Davis.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Conor Benn hits out at Ryan Garcia for 'bottling it' after American fails to show up for face-off in Las Vegas. Credit: @Zuffa Boxing

But Nelson is refusing to rule out a stunning victory for Benn.

"Never say never," Nelson told Sky Sports. "Right now, it seems like an impossible mountain to climb, because Conor Benn hasn't answered the questions that needed answering. Has he got that depth of experience? He hasn't. Can he dig deep? We know he can. Is he that level of a fighter? That's a question we don't know the answer to.

"What we do know is, historically, this has happened time and time again before. Lloyd Honeyghan going over to America and winning the world title shocked everybody. Conor's dad, Nigel Benn, going over and beating Iran Barkley. You know, Barkley had a bit of a name for himself; could Nigel do it? He did do it, and he did it after getting knocked out by Michael Watson.

"So, because the style is probably so crude and rugged, you'd think, has this kid [Conor Benn] got the class to become a world champion and be, what looks like, a class act?

"It just has to be his night. Obviously, you'd understand people leaning towards Ryan Garcia because Garcia is proven. Conor isn't. So you're going to give a man a chance to prove himself, not write him off."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Logan and Joe Gallagher agree that Ryan Garcia may be complacent about facing Conor Benn and any lack of focus could cost him dearly

Benn stepped up to middleweight to settle his rivalry with Chris Eubank Jr, losing the first fight on points before avenging the defeat with a dominant victory on the scorecards in the rematch.

The 29-year-old endured a tough weight cut to drop down towards 147lbs for the Garcia fight, but Nelson insists the all-action Brit will be a 'machine' in the ring.

"I don't believe the weight will take away his armoury," said Nelson. "It will obviously take away the natural strength that he had at a higher weight.

"He won't be completely depleted. I think he'll still be a machine. He'll be faster. He'll not be stronger. I think he'll have the speed, but not have the strength that he showed when we saw him box Eubank Jr.

"I think speed creates power, and the attrition, the number of shots that he throws, they are blistering.

"We've seen him take people out before; we've seen him concussively take people out.

"But I think speed creates power, and it's navigating that. It's about how he goes about that."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Conor Benn and Ryan Garcia exchanged heated words and then had to be separated by security during their Zuffa press conference and face-off

Benn floored Eubank Jr twice in their second fight, while he also demolished former world champion Chris Algieri, but Nelson believes Garcia will be a far more challenging proposition.

"This is graduation day for Conor Benn," said Nelson. "I expect Garcia to be a class above. I expect Garcia to take Conor seriously, and I expect him to go out and be fast and be sharp and be dominant.

"So, this is for Ryan Garcia to lose because if there's any scent of arrogance, complacency, or dismissiveness from him in regard to Conor, that will be his reckoning. That will be his downfall.

"This is one of those fights where you've got to be on your A-game. Ryan Garcia has to go in there and respect Conor. What I've seen and what I've heard doesn't tell me that; he thinks this is easy work.

"This might be just talk. It might be fighting talk, but I hope he's taking Conor seriously because if he hasn't, he's giving a man a chance who, on paper, shouldn't have one."

now 05.27 EDT Jacob Steinberg Ballon d’Or shortlist shows up Premier League’s attacking failings – but tide could be turning Premier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut. The trio giving Arsenal a presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neutrals. There was respect rather than admiration for their defensive rigour. There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final. It was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces. 49m ago 04.39 EDT David Hytner Our chief football correspondent has been writing about how the overlooked England midfielder is key to Manchester United in derby… Mainoo moves from outsider to main man after summer of hurt It was a sight the England press pack became increasingly used to seeing after the team’s World Cup matches over the summer. Kobbie Mainoo was invariably the first to leave the dressing room, walk through the mixed zone – eyes dead ahead, features impassive – and board the bus. It was as if he could not get out of the stadiums quick enough and the further England progressed the more pronounced it started to feel. There was a real gap between Mainoo and the next England player to depart the stadium in the knockout rounds. The Manchester United midfielder is inscrutable, even in the heat of battle. It is part of his enviably unflappable temperament. It was no great leap to imagine what lay behind the mask – tremendous frustration as Thomas Tuchel kept on leaving him out. Mainoo did not play a single minute at the tournament. He was an unused substitute all the way to the semi-final exit against Argentina, and when everyone expected to see him in the third-place playoff against France he did not make the bench. The Football Association said before the game he had picked up an unspecified injury. For Mainoo it was a lost summer and yet it was physically and mentally draining all the same, what with the training and travel; the demand to stay focused as he waited and waited. Sports.title: Football lends voice to message worth relaying: men should talk about their pain | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
If you watched US television adverts during the World Cup for any length of time one thing just kept leaping out. I’ve mentioned this before here, but it still seems both jarring and significant. Every third or fourth rotation in that endless daytime scroll, in between the Chicken Megadeth Hyper-Box Family Meal Deal, either side of David Beckham expertly consuming a light beer, is an advert for antidepressants.

The format for these is always the same kind of thing: contented, wholesome people throwing frisbees, or strolling through a small-town antiques fair, while a warm, honeyed, reassuring voiceover talks about how horrifying their lives are, with the suggestion that only a lengthy course of Smileothorium can solve this.

In another world there would be a call to study this phenomenon, to consider why a nation of such dazzling abundance and opportunity should also feel glazed, worthless and deprived of hope. But this is not that world. More than 50 million Americans have depression. This is demand and supply in action, a battle for market share in a £6bn industry. The US often worries about itself in its post-industrial age. What are we now? What can we still make? Where is the new frontier? Well, human misery is looking pretty hot right now.

The reason for talking about this here is that English football is doing a good thing this week. Between 4-14 September the Premier League is sponsoring the Together Against Suicide campaign. Harry Kane and Prince William have spoken warmly in support. The league is posting words of solidarity on its X account, which is probably not the best way to cheer yourself up if we’re being honest.

This is simple, useful messaging. It applies to people of any age, sex or background. But it applies in particular to men, and to middle-aged men, who are more likely to die by suicide than any other age group. Middle-aged men are more likely to experience depression and anxiety in those years. They can be hard to reach because this often happens out of sight or, most heartbreaking of all, without any indication there was even a problem.

It might be a little blunt in its styling. But what football is doing here is unequivocally good. Nothing else has the same level of reach and cut-through. If one person in the line of that message is touched by it, this seems like a happy outcome.

I think I have locus standi to talk about this. Everyone does. It’s universal. But I’m also unarguably a middle-aged man. I have two sons who are also now men. I have middle-aged male friends, many of whom are, with all due respect, a bit loopy. And like so many other people I’ve been down that road some of the way.

Life in Covid really did it for me. Exhaustion, isolation, the inescapable fact of having to carry on existing. Do you really have to, though? This kind of thing can creep into your mind like a shadow, just another idle thought. Until at some point you realise there’s a shadow in the corner of the room, a ghost in the chair, and it’s talking to you.

The fact is, it’s hard to be a man at any age. Or at least, it’s hard in a way that is distinct from other forms of hardness. And yes this statement might fail to draw an overwhelming wave of sympathy, but this is part of the problem. Pain comes for everyone. There’s no hierarchy of suffering. And male pain, male alienation is often carried around like a dead weight for exactly this reason.

double quotation mark Being able to talk about this stuff is the direct opposite of weakness. There is always someone willing to do this with you

As you get older this can be related to a sense of obsolescence. Men want to do stuff. There’s a kind of programming to feel useful, to serve some kind of function. Frankly, most middle-aged men would be happier if someone just gave them a big piece of wood and told them to saw it in half, then at the end of the day told them they’ve done a really good job, they’re good boys and everyone’s proud of them. Tomorrow you can come back and put it together again.

Instead it can feel like every part of the world is independently conspiring to make you feel like crap. Diminishing work, vanished usefulness, isolation, the way life can exhaust you quietly, without any obvious trauma. Men are not good at processing this. The key method, the strategy we’ve worked out over the years is: don’t process it at all. Carry on. Keep running through the red zone. Lads, it’s not a long-term plan.

I have two pieces of aged wisdom on this front. First, the obvious one. Embrace the feeling and talk about it. Sounds like a cliche. Is actually true. Feeling bad isn’t some deeper, truer version of you. The good stuff also exists and is just as real. Both will pass, and pass again.

Small things do help. Muscular, loud, well‑meaning men on the internet are actually right. Don’t eat rubbish. Get outside. Speak to other people. Remember that the sun also rises, that feeling terrible is also evidence of the ability to feel good. Prince William is right: being able to talk about this stuff is the direct opposite of weakness. There is always someone willing to do this with you, who will like and admire you even more as a result.

The second thing is: you do also have to fight. Those outmoded forms of masculinity – being stoic, resisting your own feelings – tend to get a bad rap. But everyone needs a bit of this. The problem is men are often not taught anything else to go with it.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Sport in Focus Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Life is brutal. It will come for you. It is heroic to fight this, even more so when you’re suffering. Old English poetry is full of epic tales shot through with melancholy warriors weeping at the sadness of the empty hall. In Roman culture the ability to embrace melancholy and fear – as well as scything off the limbs of your enemies – was seen as a sign of great and crowning masculinity. Scipio burnt Carthage to the ground, then sank into a massive depression, at which point he was seen as even more masculine, even more thrillingly in touch with his depths.

View image in fullscreen Prince William makes a speech at Everton’s Hill Dickinson Stadium on World Suicide Prevention Day. Photograph: Shirlaine Forrest/PA

Letting it out is strong. Would you like to be a Viking? Or a Roman hero with a sword? Well, those guys spent half their lives in a state of profound inner doubt, telling people all about it, then feeling so much more able to ride off on a horse and do something ostensibly useful.

There is something worth saying about sport in the middle of this. I was at Arsenal last weekend and before kick-off a bubbly and cheerful voice announced: “Suicide is NOT inevitable!” as though what we’re talking about here is having dandruff or not drinking enough water. The messaging is good. The messaging is great. The messaging is also, let’s be honest, an attempt to soothe the effects of the world in which big sport thrives and makes its fortunes. Is this a nice place?

It isn’t hard to work out why American TV is so full of adverts for antidepressants. Take a look at the stuff in between. Terrible, degrading food. Consumer goods you don’t need but must be made to crave. Pills to get you off that addiction to opioids we’ve already given you. Endless excitable messaging from corporations that secretly hate you.

Big Sport does not exist outside of this world. It is part of the same system. Oh, now you care about sad middle-aged men? The same ones who can’t afford to go any more, who feel alienated from what was once a bit of a lark and a chance to get together, whose brains must be subjected to the curated rage of the online idiot-scape?

The note of regret here is that sport still has so much power to be warm, to act as a source of contact. Witness for example the rush of love a few years back when Ben Stokes was able to talk about being depressed while simultaneously operating at his peak as England captain. It felt like a message no one had ever really sent in the same way, that you can feel like this and still be OK, or even heroically functional; that feeling all those things is really just a part of feeling.

Sports.title: All change for Maresca: the data behind Manchester City’s rapid player turnover
Sports.content:
Manchester City have experienced a level of player turnover unthinkable in the Pep Guardiola era. Where Arne Slot benefited in his first Liverpool season by retaining the squad Jürgen Klopp bequeathed, Enzo Maresca must oversee the evolution of City while winning every week. Relying on relatively new players has not cost them Premier League points yet, but there could be reasons for concern before their derby at Old Trafford on Sunday.

Most people assumed City would demolish Coventry. Fantasy Premier League players set a record last weekend for the number who used their one-off option of triple-captaining a player to multiply his points by three. More than 91% used this bonus on Erling Haaland, expecting goals galore. He scored, but that was the only goal of the game. The match was closer than anyone anticipated.

Coventry’s chances were valued at 1.37 xG by Opta, suggesting they deserved to score. The more notable statistic was the visitors having 12 shots. Visitors to the Etihad hit that benchmark 17 times in the Premier League in a decade of Guardiola and none of those that did were newly promoted.

It is inevitable that a team containing many new players are less solid. City’s starting XI against Coventry was full of familiar names; it’s just that several are known for their achievements elsewhere.

Rayan Cherki was the fifth-longest-serving player and he joined the club last summer. Only one of the five men in the key defensive positions of goalkeeper, centre-back or holding midfield was a City player when the 2025-26 season began. It would have been different had Enzo Fernández not needed to start in place of Nico O’Reilly, who was injured in the warm-up, but not by much.

Here is one way we can attempt to quantify turnover within a squad. With 11 men playing 90 minutes for 38 games, a club’s Premier League campaign consists of 37,620 player minutes. There are players who covered 13,998 minutes for City in 2025-26 who have not appeared for them in the league this season, and most of them will not because they have left. This means that 37.2% of the club’s minutes need replacing – this is their turnover rate.

Across Guardiola’s 10 seasons, this figure averaged 14.5% and was no higher than 7.5% four times. Almost everyone who contributed significant playing time in a given season would do so the following season. There was a seven-season period of supreme stability in the middle of Guardiola’s tenure, though the current squad evolution had begun in his final campaign.

Consider who has left since May. Bernardo Silva and Rodri were pivotal to City’s success and played hundreds of matches before leaving. Nico González lasted 18 months, Tijjani Reijnders even less. He came, he saw, he conquered Wolves but very few others and is now in the Saudi Pro League. Omar Marmoush and Sávio (with 50 league starts between them) have been shipped to Tottenham. City’s financial power largely protects them against the cost of transfer failures but their recent recruitment has been flawed in many areas.

In fairness, Marc Guéhi and Antoine Semenyo played only half of 2025-26 for City and quickly established themselves in the first‑choice XI. There is also Jérémy Doku, a key player from last season who has not featured in the league this term. His return from injury will lift the retention rate, though it will not bring City up to the Premier League average (31.9%).

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The only teams experiencing more turnover by this measure are Aston Villa, Tottenham, Newcastle and Brighton. They are also the only clubs who can match (or top) City for having five players who logged at least 1,500 league minutes last season but have not featured in 2026-27.

Those clubs, unlike City, are not expected to challenge for the league title or Champions League. Arsenal have kept a more settled squad, which should help them pursue those goals. The far more immediate hurdle for City is the derby with Manchester United, another of the clubs with above-average retention rate. They are fifth in the standings. Marcus Rashford doesn’t count because he spent last season on loan and did not feature in the Premier League.

Maresca may opt to use more of City’s established players for this testing fixture than he did against Coventry. Phil Foden has more goals only against Brighton than he has against United and O’Reilly is fit to return. It is one thing to rotate against a relative minnow, another to take chances in a derby.

Whatever the outcome at Old Trafford, the man charged with the impossible task of following Guardiola has to tackle the challenge with a squad that has undergone greater turnover than any his predecessor handled.

Sports.title: Kobbie Mainoo moves from outsider to main man after summer of hurt
Sports.content:
It was a sight the England press pack became increasingly used to seeing after the team’s World Cup matches over the summer. Kobbie Mainoo was invariably the first to leave the dressing room, walk through the mixed zone – eyes dead ahead, features impassive – and board the bus.

It was as if he could not get out of the stadiums quick enough and the further England progressed the more pronounced it started to feel. There was a real gap between Mainoo and the next England player to depart the stadium in the knockout rounds. The Manchester United midfielder is inscrutable, even in the heat of battle. It is part of his enviably unflappable temperament. It was no great leap to imagine what lay behind the mask – tremendous frustration as Thomas Tuchel kept on leaving him out.

Mainoo did not play a single minute at the tournament. He was an unused substitute all the way to the semi-final exit against Argentina, and when everyone expected to see him in the third-place playoff against France he did not make the bench. The Football Association said before the game he had picked up an unspecified injury.

For Mainoo it was a lost summer and yet it was physically and mentally draining all the same, what with the training and travel; the demand to stay focused as he waited and waited. Like every player who was part of a squad that reached the final weekend of the World Cup, he reported late for pre-season training with his club. Mainoo played the last half hour of United’s final friendly against Milan and that was it. On the opening weekend of the season, he was fit enough only to be a substitute at Hull, coming on with 23 minutes to go and United 2-0 down, en route to a damaging defeat.

There has been a spotlight on Mainoo, with some fans wondering how he would react to the suffocation of his World Cup dream; his treatment by Tuchel, who preferred Elliot Anderson and Declan Rice in the deeper midfield positions and, also, at various times, Reece James, Jude Bellingham, Jordan Henderson, Morgan Rogers and Nico O’Reilly. Nobody should have worried. Mainoo is made of stern stuff. United regeared their midfield to the tune of £155m during the transfer window, adding Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba. Baleba has not yet played because of injury, but as United prepare for Sunday’s derby at Old Trafford, it is Mainoo who has reasserted himself.

The 21-year-old has been outstanding in each of United’s matches since the opener at Hull – against Ipswich, Everton and then Sabah in the Champions League on Thursday night. The question for Michael Carrick in the derby will be Mainoo and who in front of the back four.

View image in fullscreen Kobbie Mainoo in action against Sabah in United’s 4-0 Champions League win. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/Sportsphoto

There is a reason why the United support have adapted the lyrics to Billy Ocean’s Love Really Hurts Without You to declare that their team cannot play without Mainoo. A couple of statistics. In the past three games, he has attempted 211 passes and completed 201, which represents extraordinary security on the ball – particularly given the frequency with which he has it. Also, the degree of risk inherent to so much of what he does.

Then there is the number that shows he made a game‑high 15 defensive contributions against Ipswich and Everton. He is improving out of possession. As much as anything, though, it is the quickness of the feet, the hip-shaking feints and changes of direction; how he simultaneously keeps his opponents on their heels and recalibrates United’s angles of attack.

Mainoo, of course, has already made his big comeback this year. Ruben Amorim could not fit him into his 3-4-2-1 system; the Portuguese did not trust him defensively. But even so, it continues to feel absurd that Amorim did not give him a single start in the Premier League last season. Mainoo’s first in the competition came in January against City at Old Trafford after Carrick had taken over.

It was the first match of Carrick’s second spell as the club’s manager and nobody really knew how it would go. “The players … maybe myself [as well], the coaches, obviously you guys in the media,” Carrick says. Everything came together in spectacular fashion, United winning 2-0, Mainoo straight back into the groove that had helped him win over Amorim’s predecessor, Erik ten Hag.

If it was an ignition point for Carrick, it was the same for Mainoo, whose form for the remainder of the season helped to drive United to a third-place finish and convince Tuchel to take him to the World Cup. As an aside, Mainoo v Anderson, who completed a £116m move from Nottingham Forest to City in July, will be box office. Anderson was a target for United before City blew them away with their offer. He called City “the kings of Manchester” on the day he signed.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

United’s dominance of the derby in January was almost total and a key takeaway was the slick first-time football they played. Remember the passing sequence when Rayan Cherki was triangulated by Matheus Cunha, Luke Shaw and Bruno Fernandes? The click was immediate for Carrick. This is the type of stuff that he wants; what he needs to see more of against City as he hopes to locate a bit of early-season momentum.

View image in fullscreen Kobbie Mainoo had a delayed start to the league season because of his involvement with England at the World Cup. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

Carrick knows a deep-sitting tempo-setter when he sees one, the player of the pass before the pass, and he doubled down on this sort of technician with his summer reboot, especially in Tielemans. It was also noticeable that when the luckless Mason Mount, who is back from his latest injury, came on for Tielemans against Sabah, he did so in a deeper midfield role. Carrick’s idea is to play through the middle. It is about balls to feet, timing, distances.

“It was nice to get Mason on in the second half and Andrey Santos [for Mainoo] and keep seeing the same things,” Carrick says. “It’s the combinations and connections. Taking the ball and playing close together at times. We have the technical ability for the boys to take the ball in the middle of the pitch. A lot of it is on wavelength and understanding … where each of them want the ball, which we are developing. It’s probably something that we’ve done a bit more of this season.”

Carrick is expected to start Tielemans alongside Mainoo with Fernandes as the third midfielder. They will be up against Anderson, Enzo Fernández and Cherki. It is a mouthwatering showdown. It will be where the derby is won or lost.

Sports.title: Ballon d’Or shortlist shows up Premier League’s attacking failings – but tide could be turning
Sports.content:
Premier League representation is low when it comes to the 16 attacking players on this year’s Ballon d’Or shortlist. Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes and Manchester City’s Erling Haaland are there but Cole Palmer, one of the nominees in 2025, is out after an injury-hit year and English football’s shift towards physicality and set pieces last season is summed up by none of the forwards from the best team in the country making the cut.

The trio giving Arsenal a presence – Gabriel Maghalhães, Declan Rice and William Saliba – are all defensive minded. Arsenal won the league but their forwards are not regarded as elite. Injuries played a part, denying Martin Ødegaard, Kai Havertz and Bukayo Saka fluency, but Mikel Arteta’s side were not loved by neutrals. There was respect rather than admiration for their defensive rigour. There was an argument that a lack of ambition after going 1-0 up stopped Arsenal from beating Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League final.

It was a close-run thing, but a second consecutive European title for PSG was a victory for attacking football over the Premier League’s attrition. Luis Enrique’s side keep beating English opponents, and there was a similar vibe at the World Cup. Games flowed more in North America, in part because of officials clamping down on the “meat wall” at set pieces.

As for England, Thomas Tuchel’s plan to tap into the Premier League’s physicality failed. England retreated in their semi-final defeat by Argentina. It is also significant that not until Anthony Gordon’s goal against Argentina did an England attacker who played in the Premier League last season score at the World Cup.

“Spanish football demands a different level of tactical and technical intelligence,” Gordon has said since leaving Newcastle for Barcelona. “In England, sometimes intensity can cover up mistakes. You can miscontrol the ball and still recover by winning the next physical battle.”

The English top flight’s appeal partly rests on those bruising qualities but the grind went too far last season. How many classic games can you remember? Some of the top sides having disappointing campaigns did not help but across the board there was grumbling about an over-reliance on set pieces and goalkeepers being squashed during elaborate corner routines. Anthony Barry, Tuchel’s assistant, noted that the game had become congealed in the middle. There was an emphasis on long throws and timewasting. The league was harder to watch.

View image in fullscreen Anthony Gordon has said Spanish football demands a ‘different level of tactical and technical intelligence’. Photograph: Newhouse Media/MB Media/Getty Images

Now comes the shift. One of the themes during the first three weeks of the campaign has been the pace quickening. Lawmakers have reacted. The five-second countdown and threat of a restart reversal at goalkicks and throw-ins have forced teams to think twice about timewasting. The 10-second time limit on players leaving the pitch at substitutions has helped and a trial with tactical timeouts mean an outfield player will have to go off for at least a minute after the restart of play if their side’s goalkeeper has gone down injured.

Early days, of course, but the football has been enjoyable and the numbers are encouraging. There have been four matches in which both teams have had 14 shots this season, compared with only one at the same stage last year. According to Opta, the average ball-in-play time has increased from 55min 23sec during the 2025-26 campaign to 57min 14sec. Delay times are down from 29.2sec to 26.7sec. Excluding penalties, the percentage of goals from set pieces has dipped from 27.5% to 23.5%.

There are more fast breaks per game (2.27 compared with 1.94), more shots per game via fast breaks (1.9 compared with 1.75) and more goals from fast breaks per game (0.43 from 0.23). Chelsea, more transitional under Xabi Alonso, are flowing and have been involved in some wild games. Liverpool have replaced Arne Slot with the counterpressing Andoni Iraola. Newcastle have been rapid under Matthias Jaissle, who has played to the strengths of Harvey Barnes and Anthony Elanga. Roberto De Zerbi seems an outlier at Tottenham, who need to speed up. Manchester City may soon want more incision from Enzo Maresca. The Italian favours a methodical style but even Pep Guardiola was moving away from obsessive control last season. There is a sense that some managers are closer in style to Jürgen Klopp than Guardiola at the moment. Alonso’s style has seemed very similar to Klopp so far. His willingness to let talent breathe is also quite like Carlo Ancelotti; Palmer has spoken about being allowed more freedom to roam under Alonso.

Perhaps there will be a correction as teams wise up to each other, Europe kicks in and injuries bite. Perhaps it will amuse you to hear that Arsenal remain top for delaying at a corner (with an average of 43.2sec). Then again, last Sunday delivered the season’s first clash between potential title rivals – Arsenal taking on Chelsea at the Emirates Stadium – and the action was breathless. Chelsea did not hold back and it was interesting that Arsenal welcomed the end-to-end openness.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Havertz was full of imagination up front and Ødegaard, Arsenal’s creative hub, dominated. It is a fascinating development. Defence was Arsenal’s greatest asset last season; Rice was more influential than Ødegaard in midfield. Now the Norwegian looks rejuvenated. Fitness helps but so does greater freedom. Chelsea did not shut the game down, so Ødegaard ran it. The best player in the best team was not a defender. At those levels Ødegaard looks as good as Fernandes.

View image in fullscreen Florian Wirtz has struggled to adapt to the pace of the Premier League. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Richard Sellers/Apl/Sportsphoto

This matters. Florian Wirtz, a star in Alonso’s champion Bayer Leverkusen side, has come to England and found the pace difficult at Liverpool. The Premier League needs top talent to feel it can shine. The three Bayern Munich forwards on the Ballon d’Or shortlist – Harry Kane, Luis Díaz and Michael Olise – moved from English teams. PSG’s Ousmane Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia are fresh for the business end of the Champions League in part because they aren’t being pushed to the limit by teams such as Brentford and Bournemouth on the weekend. Jude Bellingham, England’s jewel, has never played in the Premier League. Vinícius Júnior toyed with moving to Arsenal but stayed with Kylian Mbappé at Real Madrid.

The Premier League is the strongest and most competitive in Europe. Yet there has been a talent drain. It is easy to imagine the best forwards feel they will have more fun creating and scoring against less intense Bundesliga defences and have the freshness to compete for the Champions League, international tournaments and for individual prizes.

Look at how the four semi-finalists at the World Cup were well represented by Premier League defenders and defensive midfielders but not by wingers and strikers. Where are the stars? Those who have left have mostly not been replaced, which is why the Premier League could do with Bradley Barcola shining at Liverpool after his arrival from PSG.

Barcola succeeding could convince others to follow. If the France winger is worn down, though, it could have the opposite effect. The Premier League has to be careful. The new measures to tackle timewasting could be a gamechanger. There were only four added minutes at the end of each half when Arsenal beat Chelsea. It felt refreshing.

Sports.title: West Ham cut loose to hit Wrexham for six and go top of Championship
Sports.content:
West Ham secured their fourth league win in a row as they returned to the top of the Championship with a thumping 6-0 win over Wrexham at the London Stadium. It was a marvellous display of attacking football from Nuno Espírito Santo’s side, who swept to victory with room to spare and six different scorers.

Jarrod Bowen got the ball rolling after 28 minutes, Joël Piroe made it two before the break, then Konstantinos Mavropanos, Taty Castellanos, Mohamadou Kanté and Manor Solomon all scored in the second half as the Welsh side were dealt a hiding. The performance was further evidence the Hammers are finding their feet in the second tier after failing to win any of their first three games following Premier League relegation.

They should have led inside seven minutes, Castellanos sending a free header from Solomon’s cross over from six yards. Bowen then got clear in the box from a quick throw, but his shot was turned against the crossbar by a reflex save from Anthony Patterson. From the corner that resulted, Mavropanos headed a foot wide at the far post.

Piroe was guilty of an awful miss midway through the half, leaning back and blasting high into the Wrexham fans behind Patterson’s goal. Bowen showed him how it was done a minute later. Morato’s cross from the right was timed perfectly into the six-yard box, where the home side’s captain was arriving ahead of Jacques Ekomié to guide it into the far corner.

Mavropanos cleared off the line from George Dobson with Mads Hermansen beaten, which proved to be the closest Wrexham would come to a goal. Castellanos stayed onside and strode on to a through pass before unselfishly squaring the ball for Piroe to make it 2-0 before the break.

Patterson prevented Solomon from putting the game beyond Wrexham in the first two minutes of the second half, racing from his goal to smother the forward’s low shot. It would be a momentary reprieve and under a minute later it was 3-0. From Bowen’s corner, Mavropanos was left free inside the six-yard box to head home.

Bowen flashed a shot inches wide after cutting inside as the besieged visitors teetered on the edge of an all-out collapse in east London. West Ham’s fourth came from a Wrexham corner. A poor ball into the box was collected by Kyle Walker-Peters, who dashed away on the counter, exchanging passes before teeing up Castellanos to slot the ball into the corner.
