World.title: The long game: What will Tinubu leave behind (III), By Adeola Akinremi
World.content:
A country undergoing difficult reforms also pays a cost during the transition. The gains are not always immediately visible, and the system may not yet be running efficiently when political pressure begins to build. But repeatedly switching off the engine and starting again can waste the progress already made… Nigeria must choose its next direction. It can remain in “Parambulator” or move toward “We Don Win.” The latter, in my estimation, is where Tinubu’s long game leads.

The future of Nigeria has always been a subject of debate. Throughout our history, the conversation has always centred on great leadership, the economy, and the kind of country we want Nigeria to become. The kind of tension that comes with this debate is not new in our history. It is because the hopes and worries of many Nigerians are inseparable from the fate of the country.

But this debate, over the years, bears evidence that Nigerians want a country that works for everyone. Yet, I have watched with growing concern how hard it is to separate sentiments from substance, especially now that we’re in an election cycle.

And part of the sadness is that arguments advanced by political actors too often become the headlines of major newspapers, without clear-eyed examination of the evidence.

That’s exactly the kind of clear-eyed exercise Nigeria’s scenario-building team attempted twenty years ago.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This leaves me with the impression that reporters these days are not doing enough to examine the claims behind the story before the headlines are cast, to interrogate the motives behind them, and demand evidence before amplifying them.

In November 2006, I had a rare opportunity to work with about 35 talented Nigerians to build scenarios for the future of Nigeria, guided by eminent leaders including Father Matthew Hassan Kukah, Frank Nweke Jr, Ifueko Omoigui-Okauru, Pat Utomi, Mallam Nasir El-Rufai, Mansur Ahmed, Morin Desalu, Adhiambo Odaga, Olugbenga Adesida, Peter Wilson, Olusegun Adeniyi, Mosunmola Layode and others serving on the Board or in the team of the African Leadership Institute. It was at the invitation of LEAP Africa, a civic organisation founded by Ndidi Nwunneli, the former Chief Executive Officer of ONE Campaign.

The team met over a period of time and crafted a set of four possible scenarios for Nigeria by 2025: Parambulator; Shine Your Eye; Jaga Jaga Republic and We Don Win.

The team made it clear that Nigeria needs fundamental change, stressing the need to make risky, quantum leaps to transform the Nigerian society and economy. The scenario-building team delivered a stark warning that “small, linear steps using traditional approaches, even if the steps are in the right direction, will not be enough.”

Today, we are in 2026, twenty years after that exercise. Nigeria has moved through cycles of political promises and debates. Yet the questions raised by those scenarios remain remarkably relevant. They offer a useful lens through which to examine what President Bola Tinubu’s long game could mean for Nigeria and, more importantly, what choices today could shape the country’s future.

The use of scenario methodology in exploring national development and leadership issues demonstrates the importance of thinking beyond the present to confront difficult choices and shape a more ambitious future for Nigeria.

Today, we are in 2026, twenty years after that exercise. Nigeria has moved through cycles of political promises and debates. Yet the questions raised by those scenarios remain remarkably relevant. They offer a useful lens through which to examine what President Bola Tinubu’s long game could mean for Nigeria and, more importantly, what choices today could shape the country’s future.

According to the African Leadership Institute, which partnered with LEAP Africa, “the overarching thrust of the scenarios is that Nigeria can be transformed. The scenarios highlight the critical role of the people, lay out the choices before Nigerians and outline how the actions or inactions could shape the future.”

A scenario is not a prediction. The purpose is to construct plausible futures and then work backward to understand what decisions today make those futures more or less likely.

What happens when a country begins a difficult reform programme but changes leadership before the reform cycle has matured?

What might Nigeria look like in 2030 or 2031 if these reforms are sustained?

Yes, the ideal outcome for Nigeria is not necessarily eight years of one man. It is eight years of institutional continuity. But given Nigeria’s history of policy reversals, which political arrangement is more likely to produce that continuity?

Indeed, one presidential candidate has said in an interview with Arise TV that despite the reform, “Nigeria is heading in the wrong direction today. I just need to reverse it.” Will policy reversal pay or pain Nigeria in the long run?

Nigeria has previously imagined its future through scenarios, and those scenarios offer a framework for thinking about today’s political choice. Arguably, what Tinubu is doing matters for the outcome of a stronger economy and a better country.

And with the state police on course, Nigeria can turn that debate into an institution that works, while putting the safeguards in place to prevent abuse…. The significance goes beyond the creation of another layer of policing. Clearly, state police would change the architecture through which security is delivered, bringing policing closer to the communities it is intended to serve.

Take, for instance, the constitutional change to decentralise the country’s police force. For decades, state police have remained one of the most contentious questions in Nigeria’s security debate. Now, the Tinubu administration has pushed the issue from a long-running political argument into a concrete constitutional path.

And with the state police on course, Nigeria can turn that debate into an institution that works, while putting the safeguards in place to prevent abuse.

The significance goes beyond the creation of another layer of policing. Clearly, state police would change the architecture through which security is delivered, bringing policing closer to the communities it is intended to serve.

Of course, it is equally important not to overlook the cooperation between the executive and the legislature in moving several consequential constitutional reform bills forward under Tinubu. From Ghali Umar Na’Abba, Aminu Bello Masari, Patricia Etteh, Dimeji Bankole, Aminu Tambuwal, Yakubu Dogara, and Femi Gbajabiamila to the current Speaker, Tajudeen Abbas, the House of Representatives Speakers have often been at loggerheads with the president on reform bills – even where the party controls both the legislature and the presidency. Reforms require more than presidential ambition; they require a mission-driven and political leadership capable of building consensus and creating institutions that can carry reforms beyond the tenure of the president who initiated them.

Think of it this way: Nigeria is like an older car with a carburetor. It uses extra fuel during startup. Turning the car on and off at every stop wastes energy.

A country undergoing difficult reforms also pays a cost during the transition. The gains are not always immediately visible, and the system may not yet be running efficiently when political pressure begins to build. But repeatedly switching off the engine and starting again can waste the progress already made.

Nigeria must choose its next direction. It can remain in “Parambulator” or move toward “We Don Win.” The latter, in my estimation, is where Tinubu’s long game leads.

With that, the long game comes full circle.

Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving businesses and diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: [email protected]

World.title: Nigerian Army investigates sexual abuse allegation against serving officer
World.content:
The Nigerian Army said it has launched an investigation into an allegation of sexual abuse involving a serving officer, Etim Essien, currently serving at the Headquarters of 3 Division in Jos, Plateau State.

The division’s spokesperson, Olumide Olukoya, disclosed this in a statement on Friday.

Mr Olukoya, a captain, said the army takes allegations of sexual abuse seriously, particularly cases involving minors and other vulnerable persons.

He did not give details about the age of the victim involved.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Accordingly, appropriate steps have been initiated to establish the facts and circumstances surrounding the reported incident,” he stated.

Mr Olukoya, however, cautioned against reaching conclusions on the officer’s culpability while the investigation is ongoing.

He said making definitive comments at this stage would be inappropriate, stressing its commitment to due process, fairness and the protection of the rights and dignity of all parties involved.

He added that relevant civil authorities are investigating the matter and assured that it would cooperate fully with them.

According to the military spokesperson, the investigation will be conducted in accordance with existing laws and military regulations.

He reiterated that the army places a high premium on discipline, professionalism and respect for human dignity, adding any personnel found to have acted contrary to the law or established service regulations would be dealt with appropriately after the conclusion of the investigation.

The military spokesperson urged members of the public to refrain from speculation and the circulation of unverified information that could prejudice the investigation.

He also urged the public to avoid actions that could compromise the privacy and wellbeing of those involved, particularly any minor.

Mr Olukoya said further information would be provided when appropriate, subject to legal requirements and the integrity of the investigative process.

World.title: Abia seeks stakeholders, citizens’ input to 2027 budget proposal
World.content:
The Abia State Government has commenced consultations with citizens and stakeholders to identify priority areas for inclusion in the state’s 2027 budget.

The Commissioner for Budget and Economic Planning, Kingsley Anosike, disclosed this at a Citizens’ Engagement Forum at the Aguiyi Ironsi Conference Centre, Umuahia, on Thursday.

Mr Anosike said the engagement was meant to ensure that the 2027 budget reflected the needs, aspirations and realities of the people.

According to him, the consultation was particularly important because the 2027 budget will be the last budget cycle of the current administration.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the citizens’ contributions would help determine the priorities and projects to be captured in the Abia State Government’s final fiscal plan.

He said the present administration would not prepare the budget solely from the perspective of government officials without considering the views of the people.

“We do not want to go into a room and build a budget that does not speak to the needs of the people we serve.

“That is why Dr Alex Otti has mandated that we invite you, a cross-section of the public, into this kind of forum.

“We want to bring you up to speed on what we have done so far—meaning January to June this year, that is the half-year scorecard—and then what we intend to do going forward to build up the 2027 budget,” he said.

Mr Anosike said previous citizens’ engagements influenced government decisions, citing the redesign of the latest batch of electric buses to include ramps for persons with disabilities.

He added that the Abia State Government cancelled an initial order for 20 buses after stakeholders raised concerns about accessibility for persons living with disabilities during an earlier engagement.

Abia’s expenditure classified into four areas

Also, the Special Adviser to the Governor on Budget and Economic Planning, Eric Egwuibe, said the state’s expenditure was classified into administration, economic, law and justice, and social development sectors.

Mr Egwuibe, while reviewing the 2026 budget performance for the first six months, said that N64 billion was allocated to administration, N550 billion to the economic sector, N13 billion to law and justice and N387 billion to the social sector.

He said the economic sector remained critical because investment in infrastructure and productive activities could stimulate economic growth and expand the state’s revenue base.

The governor’s aide said that the Otti administration had made budget documents and quarterly implementation reports accessible to the public as part of its commitment to transparency.

On the 2027 budget outlook, Mr Egwuibe said the state government was working with key economic assumptions provided by the National Bureau of Statistics.

He listed the assumptions as 15.9 per cent inflation, 4.3 per cent GDP growth, $60 per barrel oil benchmark, crude oil production of 1.7 million barrels per day and an exchange rate of N1,432 to the US dollar.

Mr Egwuibe said the assumptions suggested that the state might have less revenue available in 2027 than in the current year.

He, therefore, urged citizens to moderate their expectations and prioritise projects capable of delivering the greatest impact.

In their separate contributions, the Acting Clerk of the Abia State House of Assembly, Promise Onwukwe and Innocent Nwaigwe of Okaiuga Alaike Autonomous Community commended the government for engaging citizens in the budget process.

They urged stakeholders to support the present administration’s New Abia initiative for the benefit of all.

In his remark, the Chairman of the Abia Disability Commission, David Anyaele, commended the government for promoting disability inclusion and improving accessibility of public infrastructure.

Mr Anyaele, represented by Ikenna Ebiri-Okoro, particularly cited the provision of ramps in government buildings as evidence of increased consideration for persons living with disabilities.

The engagement was attended by top government officials, traditional rulers, civil society groups and other stakeholders.

It featured an interactive session during which participants raised concerns and made recommendations on policies, budget priorities and service delivery.

World.title: ‘It’s going to be bloody’ – Amusan warns of tougher women’s hurdles in 2027
World.content:
Nigerian sprint hurdling star Tobi Amusan says she is determined to end the 2026 season on a high after claiming silver at the World Athletics Ultimate Championships, while admitting that the women’s 100m hurdles is becoming increasingly competitive.

Amusan produced a strong performance to finish second at the championship, adding another medal to a season that has tested her physically and mentally.

The Nigerian had earlier finished third at the Commonwealth Games before seeing her long-standing world record fall, but she managed to put those disappointments behind her and rebuild her momentum one race at a time.

Reflecting on her silver-medal finish, Amusan while speaking with Making of Champions in Budapest gave credit to God while acknowledging the challenges she experienced during the season.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“First, God is good,” Amusan said.

“What started off as an amazing season, in between I had some nippings here and there. You know, I’m not a robot. The body did shut down at a point. And I got back, built the momentum one race at a time.”

The Nigerian revealed that she approached the Ultimate Championships with a determined mindset, knowing she had to produce her best performance regardless of what had happened earlier in the season.

“Coming into this championship, my mindset going to the line was, we die here. I just kept telling myself I have to give it my all. I mean, I’ve always given my all at every meet,” she said.

“Today is just one of those days where I have to bring my A-plus game. And I don’t care what happened in the race. All I knew was, look, I did it. That’s all I knew. And I looked up and I saw the silver medal place finish.

“I was like, look, I came in second place. God is good.”

Amusan opens up on difficult period

The 2026 season has not been without setbacks for the Nigerian, particularly after she finished third at the Commonwealth Games before losing her world record.

Amusan admitted that the period was difficult but said the encouragement she received from those closest to her helped her remain focused and continue competing.

“I’m not going to lie. It was very rough. It was very rough,” she told MakingofChampions.

“I mean, to my family, to my mentor, to my coach, to my boyfriend. They spoke the life back into me. And, you know, this morning it was all about put the past behind you and just go for it.

“And those few sentences that I got here and there got me through this finish line today, and God.”

Despite the disappointment of losing the world record, Amusan was pleased to leave the Ultimate Championships with a medal and is now looking forward to completing the season strongly.

Asked whether her top-two finish was a statement, the Nigerian responded with her characteristic humour.

“A statement kwa? I’m coming home with a medal, you are talking about making a statement? I don’t know the statement you are looking for,” she said.

“But, I mean, I’m looking forward to end the season on a high note. I still have one more meet, I know.

“I’m still there, and we’d go get recharged for 2027 after that.”

World.title: Hot tea, coffee linked to higher risk of oesophageal cancer — Study
World.content:
People who regularly drink very hot tea or coffee may face a significantly higher risk of developing oesophageal cancer, a study has found.

The researchers found that people who preferred their beverages very hot had more than three times the risk of developing oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) compared with those who preferred warm drinks.

The study, involving nearly 980,000 middle-aged adults in the United Kingdom, was published in the International Journal of Cancer.

Oesophageal cancer affects the tube that carries food and drinks from the mouth to the stomach. Oesophageal SCC is the most common form of the disease globally.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

How hot is too hot?

The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), the cancer research arm of the World Health Organisation (WHO), classifies beverages consumed at temperatures above 65°C as “probably carcinogenic to humans”.

For the new study, researchers used data from participants in the UK Biobank and Million Women Study.

Participants reported how hot they usually preferred their tea, coffee and other hot drinks, choosing from “very hot”, “hot” and “warm”. They also reported whether they consumed fewer than six or at least six hot drinks each day.

Over the follow-up period, 2,348 cases of oesophageal cancer were recorded among the participants.

The analysis showed that the risk increased with the preferred temperature of the drinks.

Those who preferred hot beverages had almost twice the risk of oesophageal SCC compared with people who preferred warm drinks, while the risk among those who preferred very hot drinks was more than three times higher.

The researchers also found that consumption frequency was associated with risk.

After taking temperature into account, participants who drank six or more hot beverages daily had a 71 per cent higher risk of oesophageal SCC than those who consumed fewer than six.

Why temperature may matter

Keren Papier, a senior nutritional epidemiologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study, said the findings add to existing evidence linking very hot beverages with oesophageal cancer.

Previous research had largely focused on populations in South America, Asia and the Middle East, where hot-drink consumption patterns differ from those in Western countries.

Ms Papier said the new findings provide evidence from typical drinking habits in the UK, where tea and coffee are commonly consumed.

The researchers said the association was not altered by whether participants added milk to their drinks, as long as the beverage remained hot.

Also sharing his thoughts, Ian Johnson, an emeritus fellow at the Quadram Institute in England, said damage to cells lining the oesophagus and inflammation caused by hot liquids could provide a possible explanation for the association.

He advised people to allow hot drinks to cool before consuming them.

Study does not prove cause

The researchers cautioned that the study did not establish that hot drinks directly cause oesophageal cancer.

One limitation was that participants did not measure the actual temperature of their beverages. Instead, they described them according to their own perception of how hot they were.

Muy-Teck Teh, a professor of molecular oral oncology at Queen Mary University of London, said differences in people’s sensitivity to heat meant the findings should be interpreted as an association rather than proof that hot beverages cause the cancer.

The researchers said allowing drinks to cool, adding milk or cold water, or simply waiting before drinking could reduce exposure to high temperatures.

Global burden

Oesophageal cancer remains a major global health concern.

According to the IARC, about 604,000 new cases and 544,000 deaths from oesophageal cancer were recorded globally in 2020.

The agency projects that annual cases could approach one million by 2040, representing an increase of more than 50 per cent.

However, the researchers noted that the absolute risk of developing oesophageal cancer remains relatively low.

The study therefore suggests that for people who enjoy tea or coffee, allowing the beverage to cool before drinking may be a simple precaution against prolonged exposure to very hot liquids.
