World.title: Botswana pensioner loses R1.7 million in shocking bank scam: How fraudsters allegedly did it
World.content:
The four suspects appeared before the Village Magistrate Court on 11 September. Images: BPS

A Botswana pensioner is at the centre of a P1.4 million (about R1.7 million) fraud investigation after four people allegedly posed as bank employees and tricked her into revealing confidential banking information.

The Botswana Police Service (BPS) says the suspects allegedly used a fake Know Your Customer (KYC) update as part of the scheme before gaining unauthorised access to the victim’s bank account.

Four suspects have since been arrested and appeared before the Village Magistrate Court on Friday, 11 September 2026, where they were charged with a single count of fraud.



They were remanded in prison and are expected back in court on 22 September.

How the alleged P1.4 million bank scam started

According to the police, the suspects allegedly contacted the pensioner while pretending to be employees of her bank.

They reportedly told her that they were assisting her with updating her Know Your Customer (KYC) information.



KYC procedures are commonly used by financial institutions to verify and update customer information.

In this case, however, police allege that the process was used to convince the pensioner to disclose confidential banking details.

The suspects allegedly obtained the information they needed and subsequently gained unauthorised access to her bank account.



Money allegedly transferred from the Botswana pensioner’s account

Once they allegedly gained access to the account, the suspects are accused of transferring more than P1.4 million.

Police say the money was moved into various bank accounts and mobile-money wallets that were either under the suspects’ control or linked to their alleged criminal enterprise.

Investigators have managed to trace part of the allegedly stolen money.



The Botswana Police Service says the recovery of some of the funds provided crucial evidence that helped investigators make the arrests.

However, the investigation is not over.

Police say they are continuing to identify additional beneficiaries and recover the remaining proceeds of the alleged crime.



Four suspects arrested in Botswana

The four accused persons were identified by police as Bame Wendy Lebo Senna, 35, of Tlokweng; Leatile McPherson Motshabi, 36, of Mochudi; Emmanuel Gaetwesepe, 40; and Orebotse Masala, 35, both of Mokatsi Village.

According to the police statement, the suspects were arrested between 9 and 10 September 2026 following investigations into what police described as a sophisticated fraud scheme.

The police allege that the four acted together with other suspects who remain at large.



That means investigators are still trying to establish the full extent of the alleged operation and identify everyone who may have benefited from the money.

Suspects remain in custody

The four suspects appeared before the Village Magistrate Court on 11 September.

They were charged with a single count of fraud and remanded in prison.



Their next court appearance is scheduled for 22 September 2026.

As the matter is before the courts, the allegations against the accused have not been tested in a full trial.

Botswana police issue warning over bank scams

The case has also prompted another warning from police about the information customers should never give to people contacting them by phone, text message or social media.



The BPS says banks will never ask customers to disclose confidential information such as One-Time Passwords (OTPs), Personal Identification Numbers (PINs), passwords or other sensitive banking credentials through those channels.

The public has been urged to end suspicious communications immediately and report them to the nearest police station or their banking institution before financial losses occur.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE | From Zambia to the world stage: Kondo Simfukwe’s lesson in humanity
World.content:
From the intensity of the US Open to the sun-soaked courts of the BNP Paribas Open, broadcaster and host Kondo Simfukwe has become a familiar presence on some of the biggest stages in world sport. Image: Dave Marshall

To understand how a broadcaster and host can seamlessly command the world’s most glamorous sporting stages, from the electric, high-stakes atmosphere of the US Open courts to the sun-drenched arenas of the BNP Paribas Open, you must first step back to an impoverished context in Zambia.

Born in England, Kondo Simfukwe spent his pivotal childhood years in Zambia, immersed in an environment that, while economically restricted, laid down a profound human foundation that continues to guide his trajectory across the globe.

Communal interdependence

For Kondo Simfukwe, growing up in a socio-economically challenged setting was never defined by deprivation or despair.



Instead, it was shaped by an organic, deeply baked sense of communal interdependence.

“It was beautiful in that we didn’t necessarily always realise that we were growing up in an impoverished context,” he reflects.

“So, I would say because of that, two things are very significant. One is the sense of community, the sense of valuing others because suddenly, for all of us to thrive, we all needed each other. What’s mine is yours, what’s yours is mine, and as one goes, so do we all. We need each other, we help each other, we survive and thrive together.”



In this setting, collaboration, camaraderie, and mutual reliance were not calculated strategies; they were the essential, everyday mechanics of human existence.

Alongside this spirit of shared living came an enduring posture of gratitude – one that operates as a safeguard against the entitlement that so often permeates modern sports culture.

When material abundance is absent, entitlement simply cannot take root.



Value system

“When you don’t have much, you don’t lay claim to much, you don’t feel entitled to much, you don’t feel owed much, you don’t feel as though comparison is the key to life or joy,” Kondo Simfukwe explains.

“So, something happens where everything you get, you feel grateful for. With a base of ‘we need each other’ and a base of ‘we don’t have much, so everything we receive feels like a bonus, feels like a gift,’ say thank you, and then figure out who you can also bring along.”

“My value for others, my perspective about other people: I’m no better than you, you’re no better than me. I value you immensely because you carry innate value.”



This innate value system leads to striking moments of clarity when Kondo interacts with world-class athletes today.

Deeply respectful

Recalling an on-court interview at a major tournament with young Filipina tennis prodigy Alex Eala, Kondo posed a question about the refreshing, deeply respectful way she treats everyone around her.

Eala’s response was one of pure, unpretentious confusion: “Outstanding? Isn’t that normal, sir? People are valuable, aren’t they?”



For Kondo Simfukwe, Eala’s candid reaction was a moment of profound alignment, a poignant recognition of an uncorrupted ethos where human dignity is assumed rather than earned through rankings, prize money, or media fanfare.

It reaffirmed that the foundational lessons absorbed in Zambia are not merely survival mechanisms for the underprivileged, but universal principles capable of grounding anyone operating under the glaring lights of global superstardom.

What’s Next: Part II shifts to Kondo’s teenage relocation to Australia, where his worldview was radically expanded through exposure to vibrant multiculturalism, forcing him to master the art of the “cultural chameleon” while discovering sports as a tool for connection.



Dave Marshall is reporting exclusively from the 2026 US Open in New York for The South African.

World.title: PREVIEW for October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants
World.content:
Here's what we can reliably report ahead of October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants. Image: File

We’re taking a look ahead to October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants. The day to earmark for payment is Friday 2 October 2026 for the nation’s four-million elderly beneficiaries.

The gap between next month’s payment and September’s is exactly 30 days. So, not as bad as the 33-day wait back in August, but not as timeous as last month’s 28 days.

Nevertheless, the topic on everyone’s minds for October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants is what’s happening with mid-cycle top-ups?



This has been a particularly frustrating sub-story ahead of next month’s disbursements.

The agency continues to be silent on the matter, and that void is allowing a slew of misinformation to fill the void on social media …

OCTOBER 2026 SASSA OLD-AGE GRANTS

Principally, there are a growing number of online petitions/protests demanding that South African Social Security Agency Old-Age Grants be increased to R5 000 per month.

A conspicuous lack of confirmation from the agency on whether October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants will be topped-up at all is only fuelling this sentiment.

What we do know for sure is that grants increased by R80 back in April 2026:

SASSA Old-Age Grants 60 to 74 years old – R2 400 (up from R2 320)

(up from R2 320) SASSA Old-Age Grants 75 years and older – R2 420 (up from R2 340)

Should the new Minister of Social Development Dina Pule surprise us all with an October 2026 top-up … time is ticking to make it official.



Over the last two years, October top-ups amounted to just R10.

Therefore, if it were to repeat, 60 to 74 would increase to R2 410 and 75 and older would be R2 430.

Although highly unlikely, a R20 increase to stave off the current inflation crisis, would see grants jump to R2 420 (60 to 74) and R2 440 (75 and older), respectively.

STRICTER REVIEWS FOR OCTOBER 2026 SASSA OLD-AGE GRANTS

The Finance Minister’s Medium-Term update is only set for Wednesday, 21 October, well after top-ups need to be confirmed. Image: File

As ever, October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants are coming under stricter scrutiny.

The National Treasury announced that the cancellation of more than 300 000 suspect profiles had saved upwards of R170 million.

However, the DSD also revealed in parliament earlier this year that the social welfare budget was underspent by R4.8 billion.

As we’ve reported before, simple arithmetic says that figure could see a R100 monthly increase for all four-million Old-Age Grant recipients without so much as a budget adjustment.

SASSA cross-references all your personal data against a host of government departments and banks.

Therefore, anyone who has been claiming a government grant that shouldn’t be will be found out eventually.

Worse still, if you are caught misrepresenting your means, not only will you lose your grant, but you will have to pay back your ill-gotten SASSA money.

So, it’s not worth the risk if you know you genuinely don’t qualify for state assistance.

WHEN DOES DEFERRED SASSA PAYMENT LAND IN OCTOBER 2026?

For those who are reviewed by the agency and clear their names in time, they receive a deferred payment on a special fourth payment date.

Next month this falls much later, on Wednesday, 7 October 2026.

To make things tougher, the agency has also increased the income (means) and asset eligibility for October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants:

Your income must be less than R9 350 (single) or R18 700 (married) per month

(single) or (married) per month This adds up to R112 200 (single) or R224 400 (married) per year

(single) or (married) per year Total assets (property) in your name cannot be worth more than R1 584 000 (single) or R3 168 000 (married)

Plus, here’s what you need to show the agency when applying for October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants:

Official RSA identity document (ID) preferably a Smart ID Card with digital ID photo.

with digital ID photo. Valid three months’ statement certified by your bank, plus copies.

statement certified by your bank, plus copies. All documents proving your marital status, plus death certificates if necessary.

Proof of residence (a utility bill with your name on it, not older than three months ).

). Documents proving your income and/or financial dividends (very important).

Comprehensive information regarding assets/valuation of any property you own.

Full declaration of any and all private pension in your name.

Unemployment Insurance Fund (UIF) membership book, or discharge certificate from your previous job.

A copy of your will, first and final liquidation and distribution accounts if your spouse has passed away in the last five years.

HOW LONG DOES IT TAKE TO BE APPROVED FOR SASSA OLD-AGE GRANTS?

Next month’s new applicants will only receive first payments in the new year. However, they will be backdated. Image: File

October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants typically take around three months to be processed, so, you will receive your first payment only in January 2027.

However, you will be back paid to the date of your first application, so, three months in the first tranche.

But that’s assuming you have all your documents correct at the first time of asking.

It is now possible to complete eLife certification and biometric verification at the agency’s online service portal HERE to save time and beat the queues.

Plus, if you’re too old, sick or live in a remote rural area you can get a loved one to help with your October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants application.

All you need is a letter from your doctor. And all of the above documentation copied and certified by a commissioner of oaths.

If you are denied the grant you do have three months to appeal the decision with the DSD HERE.

You can always try to contact SASSA directly here:

SASSA toll-free line: 0800 601 011

Head Office of SASSA: 012 400 2322

Email SASSA: grantsenquiries@sassa.gov.za

But what do you think? Will October 2026 SASSA Old-Age Grants benefit from a top-up? Be sure to share your ideas in the comments section below …

World.title: Fuel tax changes: What this means for your petrol price
World.content:
South African motorists are once again feeling the sting of tax-driven price surges. The latest round of fuel levy adjustments came to effect from Wednesday 2 September 2026 with an increase pushed by rising global oil prices.

WHAT IS DRIVING THE SEPTEMBER HIKE?

Petrol rose by R1.34 per litre and diesel by between R2.94 and R3.15 per litre, depending on the grade. The Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources stated that most of the increase (roughly 80% of the petrol hike and around 93% of the diesel hike) was due to a higher international refined product prices. This was driven by ongoing US-Iran tensions and continued disruption risk around the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude climbed from $82.37 to $87.88 a barrel during the review period.

THE FUEL TAX COMPONENT

Beyond global oil movements, two domestic levy mechanisms added directly to the price at the pump. The Self-Adjusting Slate Levy rose by 21.90 cents per litre, from 61.38 to 83.28 cents, after the balance fell to a negative R9.519 billion by the end of July. Also, a 4.9 cents per litre increase was added to petrol prices specifically to fund a wage adjustment for forecourt employees under the Motor Industry Bargaining Council’s agreement.



This latest hike caps a volatile year for fuel taxation. Earlier in 2026, Treasury temporarily slashed the General Fuel Levy by R3.00 per litre for petrol and R3.93 for diesel to cushion consumers from a spike in oil prices. This was a result of the then-escalating Middle East tensions. That relief was phased out in two stages with half withdrawn in June, the rest in July. This was before the General Fuel Levy returned fully to its baseline rate of R4.10 per litre for petrol and R3.93 for diesel.

For motorists, the upshot is that pump prices are being squeezed from two directions at the same time, global oil costs remain elevated due to geopolitical tension. While the temporary tax relief that softened the blow earlier in the year has now fully unwound.



October fuel prices are set to ‘smash’ South African records.

World.title: President Ramaphosa under pressure: What’s driving the heat?
World.content:
President Cyril Ramaphosa is facing one of the most consequential stretches of his presidency, with legal, political and economic pressures converging just as South Africa heads toward its November local government elections.

THE PHALA PHALA SCANDAL

At the centre of the storm is the long-running Phala Phala scandal. Ramaphosa’s legal team has mounted a court challenge to Parliament’s Section 89 independent panel report, arguing it failed to properly weigh the evidence and that reviving public impeachment hearings would cause irreparable reputational harm.

His review was set down for three days in the Western Cape High Court in early September. Opponents argue Parliament has a duty to fully examine the cash-theft affair and the president’s conduct.The stakes are real: if the court sets the report aside, a new panel with a fresh mandate could be convened, effectively restarting the process.



IMPEACHMENT TIMELINE WORKING AGAINST HIM … AND FOR HIM?

An interdict has paused public impeachment hearings until the review is resolved, and legal analysts note the broader process could stretch on for years. That cuts both ways politically. Critics say the delay lets Ramaphosa dodge accountability. While allies within the ANC arguably benefit from the drawn-out timeline, since it keeps him in office through a politically sensitive election period without a resolved scandal hanging over the party’s own campaign.

Despite public calls for his resignation from opposition parties, analysts point out the ANC’s internal calculus favours keeping Ramaphosa in place, at least for now. Some suggest party leaders may quietly offer him protection in exchange for stability heading into the vote. That tension between public pressure and internal party interest is arguably the most complicated part of the story.

Adding to the mix is pressure of a different kind, business leaders are publicly pushing Ramaphosa to lock in his economic reform agenda before his final term ends. Business Leadership South Africa’s CEO has described the reform project as the most important thing happening in the country, warning that momentum built under Ramaphosa needs to be enshrined in law rather than left dependent on political continuity.

PRESIDENT CYRIL RAMAPHOSA ON THE GLOBAL STAGE

None of this has kept Ramaphosa out of international view. This week he’s in New Delhi for the BRICS Summit, pushing for deeper investment into African beneficiation and industrial development. This serves as a reminder that his presidency is still trying to operate on two fronts: defending his domestic legitimacy while continuing to position South Africa internationally.

Taken together, it’s a presidency being pulled in multiple directions at once, legally exposed, politically protected, and economically pressured to cement a legacy before time runs out.

World.title: ‘Colonialists, you have lost’: Zimbabweans spark debate in UK
World.content:
A video showing Zimbabweans singing a liberation song in Shona on the London Underground has sparked a heated debate on social media.

The group can be seen singing together on a train, with the song carrying a message directed at colonialists.

The performance has attracted attention because of its setting, with the Zimbabweans singing about colonialism while surrounded by passengers in London.



The song includes the phrase “maruza imi vapambepfumi”, which carries the meaning that the colonialists or exploiters have lost.

Liberation songs have a long history in Zimbabwe, where music was used to express resistance to colonial rule and celebrate the country’s struggle for independence.

Zimbabweans defend London Tube performance

The video has divided opinion, with some social media users defending the group and arguing that the song should be understood within its historical context.



One commenter, Farai Keith, wrote: “This is simply a liberation song. Doesn’t the USA celebrate independence? Have you ever condemned them?”

Another user, Prince RK Mhlanga, took a different view, accusing the singers of behaving like the people they criticise.

“It’s so surprising to see you behave like the very Israel you criticise day in and day out,” he wrote, while also questioning the message of the song.



The discussion has also focused on whether the people in the video were Zimbabwean musicians visiting Britain.

Tembelani Sibanda claimed that the people featured had travelled to the UK and had since returned to Zimbabwe, although this detail has not been independently verified.

‘Imperialists get angry’

Other commenters argued that the reaction to the video reflected the continuing sensitivity surrounding Britain’s colonial history in Africa.



One user, Sharp, wrote: “These guys are too lazy to sustain a drawn out conquest. The country is nearly bankrupt. So once their benos run dry, so will they.”

Another commenter, Thalex, responded: “The only thing holding them back from being our lunch meat, is our respect for law and order.”

Those comments themselves generated further debate, with some users arguing that the conversation had moved beyond the original video into broader arguments about colonialism, migration and race.



One particularly inflammatory response described Africans using racist language.

Rather than focusing on that comment, the wider reaction demonstrates how quickly the short video has become a flashpoint for discussions about Britain’s colonial past and modern African migration.

Zimbabweans’ liberation song in a very different setting

For many Zimbabweans, songs from the liberation era remain an important part of the country’s cultural memory.



The timing and location of the performance have nevertheless made it particularly striking.

A song associated with Zimbabwe’s liberation struggle was being sung in the heart of the former colonial power, while commuters appeared to carry on with their journeys.

The video has therefore prompted a much bigger conversation than the performance itself, with social media users debating colonialism, Zimbabwean identity, migration and whether liberation songs still have a place in modern Britain.

World.title: SA’s cybercrime laws put to the test amid capacity concerns
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - South Africa’s extradition of six Nigerian nationals to the US shows its cybercrime laws in action.

The Hawks and Interpol apprehended the group for alleged involvement in an online love scam where dozens of US women were defrauded of more than R100 million.

One expert warns that while the laws exist, a lack of human resources to address the issue remains a concern.

Jason Jordaan, a cybercrime investigator, said South Africa has exceptional legislation.

“In fact, I'd like to almost postulate that our legislation is probably superior to some of the legislation I see in countries like Europe and the United States as far as cybercrime goes. But I think the big difference is, like I said, it comes down to capacity. We struggle with capacity in this particular regard.

“Oftentimes, when we do build up capacity within the government sector, it gets poached to the private sector where salaries are significantly higher sometimes in this regard. And I think that costs us in the long run. But I don't think as a country we need to step back from a legislative point of view in terms of our ability to deal with this."

World.title: Four arrested for driver’s licence fraud
World.content:
THOHOYANDOU - Police in Limpopo have arrested four suspects involved in a cash-for-driver’s licence scheme.

The group had allegedly been operating at the Marble Hall Licence Testing Centre in Limpopo.

The syndicate is alleged to have fast-tracked bulk transactions involving between 20 and 30 learner licences at a time, bypassing lawful licensing procedures.

World.title: "Lack of character and leadership" : EFF reacts to Majodina's outburst
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF) have slammed Minister of Water and Sanitation Pemmy Majodina’s profane shouting match with a Kouga resident.

The party said in a statement that such behaviour is unacceptable for a public representative to insult a member of the public.

At the centre of the red berates condemnation of the minister's conduct was the treatment towards the member of the community, who the EFF deemed was treated with 'indignity, disdain and lack of respect'.

READ | 'Arrogance of power' | Politicians under scrutiny over public outbursts

The profanity exchange between Majodina and a community member happened during the launch of an upgraded pump station.

The incident captured in a video, saw a community member who was being escorted out of the venue shouting "jou ma se ****" to Majodina, who then responded by saying "Phuma! Jou ma se **** ook."

“The people of South Africa are rightly frustrated with the slow pace of service delivery, corruption and absence of government and to be irritated by their frustration, regardless of how it is expressed, reveals a lack of character and leadership.”

The incident has already triggered fierce opposition backlash, with the DA and ActionSA lodging ethics complaints over the incident.

In the meantime, critics have called on the President Cyril Ramaphosa to address the vulgar outburst, with one political analyst suggesting that a mandatory public apology and formal disciplinary consequences are required to restore dignity to public office.

World.title: No water, power and high crime | Poor service delivery could erode property value
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Poor service delivery in an area could hit homeowners twice.

On one end, it's the disruption brought onto their daily life, leaving residents scrambling for backup power or needing to buy water.

On the other end, it's the possible reality that the value of their homes could slowly erode

This is a bleak picture which real estate practitioner TT Mbha painted as he outlined the ripple effect poor service delivery has on the property market.

READ | Joburg power crisis: Residents demand action, not more promises

His comments come at the back of already exiting issues facing various communities throughout the country from water outages, prolonged power cuts and high crime rates. It could even be crumbling infrastructure from roads riddled with potholes, hijacked buildings and streetlights that are not working.

Mbha said when buyers are looking for a home, they are not just looking at the house.

They are looking at what comes with living in that neighbourhood, including amenities such as schools, hospitals, recreational facilities, sporting facilities and restaurants.

Outside of what is available to them is also where it is situated and how safe it is. But more importantly, service delivery and the efficiency of a municipality to act on the problems at hand.

“Nobody wants to invest in an area that is declining in terms of basic services,” Mbha said.

He said property owners in such cases find themselves in two battles: Having buyers who lack interest in the property or having to settle for a lower price when selling their property.

While some homeowners may try to look at alternatives like boreholes or solar power to protect themselves from unreliable services, Mbha said the “reality of that is not everyone can afford that”.

READ | Tired of potholes, Sandown residents take repairs into their own hands

And for those who can afford these options, they then find themselves being able to negotiate prices but even so, Mbha said there is still a vacuum gap in the property prices.

This refers once again to the significant decrease in the value of a property from the original agreed price because of the negative information discovered about the area.

“You are definitely going to sell it at a loss. Considering the issues at hand, nobody is going to want to offer you the full asking price, already knowing what the issues are in that area. That's the reality of it all as a property owner. "If you are supposed to get a million for that property, you'll be lucky even if you get R800,000 because people are now educated about what's happening around them. They'll know that you're selling because there's a crime issue or there's a crisis in terms of service delivery," he explained.

Mbha said that while it would be difficult to quantify the exact loss, one could judge the impact from property sales in the area, which may be ‘going through a decline’.

READ | Johannesburg, the City of Gold, is starting to look more like the City of Potholes

Despite this, Mbha does shed a glimmer of hope for homeowners.

This, he said, means the communities reclaiming their neighbourhoods.

World.title: India welcomes leaders for BRICS Summit
World.content:
NEW DELHI - The presidents of Russia and Iran were in India for talks Friday ahead of a BRICS summit that will bring together leaders including China's Xi Jinping, with wars, trade and energy expected to dominate the agenda.

"The world today is going through a period of unprecedented complexity", Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said, speaking in New Delhi at a forum, ahead of the main summit on Saturday.

Wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, as well as global trade turbulence and oil, are expected to feature prominently at the two-day annual summit.

BRICS was created in 2009 as a forum for major emerging economies seeking greater influence in institutions dominated by Western powers.

"BRICS was established to counter unilateralism", said Pezeshkian, who also met with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The Iranian president said that pressure on his country "has reached a critical and dangerous stage in recent months following the military aggression by the United States and Israel".

When the summit begins Saturday, Xi's attendance will be key.

Set to arrive on Saturday, it will be his first visit to India since 2019, marking the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between the rival neighbours, six years after a deadly military clash along their disputed Tibetan border.

Ties between the nuclear-armed Asian giants have been warming again, with flights, visas and high-level contacts gradually being restored.

"China stands ready to work with India... by strengthening communication, enhancing cooperation, and properly handling differences," Beijing's foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said Friday.

Deep mistrust remains, with their contested Himalayan frontier, a widening trade deficit and strategic rivalry still complicating ties.

Dozens of Tibetans protested in New Delhi on Friday, exiles, like their Buddhist leader the Dalai Lama, who has lived in India since fleeing a Chinese crackdown in 1959, waving placards against Xi's visit.

Modi embraced President Vladimir Putin on Friday before talks. Putin, who last visited India in December 2025, is one of New Delhi's most important strategic partners.

"One should engage in debate and friendship only with the virtuous, and nothing whatsoever with the unvirtuous," Modi wrote Friday, in a social media message in Sanskrit to welcome leaders to the 11-nation summit.

Posters of a beaming Modi line streets across New Delhi, with heavy deployments of security forces across the capital and widespread traffic restrictions.

- 'Fault line' -

As well as Iran, BRICS includes Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, countries with sharply differing positions on the war launched by the United States and Israel in February.

All three have been admitted to the group in recent years, joining founding member states that include India, China and Russia.

"The Gulf conflict is going to be the central fault line this time during the BRICS summit," said Harsh V. Pant of India's Observer Research Foundation.

"What was seen until last year as an achievement, the expansion of BRICS, today looks like a big constraint on BRICS," Pant said.

Pezeshkian's participation, his first visit to India as Iranian president, has put the Middle East conflict firmly on the agenda.

"The war in Iran will provide a stern test of the group's cohesion," said Shilan Shah of Capital Economics, noting the failure of the BRICS foreign ministers to agree on a joint statement when they met in New Delhi in May.

UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi are also to attend.

India maintains cordial relations with Iran and Israel, but is also careful to strike a delicate balance in its ties with Washington.

New Delhi has navigated the energy crisis sparked by the US-Iran war in part by turning to Russia for fuel despite Western sanctions as the war against Ukraine drags on.

World.content:
Burundian nationals in Kenya at their embassy at Dennis Pritt road on September 8, 2026 [David Gichuru, Standard]

World.title: ODM vows not to interfere with Linda Mwananchi rally in Nairobi
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Linda Mwananchi leaders during a rally in Western Kenya. [Linda Mwananchi, X]

The Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) has said it will not disrupt the planned Linda Mwananchi rally scheduled for Sunday at Jacaranda Grounds.

In a statement on Friday, September 11, ODM Nairobi Chairman George Aladwa said the party had no business interfering with the rally, noting that Linda Mwananchi had a right to speak to Nairobi residents.

“I want to make it clear that nobody in ODM has any intention of disrupting or interfering with the Linda Mwananchi rally,” Aladwa stated.

He added: “We believe that political competition should be about ideas, policies and the ability to convince Kenyans, rather than confrontations between supporters of different political formations.”

Aladwa said ODM’s opponents had a right to tell Nairobi residents what they stood for and what they intended to offer Kenyans.

“The people are intelligent enough to listen to different political messages and make their own decisions,” Aladwa said.

At the same time, Aladwa said ODM was engaged in an extensive programme to market and strengthen the party across Nairobi as it prepared for activities to commemorate the anniversary of the death of its former party leader, the late Raila Amolo Odinga.

The chairman lauded Odinga for his contribution to Kenya’s democracy, the struggle for constitutional reforms and the political transformation of the country, saying his contribution could not be erased.

“His legacy remains an important part of ODM and Kenya’s political history. As we approach the 2027 General Election, our responsibility is to ensure that ODM remains strong, organised and firmly rooted across Nairobi,” the chairman stated.

“We will continue engaging residents in all constituencies and wards and explaining the party’s agenda to the people. I appeal to ODM supporters to remain calm and focused. Do not allow yourselves to be provoked into unnecessary political confrontations,” he added.

World.title: Ndindi Nyoro tells Ruto to keep off Tata Chemicals
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

PPK leader Ndindi Nyoro addresses a rally at Nambale market in Busia on August 30, 2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro has cautioned President William Ruto against meddling in the affairs of Tata Chemicals, Africa’s largest soda ash plant in Lake Magadi, Kajiado County.

Nyoro, who is the Peoples’ Party of Kenya leader, has accused President Ruto of an alleged plot to take control of Tata Chemicals through a shareholding scheme.

He said Ruto’s directive on Tata Chemicals closure raises concerns over the future of multinational firms and their operations in the country.

Speaking during a tour of Wote, Makueni County, on Thursday, Nyoro termed the Head of State’s move selfish, saying even if he had since softened his stance on the firm, it remains wanting for investors.

“His utterances were and remain wanting for external and internal investors. We don’t want investors to work in a bad political environment. Even if he seems to have made a U-turn on the matter, we are aware he has been pushing to be a shareholder in the company. We don’t want investors to be interfered with politically because we must create an environment where our people have access to job opportunities. It is almost reaching a catastrophic level in terms of lack of jobs for our people,” he said

The PPK leader warned that the country is in a bad economic state with a Sh13.5 trillion debt that is projected to grow further by next year.

“When Ruto exits next year the debt will be more than Sh15 trillion. The next president, who will be coming from the opposition, will have hard times in running this country. For every Sh100 that will be collected as tax from 2028, Sh91 will be used to repay government debts. We should not have time now to fight as opposition and also as Kenyans. We must hold hands and send the president back home because of his failures,” Nyoro said.

The MP urged opposition leaders to put aside their political differences and unite behind a single presidential candidate ahead of the 2027 General Election, saying that a united opposition would have a better chance of defeating President Ruto.

“If the opposition wants to defeat President Ruto, they must come together and present one presidential candidate. I am ready to talk to all the opposition principals,” Nyoro said.

Nyoro also outlined a raft of proposals he says could help revive Kenya’s economy and ease the financial burden on ordinary citizens.

Among his proposals is the use of the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) to strengthen the health sector. He argued that Kenyans should be able to access quality healthcare without being forced to bear the full cost of medical services.

Nyoro further proposed changes to the way education is financed, suggesting that bursaries currently administered through the National Government Constituencies Development Fund (NG-CDF) and county governments be channelled towards financing free primary and secondary education.

He said such an approach would create a more uniform education financing system and ensure that children from poor households are not disadvantaged because of their parents' inability to meet school-related expenses.

Nyoro's proposals come amid growing debate over the country's economic direction, the cost of living, access to healthcare and the financing of education.

World.title: Mama Tutam acquitted of Sh25m fraud, says Nigerian tycoon cost her marriage
World.content:
Nairobi Woman Representative aspirant Faith Mwikali Ndiwa, alias Faith Nguthu addresses journalists at the Milimani Law Courts in Nairobi on September 9, 2026. [David Gichuru, Standard]

A Nairobi Woman Representative aspirant has confessed the frustrations and embarrassment that befell her after befriending a wealthy Nigerian businessman who later accused her of defrauding him of Sh25 million.

Faith Mwikali Ndiwa, alias Faith Nguthu, popularly known as Mama Tutam, said she was kicked out of her marriage after the father of her three children discovered reports linking her to an alleged love affair with Nigerian investor Jude Olabayo Veracruz.

World.title: Sifuna hits back at Ruto over opposition agenda
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna promised to introduce austerity measures if the opposition takes power.

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has hit back at President William Ruto after the Head of State accused the united opposition of lacking a clear policy agenda ahead of the 2027 General Election.

Speaking in the Senate, Sifuna, who has been fronted as a potential presidential candidate in the coming elections, said the opposition’s immediate plan was to restore meritocracy in government and remove Ruto from power.

Sifuna also questioned government spending, citing claims that Sh12 billion had been spent on hospitality at State House at a time when the country was facing financial constraints.

“We are being told that Sh12 billion was spent on hospitality at State House, in a country where we are told we have no cash for capitation. So those of you who ask us for a plan, ours is to send you home,” Sifuna said.

The senator further promised to introduce austerity measures if the opposition takes power, arguing that government spending could be streamlined to free up resources for essential services.

“I believe in the first 100 days after we kick this government out, we should be able to cut out the fat that is being utilised at State House so that we can pay our teachers and fund our hospitals,” he said.

Sifuna’s remarks came a day after Ruto accused opposition leaders of using ethnic profiling and intimidation to influence voters in areas perceived to be opposition strongholds.

Speaking in Ngong and Ongata Rongai in Kajiado County, Ruto defended the broad-based UDA-ODM political arrangement, saying the pact was aimed at promoting national unity and ensuring equitable distribution of national resources.

“They are intimidating people along ethnic lines, telling them they must vote a certain way. Do not allow yourselves to be divided through tribalism and hatred. Their agenda is to spread tribalism and hatred,” Ruto said.

The exchange comes as political parties and leaders intensify preparations for the 2027 General Election, with the opposition seeking to consolidate its support base while the Kenya Kwanza administration defends its record and broad-based political arrangement.

World.title: Centum taps insider as Mworia exits after nearly two decades
World.content:
Centum Investment Company PLC acting Group Chief Executive Thomas Omondi-Achola. [Courtesy]

Centum Investment Company PLC has appointed Thomas Omondi-Achola as acting group chief executive, tapping an internal candidate to succeed long-serving CEO James Mworia, who is leaving to head Kenya’s newly established National Infrastructure Fund (NIF).

The transition, effective immediately, marks the end of an 18-year tenure during which Mworia transformed Centum from a small investment firm into East Africa’s largest diversified investment platform, the company said in a statement.

World.title: Ruto: Kenya to end raw mineral exports
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during a thanksgiving service in South Horr, Samburu County on September 6, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto says Kenya will no longer allow its mineral wealth to leave the country in raw form, coming days after the controversial saga surrounding Tata Chemicals’ operations at Lake Magadi.

Ruto defended the government’s decision to suspend Tata Chemicals’ operations at Lake Magadi, Kajiado County, arguing that Kenya has not been receiving sufficient value from the natural resource and that more investors should be given an opportunity to develop the area.

“We want to give five, six or even 10 companies an opportunity to use the resources there to create jobs, value, create wealth and reduce poverty,” Ruto said.

The President made the remarks during a thanksgiving service in South Horr, Samburu County, on Sunday, where he announced a broader government policy aimed at shifting Kenya from exporting raw materials to processing them locally.

“Going into the future, our position as the government. Whether we are talking about Magadi Soda or oil or all our minerals, we have taken the decision that we will no longer export raw materials,” Ruto said.

“We are going to process all minerals available in Kenya.”

The declaration puts the long-running Lake Magadi dispute at the centre of a much wider economic strategy.

Tata Chemicals has been associated with soda ash production at the lake for more than a century. Its Kenyan operations trace their history to 1911, when the Magadi Soda Company began extracting trona from Lake Magadi.

Operations were suspended on July 28, 2026, following a directive from the Ministry of Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs over compliance and licensing issues.

Ruto has argued that the resource should generate greater benefits for Kenyans through expanded investment, job creation and local value addition.

He accused the existing model of allowing valuable resources to leave the country while Kenya receives less economic benefit than it could.

The President’s comments reflect a longstanding challenge facing Kenya’s extractive sector: how to turn mineral deposits into manufacturing opportunities rather than simply exporting commodities.

Under the proposed approach, minerals such as gold, limestone, iron ore, graphite, titanium and soda ash would be processed or refined in Kenya before being exported.

The government says this would create industrial jobs, strengthen local supply chains and increase the value of exports.

Ruto cited planned cooperation with Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote as an example of the investment model the government wants to pursue.

He said talks were underway to establish an oil refinery and petrochemical complex in Lamu, alongside efforts to attract investors into mineral refining.

“It is imprudent for any government to export raw materials, create jobs and value in other countries while we have a big population of young people who need jobs,” Ruto said.

World.title: Sifuna condemns abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Busia County Senator Okiya Omtata, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, Bumula MP Jack Wamboka during the burial service of Mary Gorreti Okiya at Kabula, in Bumula on September 5,2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has declared that the fight to restore democracy, media freedom and the rule of law following the abduction of Standard Group Senior Editor will form the centrepiece of the Linda Mwananchi government vowing to defeat President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election.

Sifuna accused President Ruto’s administration of undermining constitutional freedoms and creating an atmosphere of fear, saying the country must be returned to what he described as “the rail of the six important values” enshrined in the Constitution.

Speaking in Bumula Constituency, Kakamega County during the burial of Mary Goreti, the sister of Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah, Sifuna strongly condemned the abduction and arrest of a Standard Group Associate Editor, Alex Kiprotich, arguing that journalists must be protected if Kenya is to remain a democratic country.

“It is impossible that you are driving on the road and you are taken away the way the way the Standard Group Journaliat and Editor Alex Kiprotich was taken. Kenyans want to live in a free country. We do not want to live in fear,” said Sifuna.

He questioned the circumstances surrounding the incident and accused the Government of failing to protect media freedom, adding that the Linda Mwananchi movement would seek to restore institutions and constitutional safeguards if elected to power, arguing that democracy could not survive where citizens, journalists and political opponents lived in fear.

"You cannot just arrest a senior journalist in the middle of the road with police carrying firearms, then you dump him some 500kilometres near the dam, a country cannot have democracy if media is not being respected and allowed to do it's work as per the constitution," said Sifuna.

He said the movement’s agenda was not merely about removing the current administration from power but it's main plan is rebuilding systems of governance around constitutionalism, democracy, individual freedoms and the rule of law.

“With less than 11 months remaining, we want to tell Kenyans that our entire plan is to return this country to the rails of the six important values contained in our Constitution, including democracy, freedom of citizens and the rule of law,” said Sifuna.

Sifuna also accused the Government of using threats against political opponents, saying leaders should not threaten citizens with arrest, expulsion or other forms of intimidation.

He challenged religious leaders to remind politicians that the power to determine the length of a person's life belongs to God.

Sifuna further linked the rule of law to economic growth, warning that investors would be reluctant to establish businesses in Kenya if government could arbitrarily order them to leave.

He said Kenya could not rely on government alone to create employment for millions of young people, arguing that the country needed both local and foreign investors.

“No investor can bring his project to a country where he can wake up one day and the President tells him, ‘Pack and go.’ It is impossible,” Sifuna said.

He argued that investor confidence was also affected by the possibility of commercial disputes being referred to foreign jurisdictions because investors lacked confidence in Kenya’s legal system.

Sifuna also criticised the government over the ongoing nurses and midwives strike, saying the rule of law required the State to honour agreements signed with workers.

World.title: Civil Aviation Minister, IFC review developments in Hurghada airport tender
World.content:
Civil Aviation Minister Sameh al-Hefny met on Friday, September 11, 2026, with International Finance Corporation (IFC) Regional Director for North Africa and the Horn of Africa Ary Naim, IFC Egypt Country Manager Saad Sabra and IFC Infrastructure Projects Specialist Mohamed Mehni on the sidelines of the EIAS 2026 International Airshow and Space Exhibition in El Alamein city, northwestern Egypt, to review the latest developments in the tendering procedures for the management, operation and development of Hurghada International Airport under a public-private partnership (PPP) scheme.

The minister said the project comes as part of the Egyptian state’s directives to continue developing the civil aviation sector, enhance services provided to passengers and improve the overall travel experience.

al-Hefny praised the IFC’s role in providing technical and advisory support for the project, highlighting its international experience in preparing and implementing public-private partnership projects.

For his part, Naim affirmed the IFC’s commitment to continuing cooperation with the Ministry of Civil Aviation and supporting the project during its upcoming stages, contributing to the completion of the tendering procedures in accordance with international standards.

World.title: EgyptAir Ground Services signs 2 strategic agreements to expand international partnerships
World.content:
EgyptAir Ground Services Company signed two strategic agreements with Rafal Aviation Handling and AuriJet Aviation Services, during the third and final day of the Egypt International Airshow and Space Exhibition (EIAS 2026).

The signing ceremony was attended by Civil Aviation Minister Sameh al-Hefny, who said the ministry is keen to attract more investment and expand cooperation with major international companies and agencies operating in the civil aviation sector.

He added that expanding such partnerships would contribute to improving operational efficiency at Egyptian airports, attracting more airlines, and increasing inbound air traffic and tourism.

The agreements form part of EgyptAir Ground Services’ plan to expand its commercial and operational presence, building on its extensive experience and advanced capabilities.

Under its partnership with Rafal Aviation Handling, EgyptAir Ground Services seeks to attract international airlines, scheduled and charter operators, and private aviation, particularly from the Far East, European, and Russian markets.

The partnership with AuriJet Aviation Services aims to leverage its extensive network across the Middle East, Turkey, Europe, and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) to support and increase air cargo, charter, and private aviation traffic at Egyptian airports.

The partnerships also seek to provide international operators with a unified professional point of contact, ensuring integrated coordination of ground handling, fueling, permits, and other services while maximizing operational efficiency and flexibility.

World.title: President Sisi participates in closed-door session of BRICS leaders
World.content:
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi will participate in the closed-door session of the leaders of the BRICS countries, hosted by the Indian capital New Delhi, under the theme “building resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability” Saturday, September 12, 2026.

The President will deliver Egypt’s statement during the closed-door session of the BRICS leaders, which is being held under the theme inclusive global governance and strengthening multilateral action.”

Following the closed-door session, the president and the BRICS leaders are scheduled to tour an exhibition marking the 20th anniversary of the launch of the BRICS grouping.

The president will also participate in a dinner banquet hosted by the Indian prime minister this evening in honor of the leaders participating in the summit.

Egypt’s priorities within BRICS include launching joint projects in vital sectors, expanding economic and financial cooperation, and reforming the global financial system.

The key outcomes of BRICS summits following Egypt’s accession included the adoption at the 2024 Kazan Summit of two documents: a political declaration and a document outlining the guiding principles, criteria, and procedures for the accession of partner countries to the grouping.

Meanwhile, the 2025 Rio de Janeiro Summit produced three documents: a declaration on “global governance of AI,” “framework on climate finance,” and the Rio de Janeiro declaration, the main concluding document.

World.title: Sisi and Putin review bilateral cooperation and regional issues
World.content:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi met on Friday with Russian President Vladimir Putin, on the sidelines of the 18th BRICS Summit held in the Indian capital, New Delhi.

Egyptian Presidency Spokesperson Mohamed al-Shennawy said that the two leaders emphasized their keenness to continue efforts to strengthen bilateral relations and cooperation across various fields, to serve the interests of both nations.

President Sisi underscored the key projects currently being implemented in Egypt within Egyptian-Russian partnership framework – such as the al-Dabaa Nuclear Power Plant and the Russian Industrial Zone in the Suez Canal Economic Zone – in addition to cooperation in the fields of energy, trade, investment, food security, and tourism.

Sisi reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to overcoming any challenges that may hinder the implementation of joint projects, and welcomed the decision by relevant Russian authorities to accredit Alexandria and al-Alamein international airports, thereby boosting Russian tourism to new destinations in Egypt.

The Russian President reiterated his country’s commitment to deepening cooperation with Egypt and supporting its efforts toward comprehensive development, including executing major projects in accordance with the agreed timelines and specifications.

Regional issues

The two leaders also exchanged views on a number of regional and international issues of common interest, particularly the Palestinian cause.

They stressed the necessity of reaching a just and comprehensive settlement based on the two-state solution and relevant international legitimacy resolutions.

President Sisi reviewed Egypt’s efforts to advance the implementation of the second-phase obligations under the agreement to halt the war in the Gaza Strip, highlighting the need to ensure the adequate and sustained delivery of humanitarian aid.

The meeting also tackled the Iranian war, with the two presidents emphasizing the priority of de-escalation and a return to the negotiating track to reach a comprehensive and sustainable agreement resolving the crisis through peaceful means.

Both leaders further discussed the latest developments in Sudan and asserted the need to preserve Sudan’s sovereignty, unity, and national institutions.

President al-Sisi stressed that any infringement upon the security, unity, or sovereignty of Sudan constitutes a red line that Egypt will not allow to be crossed.

World.title: Trump on 9/11 reposts video of him asking January 6 rioters to go home
World.content:
After spending the morning at the Pentagon to mark the 25th anniversary of the September 11th tragedy, President Donald Trump apparently had another attack on his mind in the afternoon — posting the 5-year-old video of him telling January 6, 2021, rioters to go home after they violently stormed the Capitol building.

The video, which was posted in full on Trump’s Truth Social account Friday without any further context, shows the president repeating his false claim that he won the 2020 election but telling rioters to go home: “We have to have peace. So go home, we love you, you’re very special.”

A White House spokesperson said Trump reposted the video Friday as “a reminder to everyone that what the Democrats did to weaponize the justice system against President Trump has been debunked thoroughly.”

It’s unclear what cases they were referencing — the criminal case against Trump concerning the Capitol attack was dismissed due to his win in the 2024 election.

Trump has been repeatedly emphasizing voter fraud in recent months, increasingly and without evidence accusing Democrats of cheating in elections. At the GOP midterm convention this week, he implored the audience to “cheat like hell” to help Republicans keep control of Congress.

The January 6 video, about a minute in length, was panned at the time for being posted hours after the attack began and for being overly sympathetic to those storming the Capitol building. Around the same time Trump posted it Friday, he also had several other posts about the midterm convention.

World.title: Iranian allies captured a strategic Red Sea island in a vital waterway. Here’s what to know
World.content:
Iran-backed rebels in Yemen captured the strategic Perim Island in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on Friday, two Yemeni government sources told CNN, potentially expanding Tehran’s influence over another key global shipping route.

A day earlier, the Huthi group captured the port town of Mocha as it sought to take control of the country’s Red Sea coast.

The news sent shockwaves worldwide over the possible impact on shipping and oil prices, as well as the risk of a new front opening in the US-Iran war.

Bab al-Mandeb is a chokepoint linking Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Although less critical to the oil trade than the Strait of Hormuz, it carries essential goods worldwide, including millions of barrels of oil each day.

Its strategic importance has grown since the US-Iran war began, as Saudi Arabia increasingly uses its Red Sea export route to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively closed to most shipping.

The development coincides with a wider regional escalation of the war between Iran and the United States, after Tehran warned this week that it would step up hostilities against the US, which maintains a stringent naval blockade of Iran and continues to launch military strikes on the country.

How did we get here?

Yemen was plunged into civil war in 2014, when Huthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, and drove the internationally recognized government into exile. Saudi Arabia led a military campaign the following year to dislodge the rebels. Iran has supplied the Huthis with weapons and training, and exercises some influence on the rebel group’s decisions.

The result is a fractured country, with the Huthis controlling the capital and the northwest, and the government and allied factions holding much of the south and east. Some 22 million people, roughly half of the population, need humanitarian assistance to this day.

After years of stalemate, fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and the Huthis flared up in recent weeks as a result of tensions caused by the wider conflict between Iran and the US. The Red Sea became a focal point as Tehran sought ways to pressure the global economy and extract more concessions from Washington.

Fighters loyal to Yemen’s Huthi group shout slogans during a rally to recruit more fighters in Sanaa on Thursday. Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty Images

Last month, the Huthis intensified an offensive to seize Mocha from Saudi-backed forces. More than 25 Huthi rockets slammed into the sprawling harbor a few weeks ago as commercial ships were unloading, according to port director Abdel Malek Al-Sharaabi.

Until Thursday morning, Mocha was under the control of the National Resistance Forces, a Saudi-backed group commanded by Tarik Saleh, a vice president in Yemen’s beleaguered, internationally-recognized government. Later in the day, the government acknowledged the Huthis had the town.

As the Huthis were marching south, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke twice on Thursday with US President Donald Trump and urged him to strike the Huthis, two sources familiar with the matter told CNN. Trump did not agree to US strikes, one of the sources said. News of the calls was first reported by Axios.

“The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests—such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea—while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges,” a senior administration official said in a statement to CNN when asked about the calls. “We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability.”

CNN reported on Thursday that the US had stepped up its intelligence and targeting support for the Saudi campaign against the Huthis in Yemen. Sources told CNN that there are currently tight limits to the US support – not participating directly in strikes or helping to refuel Saudi warplanes or provide other operational support.

In an exclusive interview with CNN earlier this month, Saleh warned that if the Huthis seized Perim Island – which lies directly on the Bab al-Mandeb chokepoint – they could gain control of the strait itself. Dislodging them would require “a massive (international) force and the navies,” he said.

A Huthi military spokesman on Friday confirmed the group had launched a push to expel Saudi-backed forces from the remaining parts of Yemen’s western coast it still occupies, and said navigation through the Bab al Mandeb Strait was “safe for all” except for Saudi vessels.

What comes next?

The capture of Perim and Mocha gives a group trained and aided by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards greater ability to halt traffic in the Red Sea – and potentially hands Iran more leverage in its war with the US.

The Huthis “are in a good position to increase their influence around Bab al-Mandeb … and they can now protect themselves from any ground operations that can come from this area,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen with the International Crisis Group think tank, told CNN.

An effective Huthi blockade of Bab al-Mandeb would open a new front in the war with Iran and could require US military intervention, potentially weakening Washington’s ability to keep ships moving through Hormuz. It could also prevent Saudi Arabia from shipping diesel to Europe at a critical moment for the fuel market.

The Huthi advance also allows Iran to increase pressure on Saudi Arabia, a US ally that hosts American troops and bases that Tehran says were used to target it. It could also prevent Saudi Arabia from shipping diesel to Europe at a critical moment for the fuel market.

A Saudi official told CNN that Saudi Arabia will continue to support Yemen’s government and is working closely with its partners to “ensure freedom of navigation in the Arabian Gulf and Red Sea.”

“The Kingdom will also take every necessary measure to ensure that its own citizens and residents are safe and its borders are secure,” the official added.

The move also adds further volatility to oil markets, already under pressure from the very low number of vessels transiting Hormuz. Oil prices jumped four percent on Thursday, with global benchmark Brent crude hitting $105, as news broke of the Huthis gaining ground along the Red Sea. It fell three percent on Friday amid reports that Gulf Arab foreign ministers plan to meet their Iranian counterpart for the first time since the war.

Beyond its geopolitical impact, the developments risk worsening Yemen’s humanitarian crisis, already designated by the United Nations as one of the world’s worst.

“The question now is how the Saudi-led coalition will react,” Nagi of the Crisis Group said. “This is not the end of the battle, we will probably see more developments in the coming days.”

World.title: ‘A f***-up of epic proportions’: Blame game begins after Iran-backed Huthis’ lightning advance down Red Sea coast
World.content:
The desperate pleas for air cover from Yemeni generals started coming mid-morning on Thursday. An advance by the Iran-backed Huthis toward Yemen’s strategic port city of Mocha was in full swing, and backup support from chief ally Saudi Arabia was nowhere in sight.

“The Huthis committed everything they had – waves upon waves of fighters … along with their available ballistic missiles and weapons,” a senior Yemeni source attached to their military forces told CNN. The source said he contacted the United States Central Command (CENTCOM) and was assured the US was “watching the situation closely and that Saudi air support was coming.”

“But the air support never came,” the source said. “And Mocha has now fallen.”

Hours later, on Friday, the Huthis captured another key coastal asset, Perim Island, at the mouth of the Red Sea. The island splits the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in two, giving Tehran de facto control over another key shipping route.

The Huthis’ rapid advance amounts to an extraordinary 36 hours in a conflict that had been largely on ice for years. But the kindling for renewed fighting had been laid for months amid the conflict between the United States and Iran, as Tehran seeks to use oil prices – and their impact on the global economy – as leverage.

Now, Yemen and the Red Sea have the potential to become a true second front in the Iran war.

Iran’s effective control of the Strait of Hormuz plus its tightening grip on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait threatens to push oil prices even higher, weeks before November’s midterm elections in the United States.

While the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, the gateway to the Suez Canal shipping route, is less critical to global energy markets than Hormuz, it still carries essential goods worldwide, including millions of barrels of oil every day. The strait has become increasingly important since the start of the Iran war, as Saudi Arabia has re-routed some exports through the waterway to bypass Hormuz.

“(The Huthis) don’t need to use advanced weapons to close Bab al-Mandeb. They can just use a cannon on a car,” said Amr Al-Bidh, the top official of Yemen’s Southern Transitional Council (STC). The STC has fought both the Huthis and Saudi-backed forces in the past, and wants an independent state in the south.

“It’s a leverage that they have without using advanced weapons,” Al-Bidh told CNN in an interview. “And they will keep it.”

‘Ghost’ army rosters and no backup support

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke twice on Thursday with US President Donald Trump and urged him to strike the Huthis, another source familiar with the matter told CNN Friday. Trump declined to intervene, according to that source.

“The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests—such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea—while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges,” the White House said in response to CNN’s questions about the calls. “We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the Republic of Yemen Government regarding regional stability.”

CNN has also reached out to the Saudi Embassy in Washington for comment.

The swift fall of Mocha and the lack of resistance have led to finger-pointing and recriminations among US allies.

“The failure this time is not with the Yemenis,” a regional source told CNN on Thursday. “It’s a disaster made in (Washington) DC and Riyadh.

The regional source told CNN that it was “a complete failure of political leadership” amid fierce squabbling and delayed decision-making in Riyadh.

“There was not one air strike throughout the day yesterday (by Saudi support forces), although there were minute-by-minute updates,” the regional source added. “It’s a Saudi-American f**k up of epic proportions.”

US President Donald Trump met with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh on May 13, 2025, during the president’s multi-nation tour of the Gulf. Win McNamee/Getty Images

Not everyone agrees. Mohammed al-Basha, who has served as an adviser to the US government and private sector on risks emerging from the Arabian Peninsula, argues that blame also rests with Yemeni leaders, whose internal divisions jeopardized their defenses.

“This goes back to a deeper problem in the anti-Huthi coalition,” the DC-based told CNN. “There is no political cohesion.”

“I think everybody was aware of the Huthis’ push towards the west coast. The writings on the wall were very clear,” he added. “There’s no united command and control in Yemen.”

Huthi fighters arrived in Mocha on Thursday to find Yemeni battalions that were severely depleted – their rosters were filled with “ghost names” receiving salaries, and the actual strength of the army was only about 20% of what it was on paper, a Western source with knowledge of the operations told CNN.

That was compounded by the fact that the United Arab Emirates – once a member of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen – withdrew its remaining forces from the country in January, after Saudi Arabia called for them to leave amid a dispute. And Saudi Arabia did not backfill those troop barracks and bases.

“It doesn’t make sense. I mean, you have the main backer of the militaries on the ground … who are really doing all of this work for 10 years, and suddenly you ask them to leave, and you don’t fill that vacuum,” Al-Bidh of Yemen’s Southern Transitional Council added. “It’s just lack of strategy and poor management.”

The senior Yemeni official told CNN on Friday that he had “warned CENTCOM repeatedly over the past few days, including yesterday, that the situation was becoming critical.” CNN has reached out to CENTCOM for response.

A sunken vessel is seen at the surface of the water in the port of Mocha the day after an attack by the Huthis on August 9, 2026. Strikes by the Iran-backed Huthi rebels have been happening on Yemen’s west coast for weeks. Khaled Ziad/AFP/Getty Images

CENTCOM chief Adm. Brad Cooper was in Saudi Arabia on Thursday for coordination meetings, two sources familiar said. CENTCOM declined to comment, citing operational security reasons.

The Saudi military had been put on high alert three weeks ago, sources told CNN, but they didn’t move key air command personnel into place. The Western source with knowledge of the battle said that Saudi Arabia never deployed the necessary service personnel to control and direct combat aircraft in the event of a serious attack.

“The Saudis threw the Yemenis under the bus,” the Western source told CNN on Thursday.

CNN has reached out to the Saudi Arabian information ministry for comment on those allegations.

The failure to defend Mocha and Perim is even more confounding in light of the recent news – reported exclusively by CNN – that more than 100 US military advisers were sent to Saudi Arabia providing intelligence and targeting support to the Kingdom in its military campaign, according to five sources familiar with the operations.

The US military personnel are working as part of a newly established joint forces command, which was formed in recent weeks amid signs Iran was ramping up its own efforts to aid Huthi attacks, said one of the sources, a US official. That official estimated the total number of US personnel in Saudia Arabia at roughly 200 troops.

The capture of the Red Sea assets gives the Huthis far greater maneuverability and leverage, as it opens up new locations from which the Iran-backed rebels can launch boats and attacks.

Asked what comes next, al-Basha, the risk analyst, told CNN: “I think the Huthis are going to be moving east. We are seeing today, via satellite and via OSINT (open-source intelligence) photography… that the Huthis are mobilizing.”

An adviser to Iran’s supreme leader on Friday described the Huthi advance on the west coast of Yemen as a “clear victory,” writing in a post on X that “the American people and Washington’s allies are paying the price for the economic crisis and Trump’s ambitions.”

CNN’s Sarah El Sirgany, Mostafa Salem, Nadeen Ebrahim, Jennifer Hansler, Zachary Cohen, Katie Bo Lillis and Kylie Atwood contributed to this report.

World.title: Even if it’s real, Trump’s new Ukraine push is already being undermined by events
World.content:
Events since the United States revived its Ukraine peace bid say more about its chances than the sunny rhetoric that accompanies it.

President Donald Trump told reporters Wednesday that Russian President Vladimir Putin “is wanting to make a deal.” He added that if Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky “is wanting to make a deal, that’d be very nice.”

But there’s nothing nice about the reality in Eastern Europe.

On Wednesday, a Russian jet-propelled drone breached Moldovan airspace and delayed the departure of a plane taking Zelensky to Norway.

And after Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff left Kyiv after a peace shuttle visit that followed a trip to Moscow, Putin’s missiles and drones on Tuesday ended a three-day halt to attacks with a new onslaught that killed five people.

Special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner attend a meeting with Ukrainian president in Kyiv on September 6, 2026, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Genya Savilov/AFP via Getty Images

The Moldovan incident didn’t appear to be a direct threat to Zelensky — although the country’s US ambassador, Vladislav Kulminski, told CNN’s Jim Sciutto the incursion by a Russian surveillance drone was likely “not an accident.” And the raids on Kyiv were just the latest act of perpetual horror inflicted on civilians.

Off-key remarks

These incidents underscore the vicious brutality of a war that CNN reported Tuesday is costing Russia some 40,000 troops each month, citing Western intelligence agencies. The conflict is also showing an alarming new propensity to spread beyond its borders amid rising fears of a NATO-Russia clash in Europe.

So any serious, sincere effort by the Trump administration to reengage in diplomacy after its attention was dragged away by the Iran war would be welcome. The president’s critics mock his hyperbolic claims to have ended multiple wars. But a fair peace in Ukraine would be a monumental achievement.

Still, public signs out of the US diplomatic duo’s meetings with Putin and Zelensky offer little hope that the entrenched factors that extended the war for more than four years have eased. And a sequence of off-key remarks and gestures raise doubts about their grasp on the nature of the war, Russia’s motives and an approach that mirrors a repeatedly failed real estate transaction.

In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia’s President Vladimir Putin attends a meeting with Witkoff and Kushner in Moscow on September 5, 2026. Mikhail Metzel/Pool/Sputnik/AFP via Getty Images

In Moscow, Witkoff’s deferential and glowing comments to Putin about how their meetings would be a highlight to remember in retirement were startling given the Russian leader’s ruthless assault on Ukrainians and warnings among US allies of Kremlin covert sabotage threatening their territory.

Kushner later spoke about the need to find a “win-win” situation for both Putin and Zelensky that would convince them stop fighting.

This might be seen as the pragmatic touch of a dealmaker who must force each side to make distasteful choices in service of peace.

But delivering a “win” to Russia would validate its choice to wage an illegal and unprovoked war to obliterate a neighbor’s territory, history and culture. And Putin restated that the “root causes” of the conflict still need to be addressed. That’s Russia’s code for ending Ukraine’s sovereignty and demilitarization while Moscow demands land in eastern provinces its troops are yet to conquer — all of which would be impossible for Zelensky to accept.

Trump’s comments, meanwhile, reflect nearly two years of blithe and demonstrably disproven assessments of a war that keeps getting worse. “The holdup is two people hating each other,” he told reporters at Andrews Air Force base — a reference to Putin and Zelensky that ignored the complex political and historical factors cited by the Russian leader when he launched the war. “I know about deals, and these are two people that are tired of fighting. It could happen.”

Despite his optimism, the prospect of new and effective US diplomacy appears as elusive as the US delivering on Trump’s apparent offer earlier in the summer to allow Ukraine to license the manufacture of Patriot anti-missile interceptors.

There are also fresh doubts about US motives amid opacity surrounding what exactly happened in the meetings with Putin, which took place amid already deep intrigue over a recent visit to Russia by CIA Director John Ratcliffe.

Various leaks have suggested the US spy chief warned Moscow that the Ukraine war was going poorly for Russia, and to not even think about moving on any NATO territory. But it’s impossible to know for sure what is going on between Moscow and Washington — or between Putin and Trump, who had a telephone conversation this week.

The US president’s history of flattering the Russian leader has long cast doubt on the administration’s motives on Ukraine.

Meanwhile, Russia sent hints after the meeting about future economic opportunities between the two nations, renewing fears in Europe that Trump is more interested in deals, perhaps related to Russian mineral and natural resources, than a just peace in Ukraine.

And any sense that the US is an honest broker was undermined recently when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent partly blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian infrastructure, alongside the Iran war, for high oil prices. This reinforced impressions the US sees Ukraine’s self-defense as an irritant rather than a legitimate right.

Emergency and municipal services clear debris and work to restore order at the site of severe destruction following a massive overnight Russian ballistic missile attack on August 19, 2026, in Kyiv, Ukraine. Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images

‘A conclusion acceptable to both sides’

On Wednesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in Colombia that there was a chance over the next few weeks to “maybe reach a conclusion there that that’s acceptable to both sides.” But he conceded that a lot of work needed to be done.

Most wars end eventually. And the terrible toll of this one for both sides may eventually weigh on negotiations. Ukraine has not only survived but is showing an increasing capacity to project force inside Russia. But Russia has also made recent advances on the battlefield, CNN reported on Wednesday — though its casualty figures are so extreme that even Putin may have to take notice.

Could the war’s shifting dynamics unlock flexibility that has so far been elusive?
