World.title: Trade 'war' or not, are Canada and the United States now dug in?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer might not like to think of it as a trade "war," but whatever you call it — a difference of opinion? an incongruity? the unpleasantness? — it's now been going on for more than 19 months.

In February 2025, Donald Trump, in defiance of a free trade deal he himself signed in 2018, first announced tariffs on a number of Canadian products.

And it seems now it could be several more months before hostilities are reduced, let alone ceased.

"I think it is more likely than not that the current situation remains unchanged until the end of the year," said Wolfgang Alschner, a professor of business and trade law at the University of Ottawa.

"From the latest rounds of talks, we know that there is a potential landing zone but also that positions are currently too far removed to easily reach an agreement. The status quo is painful, but not so painful as to drive either side into forcing a change in position."

Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Mark Carney described the latest round of American tariffs announced earlier this week as " relatively modest ," at least "in the context of other things that the U.S. administration has done."

That might suggest Carney doesn't see a need to respond with further measures against American imports. The recent cycle of escalation may have reached a kind of equilibrium.

Carney also said Canada is "always ready to strike a fair deal." But if one is willing to entertain war analogies, it might be said that both sides now seem dug in.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc and United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer leave a meeting in Washington, D.C., in mid-August. (Kelly Geraldine Malone/The Canadian Press)

The fact that the principal negotiators — Greer on the American side, Dominic LeBlanc and Janice Charette for the Canadian government — have largely avoided the political fray and acted professionally may serve to keep a door open to negotiations, suggests Meredith Lilly, a professor of international economic policy at Carleton University and a former foreign policy and trade adviser to Stephen Harper.

Lilly also sees a few potential "trigger moments" in the months ahead that could restart talks. If the United States and Mexico were to come to an agreement on their issues, for instance, that could put pressure on Canada. The results of the midterm elections in the United States could also change the political calculus on the American side. And lingering in the distance is an American threat to impose new auto and truck tariffs on Jan. 1, 2027.

Trump could also conceivably try to force the issue with a new threat of tariffs, like he did this summer.

Perhaps less optimistically, there is Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew's account that provinces have been told to plan for "two-plus years" of turmoil.

Is anyone winning this fight?

American officials may believe that U.S. economic power ultimately gives them the advantage — U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has likened Canada to a "yippy" dachshund trying to pick a fight with a German shepherd.

But both Paul Krugman , the American economist, and Roland Paris , the Canadian foreign policy scholar, argued this week that Canada may have the motivational or political advantage, with Canadians largely united against a clear and potentially existential threat.

"Trade wars test not only economic strength but also political resolve," Paris wrote.

Recent polls have shown high support among Canadians for taking a tough approach with the United States. And the Angus Reid Institute found a significant bump in support for Carney's Liberals in the wake of trade talks collapsing.

That may strengthen Carney's hand at the negotiating table, but could the Canadian public's reaction conceivably make it harder to get to some kind of deal with the United States?

WATCH | Carney 'looking closely' at Trump's import bans, tariffs: 'We're looking closely' at Trump's import bans and tariffs, Carney says | Duration 1:03 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday that the government is looking at U.S. President Donald Trump's recent measures which include bans on Canadian imports including most alcohol products and new 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products. 'We fully recognize that for individual companies and in individual sectors these are significant, and there's a response there,' Carney said.

Before negotiations were formally suspended, Charette reportedly warned her American counterparts that a breakdown in talks and the imposition of new American tariffs could push discussions over a cliff — the public and political reaction, she said, would only shrink the Canadian side's room to negotiate.

David Coletto of Abacus Data has now made a similar argument, suggesting that public sentiment could be a serious impediment to a new deal.

"My sincere hope is that the temperature is turned down in both countries," Lilly said. "In particular, the president really needs to reduce this very aggressive social media campaign that he's pursuing. It makes it politically very difficult, if not impossible, for the Canadian side to engage."

Lilly said she wonders if it would be harder now to even get back to whatever deal the two sides were broadly in agreement about when Trump first announced in August that one was likely .

A fight that will take the measure of Carney and Canada

Some Canadians may trust Carney enough to defer to his judgment on what constitutes a good deal — or the best possible deal under the circumstances. And public opinion polling would suggest he has ample political capital to draw on right now.

But no level of support ever amounts to a blank check. The Carney government may have been acknowledging as much with its decision this week to not move forward with at least some of its most controversial proposals to amend environmental assessment laws.

For the sake of maintaining a strong hand, there might be more Carney could do in the days and weeks ahead.

The Liberal government obviously didn't heed the Conservative opposition's calls to reconvene Parliament, while releasing the text of any draft agreement, as the Conservatives also demanded, may have been impractical or unwise.

But there is also something to be said for the emphasis Conservatives have put on transparency, not only as a matter of accountability, but for the sake of building trust. That might be particularly important for Carney if this fight is to only get longer and harder — and after he was criticized for his handling of the agreement to open the Gordie Howe Bridge.

On a larger scale, the collapse of trade talks and everything that has ensued over the last two weeks may only add credence to Carney's contention that there has been a "rupture" and that Canada's "old relationship" with the United States is over.

Much of the onus for responding to that falls on the prime minister, and it's still too early to know exactly what path Canada will set out on.

WATCH | Poilievre calls on PM to release cost analysis of counter-tariffs: Poilievre calls on PM to release cost analysis of counter-tariffs | Duration 1:15 When asked at a news conference if he supports the federal government's planned counter-tariffs on the U.S., Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Canadians need to see how much the counter-tariffs will cost families and businesses, and what measures Prime Minister Mark Carney is taking to offset those costs.

But it is perhaps not too early to wonder if this moment is already leaving a mark on the Canadian psyche.

According to polling by the Environics Institute , Canadians held a decidedly favourable view of the United States for some 20 years, from the early 1980s to the early 2000s — from the presidency of Ronald Reagan through to the election of George W. Bush.

Canadian attitudes then plummeted around the time of the American invasion of Iraq, but more or less fully recovered with the election of Barack Obama as president.

There was another marked drop when Trump became president. But unlike the rebound when Obama came to office, the Canadian view of the United States did not fully recover when Joe Biden succeeded Trump, suggesting perhaps that some lasting damage was done.

If anything, the second four years of Trump have been more contentious among Canadians than the first four. And so even if a deal is reached in the next few months, it might be a long while before this trade war — for that is how people on this side of the border will surely remember it — is either forgiven or forgotten.

World.title: Zelenskyy describes Canada-U.S. tensions as 'strange,' draws comparison to Ukraine and Russia
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy calls U.S. threats to annex Canada 'very dangerous' and urges the two neighbours to work their differences.

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday described the unfolding tension between Canada and the United States as a "strange" sight to behold, drawing a comparison to his own country's fight with neighbouring Russia.

In a wide-ranging, exclusive interview with CBC News, Zelenskyy described American threats to annex Canada as "dangerous" and said both countries have a duty to resolve their differences.

"Strange," the president told CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, speaking to the tension in North America.

"It's very dangerous [when] there are some problems between neighbours and we [Ukraine and Russia] are the example."

Russia and Ukraine are, like Canada and the U.S., neighbours with a lengthy border and history, though their current tensions are vastly different: Moscow's four-and-a-half year invasion of Ukraine is a deadly war, while the issues in Ottawa and Washington are largely economic.

"I think that the United States and Canada, will have to have … very constructive dialogue. They have to have it. It's dangerous. [There's] no choice," he said.

Zelenskyy's remarks come at the end of a visit to Canada, which was focused on Ukrainian air defences and winter preparation as the war with Russia enters its fourth year.

He spoke about Ukraine's new strategic partnership with Canada, efforts to revive peace talks with Moscow and his view on any potential face-to-face meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

WATCH | No 'win-win' in war: Zelenskyy says war holds no 'win-win' scenario for Russia and Ukraine | Duration 1:24 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejects comments from U.S. officials about finding a 'win-win' solution to the war with Russia, saying too many lives have already been lost.

100-year partnership with Canada

Canada and Ukraine signed a long-term strategic and political partnership on Thursday that lays the foundation for the construction of millions of drones to defend both countries. The declaration established a 100-year partnership that stretches across defence and security, trade and investment, as well as energy and critical minerals.

On Friday, Zelenskyy said the length of the deal with Canada, one of Ukraine's most vocal supporters in the war, was chosen as a symbolic gesture.

"It's about roots," he said. "It says that we will be together for a long period of time. Our children and our grandchildren, we will work together. We will share the experience of security [and] a lot of different things."

WATCH | No desire to meet Putin: Why Zelenskyy has no desire to sit down with Vladimir Putin | Duration 2:02 Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has no desire to sit across the negotiating table from Russian President Vladimir Putin since only Russia's defeat will stop his aggression.

Zelenskyy's visit to Canada came not only as the relationship between Canada and the U.S. hit another low, but as the Trump administration renews its push to end Russia's war in Ukraine.

After U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump 's son-in-law Jared Kushner discussed potential proposals to end the war during visits to Moscow and Kyiv, Trump said the Russian leader wanted to make a deal.

But on Friday, Zelenskyy expressed doubts the Kremlin is interested in ending the war. He said he believes Russia maintains its goal of occupying Ukraine, but said he would sit face-to-face with Putin if trilateral negotiations came to fruition — though he said he doesn't expect any movement until after Russian parliamentary elections on Sept. 20.

"It's not my wish … Better to sit with my family," he said of a possible meeting with the Russian president. He described Putin as an "enemy," but said sitting down with an enemy "can bring us closer" to peace.

Diplomatic efforts to end the war have been stalled for months, while both countries have escalated attacks on the other. Moscow has continued its bombardment of Ukrainian cities, while Kyiv has intensified its strikes inside Russia in an effort to reduce its economic ability to continue with the war.

"To be honest, there is no win-win in this war. It can't be so because [there's been] so many human losses. It stopped being win-win at the first day of this war between us," Zelenskyy said.

"The most important victory for everybody, it's not for Ukraine and Russia ... For the world, it's peace. To stop this war. And this is a victory for a human lives."

World.title: Your guide to the U.S. midterms, and why they're crucial for Donald Trump
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The upcoming U.S. midterm elections will determine whether Republican President Donald Trump will be free to pursue his agenda during his final two years in office or whether he'll face constraints from a Congress where the Democrats hold new power.

Here's what you need to know about the midterms.

Why do U.S. midterms matter?

The midterms are a contest for control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, which together make up the U.S. Congress.

The party that controls the Senate holds sway over presidential appointments to cabinet, the courts and senior posts in federal agencies. The party that controls the House can launch impeachment proceedings and has the power to initiate budget bills .

If one party controls both, it has broad influence over legislation as well as the potential to thwart some presidential actions.

How is the race shaping up?

The Democrats are generally excited about their prospects in the midterms and the Republicans a little worried.

History gives the Republicans plenty of reason to fret. The incumbent president's party has suffered a net loss of seats in Congress in all but two midterms since the 1930s. The only exceptions were Bill Clinton (1998) and George W. Bush (2002), when each had sky-high approval ratings.

Trump's approval rating is anything but sky-high .

What's at stake?

With slim majorities in each chamber, the Republicans have little wiggle room to lose seats and still maintain their hold on Congress.

The Democrats need to flip just four districts to take control of the House (if they hold on to all their current seats). The Democrats also need to take just four Republican-held states to win control of the Senate. But that's a tougher task than flipping the House because there are far fewer Senate seats up for election and winning each requires a statewide victory.

A person votes in a primary election in Oak Park, Mich., on Aug. 4. (Nic Antaya/The Associated Press)

All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are up for grabs, as members of the House are elected to two-year terms.

Only 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election this fall. U.S. senators are elected to six-year terms.

When does voting happen?

Midterms, like the word implies, come at the two-year mark of a president's four-year term. This year, midterm election day is Nov. 3.

Many U.S. voters will choose to vote before then, either in advance polls or by mail-in ballots, a method the Trump administration is trying to restrict.

You may also have heard that people across the U.S. have been voting at various times since the spring in primaries, which are the contests to select each party's candidates. In most states, only people who are registered Republicans or Democrats can vote in the party's primaries.

How does Trump factor in?

Trump is not on the ballot in the midterms, but his influence on the campaign will be unavoidable.

Only one president si nce 1950 has headed into a midterm with an approval rating below 40 per cent: George W. Bush in 2006 (at 37 per cent), when his Republicans lost 30 seats in the House and six in the Senate.

Despite his low polling numbers, Trump is vowing to give "a lot of speeches" in states and districts where the races are tight to help Republican candidates. Some of those candidates are quietly asking the White House to keep him away, according to reporting by Politico.

What are the key issues in the midterms?

While U.S. polls differ slightly on the precise numbers, there's a strong thread of consistency suggesting the top issue of concern among voters right now is the cost of living.

Whether it's gas prices pushed up as a result of the war against Iran or the prices of consumer goods rising because of Trump's tariffs, pocketbook issues predominate the midterm polling.

Only one U.S. president since 1950 has held a polling approval rating below 40 per cent on the day of a midterm election. Trump is on track to be the second. (Mark Schiefelbein/The Associated Press)

Trump, as the dominant figure in U.S. politics for the past decade, will undoubtedly be an issue, particularly for moderate Republican or swing voters who backed him in the 2024 presidential election but have soured on him since then, according to polling.

Turnout in midterms is always lower than during presidential election years, so each party will be striving for ways to motivate their base. For the Democrats, weakening Trump's power could be that driving force. For the Republicans, stoking fear about what a Democratic-controlled Congress would do to the economy is a key advertising message.

Where are the key Senate races?

Of the 35 Senate seats up for election this time, fewer than 10 are considered by campaign analysts to be at risk of changing hands.

The Republicans are considered most vulnerable in North Carolina and Maine, but polling suggests they also are in tough to hang on to their Senate seats in Ohio, Alaska, Iowa and even Texas, where no Democrat has won a statewide election since 1988.

The Democrats' biggest challenges to hold appear to be in the Senate races in Michigan and New Hampshire.

Where are the key House races?

More than 80 per cent of House seats are considered safe for either the Republicans or the Democrats, according to the University of Virginia Center for Politics newsletter Crystal Ball, which has forecast and analyzed every election for U.S. president, House, Senate and state governors since 2002.

That political inertia leaves only a few dozen districts across the country truly "in play," as campaign strategists describe races where the outcome is in doubt.

Crystal Ball has labelled 17 Republican-held districts as toss-ups, including three in Pennsylvania and two in Michigan. All will be races to watch because they're prime targets for the Democrats as they try to win back control of the House.

World.title: Two uniforms, one deadly morning: How this firefighter and former soldier is reflecting on 9/11
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Twenty-five years ago, Shawn Matheson had a foot in two worlds.

As a firefighter with Mississauga Fire and Emergency Services, he and his colleagues watched the collapse of the twin towers in New York City live on television with a deeper appreciation of the horror than most others.

A an officer in the reserves, Matheson knew instinctively where events were headed.

"Like any of us in the fire service, we were trying to figure out just what was all going down and what it meant," Matheson said.

"And I guess my thoughts were sort of switching between the tragedy of what I was seeing unfold on live TV ... as well [as] about being a soldier and what that meant."

Like countless others this week, Matheson has been reflecting on the attacks of Sept. 11, 2001, that resulted in the deaths of nearly 3,000 people — including 24 Canadian citizens.

Being both a firefighter and a soldier has made him keenly aware of the risks and the cost of service, which eventually led him to volunteer for mental health non-profit Wounded Warriors Canada.

As fate would have it, on the day of the attacks a portion of his station was asked to spell off firefighters at a station near Pearson International Airport as the U.S. airspace was closing and aircraft were touching down all across Canada.

The attacks happened on a Tuesday, which also happened to be parade night for his Toronto-based reserve unit, the Governor General's Horse Guards (GGHG).

It was, he said, a surreal feeling.

'Those hours of the unknown'

"It was a very unique day to be putting on our uniform, realizing that in all likelihood, Canada would be going to war," said Matheson, who started out as a full-time armoured soldier in the 1980s and served in Bosnia before becoming a reservist and firefighter.

"In those hours of the unknown, you know, what we realized was, who knows what was going to happen next."

In the weeks after the terrorist attacks, Matheson travelled with fellow firefighters to New York to attend funerals as remains were recovered from the ruins.

"There's some incredible strong connections in the fire community amongst different departments, not only in Canada, but south of the border," he recalled. "So there were firefighters in Mississauga that had friends in the New York Fire Department [and the] surrounding departments around New York City. They played in hockey tournaments together."

While they were at Ground Zero, the remains of six more people were recovered, Matheson said.

The sense of loss was palpable.

During the Afghan war, Matheson commanded the Governor General's Horse Guards and watched as 14 of his soldiers were deployed overseas to fight. (Wounded Warrior Canada)

Later, as Canada's involvement in the Afghan war became deeper and deadlier, he commanded the GGHG and watched as 14 soldiers from his unit were sent to buttress regular force units fighting in Kandahar.

Luckily, he said, they all returned.

As the 25th anniversary of 9/11 unfolded, Matheson was on a Wounded Warriors fundraising bike ride through Canadian First World War battlefields in Belgium.

He couldn't help but reflect on how support services for both the military and first responders have evolved since the events two and a half decades ago.

Recognition that first responders are affected by the harrowing events they face, Matheson said, is something that was long overdue.

And in many ways, for Matheson, that was the lesson of 9/11.

"They do get exposed to a lot of trauma," said Matheson. "These people on fire rigs and police cars and ambulance buses. they're going to war every day. They don't know at the end of the day, the end of a shift, how things are going to play out in terms of going back home."

World.title: Céline Dion has electrified Paris — and beyond — for her big comeback
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's become a daily ritual in Paris for the past few weeks: crowds gathering outside the famed Royal Monceau hotel near the Arc de Triomphe, patiently waiting for a glimpse of arguably the world's biggest superstar right now — Céline Dion.

"Céline, Céline, Céline!" the crowds have chanted as she's appeared in various outfits, waving, signing autographs and, sometimes, even singing.

Paris, the City of Light, is electric with anticipation for the singer's return to the stage on Saturday, the first of her residency concerts in Paris, which many thought would be impossible.

"I have never, ever seen a comeback like Céline Dion's comeback in Paris, never," said Léna Lutaud, a culture reporter for France's oldest national newspaper Le Figaro.

"Paris is really a Céline Dion city right now."

Walk the length of the Champs-Élysées or along the famed Seine river and you won't miss the signs.

"Bonjour, Paris, Merci!" accompanied by a giant photo of Dion.

The initial series of 16 concerts in September and October will be followed by 10 additional shows starting in May of 2027, all at Europe's biggest indoor concert venue, Plenitude Arena. (Sarah Leavitt/CBC)

Besides the daily interactions outside Dion's hotel, Paris has been preparing for this comeback for weeks.

Themed boat rides along the Seine, pre-parties ahead of the concert, and of course, massive karaoke parties.

"She's the queen, obviously, and we've been waiting for her for such a long time," says Natacha Campana, founder of L'Écran Pop, which hosted a karaoke night with more than 2,000 guests.

"We love singing Céline in karaoke, for sure, because those songs can liberate us and it feels good."

A long-awaited comeback

When Dion stepped off a New Jersey stage in March 2020 during part of her Courage World Tour, few had any idea it would be years before she’d perform again, let alone the shocking revelation of a diagnosis that could very well have ended her career.

"I'm sorry it's taken me so long to reach out to you," Dion said in a video addressed to her fans recorded in December 2022.

"Recently, I've been diagnosed with a very rare neurological disorder called stiff person syndrome."

The disorder can cause severe muscle spasms, including of the vocal chords, which she let the world see in an Amazon Prime documentary.

But Dion says she was determined to come back , and she did, closing out the 2024 Paris Olympic Games opening ceremony, on the Eiffel Tower.

WATCH | Céline Dion opens up about coping with stiff person syndrome: Céline Dion: I Will Sing Again | Duration 44:10 In this intensely personal, candid and revealing exclusive from the team at The National, Céline Dion opens up to CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault about coping with stiff person syndrome, losing the voice that has guided her life and how she is determined to perform again. [I Am: Celine Dion, the documentary featured in this interview, premieres June 25 on Prime Video.]

A full return to concerts in front of audiences was undetermined, however, until March.

"This year, I'm getting the best gift of my life. I'm getting the chance to see you, to perform for you once again, in Paris," Dion wrote on her social media, announcing the residency on her 58th birthday.

The initial series of 16 concerts in September and October will be followed by 10 additional shows starting in May of 2027, all at Europe's biggest indoor concert venue, Plenitude Arena.

Dion fan to see their 100th show

As Estevam Peric landed in Paris, he says he felt a rush of emotions.

There was fatigue from the overnight flight from Montreal certainly, but mainly, he says he felt overwhelmingly excited.

The self-proclaimed Dion superfan made the trek across the Atlantic to see his favourite celebrated diva — for the 100th time.

Estevam Peric, a self-proclaimed Céline Dion superfan, says he travelled to Paris to see the singer for the 100th time. (Sarah Leavitt/CBC)

"I'm very, very, nervous, very excited, very emotional," Peric said, holding back tears.

"It's the soundtrack of my life. I've been following her since my teenage era, and each song, each album, there's always something special that connects to my life each time."

He says he's met Dion at least 10 times, describing her as humble and kind. Every concert is different, he says.

"The voice, it's like oxygen and the rest is just magic."

Peric has managed to snag tickets for seven of her concerts in Paris, which is no easy feat as all the performances quickly sold out. The arena has a capacity of up to 45,000 seats.

Dion waves to fans as she exits the Royal Monceau hotel in Paris on Sept. 3, ahead of a series of concerts in the French capital. (Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP/Getty Images)

Lead-up to first concert filled with excitement

Dion's love affair with France spans decades. French songwriter Eddy Marnay was among one of the very first to work alongside a teenage Dion. She also has a penchant for fashion, often partnering with French haute couture labels, like Dior and Chanel.

"I understand she's a huge star in Quebec, but here she's also a very big star because she's the only star at her level to have lots of great songs, both in English and in French," says Lutaud from Le Figaro.

It's that star power that has so many fans invested in Dion's comeback, with the hope of more concerts to come.

World.title: Jean Chrétien says 'we bow to no one' in fiery 9/11 speech in Gander, N.L.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former prime minister Jean Chrétien had a message for 'our American friends' while speaking in Gander, N.L., at the 25-year commemoration of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. 'Canadians are tolerant and kind,' said Chrétien at the event, which was attended by U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra. '[But] never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination. And never, never mistake our kindness for softness.'

'Never mistake our generosity for weakness,' Chrétien says at 9/11 memorial

Former Canadian prime minister Jean Chrétien drew thunderous applause on Friday during a fiery and patriotic speech in Gander, N.L., where many had gathered at a sports arena to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, and the legendary humanitarian response as thousands of stranded air travellers had their flights diverted to more than a dozen Canadian airports.

Chrétien was the final speaker during a lengthy and nationally televised event. He began his speech by describing Sept. 11, 2001 "like a nightmare … one that can never be erased." And then recounted how Canadians stepped up, fought side-by-side with U.S. troops in Afghanistan — which drew loud applause.

But then, Chrétien's became the first person to speak on a subject no one else who stepped to the microphone would: the fractured political relationship between Canada and the United States.

"We bow to no one," Chrétien said to an audience that included Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. ambassador to Canada.

"And the more we are insulted or threatened and abused, the more we will stand up for ourselves and stand united."

It was a powerful moment in an two-hour event filled with stories of remembrance, honour and sacrifice.

Trade war ongoing

U.S. President Donald Trump initiated a trade war with Canada, and has hurled insults at Prime Minister Mark Carney. Trump has also threatened Canada’s sovereignty by expressing his desire to make Canada’s the 51st U.S. state.

Hoekstra has amplified the rhetoric through his own public comments and by sharing Trump’s social media posts.

Hoekstra avoided the issue of trade and tariffs during his visit to Gander, and praised the longstanding partnership between the two countries. He offered thanks for the kindness and compassion shown to thousands of stranded American travellers in the wake of the terrorist attacks.

"This is to say one more time, thank you," he said, when asked about his visit to the central Newfoundland town. "We’ll get back to the economic issues from, at least our standpoint, when we get past 9/11."

Former Prime Minister Jean Chrétien received multiple standing ovations during his speech in Gander. (CBC)

Chrétien, 92, described the U.S. as a "neighbour and our closest friend," and said a massive rally in Ottawa in the days after the 9/11 attacks was "one of the most emotional moments of my life."

Chrétien’s government initiated the process in 2001 to invoke the so-called Article 5, which stipulates that an attack on one member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) is an attack on all members.

Chrétien also ordered Canadian troops into battle in Afghanistan, fighting alongside U.S. allies, and 158 of those soldiers were killed, including 13 from Newfoundland and Labrador.

WATCH | Chrétien recounts his reaction to 9/11 to the CBC's Adrienne Arsenault: Jean Chrétien recounts his reaction to 9/11 and its aftermath | Duration 7:46 As Prime Minister during 9/11, Jean Chrétien faced criticism for waiting to visit the U.S. — a decision he says he made out of respect for the victims. In a conversation with The National's Adrienne Arsenault, Chrétien recounts the decisions he made during and after the attacks and how they affected the Canada-U.S. relationship.

"Our friends were hurt, and we were hurting with them," Chrétien said. "I was proud of how we stepped up."

He described the response to 9/11 as "the Canadian way."

But 25 years later, the world has changed, and Canada’s relationship with its powerful southern neighbour has also grown more distant.

So Chrétien concluded his speech — which received no less than three standing ovations — with a strong message "to our American friends."

He said Canada is an open, generous country, and the response to 9/11 in communities such as Gander is an example of this. But he said Canada’s generosity should not be mistaken for weakness.

Former prime minister Jean Chrétien and U.S Ambassador Pete Hoekstra embrace after a fiery speech by Chrétien at Gander's 9/11 commemorative ceremony. (CBC)

"Never mistake our tolerance for lack of determination. And never mistake our kindness for softness. We know who we are and we are proud of it," he said.

Chrétien said building a country like Canada, welcoming people from around the globe, and caring for the weakest, "is a sign of strength."

Chrétien said his "honest" message was "from one friend to another," and he called on the U.S. to "respect the friendship" and "be a good neighbour."

He concluded with the following words in French: "Long live the United States and long live Canada."

World.title: Spain's soccer federation will fund egg freezing. Is this a win for female athletes?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Should professional sporting bodies encourage female athletes to freeze their eggs?

That's part of the evolving conversation around athletes and motherhood as Spain's football federation becomes the latest organization to support fertility treatment for female players.

As part of its agreement, the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) said Tuesday that it will cover the full cost of egg-freezing treatment for all international players who have been called up at least twice.

"It's important that female athletes feel they don't have to choose between their professional and personal lives," Barcelona midfielder Patri Guijarro said at Tuesday's announcement.

For female athletes, the window of peak performance and the window for fertility overlap, which researchers have noted has often made athletes feel as though they have to choose one or the other.

An Instagram post by Chelsea FC Women from Aug. 14, 2026, announces the team's partnership with Fertility Plus. (@ChelseaFCW/Instagram)

The RFEF's move follows similar fertility provisions recently announced by several other soccer teams and federations — s uch as the National Women's Soccer League and the Chelsea FC women's team — and other leagues like the WNBA and Women's Tennis Association.

But while fertility preservation measures like egg freezing are typically presented as another way to give women in elite sport greater freedom to decide if and when to become mothers, some experts and advocates worry it could perpetuate the attitude that women should wait for retirement to do so.

Exciting step, but more supports needed: Olympian

In some ways, any time a sporting body or team announces fertility funding, it's an exciting step forward for women athletes, says two-time Olympic rower Jill Moffatt, the co-founder of the Canadian non-profit MOMentum, which supports athlete mothers.

At the same time, Moffatt says it's only a true feminist "win" if they offer the same level of support, such as maternity leave and child care options, for athletes who choose to have children while competing at a high level of sport.

"Otherwise, it's kind of a double-edged sword," she told CBC News.

"Physiologically, it's totally doable to have a child and come back and compete at the highest level … but there are still so many barriers."

Canada's Jill Moffatt, back, and Jenny Casson, compete in the lightweight women's double sculls rowing heat at the 2024 Summer Olympics in Vaires-sur-Marne, France. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)

Moffatt says it's also important to remember that for many 2SLGBTQ+ athletes, IVF is sometimes a necessary part of family planning regardless of whether they choose to wait. So in that sense, she says funding egg freezing and fertility treatments is a "huge win."

There's also the fact that fertility treatments are expensive, Moffatt says, and many female athletes probably couldn't afford it without funding. For instance, CBC Sports has previously reported that 65 per cent of PWHL players earned less than $60,000 annually last season.

Most Olympic and Paralympic athletes are "just trying to keep their lights on," Moffatt said

'Felt incompatible with a career'

For many female athletes, being offered the option at all may feel like a major step forward given what researchers have noted is a longstanding attitude in sports culture that getting pregnant is the end of an athlete's career.

"Pregnancy and motherhood have long felt incompatible with a career as a pro or elite athlete because policies were either lacking or treated women unfairly," Allison Sandmeyer-Graves, the CEO of Canadian Women & Sport, told CBC News.

As a result, women who wanted to start families would often end their careers early or wait until retirement, she says, adding that waiting too long also carries a risk to a woman's ability to conceive.

For some, waiting to start their families until they're done playing is the right choice, and egg freezing offers them some assurances, Sandmeyer-Graves said.

That's echoed by Margie Davenport, a kinesiology professor at the University of Alberta who recently helped FIFA develop guidelines to support pregnant and postpartum soccer players.

"Pregnancy during an active playing career isn't the right choice for every athlete. Egg freezing has gained momentum as a practical alternative for those who prefer to wait until retirement," Davenport told CBC News.

" Ensuring female athletes don't have to choose between a career and motherhood is fundamental to athlete wellbeing and the growth of women’s sport."

And that's reassuring, according to British rugby player Natasha Hunt.

"It's the thought process behind it, like it's an OK thing to do. Like, we want to support you in this journey as well and that your contracts will still be there," Hunt said in Thursday's episode of The Good, The Scaz & The Rugby podcast.

In the same episode, when asked if she would freeze her eggs, British player Megan Jones answered, "100 per cent, yes," but she said there should be more education around it.

WATCH | Paralympian on balancing motherhood and sports: Paralympian Leanne Taylor on balancing motherhood and sports | Duration 1:29 Canadian Para triathlete shares her experiences on social media as an athlete and new mom.

Medical, ethical considerations

Athlete education is also a concern for some medical experts, who have cautioned that egg retrieval is far from straightforward, involving hormone medications and a surgical procedure.

IVF is also not a fail-proof plan. Live birth rates for those who undergo at least one embryo transfer within a year can range between 38 and 50 per cent, according to a September 2025 news release from the Canadian Fertility and Andrology Society (CFAS) discussing the most recent findings from the Canadian Assisted Reproductive Technologies Register. CFAS noted that these rates vary by age, and success rates decline as age increases.

The CFAS release also said those findings show that the number of elective egg freezing procedures more than doubled between 2019 and 2024.

"There's no guarantee that when you defrost or thaw those eggs, turn them into embryos, that they'll actually be successful and result in a successful live birth," Dr. Lamia Zafrani, an athlete gynecologist in London, told Germany broadcaster DW this week.

Zafrani said that there are also ethical considerations when an organization offers egg freezing.

"It always does bring up the question of whether by offering egg freezing and fertility preservation, the underlying message is that you're telling your players 'don't get pregnant whilst you're working for us,' " Zafrani told DW.

Seattle Storms players Sue Bird, left, and Breanna Stewart talk during the WNBA team's media day in Seattle on May 9, 2018. The Storm teammates were among a half-dozen WNBA players who had frozen their eggs, according to the players union. (Elaine Thompson/The Associated Press)

That's why it's so important to also support athletes who are pregnant or postpartum, said Moffatt, with MOMentum. She says there needs to be more child care options, specialized physical training, breastfeeding facilities and acceptance around athletes bringing children to sporting events and training camps.

In 2025, the federal government changed its policy of treating pregnancy like an injury within the athlete funding model. Advocates called it a huge step for gender equity in sport.

"There is more work to be done in Canada and internationally on this topic, but we're heading in the right direction," Sandmeyer-Graves said Friday.

'Every choice comes with trade-offs'

Spain's football federation said Tuesday its agreement was not designed to discourage footballers from having children while they're active, but to offer another option so they don't have to rule out motherhood because of their sporting career.

It said the initiative complements existing work-life balance measures, including support that allows players who have become mothers to have their children close by during away trips, training camps and tournaments.

"Every choice comes with trade-offs," said Davenport, the University of Alberta researcher. These can include managing training through postpartum recovery, navigating uncertain success rates of egg preservation, or facing age-related fertility declines later in life.

But she says that ultimately, "true autonomy means recognizing that no single timeline fits every athlete."

World.title: B.C. judge tosses drug case, says U.S. agents broke law and violated Canadian sovereignty
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. federal agents pressured a Canadian into a money-laundering conspiracy while concealing their efforts from the RCMP, amounting to "shocking and flagrant" illegal behaviour and a violation of Canadian sovereignty, a B.C. judge has found.

In her scathing decision, B.C. Supreme Court Justice Catherine Murray ordered a stay of proceedings against the Canadian, due to the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA)'s "egregious" conduct.

The man had been facing extradition to the U.S. on drug trafficking charges stemming from a plot dating back to 2015.

Murray's decision, dated April 1, was posted on the court's website this week. The case was first reported by the Vancouver Sun.

Specifics, including the alleged drug trafficker's identity, his hometown and even the narcotic he is accused of smuggling from the U.S. into Canada are redacted in the public version of the ruling.

The "experienced" DEA special agent at the centre of the case is referred to only as "Jane Doe."

The DEA says it operates two offices in Canada, including one at the U.S. Embassy in Ottawa. (Fred Chartrand/The Canadian Press)

According to the judge's decision, the American agent showed up at the man's door with two Canadian detectives who were also operating outside of their jurisdiction. The man, identified in the court documents as "named person," said he was later summoned to meet with U.S. investigators three times.

He ultimately signed an agreement to help in their probe focused on another unnamed target.

As part of that investigation, the DEA directed the Canadian to set up a deal to move an unspecified amount of cash for the target. Agents sent the man abroad to take part in the scheme and by the time he returned home, "he felt that his life was in jeopardy," the judge's decision says.

Murray said the plan amounted to a money-laundering conspiracy and that "the DEA was leading him into criminal conduct" without Canadian oversight or authorization.

"The DEA was aware of the protocols but chose to operate in Canada behind the back of the RCMP," the judge wrote. She said the DEA provided the Mounties with misleading information about the investigation — and it only did so months after pressuring the Canadian to co-operate.

"The DEA committed a deliberate, calculated and ongoing infringement of [named person]'s constitutional rights which was unlawful and conducted in violation of Canadian sovereignty," Murray wrote.

Foreign investigators cannot act as police in Canada. They're required to follow a series of guidelines while operating here, including having Canadian law enforcement supervise their operations.

'Public would be outraged' by DEA's conduct, judge says

Despite any deal the man may have had with the DEA, U.S. prosecutors still sought his extradition to stand trial. At the man's request, the B.C. judge ordered those proceedings to be halted.

"The public would be outraged by the conduct of the DEA in this case," Murray wrote.

"While there is a high public interest in seeing trafficking and exporting charges prosecuted, the behaviour of the DEA in this case is so shocking and flagrant that the justice system must distance itself from it. To allow the proceedings to continue would be to condone it."

Murray underlined it's not the first time a Canadian's case has been tossed due to the DEA's conduct. She pointed to a similar decision from a B.C. judge in 2002, after U.S. agents continued undercover work in Canada even though the RCMP had refused to approve the operations.

U.S. investigators seized 201 kilograms of suspected cocaine in August 2024 as part of a sweeping investigation dubbed Operation Giant Slalom, centred around former elite snowboarder Ryan Wedding. (U.S. District Court, Central District of California)

DEA agents have since contributed to high-profile investigations involving Canadian targets, including the FBI-led Operation Giant Slalom — centred around alleged cocaine kingpin Ryan Wedding — and the Ontario Provincial Police's recent Project Bay , which seized illegal street drugs with a street value of $139 million.

The DEA did not immediately respond to emailed questions from CBC News on Friday. The U.S. Embassy in Ottawa declined to comment on the B.C. decision.

A large anti-tank rifle, other firearms and nearly $139 million worth of illegal drugs were seized as a part of the multi-jurisdiction police investigation called Project Bay. (Camille Cottais/Radio-Canada)

In a social media post , former CSIS analyst Jessica Davis described the case as "outrageous" and "a bad sign for the future of law enforcement co-operation between Canada and the U.S."

The DEA's website lists offices at the U.S. Embassy and the consulate in Vancouver. The agency says its role in Canada "is to co-ordinate international drug-trafficking investigations between the United States and Canadian law enforcement."

"Both DEA offices in Canada work with Canadians on a full complement of cases while ensuring that our activities are in keeping with Canadian laws and existing agreements," the website says.

World.title: Colombia announces new aerial fumigation pilot program
World.content:
Colombia’s National Narcotics Council (CNE) ordered the National Police to restart the aerial fumigation of coca, the base ingredient for cocaine.

In a resolution, the CNE ordered “as a controlled, limited, temporary, and evaluable experimental phase, the implementation of a pilot plan for the eradication of illicit crops through aerial spraying using a manned aircraft and the formulated product Glufosinate Ammonium 200 SL.”

In a public statement, the National Police’s counternarcotics unit said that the 10km2 pilot area was located in Putumayo and would not affect indigenous and afro-descendant communities, who would need to be asked permission.

The exclusion of environmental protection zones and protected areas, zones associated with bodies of water, rivers, and other environmentally sensitive areas is contemplated, as well as those territories that, in accordance with current regulations and the corresponding technical studies, must be excluded. National Police Counternarcotics

The purpose of the pilot program is to “evaluate the effectiveness of aerial spraying, as well as its application under the established technical and operational conditions, said the police.

The police stressed that “this experimental phase does not constitute the resumption, adoption, or definitive authorization of a widespread or nationwide aerial spraying program,” which was banned by the Constitutional Court in 2015.

In order to resume aerial fumigation, health and environmental authorities must sign off on the program and the police would only be allowed to use airplanes with the approval of the court and local communities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella vowed to resume aerial spraying more than 330,000 hectares while on campaign and after taking office last month as part of his hardline approach to organized crime.

Former President Ivan Duque also vowed to resume aerial spraying, but failed to comply with the norms established by the court.

World.title: Court orders Colombia’s government to remove images of slain “narcoterrorists”
World.content:
A Bogota judge ordered Colombia’s government to remove images and videos of President Abelardo de la Espriella walking through the remains of slain suspected guerrillas from its social media accounts.

The judge also ordered the government to remove images and videos of the body bags containing the lifeless remains of four members of organized crime group ACSN who were killed in La Guajira.

According to the judge, the images could be harmful to minors.

The decision was celebrated by congressman Santiago Osorio (Green Alliance), who sued the government over the controversial social media posts.

The State and the National Government cannot engage in a contest with crime to see which of the two is the most cruel; in this regard, the Office of the President of the Republic, Mr. Abelardo de la Espriella, were ordered to promptly remove images that may have reached the cell phones of children across the country, showing a state displaying corpses as trophies. Congressman Santiago Osorio

Th publications were previously rejected by the Ombudsman’s Office, whose director, Iris Marin, urged the government not to “compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power.”

In the first video, De la Espriella and Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora walked through rows of body bags, displaying the remains of 23 alleged members of FARC dissident organizations EMC who were killed in the southern Guaviare province.

Among those killed in Operation Azarias were two minor victims of forced recruitment by the guerrillas.

The videos sought to promote the government’s hardline security policy, which vows to kill “narcoterrorists” who refuse to surrender.

World.title: US, Colombia sign memorandums of understanding amid “rebirth” of relations
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hailed the “rebirth” of bilateral relations as they signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear energy and rare earths.

The two leaders met in Barranquilla, where De la Espriella lives, as part of Rubio’s tour through allied countries in the Andean region.

The president and the secretary of state hailed the improvement of ties that were severely disrupted when former President Gustavo Petro was in office.

During a joint press conference, Rubio stressed the need for security in the region, claiming that “the same networks, the same criminal groups that, although they commit their crimes here, they also commit crimes in the U.S., and they damage our people.”

De la Espriella said that as part of the “Barranquilla Agreements,” he asked the US for support for his hardline security policy.

We have proposed to the government—and today I reiterated this proposal to the secretary—the 21st-Century Patriot Plan to modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president promised to “start spraying, we are going to target the laboratories, the precursors, the trafficking routes, the drug trafficking kingpins, the armed narco-terrorist organizations—we are going after the money launderers, their criminal assets, and those international networks that pose a grave danger not only to the hemisphere but also to humanity.”

Rubio did not openly commit any US support other than the memorandums of understanding.

The unbinding agreements were part of Rubio’s wish list as the US seeks new sources for rare earths and miners that can be processed outside of China, which the US Government sees as its rival.

With the nuclear energy agenda, Colombia seeks to “strengthen its capacities” with US support. Both governments “reaffirm their commitment to international development and the peaceful use of nuclear energy.”

In order to create policy regarding the memorandums, De la Espriella would need congressional support, which he has yet to seek openly.

World.title: De la Espriella lifts Colombia’s 10-year gun ban
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella lifted a gun ban that had been in place since 2015.

According to De la Espriella, the decision seeks to give “good citizens” a way to defend themselves against “criminals.”

“For years, law-abiding citizens were restricted, while criminals continued to arm themselves to the teeth illegally. That has to change,” said the president on social media platform X.

99.9% of crimes committed with weapons are committed with unlicensed, illegal weapons. Anything said beyond the mathematics is just opinion. Mathematics is an exact science. So I am pleased to sign this decree. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president said that those who want to carry guns legally must comply with strict regulations and can’t have criminal records.

The ban reactivates previously approved gun licenses and allows citizens older than 25 to purchase approved hand guns from Colombia’s State military industry.

In order to be given a license, a potential gun owner must undergo fitness tests and convince the military authority that his position in society merits a firearm.

The decision has long been awaited by conservative and far-right elements in society, who have claimed that the gun ban made them sitting ducks for extortionists, particularly in the countryside.

Experts consulted by newspaper El Colombiano warned that lifting the gun ban could increase deadly violence, particularly considering Colombia’s violent history and evidence obtained in countries where guns are legal.

“There is no evidence showing that these countries have seen a decrease in theft, extortion, and threats following these measures,” said the director of the Central University’s Security Observatory, Andres Nieto. “On the contrary, the evidence does show an increase in violence among citizens,” the scholar added.

The ban was initially imposed by former President Juan Manuel Santos in 2015 and has since been upheld by his successors.

World.title: Liberal Party joins Colombia’s far-right to form majority coalition
World.content:
The Liberal Party announced that it had joined the congressional coalition of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella.

The party, which also supported De la Espriella’s presidential bid, said that it would join the coalition after “extensive deliberation and arduous debate among representatives, senators, and leadership” of Colombia’s oldest political party.

It is worth noting that the discussions between representatives and senators over the past several weeks have revealed disagreements among some members of our caucuses with the current administration, but they also acknowledge President Espriella’s ability to work toward stimulating economic growth, building a talent pool to provide real opportunities for Colombians, and restoring security and respect for institutions. Liberal Party

The liberals’ decision gives the government broad support in Congress and marginalizes the opposition led by the leftist Historic Pact Party.

In the senate, De la Espriella’s right-wing coalition can count on the support of 63 of 103 lawmakers. In the House of Representatives, the coalition consists of 123 of 183 lawmakers.

The Historic Pact, which won the elections and became the biggest party in Congress, was abandoned by the left-liberal Green Alliance party and can count of the support of 28 senators and 44 representatives.

The opposition party has been able to make temporary anti-government alliances with, for example, the far-right Democratic Center party of former President Alvaro Uribe.

World.title: Colombia’s president appoints controversial new spy chief
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella appointed retired army General Jorge Andres Zuluaga as director of the National Intelligence Directorate (DNI) despite pending criminal investigations.

Zuluaga, who spent 30 years with military intelligence, is best known for his participation in Operation Jaque, which liberated former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, three American military contractors and 11 soldiers.

Throughout his career, the 61-year-old former general was deputy commander of the now-defunct Charry Solano intelligence school, commander of the Regional Intelligence #5 and the director of the National Army’s Technical Intelligence Center (CITEC).

Zuluaga received training in the United States and was a diplomatic aide at the Organization of American States.

He was removed as CITEC director in 2014 after prosecution investigators found out that he received intelligence illegally obtained from “Andromeda,” a clandestine intelligence unit that operated from a Bogota internet café.

In October 2024, war crimes tribunal JEP ordered the Prosecutor General’s Office to investigate Zuluaga for his alleged participation in the extermination of the leftist Patriotic Union party when he was the CITEC’s director between 2004 and 2005.

The prosecution has yet to decide whether or not to formally charge the retired general with the crimes he allegedly committed.

Zuluaga, who became a member of the far-right Democratic Center party after he was ejected from the army, has always sustained that he acted within the boundaries of the law.

World.title: Colombia’s government clashes with ombudsman over De la Espriella walking among corpses
World.content:
Colombia’s chief ombudsman, Iris Marin, clashed with the national government after she criticized President Abelardo de la Espriella for walking among the corpses of people killed by the military.

In a public statement, Marin reiterated that “in recent days, we saw the president of the Republic walking among the bodies—in white body bags—of people who were killed during Operation “Azarías” in Guaviare.”

“I don’t recall ever seeing a president walking among the dead and taking pride in those deaths,” said the ombudsman, whose office is independent from the government.

The state and the government cannot allow themselves to be drawn into a competition to see who can be the cruelest. They cannot compete with armed groups over who instills the most fear, who humiliates the adversary the most, or who turns death into a display of power. Ombudsman Iris Marin

According to Marin, the military has the right to kill citizens, but must do so with respect for the Constitution and International Humanitarian Law, and is responsible for “the way that the State exercizes power and communicates its results.”

In a response, Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara said that the Ombudman falsely equated the State with “narcoterrorist groups as if it wer competing with them in cruelty.”

“Such an equivalence is inappropriate,” said Lara and called on the Ombudsman’s Office to be “an ally of the victims and of our mission to protect them and to liberate them from the terror regime of crime.”

Marin told Lara that she trusted that “the President and the Government will reflect on the way they communicate operational results, as I requested in my statement.”

De la Espriella’s stroll through the 23 body bags, including those of two minors, was also fiercely criticized in independent and foreign media.
