World.title: Officials report 63% drop in Chiapas homicides: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📉 Chiapas homicides down 63% : Speaking from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, Sheinbaum touted security gains under Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, saying “people feel safer in Chiapas today than they did two years ago.” Officials reported the daily homicide rate fell 63% in the first eight months of 2026 compared to 2024, with 9,949 arrests and 18.6 tonnes of drugs seized in the southern state since Sheinbaum took office.

: Speaking from Tuxtla Gutiérrez, Sheinbaum touted security gains under Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar, saying “people feel safer in Chiapas today than they did two years ago.” Officials reported the daily homicide rate fell 63% in the first eight months of 2026 compared to 2024, with 9,949 arrests and 18.6 tonnes of drugs seized in the southern state since Sheinbaum took office. 📚 Pencils over screens after poor PISA scores : Responding to this week’s PISA results showing 41.8% of Mexican 15-year-olds scored below basic level in math, science and reading, Sheinbaum announced new math and reading textbooks for teachers and students, and highlighted plans to regulate device use in schools while pushing a “return to pencil and paper.”

: Responding to this week’s PISA results showing 41.8% of Mexican 15-year-olds scored below basic level in math, science and reading, Sheinbaum announced new math and reading textbooks for teachers and students, and highlighted plans to regulate device use in schools while pushing a “return to pencil and paper.” 🏥 CJNG ‘clandestine hospital’ found in Jalisco: García Harfuch confirmed that a property in Tecalitlán used by the Jalisco New Generation Cartel to treat injured members was uncovered during the search for a missing 20-year-old man, who was among eight people freed from the site.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Tuxtla Gutiérrez, capital of the southern state of Chiapas.

At the start of the mañanera, Sheinbaum said that since Governor Eduardo Ramírez Aguilar took office in December 2024, and “with the coordination with the federal [Security] Cabinet,” the security results in Chiapas have been “very good, not just in the reduction of homicides and other high-impact crimes, but also in the perception [of insecurity].”

“People feel safer in Chiapas today than they did two years ago,” she said.

Later in the press conference, security officials presented the latest data on homicides, high-impact crimes and arrests in Chiapas, a state where violence increased significantly in 2024, especially near the border with Guatemala.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks on how the government plans to improve both the teaching and learning of mathematics and reading in Mexican schools. Her comments came three days after the publication of PISA testing results that showed that around four in 10 Mexicans 15-year-olds scored below the basic level in science, mathematics and reading.

Homicides down 63% in Chiapas compared to 2024

National Public Security System chief Marcela Figueroa noted that the homicide rate in Chiapas remained “quite stable” between 2015 and 2023 before increasing significantly in 2024, a year in which an average of 2.4 murders per day were committed in the state.

She noted that the daily homicide rate in the first eight months of this year was 0.9, representing a reduction of 63% compared to 2024. The year-over-year decline was 10%, according to the data presented.

Figueroa also reported that the daily homicide rate in Chiapas in August — 0.9 — was 64% lower than the rate in December 2024, the month Ramírez was sworn in as governor.

With regard to high-impact crimes, among which are homicides, kidnappings, violent robberies and acts of extortion, the daily incidence in Chiapas in August was 2.7, a reduction of 44% compared to November 2024. The data presented by Figueroa showed that the daily incidence of high-impact crimes rose 8% between August 2025 and August 2026.

Later in the press conference, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch reported that 9,949 people were arrested in Chiapas between Oct. 1, 2024 — the date Sheinbaum took office — and Aug. 31, 2026, for allegedly committing high-impact crimes. Authorities seized 1,545 firearms and 18.6 tonnes of drugs in the state in the same period.

Sheinbaum outlines strategies to improve educational outcomes

A reporter asked the president whether Mexico’s education system needs to be strengthened in light of the PISA results published this week. In testing for the OECD’s Program for International Student Assessment, 41.8% of Mexican 15-year-olds scored below the basic level in the science/math/reading triad, more than double the 19.7% average across OECD countries. Education Minister Mario Delgado on Wednesday addressed the low scores earned by Mexican students by blaming “the excessive use of cell phones and computer screens.”

Sheinbaum asserted that “education in Mexico is getting stronger,” before acknowledging that Mexican students have ground to make up.

“We have to make progress in mathematics. We’re going to have a special textbook next year for the learning of mathematics, to help the teachers and the students,” she said.

Sheinbaum subsequently highlighted that Mexico wasn’t the only country to score poorly in the reading domain of the PISA testing.

She said that “all the countries of the world” scored poorly on reading, “with the exception of four or five, due to the use of digital platforms.”

“[That was] acknowledged by the education area of the OECD. Young people, girls and boys, stopped reading and understanding what they read due to the excessive use of digital platforms, which is something that we’re now addressing,” Sheinbaum said, referring to a plan to implement national regulations on the use of devices in schools.

“[We’re going to] return to pencil and paper, pen and paper, and reading,” she said.

Sheinbaum said the teaching of reading and writing in Mexican schools will also be supported by a new textbook.

She said that the new textbook (or likely textbooks for different grades) will include poems and short stories that girls and boys “should know.”

Clandestine CJNG hospital discovered in Jalisco

A reporter asked García Harfuch about the discovery of a clandestine Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) hospital in the state of Jalisco.

🚔 En rueda de prensa se informó que la Vicefiscalía en Personas Desaparecidas, en coordinación con la Guardia Nacional y la Secretaría de la Defensa Nacional, realizó un operativo en Tecalitlán que permitió rescatar a ocho hombres y detener a seis personas. (1-3) pic.twitter.com/Vbe47OAf8T — Fiscalía del Estado de Jalisco (@FiscaliaJal) September 10, 2026

The Informador newspaper reported on Thursday that the search for a 20-year-old man who went missing in Tlaquepaque in July led authorities to a property in the municipality of Tecalitlán that was used as a clandestine hospital by the CJNG. Informador noted that six people were detained at the property. Eight alleged victims of forced recruitment, including the missing 20-year-old, were freed.

García Harfuch confirmed that injured “organized crime people” were treated at the property. He added that investigations related to the discovery of the property are still being carried out.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: The ultimate guide to contemporary Mexican restaurants in Guadalajara
World.content:
Mexican Independence Day celebrations this month offer a great opportunity to celebrate and rediscover Mexican food, and what better way to do it than through five restaurants that are putting a contemporary spin on traditional Mexican cuisine?

From chilaquiles with poblano chile sauce to eggplant tamales and corn pancakes, here are some of the best contemporary Mexican restaurants in Guadalajara to try right now.

Ixtle

Located in Zapopan, Ixtle defines itself as a kitchen true to its roots: A relaxed concept that takes corn and Mexican ingredients as its starting point, reinterpreting them through international techniques and references.

In the mornings, guests can enjoy innovative dishes such as the Jarocho Breakfast, featuring eggs in hoja santa with longaniza, banana and confit mushrooms, or waffles made from maize accompanied by a blend of caramelized miso, maple syrup, honey, mascarpone and macadamia butter.

Lovers of traditional hot café de olla will appreciate Ixtle’s reinterpretation of a staple of Mexican cuisine — the café de olla latte, served cold with orange peel and a touch of foamy milk.

At night, the menu becomes more elaborate, drawing on a wider range of international influences and featuring dishes that are designed to be shared. The Mediterranean tuna tiradito, served with red peppers in pil-pil sauce and nixtamalized tomato paste, is a must-try.

Best for: Breakfasts with friends or a date night

Breakfasts with friends or a date night Location: C. Miguel León Portilla 478, Santa Fe, 45168 Zapopan, Jalisco

C. Miguel León Portilla 478, Santa Fe, 45168 Zapopan, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/ixtle_rest

Teté Cocina de Barrio

Spearheaded by siblings Mario and Karla Papa, Teté has been delighting tapatíos for over a decade through a cuisine that blends Mexico’s culinary heritage with flavors introduced by the different cultures that have settled in the country.

With an approach that prioritizes seasonal ingredients, the menu at Teté not only changes every month, but it is a complete surprise for diners, who do not know what they will have for dinner until dishes start arriving.

Guests are also in for another surprise: Teté does not have waiters. Instead, everyone does a bit of everything, with the chefs themselves guiding diners throughout the meal.

With no waiters and no menu, Teté defines itself as a restaurant that “doesn’t repeat menus, but experiences.” It’s no wonder this unpretentious restaurant in the Moderna neighborhood has made it to coveted culinary rankings around the world.

Best for: Date night

Date night Location: C. Rayón 830, Moderna, 44170 Guadalajara, Jalisco

C. Rayón 830, Moderna, 44170 Guadalajara, Jalisco Website: tete-cocina-de-barrio.mailchimpsites.com

Amorcito Mío

Located in the heart of Zapopan Centro and just steps away from the Zapopan Basílica, Amorcito Mío offers a warm atmosphere and home-cooked-style recipes.

Although the breakfast menu offers international dishes such as sandwiches and paninis, it is simultaneously a celebration of Mexican food, albeit with a twist.

Guests will be surprised by the variety of sauces featured on the chilaquiles menu beyond the traditional red and green. Expect chilaquiles with poblano chile sauce, spicy peanut sauce and a super spicy sauce made from güero chiles and habanero.

To balance the heat, Amorcito Mío offers a varied selection of Mexican breads, including pan dulce staples like conchas, as well as traditional bolillo and birote.

While breakfasts highlight authentic Mexican flavors, the menu shifts in the afternoon and evening to feature wood-fired pizzas and a blend of Italian and Mediterranean dishes.

Best for: Casual gatherings with friends

Casual gatherings with friends Location: Calle 5 de Mayo 275, Zapopan, 45100 Zapopan, Jalisco

Calle 5 de Mayo 275, Zapopan, 45100 Zapopan, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/amorcito_mi

Bruna

View this post on Instagram A post shared by BRUNA (@bruna_mx)

With a terrace surrounded by lush gardens and sculptures, Bruna generates excitement from the very first moment, offering diners an almost theatrical experience.

Since opening in 2015, chef Óscar Garza has drawn inspiration from Mexican abuelitas’ recipes and street-food flavors, reinterpreting them with contemporary techniques and an artistic presentation.

Among the dishes that stand out for their meticulous presentation is the chile en nogada, which returns to the menu each year during the patriotic month. Las probaditas de mole, literally meaning “little tastes of mole,” features a rainbow of colors and flavors that pushes the boundaries of classic mole poblano.

If you are looking for something sweet and original, be sure to try the bruleated corn cream, a dessert that blends the traditional flavor of corn with the classic French twist of crème brûlée.

Best for: Special occasions

Special occasions Location: Lerdo de Tejada No. 2418, Col. Lafayette, Guadalajara, Jalisco

Lerdo de Tejada No. 2418, Col. Lafayette, Guadalajara, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/bruna_mx

Tikuun Comedor Local

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Tikuun comedor (@tikuun.comedor)

Spearheaded by chef Carlos Espinosa, Tikuun has been open for over a decade, but only recently began receiving the recognition it deserves.

Situated in the trendy Colonia Americana, it features a constantly rotating menu that showcases new preparations and seasonal variations throughout the year. Although the menu draws inspiration from different cultures and cuisines, the restaurant’s manifesto promises a distinctly Mexican essence in each dish.

Standout recent offerings include roasted eggplant with cured nopal, aged cotija, salsa macha made with chia and Kalamata olives, requesón cheese and garlic confit, as well as octopus with recado negro, chinchayote, sweet potato and beet.

The intimate, almost home-like atmosphere allows guests to savor the experience at a leisurely pace, whether ordering a la carte or opting for the tasting menu.

Best for: An intimate dinner with friends

An intimate dinner with friends Location: Emeterio Robles Gil 50, Col. Americana, 44600 Guadalajara, Jalisco

Emeterio Robles Gil 50, Col. Americana, 44600 Guadalajara, Jalisco Instagram: instagram.com/tikuun.comedor

World.title: A Gang Built a Fake Police Station in a Basement in Chile and Used It to Kidnap People
World.content:
CHILE · CRIME

Key Facts — The setup A fake precinct of Chile’s investigative police, built in the basement of a building.

— The detained Seven people, including a former prosecutor, Vinko Fodich, and serving police officers.

— The victims Chinese nationals, held and threatened with fictitious investigations by American authorities.

— The props Police uniforms, unauthorised firearms and photographs of Donald Trump hung on the walls.

— The catch Fodich was acting as lawyer for the man he is accused of helping to extort people alongside.

— The status Three were ordered into preventive detention. The rest were held for a Saturday hearing.

The uniforms were real enough to work. So were three of the men wearing them, who serve in Chile’s investigative police, and the lawyer who allegedly ran the operation used to be a state prosecutor.

A building of Chile’s investigative police, the PDI. Three serving officers are among those detained. (Photo: “PDI Derechos Humanos, Providencia, Santiago 20230816” by Carlos Figueroa Rojas, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

A gang in Chile built a fake police station in a building basement. They used it to detain people and demand money from them.

Seven people have been detained. Three of them serve in Chile’s investigative police, and one is a former state prosecutor.

Cooperativa, Emol and Meganoticias reported the case this week. The detentions and custody hearings ran across Thursday and Friday.

How the Operation Worked

The set was assembled between 3 and 5 August. It was made to pass as a precinct of the Policía de Investigaciones, Chile’s plain-clothes detective force.

The men wore PDI uniforms and displayed firearms they were not authorised to carry. Photographs of Donald Trump were hung on the walls.

That last detail sounds absurd and was functional. The victims were told they were subjects of an investigation by American federal authorities.

The threat was invented. No such investigation existed, and the props were there to make the story credible to people unfamiliar with Chilean policing.

Who the Victims Were

The victims are Chinese nationals named in reporting as Mingkai Fu and Mingxia Fu, who are siblings. A brother-in-law was also involved.

They were falsely detained on 6 August. Payment demands followed on 7 and 8 August.

Cooperativa reported an initial demand of around 300 million Chilean pesos per victim, about US$320,000. That was later reduced to 200 million pesos, some US$213,000.

A promissory note of roughly 43 million pesos, about US$46,000, features separately. The figures are as reported by Cooperativa.

The sum actually extorted, according to Cooperativa, was 30 million pesos in cash, roughly US$32,000. Conversions use the rate of 12 September.

The PDI is Chile’s plain-clothes investigative force, distinct from the uniformed Carabineros. (Photo: “PDI, Viña del Mar 20231002” by Carlos yo, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

The Former Prosecutor

Vinko Fodich is a former prosecutor who was working as a lawyer. His client was Yongjie Chen, described in reporting as the leader of a group known as the Chen clan.

That is the conflict at the centre of the case. A lawyer for one party is accused of participating in the extortion of others.

Fodich, along with a PDI inspector and a third man, was ordered into preventive detention across Thursday and Friday. His defence accepted the detention temporarily while preparing appeals.

The remaining four were held for a hearing on Saturday. Outlets differ on exactly which three officers were involved, and that discrepancy has not been resolved.

What the Police Said

The director of the PDI, Eduardo Cerna, addressed the involvement of former officials. He said it pained the force that former officers had strayed from ethics, probity and doctrine.

He added that there is no place in the institution for such conduct. That is a standard formulation and it does not answer the harder question.

The harder question is how serving officers took part. A fake police station staffed partly by real police is not an impersonation problem.

It is an internal control problem, and Chile has had several of those this year. The Supreme Court spent the same week removing eleven judges over a separate scandal.

Why This Case Travels

Extortion of Chinese nationals in Latin America is not new, and it works on a specific vulnerability. Recent migrants often do not know how local policing looks or what rights they hold.

The set only needed to convince someone who had never seen a real precinct. Adding genuine officers and genuine uniforms closed the remaining gap.

Chile has seen a sharp rise in organised extortion over the past three years. Cases involving foreign victims are systematically under-reported because victims fear immigration consequences.

The case will now move through custody hearings and a formal investigation period. Nobody has been convicted, and the accounts published so far come from prosecutors and police.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the PDI?

The Policía de Investigaciones de Chile is the country’s plain-clothes detective force, responsible for criminal investigation. It is separate from the uniformed Carabineros.

Who is Vinko Fodich?

A former Chilean state prosecutor working as a defence lawyer. He was ordered into preventive detention this week over the alleged kidnapping and extortion.

Have the accused been convicted?

No. They have been detained and some placed in preventive detention while the investigation proceeds. The allegations come from prosecutors.

Why were photographs of Donald Trump used?

The victims were told they faced an investigation by American authorities. The props were part of making that fabricated threat believable.

Sources: Cooperativa, Emol, Meganoticias.

World.title: Chilean Judges Sacked by Their Own Supreme Court for Going Abroad on Sick Leave
World.content:
CHILE · JUSTICE

Key Facts — The count Three removals were agreed on Thursday and eight more on Friday, for a total of eleven.

— The offence Travelling abroad while signed off work on medical leave, known in Chile as licencias médicas.

— The rule Article 80 of the constitution requires judges to maintain good behaviour in office.

— The threshold Each removal needs at least eleven favourable votes of the full Supreme Court.

— The catch Twenty-six proposed removals failed. Seven fell short of the quorum, fifteen lost a majority and four tied.

— The gap The names of the eleven have not been published, and outlets disagree on how many cases remain frozen.

No outside body did this. Chile’s Supreme Court used its own constitutional power to remove members of the judiciary it runs, and most of the proposals it considered were rejected.

The Palace of the Courts of Justice in Santiago, seat of Chile’s Supreme Court. (Photo: “Palacio de los tribunales de justicia desde calle Bandera 01” by usachino, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

Eleven Chilean judges were removed from office this week. Their own Supreme Court did it, using a power the constitution gives it over the judiciary it heads.

The offence was not corruption and not a decision in a case. The judges travelled abroad while signed off work on medical leave.

Three removals were agreed on Thursday and eight more on Friday. La Tercera called them the first Chilean judges expelled over the practice.

How the Court Did It

The instrument is article 80 of the Chilean constitution. It says judges hold office while they maintain good behaviour, and it lets the Supreme Court end that tenure.

The procedure is a vote of the full bench, not of a panel. Each removal requires at least eleven favourable votes.

That is a high bar and it showed. Cooperativa reported that 26 proposed removals of Chilean judges were rejected in the same process.

Of those, seven failed to reach the eleven-vote quorum and fifteen were rejected by majority. Four ended in a tie.

So the court refused more removals than it granted. That detail has been largely lost in the coverage of a purge.

How Big the Review Was

Outlets disagree on the scale, and the disagreement is worth carrying rather than resolving. La Tercera counted 58 removal proceedings opened, of which 45 were reviewed in this phase.

The Clinic counted 56 proceedings opened in June, following a review of more than a hundred officials. Neither figure has been corrected by the other outlet.

Cases still suspended by the Constitutional Tribunal are also counted differently. La Tercera says thirteen, Cooperativa eleven, and The Clinic and Mi Radio ten.

The Clinic named five judges whose cases remain suspended. They are Daniel Urrutia, Jorge Saavedra, Erna Fuentes, Eduardo Fritz and Óscar Pacheco.

The main gallery of the courts building. The removals were agreed by the full bench meeting over two days. (Photo: “Palacio de los Tribunales de Justicia, galería principal” by AlBustos, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.)

Who Was Removed Is Not Public

The full list of eleven has not been published by any outlet. That is unusual for a disciplinary action of this scale.

La Tercera named José Delgado, a minister of the Court of Appeals of Arica, as one figure in the process. Mi Radio reported that Gloria Negroni, president of the Court of Appeals of La Serena, was investigated.

It cautioned explicitly that being investigated does not mean she was removed. That caution is worth repeating rather than quietly dropping.

Until the court publishes the list, any named individual beyond those attributions is inference. Chilean outlets have so far declined to make it.

Why Sick Leave Became a Judicial Scandal

Medical leave abuse has been a running Chilean scandal since 2025. Auditors cross-checked leave records against border crossings and found public employees abroad while certified unfit for work.

The practice implicated thousands across the public sector. What makes Chilean judges different is that no employer can dismiss them.

Judges hold tenure precisely so that governments cannot remove them. The only body that can act is the Supreme Court itself, and that is what this week’s votes were.

The institutional cost is visible. A court that spends two days removing its own members is a court publicly conceding that its internal controls failed.

What Happens Next

Those whose cases sit with the Constitutional Tribunal remain in post for now. The tribunal froze them on procedural grounds and has not resolved them.

The removed judges may pursue remedies, and the court has not said whether further tranches are coming. More than a hundred officials were reviewed to produce this many cases.

For Chile the broader question is one of proportion. The same week the court expelled eleven of its own, it also rejected more than twice that number of proposed removals.

Both halves of that are the story. A disciplinary system that removes everyone accused is not working either.

More: Chile news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can Chile’s government remove judges?

No. Judges hold tenure under article 80 of the constitution while they maintain good behaviour, and only the Supreme Court can end that tenure.

How many votes does a removal need?

At least eleven favourable votes of the full Supreme Court. That threshold is why most of the proposed removals this week failed.

What did the judges actually do?

They travelled abroad while signed off work on medical leave. Chile has been auditing that practice across the public sector since 2025.

Are the names public?

No. As of this weekend no Chilean outlet had published the full list of the eleven removed judges.

Sources: La Tercera, Cooperativa, The Clinic, Mi Radio La Serena.

World.title: A Small-Town Judge Just Grounded Colombia’s Return to Aerial Spraying of Coca
World.content:
COLOMBIA · DRUG POLICY

Key Facts — The order A circuit court in Puerto Asís, Putumayo, provisionally suspended all aerial spraying of glufosinate in the department.

— The instrument A tutela, Colombia’s fast constitutional rights action. This is a provisional measure, not a final judgment.

— The target Resolution 007 of 2026 of the National Drug Council, which authorised a seven-day pilot.

— The history Colombia banned aerial glyphosate in 2015 after the World Health Organization called it probably carcinogenic.

— The catch The government swapped the chemical, not the method. The court suspended the method anyway.

— The test Any restart must satisfy conditions the Constitutional Court set in 2017, including prior consultation.

The government had approved a seven-day pilot using a different chemical to the one banned in 2015. A provisional order from a Putumayo court stopped it before it started.

Aerial crop spraying. Colombia flew eradication missions for two decades before halting them in 2015. (Photo: “Agricultural aircraft fertilizing a rice field in Glenn County-104A2037” by Frank Schulenburg, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

Colombia’s president spent five weeks dismantling his predecessor’s peace policy. A circuit court in a border town has now grounded his aerial spraying plan.

The Juzgado Tercero Promiscuo del Circuito de Puerto Asís suspended the spraying of coca crops across Putumayo. Infobae and Pulzo reported the order on 11 September.

It is provisional, not final. The judge suspended the operation while gathering technical information before deciding the underlying case.

What Was Stopped

The order covers any spraying of glufosinate ammonium from the air in that department. It names the legal instrument the programme rests on.

That instrument is Resolution 007 of 2026, issued by Colombia’s National Drug Council. The City Paper Bogotá reported that it authorised a seven-day pilot project.

The pilot was a test, not the start of routine fumigation. It carried its own limits, excluding protected environmental areas.

It also excluded territories of Indigenous or Afro-Colombian communities unless prior consultation had been completed. Consulta previa is a constitutional requirement in Colombia, not an administrative courtesy.

Why Colombia Stopped Spraying in the First Place

For two decades Colombia sprayed coca from aircraft using glyphosate. The programme was known by its Spanish acronym, PECIG.

The National Drug Council suspended it by resolution in 2015. The trigger was the World Health Organization’s cancer agency classifying glyphosate as probably carcinogenic to humans.

Colombia’s health ministry recommended stopping aerial use. Communities in spray zones had reported miscarriages, birth defects and contaminated water, claims that remain contested.

Two years later the Constitutional Court set the terms for any return. Judgment T-236 of 2017 found objective evidence of significant risk to health.

Rural Putumayo, on Colombia’s southern border. The department has been at the centre of coca policy for thirty years. (Photo: “Anuncio de hornos de coca” by JEHC15, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.)

The Conditions Nobody Has Met

The 2017 ruling did not ban spraying forever. It made restarting conditional, and the conditions are demanding.

Any decision to resume must rest on objective and conclusive evidence that there is no harm to health or the environment. The burden sits with the government, not with the communities.

Risk must be regulated by an authority independent of the body doing the spraying. Evaluation must be permanent and the science impartial.

Prior consultation with affected ethnic communities is mandatory before resumption. The court also required consultation afterwards where impacts are direct.

A Different Chemical, the Same Argument

This is where the government’s manoeuvre becomes visible. Glufosinate ammonium is not glyphosate, and the 2015 suspension named glyphosate.

Swapping the herbicide sidesteps the specific resolution. It does not obviously sidestep the constitutional reasoning.

That reasoning was about the method and about the rights of the people underneath it. The chemical was the occasion, not the principle.

Glufosinate is a broad-spectrum herbicide with its own regulatory history. It has been withdrawn from approved use in the European Union.

That is not a finding about Colombian conditions. It is not nothing either.

The Puerto Asís court did not rule on toxicity. It suspended the operation until the agencies involved hand over the technical information the judge asked for.

What This Means for the Security Plan

Abelardo de la Espriella took office on 7 August promising force where his predecessor promised negotiation. Aerial eradication was the visible half of that.

The other half was closing every peace process, which he completed this week. Both halves are now running into courts rather than into armed groups.

A provisional tutela measure from a circuit court is not the end of the programme. The government can supply the information, contest the ruling, or move the pilot elsewhere.

But it establishes the shape of the fight. Colombia’s constitutional architecture makes a president’s drug policy answerable to the communities it is flown over.

That is unusual by regional standards, and it is why the 2017 judgment matters more than any single resolution. Whoever wants to spray has to prove the case first.

More: Colombia news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a tutela?

It is Colombia’s fast-track constitutional action for protecting fundamental rights. Any judge can hear one, decisions come quickly, and provisional measures can be issued before the case is decided.

Is aerial spraying banned in Colombia?

Not permanently. It was suspended in 2015, and the Constitutional Court ruled in 2017 that it may resume only if strict evidentiary, regulatory and consultation conditions are met.

What is glufosinate ammonium?

A broad-spectrum herbicide, distinct from glyphosate, which the government proposed using in place of it. It has been withdrawn from approved use in the European Union.

Does this stop eradication altogether?

No. Manual eradication and interdiction continue. The order suspends aerial spraying in one department while a judge examines the case.

Sources: Infobae Colombia, Pulzo, The City Paper Bogotá, El País, Corte Constitucional de Colombia, Consejo Nacional de Estupefacientes, UNODC.

World.title: Brazil’s Leading Challenger Is Under Investigation Over Dark Horse, a Film About His Father
World.content:
BRAZIL · ELECTION 2026

Key Facts — The status An inquiry, not a charge. No indictment, no prosecution and no defendant in this matter.

— The offences Police are examining money laundering, unauthorised transfers abroad, and active and passive corruption.

— The film Dark Horse, a biopic of Jair Bolsonaro starring Jim Caviezel, financed by banker Daniel Vorcaro.

— The sum A contract for US$24 million in 14 instalments. Police say about US$12.3 million was actually paid.

— The wording Police call the senator Vorcaro’s “interlocutor direto” rather than a name in other people’s messages.

— The catch The distributor suspended the film’s release on Friday. It was due out the same day.

Nobody has been charged. But an inquiry authorised in July became documentary fact on Friday, and it names the man polling level with Lula three weeks before the vote.

Flávio Bolsonaro, senator for Rio de Janeiro. He is the eldest son of Jair Bolsonaro and the main challenger to Lula. (Photo: “Foto oficial do senador Flávio Bolsonaro (v. AgSen)” by Agência Senado, via Wikimedia Commons, Attribution.)

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The man most likely to face Lula in Brazil’s presidential runoff is under criminal investigation. The subject is Dark Horse, a film about his father.

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro has not been charged. There is no indictment, no prosecution and no defendant, and an inquiry in Brazil can be archived without any charge at all.

What exists is an inquérito, opened on 22 July at the request of the Federal Police. It became documentary fact on Friday, when parts of the Banco Master file were unsealed.

What Is Actually Being Investigated

G1 and BBC News Brasil set out the suspected offences. They are money laundering, unauthorised transfers abroad, and active and passive corruption.

That second item matters and is often mistranslated. Evasão de divisas means sending money or assets abroad without declaring them.

It is an offence against Brazil’s financial system. It is not tax evasion, which is a separate crime under separate law.

The distinction is the whole theory of the case. Police are tracing money that left Brazil, not money withheld from the tax authorities.

The Federal Police requested the inquiry on 8 July. The prosecutor general’s office did not oppose it on 21 July, and Justice André Mendonça authorised it the following day.

What Dark Horse Is

Dark Horse is a biographical film about Jair Bolsonaro. The American actor Jim Caviezel plays him and Cyrus Nowrasteh directs.

The project originated with Mário Frias, a former culture secretary who is now a federal deputy for the PL. It is produced by Go Up Entertainment.

Its financing came from Daniel Vorcaro, the former controlling shareholder of Banco Master. That bank no longer exists.

Brazil’s central bank decreed its extrajudicial liquidation on 18 November 2025 and police arrested Vorcaro the same day. He was later moved to house arrest, then returned to preventive detention on 4 March 2026, where he remains.

The Money, as Police Describe It

Every figure here is an allegation in an open inquiry. None has been tested in court.

The Intercept Brasil first reported the arrangement on 13 May 2026. A contract found on Vorcaro’s phone provided for US$24 million in fourteen instalments.

That was about 134 million reais at the time, roughly US$26 million today. Rather less than that was paid.

Police say about 62.8 million reais, some US$12.3 million, was actually paid. The producer says 75.1 million reais, about US$14.7 million, was spent.

Investigators traced US$12,333,335 moving from a company called Entre Investimentos to the Havengate Development Fund in Texas. The transfers ran from February to September 2025.

The Senate plenary in Brasília. Because the allegations touch his conduct in office, the case sits with the Supreme Court. (Photo: “Plenário do Senado (47572923052)” by Senado Federal from Brasilia, Brazil, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.)

The Business Plan Police Do Not Believe

The clearest laundering indicator investigators point to is the revenue forecast. Valor Econômico reported on the film’s business plan.

Its optimistic scenario would beat Brazil’s all-time box-office record by more than three times. No Brazilian film has come close.

That record belongs to Minha Mãe é uma Peça 3. Metrópoles reported the plan projected up to 500 million reais, about US$98 million.

Police call this a descompasso with realistic market parameters. In plain terms, they do not believe anyone expected the film to make that money.

A forecast nobody believes is a classic laundering marker, because it justifies moving a sum far larger than the underlying business supports. It is an argument, not a finding.

What the Police Say the Senator Did

The distinction they draw is the heart of the case. They say he was not simply a name in other people’s messages.

Their phrase, quoted by Poder360 and Valor, is that he was Vorcaro’s “interlocutor direto”. His conduct is described as “cobranças de pagamentos, reuniões presenciais e acompanhamento do andamento das gravações”.

In English: chasing payments, meeting in person, and following the progress of filming. That is the allegation the inquiry was opened to test.

There Are Two Inquiries, Not One

A great deal of coverage has collapsed them. The distinction matters because they concern different money.

Mendonça supervises the first, into Vorcaro’s private transfers. That is the one in which the senator is an investigated party.

Justice Flávio Dino supervises the second, into whether public money reached the producer through parliamentary budget amendments. He authorised an operation on 10 September involving 49 search warrants.

Its targets included Mário Frias and the producer Karina Gama. Investigators allege budget amendments of 2 million reais from Frias, about US$393,000.

They allege one million reais from deputy Marcos Pollon, some US$196,000. A further 150,000 reais, about US$29,000, is attributed to deputy Bia Kicis.

What the Senator Says

He has not denied approaching Vorcaro, though he did deny it initially before the contacts were documented. He denies that doing so was improper.

On 13 May he framed it as private sponsorship with no state support. His line was “Zero de dinheiro público, zero de lei Rouanet”.

The Rouanet law is Brazil’s cultural tax incentive. Attacking it is a familiar move on the Brazilian right.

That defence is now directly contested. The 10 September operation rests on the allegation that public money did reach the producer.

The route alleged is budget amendments, not the Rouanet law. On that reading the denial is technically true and substantively beside the point.

In a televised interview on 28 August he called the matter closed. He described it as a son seeking private sponsorship for a private film about his own father.

He responded again on 11 September while campaigning in Manaus. He said he faced the disclosure with “muita tranquilidade” and called total transparency the best thing that could have happened.

He also framed the timing politically. In an election, he said, people will try anything to destabilise and will invent things where there is nothing.

Eduardo Bolsonaro’s Role

His brother appears in the file, and the attribution needs care. A contract reported by The Intercept Brasil listed Eduardo Bolsonaro as an executive producer with fundraising duties.

He denies having acted as a producer. He says the contract existed only to keep the Hollywood director attached, and that he later left the role.

What investigators themselves say is narrower and more specific. Police state that he directed how the film’s money was managed abroad.

He has acknowledged putting US$50,000 of his own money in at the outset, after an initial denial, and says he was repaid. He denies receiving money from Vorcaro or from the American fund.

He is no longer a federal deputy. His mandate was annulled and he was convicted of coercion, receiving four years in a semi-open regime.

The Film Will Not Be Released

Dark Horse was due out on 11 September, three weeks before the vote. It did not open.

Paris Filmes refused to distribute it on 23 June. On 26 August the release was pushed back until after the election.

The premiere was postponed again on 10 September, after the police operation. The distributor suspended the release entirely on 11 September.

The timing had already drawn a legal challenge. An attempt to bar the film during the campaign reached the electoral court.

Justice Kassio Nunes Marques declined to block it. He did not rule on the merits.

Where It Stands This Weekend

On Saturday Mendonça lifted secrecy on roughly forty further proceedings tied to the Banco Master case. He acted on a request from the prosecutor general relayed through the court’s president.

He also said he had released everything available to him. The film’s American producer told police he will not hand over documents without an order from a United States court.

The Supreme Court sits on Tuesday 15 September on a separate question. It will decide whether to open an investigation into Justice Alexandre de Moraes and his own dealings with Vorcaro.

Why the Timing Is the Story

Brazil votes on 4 October. Datafolha’s poll of 11 September put Lula on 46% against the senator’s 44% in a runoff.

The pollster itself reports that as a tie. Rejection rates for the two men are identical at 46%.

Two other surveys this week put him marginally ahead. AtlasIntel had 46.4% to 46.2% and Futura had a similar gap, all inside the margins of error.

So a criminal inquiry became public three weeks before a presidential vote, into a candidate level in the polls. It emerged from files a justice was ordered to release by the court’s president.

Supporters read the disclosure as interference; opponents read the conduct as disqualifying. Both readings can be argued from the same documents.

That is the problem when a country’s courts and its election collide. What is not in dispute is that money moved, and that nobody has yet been charged with anything.

More: Brazil news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Dark Horse?

It is a biographical film about former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, financed by Daniel Vorcaro of Banco Master. Jim Caviezel stars and Cyrus Nowrasteh directs. Its release was suspended on 11 September 2026.

Is Flávio Bolsonaro charged with a crime?

No. He is subject to a formal police inquiry authorised by the Supreme Court on 22 July 2026. There is no indictment, no prosecution and no defendant, and an inquiry may end without charges.

What offences are being investigated?

Money laundering, unauthorised transfer of funds abroad, and active and passive corruption. Unauthorised transfer abroad is an offence against Brazil’s financial system and is not the same as tax evasion.

What does he say?

That he sought private sponsorship for a private film about his father, that no public money or cultural tax incentive was involved, and that the disclosure vindicates him.

Does this stop him running?

No. An open investigation does not bar a candidacy in Brazil, and he remains the main challenger to Lula for the 4 October vote.

Sources: Reuters, BBC News Brasil, G1, Valor Econômico, Poder360, CartaCapital, Agência Pública, The Intercept Brasil, Metrópoles, Congresso em Foco, Al Jazeera, Agência Senado.

World.title: Buying Property in Morocco as a Foreigner in 2026
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio.

Guides · Morocco

—The stakes. A registered titre foncier is the only ownership document that gives foreign buyers secure title, clean transferability, and dependable resale protection. —The law. Foreigners can freely buy titled residential and commercial urban property, while agricultural land normally requires AVNA reclassification away from farm use. —The costs. Buyer transaction costs commonly fall in the 8 to 11 percent range of the purchase price, though allocations vary by transaction and current practice. —The markets. Marrakech medina riads, Essaouira lifestyle properties, Tangier revived districts, Agadir resorts, and Rabat premium areas all attract distinct foreign demand. —The money rule. Repatriation of resale proceeds depends on proving the original purchase was funded with foreign currency imported through official Moroccan banking channels.

The single most important act for a foreign buyer in Morocco is not choosing a city or a price bracket. It is confirming that the property carries a registered titre foncier rather than customary or shared rights, because that title is the gateway to secure ownership and later repatriation.

A traditional Moroccan medina building with ornate arches and tiled walls in an old city street.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

The Legal Framework for Foreign Buyers

Morocco generally allows foreigners to acquire residential and commercial property, provided the asset itself is properly titled and registered.

The core rule is simple: foreign ownership is workable when the property falls within the registered urban system.

Agricultural land is not the normal target for foreign ownership and remains restricted in practice.

When agricultural land is bought for a non-agricultural project, the usual route is reclassification or authorization through the AVNA framework.

The AVNA mechanism is the legal channel used to permit foreign investment on land that is not yet in a suitable urban or non-agricultural status.

For most foreign buyers, the practical conclusion is to ignore agricultural land unless the reclassification has already been completed and the title reflects that change.

The Title System: Titre Foncier versus Melkia

The gold-standard ownership document is the titre foncier registered with the Conservation Foncière, the Moroccan land registry authority.

A titre foncier gives clear ownership, cleaner transferability, and better protection for later resale.

Customary melkia ownership exists outside the fully registered system and is weaker for foreign buyers.

A melkia document is not the same as a fully registered title and creates more legal friction.

Foreign buyers should insist on titled property because the registered title is the basis for secure ownership, registration, and resale.

The single most important due-diligence item is confirming that the property carries a registered titre foncier before signing anything.

The Purchase Process Step by Step

The typical sequence begins with agreeing on price and terms, then verifying title and ownership.

After due diligence, the parties sign a preliminary agreement known as a compromis de vente and pay a deposit.

A deposit of about 10 percent is commonly cited at the compromis de vente stage, though market practice may vary.

The notary prepares the deed, checks title and ownership, coordinates completion, and handles the formalities for registration.

Funds move through official banking channels before the final deed is signed.

The transfer is then registered with the land registry, and completion is driven by title verification, payments, and registration formalities rather than a fixed legal deadline.

Foreigners buy residential and commercial property freely. Agricultural land is the exception.

Transaction Costs and Who Pays What

Commonly cited buyer costs include registration or transfer duty, Conservation Foncière fees, notary fees, and sometimes stamp duty.

Agency commission can also enter the calculation depending on how the sale was arranged.

Several current guides put the buyer’s all-in acquisition cost at roughly 8 to 11 percent of the purchase price.

Other guides place the figure closer to 7 to 8 percent depending on assumptions and whether agency commission is included.

Exact allocations vary, and final charges depend on the transaction and current practice.

Buyers should treat percentages as planning ranges, not fixed statutory rates.

Where Foreigners Buy in Morocco

Marrakech attracts strong foreign demand for renovated medina riads, villa districts, and newer apartments in areas like Guéliz and Hivernage.

Essaouira is commonly positioned as a smaller lifestyle and retirement market with lower entry prices than Marrakech but a narrower buyer pool.

Tangier is often described as a revived and dynamic market with strong interest from expatriates and cross-border buyers, especially in newer or central areas.

Agadir is a coastal resort and retirement market with comparatively more affordable prices than Rabat or top Marrakech districts.

Rabat is a higher-priced, more stable administrative market with strong demand in premium neighbourhoods.

Each city serves a different buyer profile, from tourism-led guesthouse investment to stable residential or retirement use.

Typical Price Ranges by Market

In Marrakech, a 2026 district-based source places medina riads to renovate around 8,000 to 14,000 MAD per square metre.

Prestige renovated riads in Marrakech range around 25,000 to 40,000 MAD per square metre, roughly US$2,450 to US$3,920 per square metre.

Tangier shows a broad citywide benchmark around 12,500 MAD per square metre in one 2026 guide, with higher figures in premium zones.

Rabat premium areas such as Souissi are described in the range of 20,000 to 35,000 MAD per square metre, while broader city averages are lower outside elite districts.

Agadir has a lower-to-mid range profile, with one 2026 ranking placing a citywide benchmark around 6,857 MAD per square metre.

Essaouira sits around 6,487 MAD per square metre on a citywide benchmark, reflecting a smaller and more niche market.

Financing Reality for Foreign Buyers

Moroccan banks may lend to non-residents selectively, but financing is not automatic and is often more constrained than in European home markets.

Foreign buyers, especially Europeans, are frequently described as cash buyers who bring substantial foreign currency and complete purchases with limited local debt.

Mortgage-related fees can include bank processing, valuation, and mortgage registration, separate from standard purchase taxes and registry fees.

A buyer with local financing should verify that the bank’s requirements align with the title and reclassification status of the property.

For a standing reference in 2026, the safest planning assumption is a cash-funded purchase completed through official banking channels.

That cash route also creates the documentary trail needed later for repatriation.

The ANCFCC issues the titre foncier, and a notaire registers the transfer.

The Rental and Riad-Guesthouse Angle

Marrakech and Essaouira are commonly used for tourism-oriented rentals, especially riads and small guesthouse-style properties.

Tourist accommodation use is not purely automatic after purchase.

Operating a riad or guesthouse normally requires the proper local and tourism-related authorization rather than simply owning the property.

Buyers should verify whether zoning, condominium rules, and local hospitality licensing allow the intended rental model before purchase.

The weakness of any undivided or customary title behind the asset can also complicate a guesthouse project.

A registered titre foncier and clear licensing path together form the realistic basis for a profitable riad operation.

Repatriation of Funds and the Office des Changes

Foreign buyers are advised to transfer purchase funds through official Moroccan banking channels.

The Office des Changes is the Moroccan exchange-control authority that governs convertibility and repatriation.

Proving the original foreign-currency import is what allows a foreign buyer to repatriate sale proceeds later in foreign currency.

The protected amount is subject to the rules applicable to the amount originally introduced.

The practical mechanism is to keep a formal banking trail and the currency-import attestation or record.

Without that record, resale proceeds may not be recognised as repatriable under exchange-control rules.

Annual Property Taxes

The taxe d’habitation is the annual housing tax, generally assessed on an official rental value rather than market price.

New homes can enjoy a temporary exemption period, after which the tax applies according to the valuation system.

The taxe de services communaux is a separate municipal services tax applied annually as well.

It is commonly described as tied to the property’s rental value, with urban rates often cited in current guides.

Both taxes are recurring ownership costs distinct from the one-time transaction duties.

Buyers should include at least one full year of these running charges when calculating the net yield on a rental or guesthouse property.

Common Pitfalls for Foreign Buyers

Medina properties can involve shared or unclear rights, old family succession issues, or undivided ownership that complicates resale and bankability.

Customary melkia paperwork is weaker than a registered titre foncier and creates more legal friction for foreigners.

Buying off-plan or incomplete projects carries delivery, quality, and title-registration risk.

Buyers should verify completion status and registry formalities carefully before committing to any unfinished development.

The recurring failure path is the same: paying for a property before confirming that a registered title exists and matches the asset.

Avoiding that mistake is more important than any price negotiation or rental projection.

World.title: Is South Africa Safe for Expats as Crime Drops
World.content:

Get the brief

Yesterday’s subject line: “Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with the UAE”

One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio.

Guides · South Africa

—The stakes. South Africa remains a high-violence, high-property-crime environment by international standards despite recent SAPS declines. —The date. Official SAPS releases cover January to March 2026, with a newer quarterly briefing flagged for late August 2026. —The geography. Gauteng, the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, and KwaZulu-Natal account for the bulk of murders and serious contact crimes. —The response. Expats and long-term residents rely on security estates, armed response, backup power, and strict driving routines. —The calm trade-off. The Garden Route, Winelands, and smaller Western Cape towns are seen as relatively calmer but not guaranteed safe.

South Africa asks foreign residents to accept a permanent trade-off: relative personal freedom inside a high-crime country, purchased through private security and constant spatial awareness. The latest SAPS quarterly numbers show several violent categories falling, but the lived baseline for expats has changed less than the headlines suggest.

A street-level view shows vehicles and pedestrians moving past commercial signage in a South African business district.

The National Crime Baseline for 2026

South Africa is best understood as a country with elevated murder, robbery, and property crime by global comparison.

SAPS releases remain the most direct public source, though they count reported crimes rather than every incident.

In the January to March 2026 quarter, SAPS recorded 5,181 murders nationally, down 9.5 percent from 5,727 a year earlier.

The same official release reported a 4.6 percent year-on-year decline in violent contact crime, with 7,405 fewer cases.

The previous quarter was also declining, with SAPS summaries showing contact crime down 6.7 percent and murder down 8.7 percent.

Reading SAPS Statistics Without Overclaiming

SAPS data are compiled by the SAPS Crime Registrar and drawn from police stations across the country.

They are population-adjusted using Statistics South Africa mid-year estimates, which allows provincial comparisons by rate.

But the figures only capture what victims report to police.

A July 2026 report noted that many crimes are never reported, meaning official counts lag lived exposure.

For expats, the practical lesson is to read trends as direction, not as a full measure of street-level risk.

The Geography of Risk

Gauteng, the Western Cape, Eastern Cape, and KwaZulu-Natal repeatedly dominate serious crime volumes.

In Q4 2025/26, the Eastern Cape had the highest murder rate per 100,000 people at 14.3, followed by the Western Cape at 12.8 and KwaZulu-Natal at 8.8.

Johannesburg shows a consistent split between high-exposure inner-city and commuter zones and more protected affluent northern suburbs.

SAPS precinct-level data list Alexandra in Johannesburg among higher-volume police-station areas, reinforcing that localised pattern.

The best comparisons come from police-station tables rather than vague city labels, since crime varies sharply within metros.

Gauteng carries the largest absolute murder count, not the highest rate.

Johannesburg, Cape Town, and Durban

Johannesburg’s inner city and dense commuter corridors carry more opportunistic and contact crime risk than the controlled northern suburbs.

Cape Town’s Atlantic Seaboard and City Bowl are not immune to property crime, but the most severe violence is concentrated in peripheral and high-risk township zones such as parts of the Cape Flats.

Durban and KwaZulu-Natal show their own pattern, with the province ranking among the top contributors to serious crime.

Late August 2026 reporting said Gauteng recorded the highest number of kidnappings, with KwaZulu-Natal second and the Western Cape third.

This means expat experience can differ enormously within a few kilometres, depending on access control and route choices.

How Expats Actually Live

Security estates and gated communities are the default housing choice for many foreign residents.

They combine perimeter controls, guarded access gates, and private response services to reduce casual entry.

Electric fencing, alarm systems, cameras, and neighbourhood watches add layered protection around the home.

Armed-response subscriptions are common because they create a commercial security backstop separate from public policing.

These measures are rational adaptations to persistent housebreaking, vehicle crime, and street-level snatching risk.

The Private Security Industry as a Parallel System

South Africa’s private security sector is large enough to function as a de facto parallel safety system.

A July 2026 report valued the industry at about R87 billion, or roughly US$4.5 billion to US$5 billion depending on exchange rate.

It is used by households and businesses alongside public policing, not as a replacement for it.

The same report said housebreaking remained the most commonly experienced household crime in Statistics South Africa survey data.

For expats, this industry is not optional; it is a core part of daily residential and commercial protection.

Common Crime Patterns Affecting Residents

Property-related crime remains central to resident risk even when quarterly numbers decline.

The Q4 2025/26 statement noted falls in burglary, theft of and from motor vehicles, and stock theft.

House robbery and robbery with aggravating circumstances also fell, but they still occur at scale.

Kidnapping is a visible current worry, with 4,638 cases recorded nationally in Q1 2026/27 and Gauteng accounting for more than half.

Phone snatching, ATM card fraud, and opportunistic theft fit the broader contact and property crime pattern in public spaces.

Eastern Cape and Western Cape run consistently above the national murder rate.

Hijacking Risk and Driving Rules Residents Follow

Carjacking, robbery with aggravating circumstances, and vehicle theft are tracked consistently in SAPS releases.

The newer Q1 2026/27 government reporting pointed to significant reductions in carjacking and residential and business robberies.

Long-term residents still follow defensive habits: keep doors locked, windows up, and avoid unnecessary stops.

They maintain distance at gates and intersections because slow movement and predictable stopping create exposure.

Night driving and isolated routes carry higher perceived risk, so routines are often varied and planned in advance.

Load-Shedding and Backup Power for Security

Load-shedding has shaped household security because alarms, electric fences, gate motors, and cameras depend on power.

Battery, inverter, and solar backup are used for security continuity rather than just comfort.

When outages disable perimeter protection or communications, armed-response monitoring becomes less reliable.

Expats treat backup power as a safety investment, not only an inconvenience solution.

The practical goal is to keep gates closed, cameras recording, and panic systems live during any outage.

Protest Action and Police Reporting Reality

Protest action is part of the public-order risk environment and can disrupt traffic, commuting, and business access.

Residents treat protests as a mobility problem first: avoid affected roads, allow extra time, and follow estate or security alerts.

SAPS statistics reflect crimes reported at police stations, compiled by the SAPS Crime Registrar.

Victims often do not report because of fear, inconvenience, or low confidence, so surveys can show wider exposure.

The gap between police counts and lived experience means expats should not treat low local figures as proof of low risk.

Calmer Towns and Practical Rules Long-Term Residents Follow

The Garden Route, the Winelands, and smaller Western Cape towns are commonly seen as calmer than the major metros.

Their relative appeal comes from lower density and a different crime profile than Johannesburg’s inner zones or Cape Town’s highest-risk peripheral areas.

This is a relative statement, not a safety guarantee, since the Western Cape still shows one of the higher murder rates.

Long-term residents live behind controlled access where possible and use layered security with backup power and armed response.

They minimise exposure at gates, ATMs, fuel stations, and intersections, keep routines unpredictable, and avoid displaying phones, laptops, watches, or cash.

World.title: Cost of Living Nairobi: Expat Budgets Jump 6%
World.content:
Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy . We never share your email.

One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio.

Guides · Kenya

—The stakes. Nairobi remains East Africa’s main expat duty station, so housing and schooling costs stay structurally high even when other East African capitals look cheaper. —The budgets. A comfortable single expat typically needs about KES 60,000 to 120,000 monthly, while families can spend far more before international school fees. —The housing split. Karen, Lavington, Westlands, Kilimani and Kileleshwa price well above satellite towns such as Ruiru, Syokimau and Embakasi. —The family breaker. International school fees are repeatedly cited as the largest single expat family cost and can exceed rent, utilities and transport combined. —The comparison. Nairobi is generally costlier than Kampala and Kigali for expat-standard living, while Dar es Salaam competes most closely in the region.

Nairobi’s expat cost structure is not a mystery, but it is sharply segmented by neighbourhood and family size. The city’s role as a UN and regional headquarters base keeps demand high in a narrow band of premium suburbs.

Aerial view of modern residential apartment buildings set among green trees in an upscale Nairobi neighbourhood.

Why Nairobi Is East Africa’s Expat Capital

Nairobi hosts the United Nations Office at Nairobi, one of the UN’s four major global duty stations. The city also serves as a regional headquarters base for multinational firms, NGOs and development organisations covering East Africa and the Horn.

That institutional density is not symbolic. It creates a permanent pool of international staff with housing allowances, school allowances and security expectations.

Employers compete for a limited supply of suitable properties in Karen, Lavington, Westlands, Kilimani, Kileleshwa, Riverside, Spring Valley, Gigiri and nearby areas. This competition is the main reason expat budgets in Nairobi diverge from ordinary local household budgets.

A 2026 property-market update said median asking rents across premium suburbs were up 2 to 6 percent year on year. Even modest percentage increases translate into large dollar amounts when monthly rents already run into thousands of dollars.

Realistic Monthly Budgets for Singles, Couples and Families

A single person can live comfortably in Nairobi for about KES 60,000 to 100,000 per month, while a family of four in a mid-range area typically needs KES 150,000 to 300,000 per month including rent, according to a 2026 relocation guide.

The same guide said budget living can start around KES 35,000 per month in satellite towns, while comfortable living in premium areas can exceed KES 200,000 per month. For a U.S. dollar framing, published 2026 material commonly clusters a comfortable single expat in the roughly $660 to $1,200 per month range, excluding or lightly including school costs.

Kenya’s own statistics give the firmer anchors. The Kenya National Bureau of Statistics put annual inflation at 6.6 percent in August 2026, with transport up 15.7 percent and food and non-alcoholic beverages up 9.0 percent. The Central Bank of Kenya posted the shilling at 129.45 to the dollar on 11 September 2026. That family baseline looks misleadingly low because it excludes the dominant cost: education.

International schooling adds about $2,000 to $3,000 per child per month equivalent in that guide’s framing. A couple without children can therefore live near the top of the single professional range, but a family with two school-age children moves into a completely different budget category.

Rent by Neighbourhood: The Expat Premium

Kilimani and Kileleshwa are consistently priced above many non-core districts. Published 2026 rent guides show one-bedroom apartments often around KES 35,000 to 70,000 and two-bedroom units around KES 55,000 to 130,000 depending on source and building quality.

Westlands and Parklands sit in a similar upper-mid market band, with one-bedroom units often around KES 35,000 to 70,000 and two-bedroom units around KES 60,000 to 130,000.

Karen and Lavington form the clearly premium residential belt. One-bedroom apartments in Karen are typically KES 65,000 to 80,000 unfurnished and KES 80,000 to 120,000 furnished, while two-bedrooms are KES 75,000 to 110,000 unfurnished and three-bedrooms are KES 110,000 to 170,000.

Family standalone homes in Karen or Runda can reach KES 400,000 to 1.2 million or more per month, according to a separate 2026 rental guide. The market premium for gated-community or standalone family housing is especially visible in Karen, Runda and similar low-density suburbs.

Cheaper districts outside the expat core sit far below these levels. Ruiru, Syokimau, Ruaka, Githurai, Embakasi and the Kangundo Road corridor offer much lower single-person budget rents, but they lack the concentration of international schools, private clinics and employer-friendly housing stock.

Annual inflation ran at 6.6 percent in August 2026, with transport up 15.7 percent.

Domestic Staff: A Household Expense, Not a Fixed Wage

In middle- and upper-income expat suburbs, domestic help is commonly hired for cleaning, cooking, childcare and compound upkeep. This is a widely used household-expense category rather than a fixed universal cost.

Published 2026 material did not include a primary-source wage schedule, so exact pay rates should be treated as variable. Pay depends on duties, live-in versus live-out status and suburb.

The practical implication for budgeting is that a family with a full-time nanny and a part-time cleaner will carry a materially higher monthly wage bill than a single tenant using occasional cleaning help.

The custom itself is well established. Expat households should not assume domestic staff are included in rent or service charge, though in some guarded compounds security personnel are already covered through the estate or building fees.

Food: Local Markets Versus Imported Supermarkets

There is a consistent cost split between everyday local shopping and premium imported-goods shopping. Local markets are cheaper for produce and staples, while imported supermarkets and premium grocers drive materially higher monthly food spend for expat households.

A 2026 expat guide budgets groceries for a single person at KES 15,000 to 25,000 per month in a comfortable scenario. That assumes a mix of local markets and standard supermarkets rather than a heavy imported basket.

Households that consistently buy imported cereals, dairy alternatives, packaged snacks and specific Western brands will move well above that range. Nairobi’s premium supermarkets serve that demand, but the landed cost of imported goods is structurally higher.

The mechanism is simple: a family that adapts to local produce and cuts back on imported packaged goods will spend far less than a household replicating a full expatriate shopping list.

International School Fees: The Budget-Breaker

Schooling is consistently identified as the biggest expense shock for expat families. One 2026 relocation guide estimates international school fees at KES 400,000 to 1,500,000 per term.

Another 2026 guide says international primary tuition can range roughly from KES 400,000 to 3,000,000 per year depending on curriculum, with British, American and IB programmes at the high end. A separate expat guide states international schools may cost about $25,000 to $37,000 per child annually.

Those figures make international school fees the single largest family line item. For a two-child household, annual school costs can dwarf rent, utilities, transport and food combined.

The budget consequence is structural. A family that looks affordable on rent alone becomes expensive once enrolment fees, deposits, uniforms, transport and activity charges are added.

Couples planning to start or move a family to Nairobi should treat school fees as a separate budget category before signing a lease or accepting a posting.

Transport: Ride-Hailing Dominance and Car Import Costs

Ride-hailing is widely used in Nairobi, and several guides explicitly treat Uber-style transport as a normal expat option. A 2026 expat budget guide puts transport for a single person at KES 5,000 to 15,000 per month when mixing ride-hailing and occasional matatu use.

Matatus remain the main mass-transit reality for most residents, but they are not the default choice for many expats who prioritise predictability and security. The network is extensive and cheap, but routing and comfort vary.

Car ownership in Nairobi is expensive relative to using ride-hailing. Imported vehicles face taxes and fees that materially raise landed cost, on top of fuel, maintenance, parking and security considerations.

No verified current Kenya car-import duty schedule was available in the available official sources, so the article describes the mechanism rather than a fixed tax rate. The practical advice is that transport budgets should assume ride-hailing as the baseline and treat car ownership as a significant premium.

The shilling stood at 129.45 to the dollar on 11 September 2026.

Private Healthcare and Insurance

Nairobi has a strong private-healthcare sector by regional standards. Private insurance or premium cover is common among expats, often provided through employer packages.

The main private hospitals to reference are Aga Khan University Hospital and The Nairobi Hospital.

Consultation fees should therefore be described as variable by specialty and facility, typically paid by insured patients through network arrangements or out-of-pocket for self-pay patients. Expats should budget for insurance premiums rather than assume a single standard consultation charge.

The practical exposure is not the routine consultation, but emergency care, specialist review and diagnostics. Those costs are where comprehensive cover matters most.

Security-Related Spending in Premium Housing

Security is a meaningful budget line in premium Nairobi housing, especially for compounds, apartment complexes and standalone homes. The most defensible framing is that expat households often pay indirectly for gated access, guards, alarm systems and response services through rent or separate service charges.

No verified current 2026 tariff for alarm response or private guarding was captured in the available official sources. The cost mechanism is therefore clearer than any single price.

In practice, a guarded compound may bundle 24-hour access control, perimeter patrols and alarm response into a single service charge. A standalone Karen or Runda house may require the tenant to arrange and pay for private guarding separately.

This line should not be underestimated. Security is not simply an amenity in the expat market; it is part of the market-clearing price for housing in preferred suburbs.

Internet and Utilities: Budget for Variability

Nairobi’s utilities are generally workable in expat areas, but households still budget for variability in electricity, water, backup power and internet quality. One 2026 expat guide budgets utilities at KES 5,000 to 10,000 and internet at KES 3,000 to 5,000 per month for a comfortable single-person lifestyle.

Another 2026 cost-of-living guide places fibre internet around KES 2,000 to 5,000 per month depending on package and provider. Power backup is increasingly common in premium compounds, but it may come as a separate cost or be embedded in service charges.

The practical point is reliability of service, not just price. Interruptions can occur, and households with generators or inverters carry higher effective utility costs than the headline tariffs suggest.

A two-bedroom apartment in Kilimani or Westlands will not have the same utility profile as a standalone family house with staff quarters in Karen.

Nairobi Versus Dar es Salaam, Kampala and Kigali

Nairobi is generally the most expensive of the four on an expat-standard basis. The presence of a major UN duty station and a deep base of regional headquarters pushes up both rent and schooling costs.

Dar es Salaam competes most closely with Nairobi among the East African capitals, particularly for prime housing. Kampala and Kigali tend to price below Nairobi for comparable expat accommodation, though availability of true expat-standard stock is smaller.

The verified side-by-side 2026 comparison was not fully captured in the available official sources, so the article frames the comparison by mechanism. Nairobi’s premium is most acute in the preferred expat belts and in international school fees.

For singles without children, the gap between Nairobi and Kampala or Kigali is narrower. For families paying international school fees, Nairobi’s institutional depth and school quality justify the premium for many employers and families.

The decision is therefore less about absolute cost than about matching the posting to school availability, medical cover and security expectations.

World.title: Retire in Morocco 2026 Residence Permit and Costs
World.content:

Get the brief

Yesterday’s subject line: “Algeria cuts diplomatic ties with the UAE”

One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio.

Guides · Morocco

—The draw. Morocco offers European retirees proximity to home, a mild climate and a lower daily cost base than many retiree areas in southern Spain and Portugal. —The permit. A retiree files for the carte de séjour at the local police prefecture with passport, legal entry, pension proof and accommodation evidence. —The property rule. Foreigners can own registered urban property with a titre foncier, while untitled melkia or customary land carries more legal risk. —The tax question. Treaties with France and Spain can assign pension taxing rights to the residence state but vary by pension type and require confirmation. —The healthcare model. Expat retirees generally rely on private clinics in Casablanca, Rabat and Marrakech and often keep European coverage for major treatment.

Morocco is becoming a standing option for retirees who want Europe’s proximity without southern Europe’s housing and service costs. But the path depends less on a single official income figure than on assembling the right local file, banking structure and titled property.

A narrow lane in an old Moroccan medina with stucco walls, a wooden door and two people walking in shadow.
