World.title: Judo Returns to Hungary for Exciting Grand Slam Action
World.content:
The Judo World Tour returns to Budapest. The Papp Lazlo Arena hosted athletes from across 67 countries for an electric first day of competition here at the Hungary Grand Slam 2026.

 

At -48Kg Kristina DUDINA was up against Sabina GILIAZOVA. In golden score, it was GILIAZOVA who dominated the technical battle to take gold.

IOC Member, Mr Mustapha BERRAF awarded the medals.

18 year old Izhak ASHPIZ was fighting in his third consecutive -60Kg Grand Slam medal match. A well timed Ura-nage saw the youngster claim his second Grand Slam gold.

He was awarded his medal by President of the Spanish National Olympic Committee, Mr Alejandro BLANCO.

The -52Kg final saw Barbara TWAROWSKA of Poland up against Ayumi LEIVA SANCHEZ of Spain. LEIVA SANCHEZ scored yuko to claim her first Gland Slam gold.

I love seeing the children, and signing their shirts and notebooks really takes me back to my own childhood. It’s always one of the most emotional parts of the finals for me. Ayumi LEIVA SANCHEZ (ESP)

IOC Member Mrs Filomena FORTES awarded the medals.

Boyan YOTOV of Bulgaria looked unstoppable throughout the day and in the -66Kg final there was no slowing down. With a Waza-ari on the board already, YOTOV caught his opponent beautifully scoring Ippon for gold.

Last year at the world championships the energy was special. I felt it, but I couldn't do my best, but here, now, I managed and it was a really special feeling for me. Boyan YOTOV (BUL)

The medals were awarded by IOC Member Mrs Petra SÖRLING.

In the -57Kg final, it was 2023 world silver medalist Haruka FUNAKUBO of Japan who struck gold. A clean yuko score quickly followed with dominant ground work secured FUNAKUBO the victory.

Vice President of the International Judo Federation Dr Laszlo TOTH awarded the medals.

The home nation put on a spectacular show throughout the day. Setting the stage for Day 2 of the Grand Slam. We’ll see you tomorrow.

World.title: ‘Recovery becomes self-propelling’: Five positive tipping points that can save the world
World.content:
The world risks irreversible damage as our reliance on planet-heating fossil fuels pushes ecosystems towards catastrophic climate tipping points.

 

A recent report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) warned that global temperature rise will exceed 1.5°C, likely within the next few years, overshooting the limit set out in the legally binding Paris climate agreement.

This would accelerate much of the environmental degradation the natural world is already experiencing, from shrinking ice sheets to rising sea levels and “unprecedented dieback” of coral reefs and rainforests.

The UNEP says that there are “no good outcomes if we remain above 1.5°C” and that governments must focus on making the overshoot as small and short as possible.

However, landmark new research from The Earthshot Prize and the University of Exeter has revealed 51 solutions that can trigger “rapid and transformative change” to repair the planet over the next five years. Out of these 51 solutions, five priority clusters – or ‘Earthshots’ – were identified.

Following the hottest August on record – tied with July 2023 – and a strong El Niño developing across the Pacific, researchers say that the study provides a “new, unifying agenda for positive action”.

“To reverse damage to our ecosystems before it’s too late, we need to unlock positive tipping points where progress builds on itself, costs fall with scale and recovery becomes self-propelling,” says Professor Tim Lenton, chair in climate change and earth system science at the University of Exeter.

Clean energy as a ‘master cascade’

Renewable energy such as solar and wind has already crossed positive tipping points in many markets – and is essential to end reliance on fossil fuels.

Last year, solar and wind accounted for a record 30 per cent of EU electricity, overtaking fossil power for the first time on record. During this time, EU solar generation hit a record 369TWh, up 20 per cent from 2025.

By 2030, solar power alone is projected to reduce EU emissions by 154 million tonnes of CO2-equivalent per year. This is the equivalent of the total greenhouse gas emissions of the Netherlands in 2023.

“Because clean power unlocks electric mobility, heat pumps, clean industry and clean air simultaneously, this is the highest-leverage transition across all five Earthshots,” the report says.

“The binding constraints are now grid expansion, permitting reform and the clean energy investment gap in the Global South.”

Despite hosting 60 per cent of the world’s best solar resources, Africa receives less than two per cent of global clean energy investment.

Some of the continent’s largest economies, such as South Africa, Morocco and Nigeria, are already accelerating plans to build more domestic solar manufacturing capacity to reduce dependence on Chinese imports that currently dominate the global market.

Morocco has doubled production to around one gigawatt a year. South Africa maintains a similar capacity, while Egypt has gigawatt-scale projects coming online.

“A few years ago, local solar manufacturing was barely on the agenda anywhere in Africa,” Benjamin Clarke, policy director at the Africa Solar Industry Association, tells news agency AP.

“It is now becoming a recognised pillar of industrial policy and green economic development.”

Clean cooking and clean household energy

Despite the clean energy boom, around 2.1 billion people still rely on solid fuels for cooking.

This is the largest source of indoor air pollution and a major source of ‘black carbon’, commonly known as soot.

“Clean cooking is close to a tipping point in several markets as pay-as-you-go solar and clean cooking businesses scale across East and Southern Africa,” the report states.

“In Latin America and parts of Asia, the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) transition is substantially complete, bringing health benefits to millions.”

How marine protected areas are becoming ‘self-reinforcing’

Researchers highlight that well-designed and well-enforced ocean conservation has produced “visible recovery” of fish stocks and biodiversity within recent years.

“As communities have reaped the benefits of marine conservation, protection areas have expanded and progress accelerated,” the report states.

“In turn, food security for coastal populations and climate resilience has strengthened with examples including the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park in Australia.”

Earlier this year, the highly anticipated High Seas Treaty came into force, marking a “historic milestone” for global ocean conservation.

The High Seas is often used to describe all areas beyond national jurisdiction, including the seafloor and water column (the vertical section of water from the surface to the bottom). This equates to international waters that cover more than two-thirds of our ocean – almost 50 per cent of the planet’s surface area.

Once considered barren and desolate, the High Seas are now regarded by scientists as one of the largest reservoirs of biodiversity on Earth. They play an important role in regulating the climate, supporting “crucial” carbon and water cycles.

A clownfish swims at Havannah Harbour, off the coast of Efate Island, Vanuatu, July 20, 2025. Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

However, human activity poses a growing problem for the High Seas. The High Seas Alliance (HSA) warns that destructive fishing practices such as bottom trawling and illegal fishing are harming High Seas marine life, along with issues such as plastic and chemical pollution, seabed mining and ocean acidification from global warming.

The Treaty now means that nations will be empowered to establish a connected network of High Seas marine protected areas (MPAs) – which can be adopted by a vote when consensus cannot be reached. This helps prevent a single nation from blocking MPAs being established.

It also supports developing countries through capacity building and the transfer of marine technology so that they are better empowered to develop, implement, monitor and manage future High Seas MPAs.

The ‘gatekeepers’ for tropical deforestation

Multiple studies have identified that rising global demand for meat, particularly beef, as a key force behind the destruction of the Amazon rainforest.

Research from the University of Manchester earlier this year, for example, found that up to 80 per cent of cleared forest land is converted into cattle pasture, while gaps in supply chain oversight allow deforestation to continue.

The ‘Positive Tipping Points’ report warns that concentrated global supply chains for beef, soy (which is often used to feed cattle), palm oil, timber, cocoa and coffee make a small number of buyers and financiers the “gatekeepers for tropical deforestation”.

However, legislation like the EU Deforestation Regulation, which “guarantees that the products EU citizens consume do not contribute to deforestation or forest degradation worldwide”, could make a significant difference – especially if it triggers a market-wide shift across other major importers such as China, the UK and the US.

How can positive tipping points be achieved?

Researchers stress that creating the right conditions for a solution area to tip is critical, outlining three prerequisites that are needed across all potential Earthshots. These are affordability, accessibility and attractiveness.

The report also states that the five Earthshots are “deeply interconnected” and often share the same conditions, infrastructure and risks within a single system.

For example, the boom in clean electricity could accelerate positive tipping points across all five Earthshots, while barriers such as a lack of investment in the Global South could stall progress in the regions that need it most.

“For too long a sense has prevailed that solutions to the climate and nature [crises] are out of reach. This new research explodes that myth once and for all,” says Jason Knauf, CEO of The Earthshot Prize.

“This pivotal research gives us reasons for optimism. This is a blueprint for turning ambition into action to place our planet on a path of rapid repair.”

World.title: From roughing it to Arctic luxury: Two sisters and three countries in two weeks
World.content:
There are probably more glamourous ways to begin a luxurious Nordic adventure than boarding a crammed Ryanair flight at London Stansted, but that’s exactly how this adventure started – a once in a lifetime tour for two weeks.

 

My sister Nyeema and I were fairly certain they had squeezed a few more seats onto the aircraft since either of us last flew with them. But there we were, two British sisters embarking on a girls-only holiday that would take us through Greenland, Iceland and Norway – from the decidedly and deliberately non-luxurious to the seriously expensive, with an extraordinary amount packed in between.

Sisters Nadira Tudor and Nyeema Yasin in Reykjavik Euronews Baku Bureau

By the end, we decided we could describe each destination in just three words.

For Nyeema, Nuuk was “remote, dystopian and mesmerising”. Mine were “sci-fi, raw and out-of-this-world”.

Reykjavík? She chose “charming, colourful and vibrant”. I went for “fresh-fishy, stunning and commercial”.

And Norway?

“Picturesque, historic and rainy,” according to my sister.

For me: “Luxurious, fairytale and quality.”

Those words turned out to say rather more about our journey than we realised.

Greenland: Raw, beautiful and suddenly everyone is talking about it

After a quick stopover in Copenhagen, we headed for Nuuk, Greenland’s capital, arriving to a spectacular bright daytime sky after midnight and a landscape that immediately felt unlike anywhere else.

There is undoubtedly something almost otherworldly about Greenland.

Famous Gulfoss Waterfall in Blaskogabyggo, Iceland on the Hvita river Euronews Baku Bureau

The scale, silence, water and mountains, punctuated by tiny splashes of colourful buildings, can make you feel as though you have landed on a film set... or the moon.

Filmmakers have already discovered it. Borgen: Power & Glory, starring Sidse Babett Knudsen put Greenland at the heart of a story about resources, Denmark and competing global interests in the Arctic.

Watching the real Greenland, those themes suddenly don’t seem particularly fictional.

Because one man seemed to be everywhere we went.

Donald Trump.

We had travelled to Greenland expecting to talk about landscapes, ice, culture and Arctic tourism. Instead, the US President’s name followed us around Nuuk.

Restaurants. Shops. Museums. Conversations with people we met and everybody seemed to have an opinion.

Some people we spoke to believed Trump’s repeated interest in taking control of Greenland had inadvertently done the country a favour. Whatever they thought of his politics, they liked the attention he had brought – and some thought it could ultimately benefit tourism.

A few were surprisingly relaxed, even telling us they didn’t particularly care if America took over. Most of the people we encountered, however, hated the idea.

What fascinated me was that a US president thousands of kilometres away had somehow become part of the everyday experience or travelling through Greenland.

Nuuk Cathedral or Church of Our Saviour, a wooden Lutheran cathedral in Old Nuuk neighbourhood Euronews Baku Bureau

We met Alice Burton, a former Head of Press Section at the US Embassy in Vienna, in our shared accommodation, who would become our partial travel companion, who had been hearing similar things from the locals.

“Nuuk is the most quiet capital I’ve ever visited,” she told me.

There are for sure few cars, little honking, hardly any sirens and remarkably few people on the streets.

“A world in itself,” Alice reflected.

Tourist Alice Burton eating whale steak in Three Coats restaurant in Reykjavik Euronews Baku Bureau

Yet politically, Greenland now feels anything but isolated.

Official tourism research estimated that just over 149,000 international tourists visited Greenland in 2024, with almost two-thirds arriving by cruise ship. Nuuk’s international airport is meanwhile transforming access to the capital.

For a destination with a population of fewer than 60,000 people, those numbers really matter.

What tourists don’t necessarily see in Greenland

It was how strongly I sensed a “them and us” relationship between Greenlanders and the Danes.

Along with Donald Trump, the divide surfaced in conversations with people we met unprompted, and in the way some Greenlanders spoke about Denmark, language, history and identity.

These individuals are not a measure of wider public opinion, but the sense of separation was striking – especially in the museums we visited.

Rather than presenting visitors with a sanitised Arctic idyll, Nuuk’s cultural institutions openly explore Greenland’s complicated relationship with Denmark.

Alice, Nyeema and I were all particularly struck by Nuna, an exhibition at Nuuk Art Museum examining land, identity and Greenland’s relationship with outside powers. At its entrance was a message requiring little explanation.

'Greenland is not for sale'

Talk to people and another Greenland begins to emerge – a society having its own conversation about identity, autonomy and Denmark while simultaneously confronting extraordinary new interest from the outside world.

Climate change, military security, natural resources, Indigenous identity, tourism and the interests of global powers increasingly collide here.

And yet everyday life carries on around the geopolitical noise.

On the water, however, there are bright blue mini-icebergs, mountains rising directly from the waves, rocks, sky and sea stretching into the distance and an undeniable silence, exactly the Greenland one imagines.

Perhaps “out of this world” wasn’t such an exaggeration after all.

Iceland: When tourism becomes a well-oiled machine

Arriving in Reykjavík after Greenland felt like jumping several stages forward in the evolution of a tourism industry.

If Greenland feels like a destination being on the cusp of something, Iceland has had years to work out what international visitors want.

And it shows.

Grimnes-og Grafningshreppur, the Kerio Volcanic Crater Lake, filled with turquoise-blue water Euronews Baku Bureau

The statistics underline just how important tourism has become. Statistics Iceland recorded an estimated 10.16 million overnight stays in registered accommodation in 2025, up 9.1% in a year.

Tourism directly accounted for 8.8% of Iceland’s GDP in 2025, while tourism consumption by domestic and international visitors reached almost ISK 914 billion, which equates to over 6.5 billion euros.

Those are substantial numbers for a small island nation and as a traveller, you can see the sophisticated industry that has grown around them.

Reykjavik is charming and colourful but also extremely tourism-savvy.

Excursions are offered everywhere and so are restaurants, shops selling Icelandic designs, outdoor clothing galore, Viking paraphernalia and row upon row of traditional woollen jumpers.

The latter look as they are going to itch and after my sister and I tried on a very wide variety of designs, we realised that they didn’t.

They do, however, shed hair like a loveable dog.

Cod with a honey and mustard sauce, at Three Coats restaurant in Reykjavik Euronews Baku Bureau

And then there was the food.

Fish was a highlight: extraordinarily fresh cod, tasting unlike any cod that you will be served in the UK, despite it being renowned for fish and chips.

There’s also smoked salmon, shrimp and warming soup served inside a bread bowl.

For the more adventurous, menus can venture into horse, whale steak and slithers of smoked puffin.

Iceland has become extremely good at turning what makes it distinctive into an experience visitors can easily access, but there is, however, one unavoidable issue.

It is very expensive.

But again, as in Greenland, there is no ignoring the disappearing glaciers, pollution of the oceans and land and the doom of climate change and for a country so dependent on both tourism and fishing, these aspects are difficult to ignore.

And perhaps at that is the contradiction at the heart of Iceland’s success. It has become supremely good at selling the experience of Iceland. But the thing that everybody has fundamentally travelled there for is something nobody has created.

Nature.

Our own excursion beyond Reykjavik may have had us packed together liked sardines, but once the city disappeared behind us it became increasingly difficult for us to complain.

Iceland straddles the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. Fissures cut through the landscape, geothermal activity bubbles beneath it and volcanoes, waterfalls and vast expanses of open land make it feel as though the planet is showing.

Hollywood clearly agrees.

Game of Thrones turned Icelandic landscapes into territory north of “the Wall”, while Christopher Nolan transformed parts of the country into another planet for Interstellar starring Matthew McConaughey and Anne Hathaway. The Star Wars universe has also found a home within Iceland’s otherworldly scenery.

Norway: When expensive starts to feel worth it

Bergen greeted us with torrential rain, which cleared the following morning.

We wanted to travel from Bergen through Myrdal to Flam, but there was one problem, and that was the direct trains we wanted were all sold out, but we found an alternative router from Bergen towards Myrdal via Voss, before joining the famous Flam Railway.

Mountains stretched beyond what the eye – or an iPhone camera – could properly absorb.

Water cascading from waterfalls and wild rivers, tiny settlements beneath enormous peaks.

The Flam Railway runs for around 20 kilometres through spectacularly dramatic mountain scenery towards the fjord below and has become one of Norway’s best-known rail experiences.

Myrdal station where you can catch the Flam Railway to the Hardangerfjord Euronews Baku Bureau

Hollywood has also exploited this country with good reason. Tom Cruise has repeatedly returned with the Mission Impossible franchise. Mission Impossible: Fallout features the spectacular clifftop finale at Preikestolen with Cruise and Henry Caville and in Dead Reckoning, Cruise launched a motorcycle from Helsetkopen. Daniel Craig’s final James Bond film, No Time to Die, also used Norwegian locations, as did the hit series Succession, featuring Brian Cox and Jeremy Strong.

The price of luxury

Norway is also expensive, but tourist don't appear to be staying away.

Norwegian commercial accommodation recorded 40.6 million guest nights in 2025 up 5.2% in a year.

International visitors accounted for a record 14.2 million guest nights – an increase of 14% – and around three quarters of foreign guest nights came from European markets.

Germany was the largest overseas market, followed by Sweden, the Netherlands, the UK and Denmark.

Bergen itself is flourishing, with the wider region recording around three million commercial guest nights in 2024, 13.5% higher than in 2019.

Eirik Gjøvåg Berge, Chief Communications Officer at Visit Bergen, told Euronews that it is important to distinguish between Norway’s reputation for high prices and what visitors are actually doing.

He points out that the evidence, does not suggest high costs are driving international travellers away.

“In fact, favourable exchange rates for many international visitors, combined with Norway's strong appeal as a nature and experience destination, have helped drive continued growth,” he says.

Does quality justify the price?

Hilde Berentsen, General Manager of Home Hotel Havnekontoret, seems to think so. “If you pay for a service then you can have a higher quality,” she told me. “If you always go for the cheapest thing, then you don’t have quality around you.”

Berentsen has watched Bergen’s tourism industry develop since the hotel opened in 2006.

Hilde Berentsen in the lobby of the popular Home Hotel Havnekontoret located next to the harbour in Bergen, Norway Euronews Baku Bureau

One of its first celebrity guests was football legend Diego Maradona, who stayed with his team and the hotel has subsequently attracted considerable publicity for its luxury suite, which became known as Bergen’s most expensive hotel room. More famous guests have since followed suit.

“Everything cannot be for everybody,” she said, pointing to camping, caravans and cheaper accommodation as alternative ways of experiencing the country.

According to Visit Bergen, tourism supports around 13000 jobs and generates approximately more than 617 million euros (NOK 6.7 billion) in annual value creation.

Three countries, three very different versions of northern tourism.

Bird’s eye view of houses dotted around the mountains skirting Bergen Euronews Baku Bureau

By the time my sister and I had reached the end of our journey, that decidedly non-luxurious flight out of Stansted seemed a very long way away.

We had travelled through three countries united by extraordinary natural beauty but offering remarkably different experiences.

There were no Mediterranean beaches, no sun loungers and frankly, not a great deal of sun on this holiday.

Instead, there were fjords, mountains, volcanoes, waterfalls, tectonic plates, Viking jumpers, fresh fish, packed trains, unexpected friendships and Donald Trump.

Two sisters beginning this journey with no expectations, but the end allowing three words to describe each location, but probably, they were nearly not enough.

World.title: Podcast: Eco-anger, France in space, world's first photograph
World.content:
A climate expert experiences eco-anxiety firsthand after living through France's hottest summer on record. France tries to find its place in the new space race. And the story of the earliest known photograph still visible today.

Advertising

Eco-anxiety is on the rise in France after a summer of unprecedented heatwaves led to wildfires, scorched crops and the deaths of at least 7,000 people as well as livestock and birds. Juliette Decq, a climate adaptation consultant, says fear is a normal response to the reality people are now facing. A mother of two young children, she experienced that reality firsthand when her own home became unsafe. She talks about her anger over France’s lack of preparedness, not least in schools, but also about the solidarity she witnessed in her local community as they helped people protect themselves. Eco-anger, she says, can be a force for change. (Listen @0')

Historically a leader in Europe’s space programme, France is reassessing its role in space. Although French astronaut Sophie Adenot is currently on the International Space Station, France’s space ambitions haven’t focused on human space flight. But as the US and China ramp up their Moon missions and space becomes increasingly industrialised, France is looking to find its place. Space policy analyst Xavier Pasco explains how Europe is positioning itself as a regulator in a rapidly changing sector that has, until now, remained largely unchecked. (Listen @20'10'')

French inventor Nicéphore Niépce took the earliest surviving photograph in July 1827: a scene from a window that might have taken days to make. He fell into obscurity, and the photo itself was lost. Now it's returning to France, as part of a celebration of 200 years of photography in his honour. (Listen @14'15'')

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Brazil: Flavio Bolsonaro faces corruption probe weeks before election
World.content:
Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, Lula's top rival in next month's election, is under investigation for alleged corruption linked to financing a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the leading right-wing challenger to President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, is under investigation for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion tied to the financing of a biopic about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, according to newly unsealed court documents.

What do we know about Bolsonaro's corruption probe?

The probe centers on funds Bolsonaro allegedly sought from Daniel Vorcaro, the disgraced banker behind the collapsed Banco Master, to help produce "Dark Horse," an unreleased film starring Jim Caviezel as the elder Bolsonaro.

Investigators are examining roughly $12 million that flowed from a Vorcaro-linked entity to a fund tied to Eduardo Bolsonaro, the senator's brother and campaign adviser, who lives in Texas. One document alleges Eduardo advised on how the money should be managed once in the United States.

Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Supreme Court Justice Andre Mendonca, a Bolsonaro appointee, opened the investigation in July at the request of federal police, but the case remained sealed until Chief Justice Luiz Edson Fachin ordered it made public this week, Reuters reported.

Federal police raided the production company behind the film and the office of congressman Mario Frias, its executive producer, on Thursday. Both have been barred from leaving the country and deny wrongdoing.

How did the Bolsonaros respond?

Flavio Bolsonaro has denied any misconduct, telling reporters at a campaign stop, "It is very positive that the documents are unsealed," the Associated Press reported

"I want transparency in everything."

Eduardo Bolsonaro similarly rejected the allegations, telling Reuters the funds were routed through the US to avoid interference from Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversaw his father's coup conviction.

"They want to frame this as bribe money, which it isn't," he said.

On social media, he said investigators “are trying to repeat the mechanism that worked against Jair Bolsonaro.”

What did Lula say?

In a Thursday television interview, Lula said Banco Master "was created in the Bolsonaro administration" and shuttered during his own term. He has called for full transparency in the case regardless of political fallout.

The disclosures come three weeks before Brazil's October 4 election, in which polls show Bolsonaro and Lula roughly tied.

Political analysts say the timing leaves Bolsonaro less room to recover than when the scandal first surfaced in May, though the fallout could also cut against Lula given the case's ties to Vorcaro's dealings with multiple political and judicial figures.

A runoff, if needed, is set for October 25.

World.title: Corals as climate archive: Are El Niños intensifying?
World.content:
Records from the past few decades show that, during this period, El Niño events have been frequent and often extreme. But is this normal, or is it the result of climate change? Corals can give us a clear indication.

A storm is gathering. Most likely a very big one. El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon occurring every two to seven years, towards the end of the year, but it comes in various different strengths, depending on the prevailing conditions.

El Niños are considered strong if the surface temperature of the water off the west coast of South America is more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above average. In July this year, the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) was already observing temperature increases of greater than three degrees Celsius in the eastern and central Pacific.

The German Meteorological Service believes this "could in all likelihood develop into one of the strongest El Niño events since records began."

But a recent article by the Max Planck Institute for Meteorology states that whether or not strong El Niño events will intensify as a result of climate change "remains the subject of ongoing research."

The data gap: What corals can tell us about El Niño

The problem is that the data on ocean surface temperatures is only truly reliable from the 1980s onward, with the start of satellite observation. And this data doesn't tell us how El Niño behaved before industrialization and the burning of fossil fuels.

US researchers say corals can help to close this knowledge gap. Julia Cole, a climate scientist and paleoclimatologist at the University of Michigan, and her team recently published a study on this subject in the journal Science.

"We've known for a long time that the last 40 or 50 years has really strong El Niño events," says Cole. "It's been hard to say whether the recent strong El Niño that we've had is part of a natural cycle, or if it's something a little bit unusual related to being in a warmer than normal world." The coral analysis points firmly in one direction: Unusual. Not normal.

Corals: A repository of 1,000 years of climate history

Cole and her team examined fossilized and living corals around the Galapagos Islands off Ecuador in the eastern Pacific. Corals grow between one and two centimeters per year, and in doing so form a structure similar to growth rings on trees. "We made use of the fact that corals record ocean temperatures as they grow, in the chemical composition of their skeleton," Cole explains.

Corals are living creatures that construct external skeletons through calcification, adding a band of new growth each year with calcium carbonate precipitated from the surrounding water. In this way, over decades and centuries, corals have formed entire reef systems. Other chemical elements are also incorporated into the skeleton during the calcification process — strontium, for example. Sometimes more is deposited, sometimes less, depending on the temperature of the water.

"In colder temperatures, it [the skeleton] absorbs more strontium, in warmer temperatures less," says Cole. The ratio of strontium to calcium in the skeleton provides information about changes in temperature.

Specific isotopes of oxygen in coral skeletons provide clues, as well. "The rare oxygen-18 and the common oxygen-16 are also taken up in a ratio that reflects temperature," says Cole. In colder conditions, more oxygen-18 is absorbed than in warmer temperatures.

In this way, researchers were able to reconstruct the changes in ocean temperatures over the past 1,000 years, according to the age of the corals. Their conclusion was that El Niño events have become markedly stronger compared to the pre-industrial period.

Scientists Julia Cole and Cameron Tripp collecting samples at the Galápagos Islands Image: Julia Cole/University of Michigan

Corals give indications, not conclusive answers

Cole's study has confirmed a long-held suspicion. "These developments correspond to the predictions of the best climate models. They predict a quantifiably higher likelihood of extreme eastern Pacific El Niño events in the 2030s," says Jens Zinke, professor of paleobiology at the University of Leicester in England.

However, other scientists are more circumspect in assessing the study's significance. "Coral data does achieve a high temporal resolution — monthly to seasonal — but its accuracy is dependent on local conditions, meaning that direct comparisons with modern measurement data are fraught with uncertainty," says Andreas Fink, professor of meteorology at the Institute for Meteorology and Climate Research in Karlsruhe. According to Fink, the significance of the study is undermined by its regional limitation to the eastern Pacific.

Cole is also aware of her study's limitations. "Our data does fill a gap, but I want to be clear that our record isn't continuous," she says. "We don't have every single year over the last millennium. We have a little bit under half of the years covered."

An NOAA scientist drilling to collect a coral core at the Galápagos Islands, Ecuador Image: NOAA

Floods, droughts, record heat — the consequences of stronger El Niños

Although the epicenter of the El Niño phenomenon is the Pacific, it changes the weather across the globe. In countries like Ecuador and Peru it can cause heavy rains and flooding, while Australia and Indonesia may experience a lack of rain, leading to drought and wildfires. El Niño also causes global temperatures to rise for a while.

If the predictions prove right and this El Nino does in fact become a Super El Niño, the coming year, 2027, will probably be another of record heatwaves, according to Thomas Felis. Felis leads the research group on coral paleoclimatology at the MARUM Center for Marine Environmental Sciences at the University of Bremen, and has conducted a similar study to Cole's.

Heat-stressed oceans: El Niño is a threat for corals

A year of record heat "will very probably lead to another global coral bleaching," says Felis. This has happened before, in the years 2023–24 and 2015–16, which were also El Niño years.

Corals get their characteristic colors from certain algae with which they live in symbiosis. Through photosynthesis, the algae provide the energy the corals need to live. If the temperature of the ocean is too high, the algae start to produce toxins, and the corals end the partnership. The coral remains, in its skeleton.

It can survive like that for a few weeks, and if the temperature drops again, the algae return. "But if this state, with abnormally high summer temperatures, goes on for too long, the coral becomes so sick that it eventually dies," Felis explains.

Worldwide coral death would mean not just the end of a unique ecosystem, but the destruction of an archive that preserves the history of the oceans.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
World.content:
Uber's departure from Nigeria and Uganda has left countless customers high and dry. But what about drivers? With fuel prices, maintenance, and other operating costs rising, many say they're struggling to make a living.

A week ago, Uber unexpectedly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending more than a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also said it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect.

With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda, Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — Egypt, Ghana, Kenya, and South Africa.

"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition," without sharing details on what this assistance would entail.

In the last year, the multinational company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania, while also cutting its global workforce by 10%.

Ride-hailing apps have gained in popularity across Africa over the past decade, but not all of them seem to be profitable Image: Afolabi Sotunde/REUTERS

Africa a difficult market to crack

Uber has not managed to grow across much of the African market despite its massive global scale. The profit-driven ride-hailing app faces stiff competition from rival platforms, including Bolt, inDrive and SafeBoda, which operate in the Nigerian and Ugandan markets and beyond.

However, it's not only Uber that is having to deal with its frustration over the current situation: Many of its drivers across Africa have been raising complaints about shrinking profit margins amid rising fuel costs, inflation and currency volatility, especially in markets like Nigeria.

In their view, Uber's business model of pocketing around 20% — 25% of any trip fare in commissions is no longer tenable.

Discontent, discombobulated and disregarded drivers

Abbas Olamide, an Uber driver in the Nigerian capital Abuja, said the company's overall service was "good," while firmly stressing that the high commission rates were adding greatly to his existing woes.

He told DW that a ride of 30,000 Naira (€20) "to the airport means the ride-hailing app would deduct 6,000 Naira as commission," still leaving him to "then pay a gate fee at the airport."

"Probably because you do not want to go back to town empty-handed, we also pay to park at the airport [to pick up another client]," he explained.

"At the end of the day, what's left is no longer enough."

Uber makes UK drivers workers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Samuel Olatunji, an Uber-driver in the megacity Lagos, also shared his concerns with DW following the abrupt announcement of Uber's exit, saying he will now have to recalibrate his own business model.

The 43-year-old driver says he'll have to join hundreds of other drivers who "have to depend on other [ride-hailing] apps now" to ensure any steady stream of income.

"But the amount I take home won't add up like before again."

In recent years, drivers like Olamide and Olatunji have staged several strikes and protests over soaring operating costs, low fares and working conditions, as well as Nigeria's fuel hikes, which this year have also been worsened by the surge in prices at the pump following the war in Iran.

Their pleas and concerns, however, remain largely unheard, as they find themselves having to prepare for a bumpy ride ahead.

Dollars versus naira

Uber meanwhile did not provide a detailed explanation for its decision; however, it comes against the backdrop of double-digit inflation in many places across Africa, which has eroded the purchasing power of millions of people while pushing them deeper and deeper into poverty.

This also makes consumers less likely to use the transport company.

Ikemesit Effiong, partner at SBM Intelligence, a consulting firm based in Lagos, explained that "[r]ising costs for such things as fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance, coupled with a currency that is less valuable now than in 2014 means that fares were climbing faster than the average Lagos or Abuja rider's willingness or ability to pay for the convenience."

Rising fuel costs due to the war in Iran coupled with Nigeria's abolition of the state fuel subsidy have led gas prices to skyrocket Image: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

Effiong added that while Uber's cost base is dollar-linked, the drivers' revenue is the shrinking naira, leading to the overall maths not working anymore, and forcing Uber to operate under unsustainably thin profit margins.

This is despite the fact that Nigeria's ride-hailing market alone is estimated to be worth around $450 million per year.

"These platforms are trying to hold fares low enough to retain price-sensitive riders, while the driver take-home shrinks in real terms. This pushes drivers toward multi-apping, off-platform negotiation, or exit altogether," he noted.

Effiong further highlighted that one of Uber's local competitors, InDrive, does actually operate under a negotiated-fare approach, resulting in "less reliance on the capital-heavy, standardized-fare template that works in wealthier markets."

The complex economics of ride-hailing

There are some striking similarities between the Nigerian and Ugandan markets: Both countries have huge populations and a growing demand for more transport solution. But both across both Kampala and Lagos, Uber's exit also creates a loss of a service many users had considered a safe and reliable option — more so than some of the other options.

Mary-Esther Anele, a Lagos resident, told DW that she knows that she is "going to start looking for alternatives."

"But most importantly, I'm going to travel less anyway now because transportation costs are going to increase," she added.

Spain restricts ride-hailing services To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

There also are questions about any knock-on effects beyond the current decision by Uber:

Will the California-based multinational leave its remaining African markets? Will its pricing dynamics change in order to bring in more money from the continent? And how will competitors respond?

In some other African countries like South Africa, ride-hailing apps like Uber have also long been a thorn in the side of taxi companies and minibuses, whose operators say they don't want to compete against those drivers, even resorting to violence at times as part of ongoing local taxi wars.

Will Uber's shrinking footprint in Africa impact these kinds of developments in other markets?

As countless drivers prepare for an unknown future, the end of their partnership with Uber might — for many — spell their journey's end.

In some markets, the competition between ride-hailing apps and traditional taxi services can have brutal consequences Image: Daniel Irungu/dpa/picture alliance

Frank Yiga from Kampala contributed to this report.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

World.title: North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles day after trilateral drills end
World.content:
North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles into the sea a day after the US, South Korea and Japan concluded joint military exercises Pyongyang had called provocative.

North Korea launched several short-range ballistic missiles toward the sea on Saturday, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said, a day after the United States, South Korea and Japan wrapped up a five-day trilateral military exercise that Pyongyang has criticized as provocative.

What do we know about the launches?

The missiles were fired from North Korea's eastern Wonsan area and traveled roughly 250 kilometers before landing in the country's eastern waters, South Korea's military said.

According to the Yonhap news agency, the North appears to have launched its Hwasong-11 series ballistic missiles alongside rounds from 600-millimeter multiple rocket launchers, with the two systems fired in succession across multiple instances, sources told the outlet.

The JCS said it had increased surveillance and was coordinating closely with the US and Japan. Meanwhile, South Korea's presidential national security council called on North Korea to halt launches that violate United Nations Security Council resolutions.

The US Pacific Command said the launches did not pose an immediate threat to American territory or regional allies, reaffirming Washington's defense commitments in the region.

What lessons is North Korea learning from the Iran war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the US-Korea drills entail?

The trilateral drills that preceded the launches, known as Freedom Edge, involved joint training across air, sea and cyber domains, including maritime maneuvers, air refueling and cyber coordination.

South Korea's military has described the exercises as defensive, intended to strengthen a coordinated response to North Korean nuclear threats.

North Korean Defense Minister Kim Song Gi had denounced the drills as "provocative" when they began earlier this week, threatening unspecified "strong and reflective countermeasures."

Saturday's launch marked North Korea's first missile test in roughly three weeks, following a similar barrage of more than 10 short-range missiles last month during a separate round of US-South Korea exercises.

Has South Korea's relationship with the US changed?

The launches also come amid a broader shift in the security dynamic on the Korean Peninsula.

Last month, President Donald Trump ordered a significant scaling back of the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise with South Korea, citing his relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who has long described the drills as rehearsals for invasion.

But Kim's sister and senior official, Kim Yo Jong, dismissed the gesture, saying a shortened drill would not change its "provocative, aggressive nature."

Last Sunday, Kim Jong Un used a ceremony marking the commissioning of North Korea's second naval destroyer to call for expanding the country's nuclear deterrent. Both of the country's destroyers are said to be capable of carrying nuclear-capable missiles.

Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Associated Press experts say Pyongyang's leader, bolstered by his advancing weapons program and closer ties with Moscow and Beijing, may be positioning himself to extract greater concessions in potential talks with Washington.

Kim has said he would consider returning to negotiations if the US drops what he calls its "hostile policy" and recognizes North Korea's status as a nuclear state.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: Russia's drone war comes to Moldova and Romania
World.content:
Incursions by Russian drones into Moldovan and Romanian airspace are increasingly common. This week the Ukrainian president's plane was stopped from taking off from Chisinau. Observers suspect the attacks are deliberate.

For Ukrainians, Russia's air war has been a bitter, bloody reality for years. People in Ukraine are being killed every day by missiles, bombs, and drones. But the country's central and southeastern European neighbors have also found themselves affected, albeit on a smaller scale: Missiles and drones sometimes invade their air space, and occasionally even crash on their territory.

Now the Russian drone war is coming dangerously close to two of Ukraine's neighbors: Romania and the Republic of Moldova, where drone incidents are now an almost daily occurrence. The drones often explode, leaving people injured, and there have also been recent attacks on Ukrainian checkpoints at the Moldovan and Romanian borders.

The attacks have now escalated to such a degree that many observers believe they can no longer be considered unintentional. They suspect the Kremlin is deliberately trying to bring the war to Ukraine's neighbors.

The latest drone incursion and crash on Tuesday caused a furore as it prevented a plane with the Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on board from taking off in the Moldovan capital Chisinau. A Russian Geran drone, which can fly as fast as 500 kilometers per hour (311 mph), took off in Crimea, then flew through Ukrainian airspace and eventually crashed in a sunflower field near the Moldovan city of Riscani.

The drone also flew over Romania, where two fighter jets were scrambled from NATO's Kogalniceanu airbase near the Black Sea port of Constanta, though it remains unclear why they did not shoot down the drone, as they had on other occasions.

Police investigate the debris from a drone that exploded on August 17, 2026, in the Moldovan village of Talmaza Image: Polizei Republik Moldau/DW

More and more incidents in Moldova and Romania

The most serious aspect of the incident was that it showed how limited Moldovan air defense is in its ability to protect the country's air space. The drones were detected and tracked by air traffic control, but it was not possible to shoot them down. According to publicly available information, the country possesses only a small number of Polish Piorun anti-aircraft missiles, and these are only able to protect certain specific targets.

There have been around three dozen drone incidents in Romania and Moldova since the beginning of August this year. The majority were airspace violations, but there have also been crashes and explosions, while debris has also been found. In Romania, several drones have also been shot down. According to official data, 17 drones crashed in August in Moldova alone – as many as in all of 2025.

Deaths at border crossings

There was also a drone strike on the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and southeastern Moldova on the night of September 8. The crossing, situated around a kilometer from Moldovan territory, and was damaged in the attack. Two people were killed and two others wounded, one of them a Moldovan citizen.

The Moldovan leadership has strongly condemned the drone attack. President Maia Sandu said on Wednesday that Russia's war had arrived at the Moldovan border.

"It is hard to understand, given this reality, that there are still voices who try to convince Moldovans that Russia is not the aggressor, or that the war in our part of the world has nothing to do with us," Sandu said.

Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The president of the Moldovan parliament, Igor Grosu, wrote on Facebook that these were incidents "we can no longer view as something remote." The threat from Russia, Grosu said, was not a "specter," and not propaganda: "It is a daily reality."

Moldova's Defense Minister Anatolie Nosatii said that the deaths of Moldovan citizens could no longer be ruled out in future.

Vladimir Bolea, the minister of infrastructure, warned that Giurgiulesti, Moldova's port on the Danube, could become a target after the Russian Foreign Ministry accused Romania and Moldova of using the port as a "transit hub" for arms shipments.

'Planned operation' by Russia?

Moldovan military and security expert Rosian Vasiloi, a former head of the Moldovan border police, wrote on Facebook in response to Tuesday's drone crash in Moldova: "This is a planned operation by the aggressor state."

He also referred to the drone's peculiar flight path: After flying from Ukraine over Moldova into Romania, it made an about-turn and flew back to Moldova.

Vasiloi concluded: "We can no longer view our airspace as separate from Ukraine's and Romania's. Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova, and Romania already form an interconnected operational area as far as air threats and their impact on regional connectivity are concerned."

The Romanian leadership has not yet reacted to the latest incidents. But in July, the Romanian government made a political and military change of course: After a long period of restraint, it started to shoot down drones in Romanian airspace.

The remains of a Russian Shahed drone shot down in Romania in July 2026. Russia's ambassador to Bucharest was summoned to receive a formal protest Image: Ministerul Afacerilor Externe

Former Romanian General Virgil Balaceanu, a regular analyst in the country's media, has urged Romania's leaders to accelerate the enhancement of Romanian air defenses. Balaceanu also believes that the drone incident on Tuesday was a deliberate maneuver.

Following this latest incident, the US Institute for the Study of War (ISW), a leading public think tank for analysis of Russia's war against Ukraine, wrote that while there was no evidence that the airspace violations were intentional, it could be said that Russia benefited from such actions.

In particular, it wrote, the incursions using Russia's latest, extremely fast Geran drone model "aim to further test NATO and Moldovan defenses and the response of the entire NATO alliance."

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: DW exclusive: Zelenskyy offers to meet Putin at G20 in Miami
World.content:
In an interview with DW, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country was in a strong position to negotiate and offered to meet Vladimir Putin in Miami.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said he would travel to Miami if his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, attended the Group of 20 (G20) leaders' summit scheduled for December.

Zelenskyy replied enthusiastically when DW's correspondent Misha Komadovsky posed the question on Friday.

"Yes, of course. We have to come. We have to meet, to speak and make decisions," he said.

Zelenskyy added that what he was going to say to Putin mattered less than results.

"It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn’t matter. It doesn’t matter. [...] Results matter. That's it."

Zelenskyy and Putin have not met in person since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of its smaller neighbor in February 2022.

The Kremlin has so far declined to say whether Putin would go to Miami for the meeting.

The Russian leader has not personally attended a G20 summit since 2019.

Last month, Russia's Finance Minister Anton Siluanov was however invited by the US to attend a meeting of G20 countries in North Carolina in a move that upset European officials.

Zelenskyy backs Putin meeting at Miami G20: 'Results matter' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

100-year partnership declaration with Canada

First up, however, Zelenskyy spoke of the deals he signed on Thursday with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, including a 100-year partnership declaration.

Zelenskyy underlined the importance of the deal, which he said covered numerous sectors, "from security, financing, energy, very important energy, veteran policy, and culture, and relationships and humanitarian issues."

"So it's a global decision, a really historic decision, and I'm happy that we have it," he said.

Zelenskyy said he had also signed a deal on collaboration on drone production with the Canadian leader involving a number of Ukrainian companies.

Zelenskyy pushes for more Patriot missiles ahead of winter

Zelenskyy's interview with DW comes as summer is nearly over and Ukraine is gearing up for the cold months of winter.

The Ukrainian president has conceded that his country has been struggling to counter flying jet-propelled drones that Russia has been increasingly deploying.

"They [US] have political will to sell and to help, but the production is not too big. So it means that stocks is a variant," he said.

"Will Americans be ready to give us (Patriots)? I don’t know. We will see."

Patriot missiles are powerful weapons that are currently the most effective defense against Russian ballistic missile attacks.

What Zelenskyy needs from US and European allies

"Russia [currently] produces 140 ballistic missiles per month. So, according to the rules of NATO, if you want to destroy 140, you need a 1-to-2 [ratio], 280 missiles," Zelenskyy told DW.

"You will never have 280 missiles per month, and between us, it’s a huge challenge to have [even] 100 missiles per month. This is what I want. I want to have 100-120 for these difficult months, especially the cold months."

Germany earlier this week said it was going to send Patriot missiles from its national stock, without specifying how many missiles that would be.

Zelenskyy called on Kyiv's European allies to provide more support.

"They have to give as much as possible. With all respect to them, they have to give to Ukrainians to save their lives."

Zelenskyy also spoke of having secured agreements with several European companies to develop a Ukrainian-led anti-missile system called Freya.

He said he was hoping that the first test phase would begin by the end of December, stressing that time was short.

Ukraine faces Patriot missile shortage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine in 'good position for negotiations'

Zelenskyy said that it was a "good signal" that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv earlier this week, and not just Moscow.

He said he had made clear to them that his country was well-placed for negotiations on ending the conflict, with Russia estimated to be losing more than 30,000 soldiers a month.

Zelenskyy said this meant that Moscow was paying a "big price" for small gains on the battlefield.

"So that’s why we think that we have now good position for negotiations," he said, adding that his country was stronger than last year.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Zelenskyy in Kyiv Image: Ukrainian Presidential Press Office/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Grain and energy top priorities

The other concern that has been coming up steadily over this summer is the shipment of grains through the Black Sea, with Moscow and Kyiv currently targeting each other's ships and hindering exports.

Russia's de facto blockade of Ukraine's Black Sea ports in the Odesa region has led to a 76% fall in Ukraine's grain exports year-on-year so far in August.

Zelenskyy said he had spoken with the two envoys about an energy and grain ceasefire that could provide a starting point for peace.

"What can bring us to any kind of negotiations? So energy and grain. This is step number one. What we can achieve," he said.

Edited by: Jenipher Camino Gonzalez

World.title: France: Sabotage suspected in train derailment
World.content:
Dozens were injured when a train derailed between Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, on Friday evening. Police believe the accident may have been deliberately caused, local media say.

A train derailed on Friday evening between the cities of Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, authorities said, with local media citing police as saying sabotage may have been at play in the incident.

At least 44 people were injured in the accident, which occurred near the municipalities of Cleon and Tourville-la-Riviere at around 7:30 p.m. local time (18:30 UTC), the Seine-Maritime prefect said in a statement .

One of ​the injured, a young woman, was in a critical state and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen, the local authority added.

The train was carrying around 180 passengers when it derailed, national rail company SNCF and the prefect said.

What else do we know about the train derailment?

French Transport Minister Tabarot said 140 firefighters were at the scene.

Local authorities have urged the public to avoid the area.

The French rail network operator SNCF Reseau said traffic on the line had been suspended.

"The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Reseau said.

​A police spokesperson said the train derailed after hitting an unidentified object.

A piece of rail that might have been involved has been found on the track, according to police reports.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Ukraine: Russian strike on Kyiv gas station kills 2
World.content:
With fighting on the front lines mostly stalled, Russia has been increasingly hitting petrol stations and other civilian targets. Ukraine has also been attacking Russia with drones, killing three people on Friday.

At least two people were killed in Kyiv after Russian jet-powered drones struck a petrol station on Friday.

A 12-year-old boy was among 12 people who were injured by the attack, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said one of the injured was a first responder who was "wounded in a double-tap strike."

Russia has turned to using jet-powered drones in near-constant attacks on Kyiv Image: Efrem Lukatsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

Russia increasingly targeting petrol stations with new, faster drones

Friday's drone strikes come a day after what is thought to be the first Russian attack on a Kyiv gas station during the war.

Russia has struck around 300 petrol stations in Ukraine in recent months, most of which were in or near frontline areas.

The attacks on petrol stations come amid a spike in Russian assaults using new, faster and harder-to-intercept jet-powered drones to strike logistics centers, warehouses and commercial supply chains.

Russia turns to jet-powered drones to wear Kyiv down To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ukraine condemns escalating Russian 'terror'

Zelenskyy said Russia was escalating these strikes on civilian energy infrastructure, calling them "increasingly terrorist in nature."

"Maximum attention must be focused on protecting the skies, finding solutions to protect people, and scaling up countermeasures against Russian drones," the Ukrainian leader said in a post on X.

The CEO of Ukrainian oil giant Ukrnafta, which owns the gas station and one other that was also struck on Friday morning, condemned Russia for "yet another deliberate strike on civilian facilities."

"There is no military objective in such attacks. This is terror against the civilian population," Bogdan Kukura said.

Russia has not publicly commented on the latest attacks, but has consistently denied targeting civilians.

Ukraine, Russia striking logistics, energy targets

More than four and a half years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion and with the fighting on the front lines in eastern Ukraine mostly stalled, Russia and Ukraine have been increasingly hitting logistics, energy and other economic targets in a bid to dent the other's war effort.

Ukraine has also stepped up its own drone attacks inside Russia. Overnight, two people were killed in Russia's Tula region, while one person was killed in Kursk on Friday, officials said.

Tula's regional governor Dmitry Milyayev added that three people were injured in the attacks.

Ozon, Russia's second-largest e-commerce platform, said a Ukrainian drone had struck a logistics hub in the city of Saratov, starting a fire.

Kyiv says its strikes against e-comms targets are aimed at disrupting Russia's supply lines Image: REUTERS

More than 20 warehouses belonging to Ozon and Wildberries, Russia's other leading online retailer, have been hit in Ukrainian attacks in recent weeks.

Kyiv says the strikes are justified as part of its campaign to undermine Russia's war effort, which has also seen Ukraine target Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko
