Following a crash between a train and a truck at a rail crossing that left one passenger dead and both drivers with serious injuries, Poland’s main train drivers’ union has announced a go-slow protest that will take place on Friday. They note that they have long been warning about a lack of sufficient safety measures at rail crossings, and say that a “red line has now been crossed”. In the wake of Wednesday’s tragedy, Prime Minister Donald Tusk has pledged that the government will introduce “very tough” new punishments for those who violate regulations at crossings. Poczułam takie jakby silne hamowanie, takie bardzo silne i nagle takie bujanie i do człowieka dociera, że zaraz się wykoleimy – mówiła pasażerka pociągu Intercity "Koziołek", jadącego z Lublina do Szczecina, który wykoleił się w miejscowości Sokolniki Suche w Mazowieckiem.… pic.twitter.com/enyjD2Wo6K — tvn24 (@tvn24) September 9, 2026 On Wednesday morning, a train travelling between the cities of Lublin and Szczecin partially derailed in the village of Sokolniki Suche in central Poland after colliding with a heavy goods vehicle that, initial findings suggest, had entered the tracks at a rail crossing despite warning lights flashing. The crossing had no barriers. The train was carrying at least 114 people, including three crew. One passenger in the first carriage, a 39-year-old woman, died in hospital from her injuries, prosecutors announced later on Wednesday. Four others, including the drivers of both the train and the truck, remain hospitalised in serious condition. Prosecutors say that, from the evidence collected so far, they will launch an investigation into the crime of unintentionally causing a rail disaster, which carries a prison sentence of six months to eight years. However, they have not yet been able to interview either driver due to their health conditions. On Thursday, the head of the Polish train drivers’ union, Leszek Miętek, announced that a protest would begin at midnight and last through the whole of Friday. “We are appealing to train drivers to travel at a safe speed of 20 km/h (12.4 mph) across every level crossing in Poland,” he said, adding that he had “received reports from across the country” that “there’s full support for this type of action”. Miętek noted that the Polish labour code allows employees to refrain from work if they believe it poses a threat to their life or health. While drivers would not go that far, they want to demonstrate in a bid to prompt “action from those responsible for safety.” He warned that train delays should be expected on Friday. Związek Zawodowy Maszynistów Kolejowych mówi "dość" i ogłasza ogólnokrajowy protest po tragicznej katastrofie w Sokolnikach Suchych. W piątek, 11 września, pociągi w całej Polsce będą zwalniać na przejazdach kolejowych do zaledwie 20 km/h. However, “a red line has [now] been crossed”, he added, quoted by news website Interia. Miętek noted that, for over 18 months, the union has been running a campaign, titled “I Want To Live”, focused on safety. Just two days before the accident, it had issued a special appeal to drivers over “growing safety concerns on Polish railways”. “We have been doing everything we can in parliament and at the infrastructure ministry to make sure this problem is noticed,” added Miętek, who also welcomed the fact that, following Wednesday’s accident, Tusk has pledged to take action. 💬 Premier @donaldtusk ⤵️ Katastrofa kolejowa w Sokolnikach miała miejsce na przejeździe kolejowym, dlatego natychmiast rozpoczniemy prace nad zaostrzeniem przepisów dla tych, którzy wjeżdżają na przejazdy kolejowe, mimo zapór i czerwonych światel. pic.twitter.com/BgaZQLEPbR — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) September 9, 2026 In those remarks, the prime minister lamented that the accident in Sokolniki Suche was “yet another case of such a catastrophe happening at a rail crossing”. “We must immediately begin urgent work on tightening regulations,” he continued. This would include “very tough” punishments “for those who, unfortunately, quite systematically drive onto railway crossings despite barriers and red lights”. Infrastructure minister Dariusz Klimczak later confirmed that they were working on “radical” measures to toughen penalties for those who violate the rules at rail crossings. He revealed that one proposal being considered is suspending for three months the licence of any driver who ignores red lights at rail crossings. However, critics noted that the ministry had already announced such plans in July 2025, and had failed to implement them since then. – Chcemy wprowadzić przepis, na podstawie którego każdy kierowca, który wjedzie na przejazd drogowo-kolejowy kiedy jest zapalone czerwone światło, straci prawo jazdy, zostanie mu ono zatrzymane na trzy miesiące. Chcemy także zmienić kodeks karny we współpracy z ministrem… pic.twitter.com/RhE8pcvlJ9 — Ministerstwo Infrastruktury (@MI_GOV_PL) September 9, 2026 The latest data from Eurostat, the European Union’s statistics agency, show that in 2024 Poland recorded the second-highest number of rail accidents, 220, among all member states, behind only Germany (366). However, 24% of Poland’s accidents took place at rail crossings, compared to 16% in Germany. In total, Poland had by far the highest number of deaths caused by accidents at rail crossings (45), ahead of Germany (26), France (20) and Hungary (18). When taking into account the size of countries’ rail networks, Poland had 4.3 rail deaths (from all causes, not just accidents at crossings) per thousand kilometres of track, which was the fifth-highest figure in the EU, behind Portugal (6.2), Hungary (5.8), Slovakia (5.7) and Lithuania (4.6). Last week, in dramatic scenes captured on camera, a train carrying almost 300 passengers hit a truck at a rail crossing in Gdańsk, luckily resulting in no injuries. The driver of the truck, who is from Bosnia and Herzegovina, has been charged. A train crashed into a lorry stuck on a railway crossing in Gdansk, Poland, after the barriers closed while the vehicle was still on the tracks. World.title: Almost 80% of Poles support helping Baltic states if Russia attacks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Almost 80% of Poles say that they would want their country to come to the aid of the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – if they were attacked by Russia. The new poll follows a controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure, former defence minister Mariusz Błaszczak, in which he refused to confirm his support for Poland fulfilling its NATO obligations by coming to the aid of the Baltic states if they were invaded. In a survey for broadcaster Radio Zet, the IBRiS agency asked: “In the event of Russian aggression, should Poland help Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia?” In response, 77.8% of those polled said that it should, while only 16.1% were opposed. Among respondents who identified as politically centrist, 92% were in favour. The figures were lower for those with left-wing (75%) or right-wing (73%) views, though in both cases a large majority still supported coming to the Baltic states’ aid. Commenting on the findings, Radio Zet wrote that “the survey shows that Poles feel responsible for the military security of their NATO allies – contrary to what some politicians have said”. That was a reference to remarks last week by Błaszczak, who is the head of the parliamentary caucus of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s largest opposition group. Between 2018 and 2023, Błaszczak served as defence minister in the former PiS-led government. In an interview with Radio Zet, Błaszczak was asked if, in the event of a Russian attack on the Baltic states, Poland should come to their aid. “Polish soldiers should defend Poland,” he responded. “We need to be strong in our alliances…We should prioritise cooperation with the United States.” The interviewer pointed out that Article 5 of the NATO treaty requires members of the alliance to come to the assistance of another member that is attacked, and again asked if Poland should help the Baltic states if such an attack occurred. “We border Russia directly, and we border a Russia that has effectively taken over Belarusian territory. So we’re also on the front line,” replied Błaszczak. “This article, of course, speaks of solidarity, but the point is that the government that governs Poland should establish the best possible relations with the United States.” With the interviewer continuing to press the question, Błaszczak simply said that “it all depends on the circumstances” and “it’s not a straightforward issue”. Błaszczak’s comments were criticised by figures from Poland’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused him of calling into question the validity of Article 5, on which Poland would rely if it were attacked. “A former defence minister who undermines the sanctity of Polish security, i.e. NATO’s Article 5, is a moron,” wrote deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk. Interior minister Marcin Kiewiński said that Błaszczak had “undermined the very purpose of NATO’s existence”. In response to the criticism, Błaszczak wrote on social media that, during the PiS government’s time in power, it had significantly enhanced security ties with the Baltic states, including stationing Polish forces in Latvia and contributing Polish F-16s to NATO’s air policing mission. “NATO’s Article 5 is activated collectively, and alliance commitments are binding, but every [Polish] defence minister’s priority should be the defence of Poland and ensuring the safety of Poles,” he added. Błaszczak to stan umysłu. Mało im było niszczenia SAFE, to dziś były szef MON podważył sens istnienia NATO wskazując, że Wojsko Polskie nie powinno bronić Litwy, Łotwy czy Estonii. Przyjaźń tego skompromitowanego środowiska z Orbanem to nie był przypadek… — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) September 1, 2026 On Wednesday, Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, visited Latvia, including the base in Ādaži where a Polish military contingent has been based since 2017 as part of a multinational NATO brigade. “Poland and Latvia face similar threats in the security domain,” said Sikorski. “We must speak with one voice and take our security seriously. Only such actions can guarantee effective protection against the threat from Russia.” “We do not want an escalation of the conflict, but Putin must know that we are not going to sit idly by and wait for his next step,” he continued. “We understand that the defence of our allies also contributes to Polish security. We stand ready to share the burden of defending the eastern flank.” 📍 Ādaži 🇱🇻 Continuing visit to Latvia, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs @sikorskiradek visited the base of the Polish Military Contingent. World.title: Polish school pupils second best at maths in EU
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Polish schoolchildren are the second best in the European Union at mathematics, the third best at reading comprehension, and the fifth best at science, according to the latest results from a major international study of pupils’ abilities. The Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) is carried out every three years by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and measures the performance of 15-year-olds. The latest instalment, based on tests taken in 2025, was published on Tuesday this week. It includes results from 91 countries and territories across the world. A total of 760,000 pupils were assessed, including 7,103 in 217 Polish schools. In maths, Polish pupils obtained a mean score of 484, which was the 12th highest in the world. The top seven places were taken by Asian countries and territories. But the only other European Union country to exceed Poland’s score was Estonia (508). Poland was just behind the United Kingdom (488) and Canada (485), but ahead of the likes of Finland (469), Germany (464) and the United States (463). In reading comprehension, Poland’s mean score of 482 was 14th in the world and third best in the EU, behind Ireland (500) and Estonia (499). Polish pupils performed slightly worse, in relative terms, in science, where their mean score of 495 was 18th in the world and fifth best in the EU. A number of Polish media outlets and Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrongly reported that Poland was third best in the EU for science. In fact, it was significantly behind Estonia (527) and Finland (504) and marginally below Ireland (500) and Austria (497). Poland’s latest results continue its recent history of performing strongly in PISA. In the 2018 instalment, Polish pupils were the third best in the EU in both maths and science, and fourth best in reading. In 2022 (when PISA took place a year later than planned due to the Covid pandemic), Poland was fourth in the EU in maths and fifth in both science and reading. In 2021, a separate assessment of reading comprehension among fourth-grade pupils – called PIRLS and carried out every five years by the International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement – found Poland had the joint best result among EU countries, equal with Finland Following the announcement of the new PISA data, Polish education minister Barbara Nowacka welcomed the fact that “Poland has maintained its high ranking among European Union countries”. However, she added a note of caution, pointing to the fact that, overall, test scores have been declining, both in Poland and globally. That shows “Polish education still has a lot of work ahead of it”. Nowacka said that her ministry’s efforts to reform the school curriculum had been based on results and recommendations from previous PISA reports. World.title: Poland secures further $4bn financing from US to buy American military equipment

Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment. Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”. The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”. .@UnderSecT took part in the signing of a $4 billion Foreign Military Financing (FMF) loan guarantee—an important step in U.S.-Polish security cooperation. Poland’s significant investments in its defense capabilities and the U.S. defense industrial base reflect our shared… pic.twitter.com/Dz3huAp8pj — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) September 9, 2026 Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery. The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”. In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself. Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”. “Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth. The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”. This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”. 💬 Obecna umowa została zawarta na korzystniejszych warunkach niż dwie poprzednie umowy z gwarancjami pożyczkowymi dzięki subsydiowaniu części kosztów finansowania w ramach grantu przyznanego w tym celu przez Rząd USA. To kolejny wyraz bardzo bliskiej, transatlantyckiej… pic.twitter.com/Ipd4cYDeFo — Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego 🇵🇱 (@BGK_pl) September 9, 2026 The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year. President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending. They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement. However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”. Amerykański sprzęt wojskowy ponownie wzmocni Wojsko Polskie i bezpieczeństwo Polaków! Właśnie zabezpieczyliśmy środki w wysokości 4 mld dolarów, czyli prawie 15 mld zł na jego zakup. Łącznie w ramach amerykańskiego programu Foreign Military Financing pozyskaliśmy już blisko 20… pic.twitter.com/hhzXcE1hoC — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) September 9, 2026 While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington. In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw. Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory. On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation, including DiNanno, was in Poland this week to discuss potential locations for the base. World.title: “We remember where Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead,” says Polish FM
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s foreign minister has expressed concern over the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at a time when Germany is rapidly rearming – suggesting that it has echoes of the build-up to World War Two. “We want Germany, under democratic leadership and as Europe’s largest economy, to play a strong role in ensuring our common security,” Radosław Sikorski told German newspaper Handelsblatt. “But we remember all too well where a rearmed Germany in the hands of a far-right, pro-Russian party can lead – and that is precisely what the AfD represents,” he added. Polens Außenminister Sikorski: „Wir wollen, dass Deutschland (…) eine starke Rolle bei der Sicherung unserer gemeinsamen Sicherheit spielt. Aber wir erinnern uns nur allzu gut daran, wohin ein wiederbewaffnetes Deutschland in den Händen einer rechtsextremen, prorussischen Partei führen kann (…)“ [image or embed] — Andreas Prause (@andreas-prause.eu) 8 September 2026 at 21:05 Poland was, on 1 September 1939, invaded by Nazi Germany, marking the start of World War Two and over five years of brutal occupation. The attack was launched in cooperation with the Soviet Union, which invaded Poland from the east two weeks later. After Hitler was defeated, Germany had no major far-right party for decades. However, that has changed in recent years. In 2024, the AfD came first in the Thuringian state election, with 33% of the vote. Last Sunday, it won in Saxony-Anhalt, with 44%. The party also came second in the federal elections of 2025, with 21%, making it the main national opposition. Opinion polls now show that the AfD is the most popular party nationally, with support of around 28%, well ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU), on 21%. The AfD’s growth has been watched with particular concern in Poland, a country that suffered enormously under Nazi-German occupation. Some senior AfD figures have sought to downplay the significance of the Nazi era. In 2025, when the German parliament approved plans for a memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of World War Two, the AfD was the only party not to vote in favour. The AfD’s sympathy towards and links with Russia have caused further disquiet in Poland. Last year, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said he “does not see any current threat to Germany from Russia” and that, in fact, “Poland could also be a threat to us”. This year, another senior AfD figure, Kay Gottschalk, called for Poland to pay his country €1.3 billion as reparations for its “complicity” in the sabotage of the Nord Stream gas pipelines that used to bring Russian gas to Germany through the Baltic Sea but were damaged by explosions in 2022. Germany’s parliament has passed a motion calling on the government to establish a permanent memorial in Berlin to Polish victims of the German-Nazi occupation. The measure was supported by all parties apart from the far-right AfD https://t.co/8dk0ZSpmjJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 3, 2025 In the wake of the AfD’s victory in Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that “only idiots or traitors” in Poland would celebrate an AfD victory. He claimed there were some such people in Law and Justice (PiS) and Confederation (Konfederacja), the two main right-wing opposition parties. However, PiS’s reaction to AfD’s rise has been mixed. On Tuesday, PiS MP Małgorzata Golińska told Polskie Radio that it represents a “kind of browning” of politics in Germany – a reference to the brown shirts of Hitler’s SA paramilitary forces that helped bring him to power in the 1920s and 1930s. “A return to very dangerous thinking is taking place there and we must observe in which direction it will all develop,” added Golińska. “From Poland’s perspective, we should not overreact with any particular emotion, but we also cannot be naive [in thinking] that nothing is happening there.” By contrast, another PiS MP, Jarosław Sellin, told Onet Radio that PiS and the AfD “say similar things” when it comes to EU climate and migration policies. But he added that “this does not mean we have to like what the AfD says about history, relations with Poland, and Russia”. Polish PM @donaldtusk has condemned as “idiots or traitors” right-wing opposition figures who have welcomed the far-right AfD's election victory in Germany However, the response from the Polish right to the election result has so far been relatively muted https://t.co/goSWlbeGA8 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026 Responses from Confederation have likewise been mixed. The group is actually made up of two main factions, one of which, a libertarian party called New Hope (Nowa Nadzieja), is allied with the AfD in the European Parliament. New Hope’s spokesman, Wojciech Machulski, told the Fakt daily that they are “united [with AfD] in our opposition to EU migration and climate policies” but at the same time “we do not accept the anti-Polish statements”. Krzysztof Mulawa, an MP from the National Movement (RN), which makes up the other half of Confederation, told the newspaper that “several of the AfD’s demands are unacceptable from the Polish perspective”. But he said that there were areas of shared interest, such as abolishing the euro. A number of figures from PiS and Confederation have also expressed hope that the AfD’s rise at the expense of establishment parties can herald a similar development in Poland, which, like Germany, is ruled by a pro-EU coalition ranging from centre-left to centre-right. Europa się budzi, a establishment wpada w panikę. Wynik AfD pokazuje, że ludzie mają dość dyktatu Brukseli, Zielonego Ładu i niszczenia państw narodowych przez nielegalną imigrację. Polityczne trzęsienie ziemi dopiero się zaczyna. Piękna, biała Europa narodów wkrótce powróci. — Włodzimierz Skalik (@Wlodek_Skalik) September 7, 2026 One party that has been unambiguously positive in its response to AfD’s victory is the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), a radical-right, pro-Russian group that broke away from Confederation last year and is currently polling support of around 9% “Europe is waking up, and the establishment is falling into panic,” wrote KKP’s deputy leader, Włodzimierz Skalik, on social media. “A beautiful, white Europe of nations will soon return.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Robots “protest” in Warsaw to demand regulation of AI and automation
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Around 30 robots protested outside Poland’s digital affairs ministry on Monday, calling for tougher regulation of artificial intelligence and robotisation. The human organisers say there needs to be greater public debate over the impact of new technologies on the labour market. Digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski met with the demonstrators, telling them that his department is working on regulations. However, one of the organisers said that plans currently being discussed by parliament contain insufficient protection for workers. Around 30 robots joined a protest in front of Poland’s digital affairs ministry, calling for stronger AI regulations. The demonstration was organised by campaigners to spark debate on how AI and robots could replace workers. pic.twitter.com/QEbvchb2RS — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) September 7, 2026 Standing in several rows, the robots waved Polish flags and chanted slogans such as “We want regulations, we want rules, we want law” and “Don’t wait, regulate, protect jobs”. The organisers, a group called Democratism, said the event was intended to highlight the need for debate and legislation before automation has a more profound impact on employment. “Some people will benefit from new opportunities, while others may need to retrain or adapt to completely different roles,” they wrote. Society needs to discuss “who is responsible for preparing people for these changes, how workers should be protected during the transition and how reskilling should work”. Democratism appears to have been launched shortly before the protest, with the announcement about the demonstration among the first material published on its social media accounts. The initiative was launched by Delta Robots, a company that rents robots for events. However, a website they have set up to gather support for greater debate over the impact of AI and robotisation has so far only obtained signatures from 61 people. Grzegorz Kuliś of Delta Robots admitted to news website Gazeta.pl that their “campaign also has public relations value” for the company. However, he added that, “even though we’re deploying robots, we’re also humans, and we have a whole host of concerns that, if we don’t regulate this, we’ll soon find ourselves in an unprecedented situation that no human being will be able to cope with”. “We are constantly debating the impact of migrants on our society, whilst the vast majority of ‘migrants’ will arrive either via undersea cables across the Atlantic in the form of AI agents, or as humanoid robots in shipping containers from China,” he warned. Gawkowski, who went out to address the organisers, said the ministry’s objectives were aligned with the protesters’ concerns. “People come first, and that is what matters most to us,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Eska. The minister also announced plans to establish a committee on AI development and safety as well as to introduce so-called sandboxes, where companies will be able to test AI solutions before deploying them more widely, reports local news website O!Polska. Kuliś, however, told Gazeta.pl that a draft law on AI systems currently being considered by the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament, contains too little practical protection for workers affected by automation. A Polish radio station that launched a channel run almost entirely by AI – including its presenters – has decided to end the project after less than a week The head of the station admitted they were "surprised by the level of emotion" the idea had caused https://t.co/9iMlRVamSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 28, 2024 The rapid development of AI and robotics has sparked debate around the world on how such technologies will impact humans, including to what extent and in what ways they will replace human labour. However, a number of recent reports have found that the impact of AI on jobs has so far been smaller than many previously predicted. Analysis by the Institute of Economic Policy Research at Stanford University, published in July, found that “AI’s effects on overall employment are likely small”. A further concern has been the prospect of AI “going rogue” by starting to act without or beyond human control. Those fears were strengthened after it emerged in July this year that some of OpenAI’s AI agents had autonomously hacked Hugging Face, another AI company. The incident prompted more than 100 companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Hugging Face, to sign an open letter calling on companies and governments to step up cybersecurity efforts amid emerging threats. A recent rise in unemployment in Poland has raised concern. But that headline figure does not tell the whole story, with experts arguing that the Polish labour market is actually in good shape, writes @AlicjaPtak4 https://t.co/Pk4y7BqGrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 24, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: EU Moves to Curb Airbnb-Style Rentals to Boost Long-Term Housing
World.content:
The EU has introduced a framework to support long-term rentals in tourist-heavy cities. Airbnb warns it creates regulatory uncertainty without improving long-term housing outcomes.

The EU has announced an affordable housing plan aimed at encouraging long-term rentals and making housing more accessible for Europeans.

Unveiled on Wednesday, the plan aims to create clarity and predictability in how rules are applied by local authorities, particularly in neighbourhoods popular with tourists where short-term rentals have displaced residents.



“Lack of affordable housing is a matter of concern for so many of our European citizens,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press statement. “Essential workers and students cannot afford to live where they serve and study. But most importantly, it is about fairness. Today, we are delivering for all Europeans.”

“The new rules are designed to help competent authorities identify ‘areas under housing stress’ using a common methodology,” a Commission press release explains.

Housing in Europe is getting worse

The latest data on access to accommodation across Europe are worrying, and have pushed the Commission to intervene.

Recent Eurobarometer data shows that 50 per cent of European city dwellers think that housing is an urgent problem they experience. House prices have skyrocketed faster than local incomes across most European capitals, rising 64.9% between 2015 and 2025 and rents 21.8%, according to EU data.

Even people who cannot afford to buy are facing rising rents, which consume 40% of household income, and middle-class families are also increasingly facing a reality where they can’t afford to buy or rent, but also aren’t eligible for social housing.

Many residents in cities like Lisbon, Barcelona and Prague complain that short-term rental platforms like Airbnb have removed homes from the market and pushed prices up, often forcing them to move.

Short-term rentals represent only 1.2% of the EU’s total housing stock, but they can account for up to 20% in some tourism hotspots. With too few homes being built where demand is strongest, Brussels estimates it needs more than 2 million new homes every year to fix the problem.

Airbnb, the largest worldwide platform for short-term rentals, has criticised the plan as not sufficiently clear.

“Airbnb shares the Commission’s ambition to make housing more affordable. But as drafted, the Affordable Housing Act will not add a single home to the long term rental market, while adding regulatory uncertainty for hosts across European cities,” the company wrote in a press statement after the Commission’s announcement.

The plan must now be negotiated by the EU co-legislators before being approved.

World.title: Prague’s Industrial Palace to Reopen to the Public for Guided Tours
World.content:
After a major renovation costing more than CZK 3 billion, Prague’s Industrial Palace at the Výstaviště exhibition grounds will open its doors to the public in two weeks.

From September 25 to October 11, visitors will be able to explore the history and architecture of the landmark and see how it has been transformed during the renovation on guided tours organised by Výstaviště Praha and Prague City Tourism.



According to Výstaviště Praha, the palace will not remain open to the public on a regular basis after the tours. Instead, it will serve as a venue for exhibitions, trade fairs and other scheduled events.

The renovation of the Industrial Palace, including the reconstruction of its fire-damaged left wing, began in February 2022, more than 13 years after the wing was destroyed by a fire in October 2008.

The approximately one-hour guided tour costs CZK 91. Organisers say the symbolic price refers to 1891, the year the Industrial Palace first opened. Tickets are available through the Prague City Tourism website. Places are limited, and some tour dates have already sold out.

The first major event scheduled at the renovated palace will be the Designblok festival in early October.

Built in Just Ten Months

The Industrial Palace was built for the 1891 Jubilee Provincial Exhibition based on designs by architect Bedřich Münzberger. It is considered an important example of both artistic and technical heritage. The building was the first in the Czech lands to feature an architectural design based on a prefabricated iron structure.

Contemporary records show that 450 workers completed the building in just ten months, despite flooding and severe frosts affecting the exhibition grounds during construction.

From the beginning, the palace served as a venue for exhibitions and cultural events, although it was originally intended as a temporary structure.

Between 1952 and 1954, the communist government decided to repurpose the building, ordering its main hall to be converted into a social and dance hall. The building was also renamed the Congress Palace and became part of the Julius Fučík Cultural and Recreation Park, which operated at the site at the time.

One Wing of the Palace Was Destroyed by Fire

On October 16, 2008, a fire destroyed the left wing of the Industrial Palace after items left on an electric hot plate caught fire. The person responsible was never identified.

The renovation did not begin until early 2022. Under the original plans, the work was supposed to be completed last year.

However, once the foundations, floors and suspended ceilings of the right wing were uncovered, it became clear that the condition of the historic building was worse than expected, leading to additional work and delays.

World.title: New York Inspired New Residential Project in Prague’s Smíchov
World.content:
A new seven-story residential building planned for Prague’s Smíchov district has moved closer to construction after securing a zoning decision.

The project, known as Smíchovská Žehlička, is being developed by BPD Partners and Top Estates and is expected to be completed in 2029.

The building will contain 66 apartments as well as eight commercial units for shops, services and restaurants. It will also include shared coworking and community spaces. The total gross floor area is expected to be close to 8,000 square meters.

The project is planned for a wedge-shaped site between Kováků and Na Zatlance streets, directly below Mrázovka Park. The unusual shape of the plot and the significant difference in elevation between the two streets have made the site particularly difficult to develop.

The project has been in preparation for more than a decade. BPD Partners, the investment group owned by Czech businessmen Vasil Bobel, Petr Pudil and Jan Dobrovský, began working with architect Patrik Hoffman on the scheme in 2010.

Inspired by New York’s Flatiron Building

The shape of Smíchovská Žehlička is largely determined by the site’s narrow, wedge-shaped plot and surrounding streets. The design also takes inspiration from New York’s Flatiron Building, whose distinctive triangular form became a response to an equally unusual urban site.

The Prague project aims to use the constraints of its location in a similar way. Rather than attempting to conceal the site’s difficult geometry, the design makes it a defining feature of the building.

The residential units and commercial premises will all be offered for sale. The development will also provide shared areas intended for coworking and community activities.

If permitting and construction follow the current schedule, Smíchovská Žehlička could be completed by the end of 2029.

World.title: Award-Winning Holocaust Documentary to Premiere in Prague
World.content:
Award-winning Holocaust documentary UnBroken will have its Czech premiere at Prague’s Edison Filmhub on Friday, September 25.

The screening will take place alongside the opening of the new “Rescuers of Children” exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum.

Director, producer and writer Beth Lane will attend the Prague screening.



The documentary tells the story of Lane’s mother, Ginger Lane, and her six siblings, who survived the Holocaust after being hidden for two years by German farmers Paula and Arthur Schmidt.

The seven Jewish children were sheltered on the couple’s farm in Brandenburg, about 60 kilometers east of Berlin. They survived the war and emigrated together to the United States in 1946.

They are believed to be the only known family of seven Jewish siblings to have survived the Holocaust and later emigrated together as a family. Ginger Lane, now 86, is one of two surviving members of the family.

Paula and Arthur Schmidt were later recognized by Yad Vashem as Righteous Among the Nations, an honor given to non-Jews who risked their lives to save Jews during the Holocaust.

Their story is also featured in “Rescuers of Children,” the new exhibition at the National Pedagogical Museum. The exhibition examines the experiences of children and other vulnerable people during the Holocaust and presents stories of individuals who risked their lives to help those facing persecution.

The Prague screening follows the documentary’s German premiere in Dachau on July 17, where UnBroken received the inaugural Lichtbrücke Prize for Human Rights in Film.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by UnBroken (@unbrokenthefilm)

The film premiered in 2023 at the Heartland International Film Festival, where it won Best Documentary Feature Premiere. It has since been screened in more than 50 cities, including at the United Nations in New York and Vienna, the Museum of Jewish Heritage in New York and the Pilecki Institute in Warsaw.

UnBroken was released on Netflix in the United States in April 2025 and has since surpassed 1.5 million streams there.

The Czech premiere will take place at Edison Filmhub in Prague on September 25, 2026.

World.title: GALLERY: One of Europe’s Largest Aquariums Set to Open in Czechia in 2028
World.content:
A new public aquarium costing around CZK 700 million is planned for the Brno Exhibition Centre, with construction expected to begin in 2027 and the first visitors arriving in the second half of 2028.

The project, called Green Planet: National Aquarium, will occupy Pavilion C at the Brno Exhibition Centre. It is expected to contain around 100 aquariums and water tanks holding more than four million liters of water.



The facility will be home to about 400,000 animals representing roughly 500 species, including rare species. Developers say the project will rank among the largest aquarium complexes in Europe.

Brno Mayor Markéta Vaňková said the aquarium could attract around 500,000 visitors during its first year of operation, including people from across the South Moravian Region and neighboring countries.

The main attraction will be a 2.5 million-liter ocean tank featuring a 55-meter underwater tunnel.

Visitors will be able to walk through the tunnel while observing marine life around and above them. The aquarium will also feature hundreds of other aquatic species across its various tanks.

The developers say the number of animals will put the complex among Europe’s largest aquariums. They estimate that it will contain around 36 times as many animals as the Barcelona Aquarium.

The project is also designed around reducing water consumption.

According to the plans, recirculation systems will clean and treat water before returning it to the tanks. The developers say efficient water management will be one of the project’s priorities.

Czech and international specialists are involved in preparing the aquarium, which is expected to include both educational and visitor-focused elements.

World.title: Prague to Host Central Europe’s First Climate Week
World.content:
Prague will host the first international climate week in Central Europe from September 14 to 20, with more than 50 conferences, seminars, workshops and other events planned across the city.

Climate Week Prague will bring together representatives from climate research, finance, government, business and other sectors to discuss how cities and economies can respond to climate change.

The official opening will take place at the Prague Planetarium on Monday, September 14, at 2:30 p.m.



Speakers will include former European Commissioner for Climate Action Connie Hedegaard, Deputy Director-General for Climate Policy at the European Commission and a former Czech environment minister Jan Dusík, and Prague Mayor Bohuslav Svoboda of the ODS party, who is supporting the event.

The program will cover a broad range of issues, including how cities can adapt to rising temperatures, water management, energy, construction, agriculture and transport.

Finance will be a major part of the agenda. The CEE Sustainable Finance Summit, running from September 14 to 16, will examine the impact of geopolitics and artificial intelligence on Europe’s economic competitiveness.

Climate Week Prague has been organized by a coalition of independent organizations led by the International Sustainable Finance Centre. The group also includes research institutions, the Climate Facts think tank, banks, investors and trade unions representing workers in the construction and energy sectors.

The organizers say the increasing effects of climate change, including more frequent heat waves, were among the main reasons for launching the event.

Data cited by Fakta o klimatu illustrates the change in Prague’s summer temperatures.

Between 1961 and 1990, the city recorded seven tropical nights, when temperatures remained at or above 20 degrees Celsius throughout the night. Over the following 35 years, that number increased to 165, according to data from the Czech Academy of Sciences’ Institute for Global Change Research.

Average summer minimum temperatures in Prague also increased during the period, rising from 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, according to Fakta o klimatu.

The local figures come as international assessments warn of further warming. Reuters reported earlier in September, citing the United Nations Environment Programme, that global temperatures are expected to exceed the key 1.5-degree-Celsius threshold above pre-industrial levels within the next few years.

Further warming is expected to contribute to more extreme weather and increase pressure on ecosystems, glaciers and low-lying coastal cities.

World.title: Prague’s Petřín Funicular to Return to Service on September 22
World.content:
Prague’s Petřín funicular will resume passenger service on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, following a two-year reconstruction of the railway and its infrastructure, the Prague Public Transit Company (DPP) has announced.

Service will begin at 7 a.m., with the new fourth-generation cars departing from both Újezd and Petřín stations.

Trains will then run according to the regular timetable, with departures every 10 minutes until 10:15 p.m.



The reopening comes almost exactly two years after the previous funicular was taken out of service. The third-generation cars made their final journey on September 13, 2024, after prolonged heavy rainfall destabilized and eroded sections of the hillside.

New cars increase capacity

The two new cars were designed by Czech designer Anna Marešová and built by Swiss manufacturer CWA Constructions SA. The vehicles cost a combined CZK 137.7 million and were delivered to Prague in April.

Each car can carry up to 120 passengers, compared with a capacity of 100 on the previous vehicles. The design also introduces glass roofs, giving passengers a clearer view of Petřín Hill during the journey.

Air conditioning, however, will not be installed. Because of technical limitations, the cars will instead use forced-air ventilation. The decision has already drawn criticism from some Prague residents, who have questioned how comfortable the cars will be during hot summer days, particularly given their large glass roofs.

The two-year reconstruction involved more than replacing the vehicles. Workers strengthened the foundations beneath the track, installed new rails and upgraded the funicular’s traction system.

How much will the new funicular cost?

A single journey will cost CZK 100 when purchased on site. Passengers using the PID Lítačka mobile application will pay CZK 90.

Passengers with valid long-term Prague public transport passes covering one month to one year will continue to ride without paying an additional fare.

The same applies to holders of 24-hour and 72-hour passes, children under 15 and passengers aged over 65.

World.title: Prague Botanical Garden to Host Grape Harvest Festival
World.content:
The Prague Botanical Garden will host its traditional grape harvest festival at St. Clare’s Vineyard on September 12 and 13, bringing two days of wine, fresh burčák, live music and activities for visitors.

The festival, known as Vinobraní na Vinici sv. Kláry, will feature wines from producers across the Czech Republic, Moravia and other countries.

Visitors will also have the chance to taste white and red burčák made from grapes harvested this year at St. Clare’s Vineyard.



The first grapes for the festival have already been picked by hand. Workers harvested 2,700 kilograms of table grapes and the Modrý Portugal variety. The grapes are now being used to produce this year’s burčák, a young wine that is still undergoing fermentation and is traditionally associated with the Czech grape harvest season.

Alongside wines from the St. Clare’s winery, the festival will present a selection of wines from other producers from the Czech Republic, Moravia and abroad.

Two days of live music

Music will be a major part of the weekend program. Saturday’s main stage lineup includes Jordan Haj and Emma Smetana, YES BROTHERS and 20 MINUTES.

On Sunday, visitors can see the Děda Mládek Illegal Band, BRASS AVENUE, MOVEBREAKERS and OFF BEAT ORCHESTRA. A second music stage will also operate near the St. Clare’s wine shop.

The festival program includes more than music and wine. Visitors can join guided tours of the vineyard, take part in workshops and creative activities, or attend the Vínohrátky educational program. The guided tours are included in the admission price.

The event will run from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both September 12 and 13. Activities will take place at St. Clare’s Vineyard and in the Ornamental Garden of the Prague Botanical Garden.

Tickets bought at the venue cost CZK 280 for adults and CZK 180 for children and young people aged 3 to 17.

Online tickets purchased by September 11 are CZK 250 for adults and CZK 150 for children and young people. Children under three can enter free of charge.

World.title: PM Magyar: Orbán government knew about child abuse but did nothing – Tisza government pledges immediate action
World.content:
The Government will submit a package of legislation to Parliament next week aimed at strengthening children’s rights and safety, Prime Minister Péter Magyar said in Budapest on Saturday. He was speaking at a press conference presenting a report on the country’s child-protection system.

Rules to be tightened

Magyar said the rules governing content accessible to minors would be tightened, including material that depicts sexual violence or sexuality explicitly, or promotes exploitation and manipulation.

Child-protection requirements covering outdoor advertising, political s and media content will also be strengthened, he added. The Prime Minister said the law would also set out stricter requirements for how the state must deal with children stranded in hospital, ensuring that no child is left there for months simply because the system has failed to find suitable care.

Photo: MTI

The state would “never again turn its head away”, Magyar said. It would no longer conceal reports or abandon children and professionals working in the field. “The era of denial is over,” he said. “From now on, there will be action, the provision of the necessary resources and strict accountability.”

Government launches emergency programme

The government will also launch an immediate child-protection crisis programme worth around 10 billion forints. “We cannot afford to wait for next year’s budget; immediate action is needed,” Magyar said at the press conference, where he outlined the report and the Government’s planned measures.

According to the Prime Minister, around 6 billion forints will be spent on direct professional programmes, while a further 3.4 billion will fund developments, preferably before the end of this year. The professional programmes will create 184 new places, or places with new functions. They will also strengthen the protection and care provided at 15 specialist children’s homes, while immediate crisis accommodation will be established for 80 children, he said.

Photo: MTI

Mr Magyar added that targeted care would be introduced for children with autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disabilities and severe psychological or behavioural problems. A residential rehabilitation programme for children with addiction problems will also be launched, while around 440 million forints will be allocated immediately to support vulnerable adolescent girls and young mothers.

If you missed – PM Magyar unveils major changes: Huge pay rises, tougher environmental fines and radical concession changes

Child abuse was systematic and ongoing

Child abuse within the child-protection system was systematic and ongoing, while the Orbán government knew about it but did nothing, Mr Magyar said at the press conference in Budapest. He said the Interior Ministry, led by Sándor Pintér, knew precisely what was happening, MTI wrote.

According to the ministry’s own internal data, 1,959 cases of child abuse were recorded in state-run child-protection institutions in 2024, followed by a further 1,684 cases in 2025. Police complaints were filed on 2,249 occasions over the two-year period – an average of more than three reports every day. The true figure could be considerably higher, as many cases of abuse remained hidden, the Prime Minister said.

As a private citizen and a father, Mr Magyar said he found it incomprehensible that the Orbán government had known about the abuse and had even created the conditions in which it occurred, yet did nothing when it saw the consequences.

In Mr Magyar’s assessment, the Orbán government had not merely failed politically; it had also failed a basic test of humanity.

Former school guard jailed in Hungary for sexually abusing two vulnerable minors

World.title: Anti-Austrian fury erupts after Hungarian Harley-Davidson rider is fined in Austria
World.content:
A Hungarian Harley-Davidson rider paid a EUR 2,400 fine — equivalent to roughly HUF 1 million — on the spot in Austria after police said her motorcycle was 10 decibels louder than the level recorded on its registration document.

The woman knew her bike was not entirely compliant with regulations, but had not expected the breach to have such serious consequences. The case has sparked outrage among Hungarian motorcyclists, while a Hungarian living in Austria said the real question should be why anyone would travel to a country known for particularly strict checks on noisy vehicles with a modified motorcycle — and then seek to stir up anti-Austrian sentiment on social media.

Motorcycle exceeded permitted noise level

The incident took place in the Faaker See area of Carinthia during European Bike Week, a Harley-Davidson gathering. According to the rider’s account, police inspected the motorcycle for more than half an hour before carrying out a noise-level test.

Hungarian Harley-Davidson rider received huge fine in Austria because of her modified motorcycle. Photo: depositphotos.com

According to the woman’s post, the measurement showed that the motorcycle was “only” 10 decibels louder than the figure recorded in its registration document.

At the end of the inspection, she was fined EUR 2,400, which she paid on the spot by bank card. The roadside technical inspection cost a further EUR 20, while the motorcycle’s number plate was removed and its registration document was withheld.

The rider was not, however, ordered to have the motorcycle taken away immediately. She was allowed to return to her accommodation under police escort, sparing her the additional cost of motorcycle recovery.

It was not “just” 10 decibels

A Hungarian living in Austria who responded to the incident pointed out in a Facebook post that the additional 10 decibels should not be dismissed as a minor discrepancy.

The decibel scale is logarithmic: according to the account, a 10-decibel increase represents ten times the sound intensity, while the human ear perceives the noise as roughly twice as loud. In other words, this was not a difference of just a few per cent.

The source said Austrian authorities, particularly in Carinthia and Tyrol, had for years been carrying out targeted checks on modified and excessively loud exhaust systems. During major motorcycling events, they apply a zero-tolerance approach.

She could have faced a far larger fine

Under Austria’s Road Traffic Act, fines for unauthorised technical modifications and excessive noise can reach as much as EUR 10,000. By comparison, the EUR 2,400 penalty was relatively moderate; it merely appears steep to a Hungarian pocket.

It is important to note, however, that the rider did not publish the official document relating to the fine. It is therefore impossible to establish with certainty which offences were involved, or on what legal grounds the final sum of EUR 2,400 was calculated.

The removal of the number plate and registration document was not an arbitrary act by the police either. In cases of substantial noise violations, Austrian regulations allow — and in certain circumstances require — authorities to prevent the vehicle from being used any further.

She knew the motorcycle was not fully compliant

One of the most significant details in the case is that, by her own account, the rider was aware that her Harley-Davidson did not fully comply with the regulations.

Despite this, she set off for the motorcycling event. That was why the Hungarian living in Austria raised the issue of self-reflection in her post. She argued that anyone planning to attend an event such as European Bike Week should take particular care to check local regulations in advance, since the authorities around Faaker See pay special attention to loud and modified motorcycles during the event.

Local residents also regularly complain about the motorcycle noise generated during the gathering, which can continue around the clock and places additional pressure on the police.

If you missed it: PHOTOS: Harley-Davidson festival in Budapest – two bikers died

Anti-Austrian sentiment spills over

The incident prompted furious reactions in Hungarian motorcycling groups. According to the account, the comments included anti-Austrian slurs, accusations of Nazism and a series of crude insults.

The author who responded to the incident said the original post had presented the case in an excessively one-sided manner and had mainly served to fuel hostility towards Austrian police. Meanwhile, the fact that the motorcycle had not been fully compliant in the first place — and that a 10-decibel excess constitutes a significant breach — had been pushed into the background.

She and several commenters stressed that, in their experience, Austrian authorities would have acted in exactly the same way against an excessively loud Austrian or German rider as they did against a Hungarian national.

World.title: 9/11 terrorist attack commemorated in Budapest – photos
World.content:
The US Embassy in Hungary commemorated the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks on Friday together with members of the Hungarian police and fire services.

9/11 terrorist attack commemorated in Budapest

Chargé d’Affaires Caroline Savage and members of the embassy community took part in the remembrance ceremony, honouring the nearly 3,000 people who lost their lives in the attacks 25 years ago.

“We remember together because we grieved together,” the embassy said, highlighting the close cooperation between Hungary and the United States in addressing the major terrorism challenges that followed 9/11.

The US flag at the embassy was lowered to half-staff in the morning, in line with the practice at American installations around the world. Embassy staff also observed a moment of silence for the victims. “We will never forget,” the embassy concluded.

World.title: Hungary sends a clear message about Ukraine, Western Balkans ahead of key EU enlargement decisions
World.content:
Foreign Minister Anita Orbán discussed the European Union’s enlargement timeline with Marta Kos, the European Commissioner for Enlargement, in Budapest on Friday.

In a post on Facebook, Orbán noted that the European Commission will present its proposals for enlargement reforms at the end of September. The European Council will address enlargement in October, followed by the publication of the annual Enlargement Package, with member states setting the direction for the next period in December, she said.

“The Western Balkan countries have waited too long for EU membership,” Orbán said. “Montenegro and Albania have made significant progress, so the European Union must continue to advance their accession processes.”

Meanwhile, the minister said that regarding Ukraine, she had reaffirmed that Kyiv needed to take concrete steps to secure the rights of the ethnic Hungarian community in Transcarpathia in order for Hungary to support the opening of further accession clusters.

World.title: Former state secretary: Former PM Orbán ordered Hungary to pay more for a telecom company than the owners had asked
World.content:
Former state secretary Vilmos Vályi-Nagy has spoken about government meetings held to resolve “problematic cases”, the increase in the purchase price of telecommunications company Antenna Hungária and what he described as massively overpriced state IT procurements in the second part of his interview with Partizán, published on Friday evening.

Vályi-Nagy, who served as a state secretary in the Orbán government between 2010 and 2014, was introduced in the programme as one of the important sources for investigative journalists over the past decade.

He said that meetings were held at Parliament every Monday morning, attended by the then prime minister and state secretaries, where “problematic cases” were dealt with and decisions considered important for the functioning of the economy were made.

According to Vályi-Nagy, the tenders for public lighting in municipalities were among the issues discussed. He said Elios, a company that became closely associated with the business interests of Orbán’s son-in-law, István Tiborcz, regularly won such tenders, while János Lázár was responsible for ensuring that the cases moved forward.

He added that problems arising in connection with the projects were dealt with immediately.

Read more about the interview: How former PM Orbán’s ex-secretary informed media about the shady businesses and was threatened with his kids

‘The proportion of bad projects started to increase’

Vályi-Nagy said that, over time, an increasing number of projects came before the meetings that he considered professionally unsound and financially loss-making for the state.

“More and more cases came up that were totally unprofessional and completely loss-making, and apart from the company implementing the project doing extremely well out of it, they were nothing but a burden and a liability on the back of the Hungarian state,” he said.

He added that the balance had gradually changed, with the proportion of bad projects increasing while the share of good projects declined.

As an example, he cited a government data centre planned for Göd, saying the state had spent HUF 15 billion on the project even though, apart from a concrete structure, nothing was ultimately completed.

Vályi-Nagy described the case as “outright theft”, adding that no one had been held responsible, no investigation had been launched and no criminal complaint had been filed.

Antenna Hungária: ‘I froze’

The former state secretary also recalled negotiations over the state’s repurchase of Antenna Hungária, which had been privatised during the premiership of Ferenc Gyurcsány.

He said that, in the early 2010s, negotiations with the foreign owner had brought the proposed purchase price down from HUF 61–62 billion to HUF 48 billion.

However, when he informed Viktor Orbán about the deal, the prime minister allegedly told him that the lower price was not acceptable and that the purchase price should instead be HUF 53 billion.

“So we had to modify the price backwards,” Vályi-Nagy said. “I froze, because anyone would have frozen in that situation. On the one hand, I did not understand it, but on the other hand, I very much understood what this story might be about,” he added.

State IT procurement became increasingly centralised

Vályi-Nagy also discussed the way the state organised IT procurement, claiming that IT purchases were concentrated among a handful of companies while contract signing was tied to a single ministry. He said the system became so centralised that operational and organisational problems were prevented from reaching the highest levels of government.

According to Vályi-Nagy, a contract for the e-ingatlan system was signed around 2016, but the system has still not worked properly, or has only functioned partially.

He also claimed that the value of active contracts connected to digital citizenship had exceeded HUF 100 billion, despite the system being capable, in his view, of being developed for one-tenth of that amount at a higher professional standard.

The former state secretary said the number of such contracts continued to grow, while in many cases private-sector companies effectively decided what developments the state would carry out.

He described this as “quite incredible”.

From around 2016–2017, he said, there was always someone who effectively took control of the market and decided which companies could enter framework agreements and which could not.

“You can get into this framework agreement, you will be the consortium leader, and you — get out of here,” he recalled the approach as being.

‘Everyone was stealing from everyone’

Vályi-Nagy described the system as a hybrid structure in which even the ultimate owners behind businesses associated with the National Cooperation System (NER) were allegedly sometimes exploited by other NER-linked oligarchs.

He claimed that the oligarchs could also be exploited by their own middle managers.

“So everyone was stealing from everyone,” he said, arguing that this was one reason why the final bill paid by the Hungarian state became so high.

Claims of political interference in investigations

The former state secretary also made allegations concerning investigations by the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV). According to Vályi-Nagy, the NAV had thoroughly investigated and traced the relevant information, collecting extensive data on those involved and carrying out raids.

He then alleged that, several weeks later, political pressure was brought to bear on the leadership of the tax authority.

“The NAV investigated everything very thoroughly and traced everything. It collected all the information about everyone and carried out raids. Then, a few weeks later, politics raided the leadership of the NAV; those who had been working on the case were sidelined, and the case was moved to a provincial investigative office and put into the hands of four to six people.”

He said that the original 100–120 people working on the case were removed from it and replaced by four to six investigators who had to start again from scratch.

“Accordingly, that was how the case continued,” he said.

Vályi-Nagy claimed that there had been hundreds of cases in which the task of people working at the NAV, police or prosecution service had effectively been to put investigations on the back burner.

Calls for scrutiny of state IT contracts

Turning specifically to state IT procurement, Vályi-Nagy alleged that contracts covering various network services and equipment purchases were significantly overpriced. He also said that licensing agreements deserved particular scrutiny, arguing that the issue “cries out for an investigation”.

World.title: Péter Magyar opens World Athletics Ultimate Championship in Budapest alongside Usain Bolt
World.content:
Budapest has welcomed some of the biggest names in athletics as the inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship got underway, with Prime Minister Péter Magyar joining athletics legend Usain Bolt and World Athletics president Sebastian Coe for the official opening.

Usain Bolt arrives in Budapest for new athletics spectacle

The three-day competition is being held at the Gyula Zsivótzky National Athletics Centre from 11 to 13 September, bringing together some of the world’s top athletes for a new-style global championship.

Magyar shared a photo on Facebook from the opening ceremony with Bolt, the eight-time Olympic champion, 11-time world champion and world record holder. Bolt is in Hungary as an ambassador for the event and is also attending the competition in person.

The Prime Minister wrote that he had welcomed the athletics legend to Budapest for the first-ever World Athletics Ultimate Championship.

The event is designed to present athletics in a new format, combining elite competition with a more spectacular presentation aimed at attracting audiences beyond the sport’s traditional fan base.

One event at a time, with a USD 10 million prize pool

According to Blikk, one of the biggest changes is the competition format. Rather than several events taking place simultaneously around the stadium, only one event will be held at a time, allowing spectators and viewers to focus entirely on the athletes competing.

The stadium itself has also undergone a striking transformation. The traditional red running track is complemented by a black competition surface, LED strips and extensive lighting effects, creating an atmosphere closer to a concert venue than a conventional athletics meeting.

The stakes are equally eye-catching. A total of USD 10 million will be distributed among the athletes, with each winner set to receive USD 150,000.

There will also be no traditional medals for the podium finishers. Only the winner of each event will receive a trophy, reflecting the organisers’ aim of putting the spotlight firmly on the athlete who reaches the top.

Sebastian Coe said the decision to abandon traditional medals was deliberate, arguing that the new global championship is about determining who is the single best athlete in each event.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

New rules promise a different kind of competition

The Budapest championship also introduces several unusual rules. In the 200-metre final, athletes can choose their lane based on their world ranking. In the high jump and pole vault, ties for first place must be settled through a jump-off, ensuring that every event has a single winner.

The organisers have also introduced changes aimed at making controversial judging decisions more transparent. Appeals must be resolved before the television broadcast window closes, while major decisions will be announced inside the stadium. Spectators will also be able to watch replays of disputed moments on the big screen.

Broadcasts will feature another new element, with viewers able to see the competitors’ chances of winning the overall title based on the results as the competition progresses.

We wrote about the championship in detail earlier: Budapest is about to host an athletics event unlike any before – $10 million in prize money and no medals

Hungarian athletes among the global stars

Hungary is also represented at the championship, including by Olympic sprinter Boglárka Takács, who will compete in the newly introduced mixed 4×100-metre relay. Takács will race alongside Zita Szentgyörgyi, Lili Brucker, Krisztián Kalics, Dominik Pázmándi, Ábel Takács and Apor Jakab in the unusual event.

Meanwhile, the international field includes Swedish pole-vault superstar Mondo Duplantis, who will compete for the Absolute Champion title on the opening night. He is also set to perform the official anthem of the World Athletics Ultimate Championship during Sunday’s closing ceremony.

The event runs from 11 to 13 September at the Gyula Zsivótzky National Athletics Centre.

World.title: Viktor Orbán has returned from his summer vacation: “I’m back”
World.content:
Former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán has announced his return to political work following the summer break, posting a short but striking message on Friday evening: “I’m back. Then let’s get cracking!”

Orbán set to speak at “Kötcse picnic”

The Fidesz leader did not provide any details about his plans, but accompanied the message with a fast-paced video featuring highlights from his previous political appearances, including scenes from earlier Fidesz gatherings and Kötcse picnics. The timing of the announcement comes just one day before Orbán is due to address an important Fidesz gathering.

Viktor Orbán is scheduled to deliver a speech at the Kötcse Picnic on Saturday, 12 September, where he is expected to outline his political strategy for the period ahead. The Kötcse meeting is considered one of the most significant events in the Fidesz political calendar.

It traditionally brings together senior party figures, politicians and members of the party’s wider intellectual and political circle. Orbán has typically used the occasion to assess the political situation and discuss the priorities and challenges facing the party, making his speech closely watched for indications of its future direction.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

A message ahead of an important political gathering

Orbán’s latest video deliberately draws on his political past, combining footage from previous speeches and Fidesz events with music from the 2010 FIFA World Cup era. The post itself offered no indication of the specific issues he intends to address at Kötcse.

The upcoming gathering is also notable because attendance is reportedly no longer compulsory for members of Fidesz’s wider political circle, making this year’s event different from previous meetings. Critics of Viktor Orbán and Fidesz argue that the party is facing political and economic challenges and that the former prime minister needs to deliver a strong message to maintain support.

Whether Saturday’s speech will provide concrete policy announcements or focus primarily on political mobilisation remains to be seen. For now, Orbán’s message is brief but unmistakable: after the summer break, he says he is back in action.

Read also: “Debt slavery is coming” — Viktor Orbán sounds alarms and attacks Tisza government

World.title: Hungarian oil giant MOL reacted to the government’s diesel support decision
World.content:
Hungarian oil and gas company MOL has backed the government’s new diesel support scheme but warned that reintroducing a fuel price freeze could lead to petrol and diesel shortages within days.

The company said the monthly HUF 5,000 (EUR 13.76) support announced by the government was a better solution than restoring the previous regulated fuel price, as it provides targeted help to consumer groups most affected by rising diesel costs without discouraging fuel imports.

Price freeze could hit imports

According to MOL, bringing back a protected fuel price would immediately reduce imports because suppliers could no longer operate profitably at the artificially lower domestic prices. The company warned that this could result in petrol and diesel shortages within just a few days. MOL said the international fuel market has also become increasingly fragile. Conflict around the Strait of Hormuz and Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure have contributed to tighter global supplies.

Based on July figures, MOL said global diesel exports were 21% lower than a year earlier, while petrol exports had fallen by 14%. Diesel deliveries from India and Turkey to the European Union have also declined, partly because of EU restrictions on products made from Russian crude. Lower water levels on important transport routes are creating an additional challenge, making it more difficult to move imported fuel into the interior of Europe, quotes Blikk.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Diesel demand set to rise

MOL also expects demand for diesel across Europe to increase significantly over the coming weeks, as the continent enters one of its strongest seasonal consumption periods. The company said the next two months are likely to bring particularly high demand at a time when supply is already constrained. The pressure is reflected in international prices. MOL reported that on 8 September, the global oil price was 53% higher, while the European diesel price was 89% higher than before the outbreak of the Iran war.

The company said maintaining a stable domestic fuel supply and ensuring continuous imports are therefore among its main priorities. Despite increasingly limited availability on international markets, Hungary has so far avoided fuel shortages.

Stay up-to-date: Péter Magyar would break away from Russian oil, but expects something in return from Brussels

MOL offers temporary premium fuel discount

MOL CEO Zsolt Hernádi and other company executives were recently invited to a government meeting to discuss how fuel prices could be contained without creating shortages or imposing an additional HUF 50–100 billion monthly burden on the state budget. Following the meeting, MOL announced a temporary HUF 35-per-litre discount on its EVO Plus premium fuels for customers using the MOL Move app and an eligible discount coupon.

The promotion is available during three weekends: 10–13 September, 17–20 September and 24–27 September. MOL said Hungarian retail fuel prices remain below the EU average, but argued that domestic prices must remain broadly aligned with those in neighbouring countries. If Hungarian fuel becomes significantly cheaper than the regional market, importers may no longer find it profitable to bring fuel into the country.
